Venerisy 7° die Decembris;

Anno 10* Anns Regime, 1711.

A MESSAGE from her Majesty, by Sir William Oldes, Gentleman Ulher of the Black Rod:

M r. Speaker,

The Queen commands this honourable House to attend her immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the whole House, went up to attend her Majesty.

And, being returned;

Several Members took the Oaths; and made and subscribed the Declaration; and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration; according to the Laws made for those Purposes.

Then a Bill for regulating the Payment of Seamen’s Wages, was read the First time.

Sefolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported. That her Majesty had been pleased to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament; and, to prevent any Mistakes, he had desired, and obtained, a Copy thereof; which he read; and is as follows; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have called you together as soon as the publick Affairs would permit: And 1 am glad, that I can now tell you. That, notwithstanding the Arts of those who delight in War, both Place and Time are appointed for opening the Treaty of a general Peace.

Our Allies, especially the States General, whose Interest I look upon as inseparable from my own, have, by their ready Concurrence, expressed their entire Confidence in me: And I have no Reason to doubt, but that my own Subjects are assured of roy particular Care of them.

My chief Concern is. That the Protestant Religion, and the I^aws and Liberties of these Nations, may be continued to you, by securing the Succession to the Crown, as it is limited by Parliament, to the House of Hanover.

I shall endeavour. That, after a War which has coil so much Blood and Treasure, you may findyourlntereil in Trade and Commerce improved and enlarged by a Peace; with all other Advantages which a tender and asseftionate Sovereign can procure for a dutiful and loyal People.

The Princes and States which have been engaged with us in this War, being, by Treaties, entitled to have their several Interests secured at a Peace, I will not only do my utmoii to procure every one of them all reasonable Satisfaction; but 1 shall also unite with them in the ilri&eil Engagements, for continuing the Alliance, in order to render the general Peace secure and tailing.

The befl Way to have this Treaty effectual, will be to make early Provision for the Campaign: Therefore I must aik of you. Gentlemen of the House of Commons, Vo a. 17.

the necessary Supplies for the next Year’s War: And I do moil earnestly recommend to you to make such Dispatch therein, as may convince our Enemies, that, if we cannot obtain a good Peace, we are prepared to carry on the War with Vigour:

Whatever you give will be dill in your own Power to apply: And I doubt not, but in a little time after the Opening of the Treaty we shall be able to judge of its Event.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

' As I nave had your cheerful Atfiftance for the carrying on this long and chargeable War, so I a flu re myself, that no true Protestant, or good Subject, will envy Britain, or Me, the Glory dhd Satisfaction of ending the fame, by a just and honourable Peace for us, and all our Allies.

Such a Peace will give new Life to our foreign Trade; and 1 shall do my utmost to improve that happy Opportunity to encourage our home Manufactures} which will tend to the Eastng of my Subjects in that excessive Charge they now lie under in maintaining the Poor; and to correct and redre(s such Abuses as may have crept into any Part of the Administration during so . long a War.

I cannot conclude without earnestly recommending to you All, Unanimity; and that you will carefully avoid every thing which may give Occasion to the Enemy to think us a People divided amongst ourselves; and, consequently, prevent our obtaining that good Peace, of which we have such reasonable Hopes, and so near a View.

I pray God direct your Consultations to this End; that, being delivered from the Hardships of War, you may become a happy and a flourishing People.

Ordered, That Candles be brought in Candler

And they were brought in accordingly.

Concern; and to express the Satisfaction of this House in what her Majesty has been pleased to declare, concerning the general Peace her Majesty has in View; and also, to allure her Majesty, That this House will give such Dispatch to the necessary Supplies, as may enable her Majesty to carry on the War with Vigour, if a good Peace cannot be obtained; and, in the mean lime, that this House will use their utmost Endeavours to preserve such an Unanimity, as may give the Enemy no Hopes from any Divisions among us;

And they are to take into Consideration all such Matters as shall or may come in Question, touching Returns,

Elections, and Privileges; and to proceed upon Double Returns, in the First Place; and to Report their Proceedings, with their Opinion therein, to the House, from time to time: And all Persons that will question Returns are to do it in Fourteen Days next; and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in: And the Committee to have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records, for their Information:

And all Members who are returned for two or more Places, are to make their Election by this Day Three Weeks, for which of the Places they will serve; provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place:

And if any thing shall come in Question touching the Return, Election, or Matter of Privilege, of any Member, he is to withdraw during the time the Matter is in Debate: And that all Members returned upon Double Returns do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That in case it shall appear, any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, as a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Persons.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respe&of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee 'thereof; or directly or indireCUy endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be an high Crime and Misdemeanor: And this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offenders.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before the House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offenders.

Resolved, That for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament, the same is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House; and the Key delivered to the Clerk of this House, to be locked up by him: And that he do not presume to deliver up the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber, every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Galleries thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, That, from Nine a Clock in the Morning to Three in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple-bar and Westmin-fier-hall, be kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care there be no Gaming, or other Disorders in hall, or Passages leaiding to the House, during the Sitting of the Parliament: And that there be no Annoyances, by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster: And that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care. That no Footmen be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That no Committees do fit in the Morning, without the special Leave of the House.

A Petition of LewisWogan Esquire was presented to

the House, and read; setting forth, That at the Election for a Burgess to serve in this Parliament for the Borough of Pembrook, Sir Arthur Owen Baronet, and the Petitioner, flood Candidates; and that the Mayor and Bur* gestes of the Borough of Wifon, in the County of brook, have a Right, together with the Mayor and Burgesses of Pembrook, and the Liberties thereof, and the Mayor and Burgesses of Tenby, and the Liberties thereof, to vote at such Election; and ought to have public Notice given them thereof: And that the said Mayor of Wiston, and divers Burgesses, appeared, and offered to vote for the Petitioner at the said Election j but were refused by the Mayor of Pembrook; who denied their Right; and admitted divers Persons to vote for Sir Arthur Owen who were not legally entitled to vote: By means whereof, and of Bribery, Corruption, and other undue Practices, the said Sir Ar Owen procured him-

self to be returned Burgess to serve in this Parliament for the said Borough of Pembrook; and the Petitioner, though chosen by a great Majority of legal Electors, is excluded from his just Right: And praying Consideration of the Premises, and Relief therein.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Mayor and divers Burgesses of the ancient Borough of Wiston, in the County of Pembroke, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Burgesses of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the said Borough is an ancient Borough by Prescription; and their Mayor and Burgesses, and also the Mayor and Burgesses of Pembrook, and the Liberties thereof together with the Mayor and Burgesses of Tenby, and the Liberties thereof, have a Right to vote at the Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Pembrook; and have frequently exercised that Right; and Notice has been given them by the Mayor of Pembrook in order thereunto: But Sir Arthur Owen Baronet, to gain the Government of Pembrook wholly into his own Hands, in 1704, procured himself to be elected Mayor, although by the Charters he was not qualified so to be; and so continued illegally for Two Years; during which time he admitted great NuYnbers of his Dependants, Tenants, and Servants, who did not live within the Liberties of Pembroke, to be Common Councilmen and Burgesses, contrary to the Charters and By-Laws of the said Borough; thereby intending to bring the Election for the said Borough into his own Power, and deprive the Petitioners of their Right therein: That Sir Arthur hath procured divers of his Dependants, of mean Fortunes, who were not Housholders in the Town, to be elected Mayors; who have irregularly admitted divers unqualified Persons Burgesses of Pembroke; and the present Mayor, Joseph Rickfon, solicited in the last Election for

Sir Arthur; and proceeded thereto, without giving the Petitioners Notice’ thereof, as the Law requires; yet they, and others, Burgesses of Wiston, resorting to the said Election, were in a riotous manner menaced by Sir Arthur Owen, and his Agents; and their Votes for Lewis Wogan Esquire were refused by the said Mayor,

who denied the Petitioners..... thereto; by which,

and other undue Practices, the said Sir Arthur Owen procured himself to be returned; and the Petitioners are in Danger of losing their just Privilege of voting in Elections to parliament for ever: And praying the Consideration of the House, and Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter

thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Major General George Hamilton was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Commissioners for the Burghs of Anfruther Easter, Piltenweem, Anfruther Weser, Kilrenny and CrailXe, in the County of Fife, did, on the 27th of October 1710, meet at Pittenweem, to choose a Burgess to represent them in Parliament: That the Petitioner was duly elected for the said District, as appears by the Minutes taken at the Election: That Three in Five, who could claim any Right to vote, voted for the Petitioner: That, without any Answer made to the Petitioner’s Protestations, founded on Law, and Matters of Fact, the Sheriff, and Clerk of the Meeting, returned Sir John Anfruther, alone, without the least Appearance of a Majority: And praying the House to examine the Merits of the Election; a pretended Commissioner for Piltenweem being permitted to vote, though he was not elected thereto; and to give such Relief as shall maintain the Rights of the Commons, and the legal Constitution of Parliaments.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Colonel Byerley reported from the Committee, to whom it was referred to draw up an Address, to be presented to her Majesty, upon the Resolution of the House Yesterday, That they bad drawn up an Address accordingly; and had directed him to report the same to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was twice read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament aflera-bled, beg Leave to return our sincere and hearty Thanks for your Majesty’s most gracious Speech from the Throne; wherein your Majesty, by expressing your great Care and Concern, in so particular a Manner, for the Protestant Religion, which, above all Things, is most dear to us; for those Laws and Liberties which make us peculiarly happy above other Nations; and for the Succession of the House of Hanover, as limited by Parliament, upon which the future Security of our Religion, Laws, and Liberties, depends; has given us a fresh Demonstration, that your Majesty has nothing so much at Heart, as the Safety and Happiness of your People.

Having an entire confidence in your Majesty’s Wisdom and Goodness; in your Honour and Justice to your Allies; and in your particular Care of your own Sub-jeds; we cannot but express our Satisfaction in what your Majesty has been pleased to declare, of the just and honourable Peace your Majesty has in View.

This was the End for which your Majesty entered into the War; and nothing can add more to the Glory of your Reign, than, after the many unparalleled Successes in the Course of this War, to have your Majesty conclude it with the Blessing of such a Peace; which, we cannot doubt, will be rendered secure and lasting, by your Majesty’s pursuing the wife Resolutiou you have taken, of entering into the strictest Engagements for continuing the Alliance to that End.

And we presume to assure your Majesty, we will take all possible care to preserve that Unanimity your Majesty has recommended to us; and use our utmost Endeavours to disappoint, as well the Arts and Designs of those who, for private Views, may delight in War, as the Hopes the Enemies may have vainly entertained of receiving Advantage from any Division among us.

We entirely concur with your Majesty, that the best Way to bring this Treaty to good Effect, is to make an early Provision for the next Campaign: For which Purpose, notwithstanding the heavy Burthens, which, during this long and expensive War, your Majesty’s Subjects have undergone, we will, with the greatest Alacrity, grant such effectual and speedy Supplies, as shall enable your Majesty to carry on the War with Vigour; and convince your Enemies, if the intended

Vol. 17.

Negotiations should prove ineffectual, that no Amusements nor Attempts whatsoever can alter our firm and stedfast Resolution of supporting the best of Sovereigns in carrying on so just a War, till a safe, tailing, and honourable Peace may be procured for your Miy'efty, and all your Allies.

Resolved, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Address.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know her Majesty’s Pleasure, when she will be attended by the House.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take into Consideration her Majesty’s most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament:

And the same was again read by Mr. Speaker.

And a Motion being made, That a Supply be granted to her Majesty;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of that Motion.

Ordered, That her Majesty’s Speech be referred to the said Committee.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, N ine a Clock.

James Mayo, on behalf of themselves, and other Members of the Company of Fullers, and Freemen of the City of Coventry; and of Ralph Whitehead, Thomas Clarke, Richard Nicklin, Henry Clarke, and Thomas Craner, in behalf of themselves, and many Score of other Freemen of the said City of Coventry; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have been Apprentices in the said City, and served Seven Years: That they, and their Mailers, always enjoyed all Privileges, and done all Duties, belonging to the Freemen thereof; but that, at the Election for Members of Parliament for the said City, the 18th of October 1710, the Petitioners were debarred, by the Sheriff, of their Right of Voting, under Pretence of a Resolution of this House; whereby it was determined, That the Right of Election was only in Freemen serving their Apprenticeships in the said City: That the Petitioners the Fullers, and their Predecessors, are, for the Benefit of their Fulling-mills, compelled to live out of

Town, and pay to the Church and Poor, and serve all Offices belonging to their Company in the said City; and the Petitioners of other Trades have been admitted to Votes, for many Years; and all of them have undoubted Claim to it, by the constant Method of Election in the said City: And praying, That their Right may be ascertained; and Reparation for the Injury sustained, by Denial of their Votes.

A Petition of Henry Hamilton Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioner ec 10"' was duly electeda Commissioner to serve in this Parliament for the Town of Edinburgh-, but Sir Patrick John.

Jtone, late Provost of the said Town, procured himself to be elected, and returned, though incapable of serving; because, by the Constitution of the said Burgh, One of the Merchants, and One of the Trades, of the said Burgh, ought to be chose by Turns; and he, being a Merchant, andferved for the said Town in the last Parliament, ought not to have been returned in this; but the Petitioner, who is One of the said Trades, ought to have been returned: Besides which, many other illegal Practices were used for Sir Patrick Johnstone's Election; for that the Eight Deacons, or Heads, of the several Companies, or Trades, who used to vote, came and offered to take the Oaths, and to vote for the Petitioner; and Adam Brown,

Provost of the said Town, refused to give them the Oaths, or allow them to poll; and refused to make patent the Records of the said Town, though required, to clear several Disputes touching Elections for the said Town; and he admitted several Persons to vote for Sir Patrick, who had no Right; in Prejudice to the Petitioner: And praying, That the House will appoint a Day for hearing the Merits of the said Election; and give such Relief therein as shall be agreeable to Justice.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections:

And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

.Mwrdeon A Petition of the Magistrates and Town Council of LamJ lax. t lie City of Aberdeen, in the Name of themselves, and the Community thereof, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Royal Boroughs of Scotland have used to pay a Sixth Part of the Land Tax of that Part of the united Kingdom; which has been proportioned by the Convention of Boroughs, without any certain Rule or Standard, other than the Discretion of the Commissioners of the Burghs met in Convention; which Practice has beeti lately so far perverted, by de-ligning Men getting themselves elected Commissioners lor Boroughs, not being Traders or redding the rein, contrary to the ancient Rights and Privileges thereof, as evidently to tend to the Opprcdion of particular Boroughs, according to the humour of prevailing Parties in the Convention, and the overturning the Liberties of these Boroughs in Election of their Magistrates and Commissioners for Parliament; it being highly reasonable all Taxes and Subddies granted to her Majesty should be equally exacted from all her Subjects, according to fume Rule: And praying, That some Method may be afeertnined, according to which the said Convention shall direct themselves, in proportioning the respective Quotas of the Boroughs; and such Relief as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee of the whole House.

THE Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the ingroSTed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for the preserving the Protestant Religion, by better securing the Church of England by Law established; and for confirming, and supplying the Defects of, the Toleration granted to Protestant Dissenters, by an Act, intituled, An Act for exempting their Majesties Protestant Subjects, diSfenting from the Church of England, from the Penalties of certain Laws; and for the further securing the Protestant Succession, by requiring the Praftifers of the Law in North Britain to taketheOaths, and subscribe the Declaration, therein mentioned.

A Petition was offered to the House on behalf of the Dutch and French Protestant Churches:

And the Question being put, That the Petition be brought up;

It passed in the Negative.

Then the House, according to Order, resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Windfortook the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Windforreported from the Committee, That they

had gone through the Bill, and made some Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same. Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Mr. Windsor, according to Order, reported the said Amendments; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Pr. 3. L. 18. after the Words " Royal Family," leave out " and shall be thereof convicted," and, instead thereof, insert " shall forfeit Forty Pounds; to be recovered, " by him or them that shall sue for the same, by any " Action of Debt, Bill, Plaint, or Information, in any *f of her Majesty’s Courts at wherein no

" Essoign, Protection, or Wager of Law, shall be allowed, or any more than one Imparlance: And be it " further Enacted, That every Person convicted in any 4* Action to be brought an aforesaid, or: "

In the Title, L. 4. leave out " and supplying the " Defects of:"

L. 10. after " Laws," insert " and for " supplying the Defects thereof."

The said Amendments, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Petition of Thomas Carr and John Esquires, Chichester and other Freeholders, Inhabitants, and honorary Free- S’le<a‘un-men, of the City of Chichester, in the County of Siiftex, who have Right of voting for Members to represent the said City in Parliament, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners and Elfon,

being prevailed with by the Electors of the said City to Hand their Representatives to serve in the ensuing Parliament, gave Notice thereof to the present Mayor, the proper Magistrate that makes the Return; but the Mayor proceeded to Election before the Time appointed by an Act of Parliament in such same provided: Whereby the Petitioners, and others, by remote Distance from the said City, were deprived of giving their Votes for Members to serve in this Parliament: And the Mayor, upon polling Four or Five Persons only, although there be as many Hundreds have Right of voting for the said City, returned Two Members of his own setting up, to the Petitioners Prejudice: And praying such Relief as the House shall think meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections:

And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

An ingrossed Bill for granting an Aid to her Majesty, Supply Bill; to be raised by a Land Tax in Great Britain, for the Lan<1 Tax* Service of the Year 1712, was read the Third time.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Bill;

P. 59. L. 14. to leave out " May," and insert " March

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and the Bill amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be.

An Act for granting an Aid to her Majesty, by a Land Tax in Great Britain for the Service of the Year 1712.

Ordered, That Mr. Conyers do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence thereunto.

Mr. Lockhart, from the Commissioners for taking, Public examining, and Hating, the publick Accounts of the Accounts. Kingdom, made a Report of some Practices, which they have discovered in their Examinations, relating Mtrlborou;!l., to the Affairs of the Array; which he read in his Place; Conduct.* and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

YOUR Commissioners humbly represent, That, though they have nfed their utmost Application in taking and examining the public Accounts, yet they are unprepared to offer any perfect State of the particular Branches of the Revenue to the House: But will endeavour to lay before you, after the Recess, a General Account of the Receipts and Iffui"s of her Majesty’s Exchequer for the current Year 1711; which, they hope, is All will, for the present, be expected from them; as well in regard of the fliortness of the Time they have been engaged in this Work, as of the great Variety and Extent of it: They beg leave also to observe, That many of the Accounts are not yet completely brought before them; particularly those of the Army, which are very large and voluminous:

But, in the course of their Examinations, relating to the Affairs of the Army, They have already discovered some Practices, which they conceive highly detrimental to the Publick, and such as they are obliged to report to you.

In Obedience therefore to your Order, of Tuesday the nth instant, your Commissioners here present a State of several Fasts; which, with their Circumstances, and Proofs, they humbly offer to the Wisdom and Justice of the House.

Some time after this Evidence was given by Sir mon de Medina, your Commissioners received a Letter

from the Duke of Marlborough, by the Hands of James

Craggv E fq 11 i r e; wherein the Duke desires vour Commissioners. That when they make their Report, they would lay some Facts before the Parliament in a true Light: And this Justice, they think, they cannot better do, than in his Grace's own Words; viz.

Gentlemen, Hague, November the loth, 1711.

HAVING been informed, on my Arrival here, That Sir Solomon de Medina has acquainted you with my having received several Sums of Money from him; That it might make the less Impression on you, I would lose no time in letting you know, that this is no more than what has always been allowed as a Perquisite to the General or Commander in Chief of t he Army in the I.oze Countries, even before the Resolution, and since: And I do allure you, at the same time. That whatever Sums I have received on that Account, have been constantly employed for the Service of the Publick, in keeping secretCorre-spondence, and in getting Intelligence of the Enemy’s Motions and Designs: And it has fallen so far short, that I take Leave to acquaint von with another Article that has been applied to the same Use, and which arises from her Majesty’s Warrant, whereof the inclosed is a Copy; though this does not properly relate to the publick Accounts, being a free Gift from the foreign d roops: You will have observed, by the several Establishments, That before the late King’s Death, when the Parliament voted Forty thousand Men, for the Quota of England in the Low Countries, Twenty-one thousand Six hundred and Twelve were to be Foreigners, and the rest English: For these lad they gaveTen thousand Pounds a Year for Intelligence, and other Contingencies, without Account: But his Majesty being sensible, by the Experience of the last War, That this Sum would not any ways answer that Service; and being unwilling to apply for more to the Parliament, lie was pleased to order, That the foreign Troops should contribute Two and an Half per Cent. towards it; and, being then his Ambassador, and Commander in Chief Abroad, lie directed me to propose it to them, with an Afi’urance, that they should have no other Stoppage made from their Pay; this they readily agreed unto; and her Majesty was afterwards pleased to confirm it, by her Warrant, upon my acquainting her with the Uses it was intended for: And it has been accordingly applied, from time to time, for Intelligence, and secret Service, with such Sneeds, that, next to the Blessing of God, and the Bravery of the Troops, we may, in a great Measure, attribute most of the Advantages of the War, in this Country, to the timely and good Advices procured with the Help of this Money.

And now, Gentlemen, as I have laid the whole Matter fairly before you; and that, I hope you will allow, I have served my Queen and Country with that. Faithfulness and Zeal which becomes an honest Man; the Favour that I intreat of you is, That when you make your Report to the Parliament, you will lay this Part before them in its trueLight; so that they may fee this necessary and important Part of the War has been provided for, and carried on, without any other Expence to the Publick, than the Fen thousand Pounds a Year.

And I flatter myself, that, when the Accounts of the Army in Flanders come under your Consideration, von will be sensible, the Service on this Side has been carried on with all the Oeconomy, and good Husbandry to the Publick, that was possible.

I am, Gentlemen,

Your moil obedient,

Humble Servant,

Marlborough.

If Mr. Sioeet, at Amsterdam, has taken upon himself

to transact the Disposition of this Two and an Half Cent, with the Duke of Marlyour Commissioners are humbly of Opinion, That he ought to have transmitted constant Accounts of it to Mr. whose Agent he only is; and not to have negotiated so large Sums of Publick Money in so clandestine a manner.

By the Warrant, this Deduction is reserved for defraying the extraordinary contingent Expences of the Troops from whom it is flopped; and if the Whole has been employed in secret Correspondence and Intelligence, there mud have been some Neglect of the other Services for which it was originally designed; and such a Disposition, being in no fort authorized by the Warrant, is a Misapplication of it: Betides, your Commissioners apprehend. That the Article for secret Service, to which this Deduction is pretended to have been applied, was always included in the Ten thousand Pounds above mentioned, for the Contingencies of the Army; and if so, the Whole remains to be accounted for; which, on a Computation made from the whole Sum of Eleven millions Two hundred Ninety-four thousand Six hundred Fifty-nine Pounds Four Shillings and a Peny Iialfpeny, paid by Britain, to and for all the foreign Forces, since the Thirteenth December 1701, according to the Returns of the Auditors and Pay-master, amounts to Two hundred eighty-two thousand Three hundred Sixty-six Pounds Nine Shillings and Seven Pence: On a Computation made from the Sum of Seven millions One hundred and Seven thousand Eight hundred and Seventy-three Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Eleven Pence Halfpeny, paid to and for the foreign Forces, since the time aforesaid, exclusive of Italy, Spain, and Portugal, amounts to One hundred Seventy-seven thousand Six hundred Ninety-five Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Three-farthings.

Your Commissioners humbly lay before you some, other Facts relating to the Forage Contracts, for the Troops in North Britain, made by Robert Walpole, Esquire, late Secretary at War, pursuant to a Power given him by Sidney Earl of Godolphin, then Lord High Treasurer of Great Britain.

By the rates allowed in these Contracts it appearing, That her Majesty had been put to an extraordinary Expence, above the Pay of the Soldiers; your Commissioners thought it their Duty to inquire, whether, in this Part of the Service, sufficient Care had been taken to procure the most advantageous Terms for the Publick.

And, being informed. That John Esquire, was concerned in these Contracts, they examined him; and he declared, upon Oath, That Colonel George Douglas, and himself, were afiumed Partners with Sir Samuel , and Mr. John

Campbell, in the Contrail made by Mr. to

provide Forage, from the Middle of May One thousand Seven hundred and Nine, to May One thousand Seven hundred and Teh, for the Troops in North Britain, at Three Pence Halfpeny a Horse, for green, and Nine Pence for dry, Forage, each Twenty-four Hours.

That the said Colonel George , and he, the

laid Mr. Montgomery, were also afiumed Partners with

Mr. John Campbell in a subsequent Contrail, commencing in May One thousand Seven hundred and Ten, and ending in May One thousand Seven hundred and Eleven, made likewise by Mr. Walpole, and at the same Rates with the former.

That the first of these Contrails was made by Mr. Walpole, in London, with Sir Samuel Macklellan; who, before he went into Scotland, told the said Montgomery, That Mr. Walpole, in making the Contrail, reserved a Share for a Friend of his, who was to have the Benefit of a Fifth Part, if not redeemed by the Contrailors with a Sum of Money; and Sir Samuel, soon after, on his Death-bed, at Edinburgh1, declared the fame;

Whereupon, Colonel Douglas, and Mr. Campbell, directed him, the said Mr. Montgomery, to pay Five hundred Guineas to the said Mr. Walpole: And, accordingly, he delivered into Mr. Walpole's own Hands a Note for that Sum, payable to Mr. Walpole, or Order: And the said Montgomery, afterwards, paid the Sum of Five hundred Guineas to one Mr. Man, Mr. Walpole's Agent; who gave him up the Note, with the Receipt on the Back of it, signed by Mr. Walpole.

That the second Contrail was made by Mr. Walpole, with Mr. John Campbells who, thereupon, directed the said Montgomery to give a Note for Five hundred Guineas, or Pounds, he could not remember which, to Mr. Walpole;which he accordingly did; and made it

payable to Mr. Walpole, or Order; and delivered it into his own Hands.

This Second Note was left with the said Mr. Man; of which the said Mr. Montgomery hath paid about Four hundred Pounds.

He further declared upon Oath, That Two Hundred Guineas were given by the Contrailors to Sir David Dalrymple, in Consideration, That his Son-in-Law, Sir Alexander Murray, was proposed, but not admitted, to be a Partner in the first Contrail:

That the Earl of Leven, Commander in Chief of her Majesty’s Forces in North Britain, had a Hundred Guineas, each Year, from the Contrailors, for regulating the Quarters of the Troops:

That a Hundred Pounds a Year were paid to Mr, Merrill, Deputy to Mr. How, for receiving the Queen’s Bounty Money, and keeping an Account of it between the Queen and the Officers:

That the said Mr. Montgomery gave a Note for Fifty Pounds to Mr. Taylor, chief Clerk to Mr. Walpole 1 which is not yet paid.

Your Commissioners cannot, exailly, state the Loft the Publick has sustained by these Contrails; but find, That if the Forage had been furnished in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Nine, and One thousand Seven hundred and Ten, at the Rates settled by the Contrail for the present Year, there had been saved to the Government more than Nine thousand Five hundred Pounds; which is near a Fourth Part of the whole Charge.

They do not apprehend. That this Difference has arisen, altogether, from the Scarcity of Forage in the Two last Years: For Captain William Preston, of Colonel Kerr's Regiment, hath declared, before them, on

Oath, That he agreed with the Contrailors to furnish green Forage for his own Troop, in those Years, at Two Pence Halfpeny an Horse, for Twenty-four Hours, which coil the Government Three Pence Halfpeny, with an Addition only of Seven Pounds, each Year, for providing extraordinary Forage for the Officers Horses belonging to that Troop; and that the Contractors af-lured him, they had made the same Agreement with other Officers.

How far these Practices have been injurious to the Publick, is humbly submitted to the Consideration of the House,

Geo. Lockhart, (L. S.)

Hen. Bertie, (L. S.j

S. Wimington, (L. S.)

Fra. Annejley, (L. S.)

Tho. Lifter, (L.S.)

Will. Shippen, (L.S.)

H. Campion, (L. S.)

And the said Dpositions were read; and are as follow; viz.

Sir Solomon De Medina Knight, being sworn on the Pentateuch, depofeth. That from the Year 1707, to this present Year 1711, both inclusive, he has been solely, or in Partnership, concerned in the Contracts for Bread, and Bread Waggons, for supplying the Forces in the ‘Low Countries, in the Queen of Great Britain's Pay:

And that he gave his Grace the Duke of Marlborough, for his ownUfe, the several Sums following; viz.

And also 21,000 Gl. for this present Year, in Part of a like Sum with those above-mentioned: All which Sums he gave his Grace, because the former Contractors had given the like>annual Sums: He further depofeth, That he allowed, yearly, Twenty-two Waggons, gratis, to the General Officers; Twelve or Fourteen of which were for the Duke of Marlbors own Use: And that the former Contractors did the fame.

This Deponent further faith, That from the said Year 1707, to this Year 1711, both inclusive, he gave yearly, on sealing the said Contracts, a Gratuity of Five hundred Gold Ducats to Mr Secretary to

the Duke of Marlborough, for his Trouble and Pains in translating the Dutch Contracts; and putting the English Contracts into Form:

And he further faith. That for all the Money he received in Holland, from Mr. Sweet, Deputy Paymaster

at Amsterdam, on Account of the said Contracts, he was

obliged to pay him One per Cent, for prompt Payment; and that the former Contrafiors did the fame: But he found him, notwithstanding, so backward in his Payments, that he complained to the Duke of Marlborough; and, at the same time, acquainted him with the Allowance he made Mr. Sweet, of One as aforesaid; and that his Grace reproved him, for not paying this Deponent more punctually:

And this Deponent further faith, That it appeared by the Accounts of Antonio Alvarez Machado, who had supplied the Bread, and Bread Waggons, for the Forces in the English Pay as aforesaid, for the Years 1702, 1703, 1704, 1705, and 1706, that he gave as large yearly Sums to the Duke of Marlborough, as this Deponent hath done since.

6* Dec. 1711,

Mr. John Montgomery, being sworn, did depose. That Colonel George Douglas, and himself, were assumed Partners with Sir Samuel Macklellan, and Mr. John Campbell, in the Contract made with Robert Walpole Esquire, late Secretary at War, to provide Forage for the Troops in Scotland, from the Middle of May 1709, to May 1710; and likewise with the said John Campbell, in a subsequent Contraft, from May 1710 to May 1711; which, by an Order from the Queen, or the Treasurer, was continued to October 1711:

That Money was given to several Persons on the Account of these Contracts; viz.

To Sir David Dalrymple, Two Hundred Guineas; in Consideration, That his Son-in-Law, Sir Alexander Murray, was proposed, but not admitted to a Share of the Contract:

To the Earl of Leven, Commander in Chief of her Majesty’s Forces in Scotland, a Hundred Guineas, yearly, for his regulating the Quarters of the Troops:

To Mr. Merrill, Deputy to Mr. How, a Hundred Pound, yearly, for keeping the Accounts between the Queen and the Officers (for the Queen paid a Peny per Diem for each Horse «t Grass, and Three Pence per Diem for each Horse at dry Forage; which, with the Stoppages from the Dragoons Pay, amounted to Three Pence Halfpeny for each Horse at Grass, and Nine Pence for each at dry Forage;) and for answering Mr bell's Bills, and receiving the Queen’s Bounty-money from the several Agents, to whom it wasfifft payable:

To Mr. Taylor, chief Clerk to Mr. Walpole, Fifty Pounds for bothContraCls; for which he gave him his Note; 'but ’tis not paid as yet:

That Sir Samuel Macklellan made the first Contract with the said Mr Walpole, whilehe was at; and,

before he went to Scotland, he told this Deponent, That

a friend of Mr. Walpole was to be a Sharer in the Contract, or to be redeemed by Sir Samuel Macklellan by a Sum of Money; and that Sir Samuel, soon after, on his Death-bed at Edinburgh, did declare the fame; and that John Campbell, and Colonel Douglas, agreed, and directed this Deponent, to pay Five hundred Guineas to Mr. Walpole; and that., accordingly, this Deponent

gave Mr. Walpole a Bill, or Note, payable to himself, or Order; and delivered it into his own Hands;and that lie paid the said Sum to Mr. Man, who delivered the Note to this Deponent, with Mr. Walpole's Receipt upon the Back of it:

Thatjo/i/i Campbell entered into the second Contract, and directed this Deponent to give a Note for Five hundred Guineas, or Pounds (but he is not sure which), to Mr. Walpole, as he had done the Year before; which he delivered also to himself; and, the Note being put into the Hands of Mr. Man, he hath paid about Four hundred Pounds thereof.

Captain William Preston, of Colonel Kerr's Regiment, being sworn, depofeth, That, by a verbal Agreement with the - Commissaries, he furnillied Grass, or green Forage, for his Horses in North Britain, at Two Pence Halfpeny per Horse per Diem, for the Summers 1709, and 1710; and that he had an Allowance of £. 7. 14$. 10 d.or thereabouts, each Year, in Consideration of providing better for the Officers Horses; and that the Commissaries told him, they allowed him the same as they allowed others; and belives several others made the like Agreements.

A Message from the Lords, by Sir William Gldes, Gentleman Uther of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of her Majesty’s Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And, being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That he had, with the House, attended in the House of Peers; and heard the Commission read, declaring and notifying the Royal Afient, in her Majesty’s Absence, to Two publick Bills:

And the same was, by the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, Lord High Treasurer of Great Britain, and other Lords commissioned by her Majesty for that purpose, declared and notified accordingly, to these Bills;

An Act for granting an Aid to her Majesty, to be raised by a Land Tax, in Great Britain, for the Service of the year 1712:

An Act for the preserving the Protestant Religion, by better securing the Church of England as by Law efta-klished; and for Confirming'of the Toleration granted to Protestant Dissenters, by an Act, intituled, An Act for exempting their Majesties Protestant Subjects dissenting from the Church of England from the Penalties of certain Laws; and for supplying the Defects thereof; and for the further securing the Protestant Succession, by requiring the PraClicers of the Law in North Britain to take the Oaths, and subscribe the Declaration,- therein mentioned.

ANNE R.

HER Majesty fully determined to have been personally present in Parliament this Day; but, being prevented by a sudden Return of the Gout, her Majesty, in Hopes (lie may, by the Blessing of God, be able to speak to both her Houses of Parliament, on Thursday next, desires this House may forthwith adjourn itself to Thursday next, the Seventeenth of this instant January.

Die Luna, 14* Januarii 1 744.

Mr. Robert Man, being sworn, deposed. That, hearing a Contract was to be made for Forage for the Troops in North. Britain, he applied, in Summer One thousand St-ven hundred and Nine, to Mr. Walpole, ihen Secretary at War, to be concerned therein; but does not know that Mr. Walpole recommended him by Name, not Being present.

That he afterwards met Sir Samuel Macklellan, at the War Office, and, being made known to Itim by Mr. Taylor, Mr. Walpole's Clerk, went with him to a Tavern:

That this was the only time he was in his Company, and no Witnesses were present: That he then pressed Sir Samuel to let him know, what Share he was to have in the Contraft; and who were to be his Partners: Sir Samuel said. He could not tell him then; but that he should have a Share liable to Profit or I.ofs; but did not know how many would be concerned till he was in Scotland, and then he would send to him; but he never heard from him: That he further dtfired to know what Money heinuft advance, on Account of the Contraft; and Sir Samuelanlwered him, What need you be so inquisitive, since you shall benefit by it

He farther deposed, That he did not know who were the other Contractors, till this Matter was brought into Dispute: That he never corresponded with Sir Samuel, or any other of the Cont; actors i or ever had any Dif-course with them; or ever meddled with the Management; nor ever saw any of the Accounts relating to this Contract: That he received the Note for the Five hundred Guineas from Mr. Walpole: That he was very cautious when in Mr. Montgomerie's Company; and never said a Word of the Contract to him when be received the Money from him: That he never did advance any Money on Account of the Contract; and never was required by the Contractors so to do: That nobody spoke to him to be concerned in the Second Contract j but that he only desired Mr. Walpole to think of him again: That he never had any Discourse with any other Person in relation to it; and did not kuow he was concerned in that Second Contraft till he received the Second Note, dated in August 1710, from Mr. j

to whom it was made payable.

He further deposed, That he is related to Mr. Walpole, has received his Rents, and transacted Business for him a great while: That he prepared an Affidavit, in order to produce to the Commissioners of publick Accounts; which Mr. Walpole and his Clerk afterwards reduced into the Form in which he presented it.

Robert Mann,

The Deposition of Mr. Robert Mann,

This Deponent, being sworn, does, upon his Oath, declare, That, in the Year 1709, he was, by the Recommendation of Mr. Walpole, the then Secretary at War, admitted and taken into a Share or Partnership of a Contraft made for furnishing green and dry Forage to the Troops in North Britain, by Sir Samuel Macklellan Vot. 17.

and others; and that, by an Agreement betwixt himself Pu,)]ic and Sir Samuel Macklellan, he was to be a Sharer in this ccount8* Undertaking, at equal Profit or Loss, as should arise or Mr. Walpole’* happen in performing the Contraft, together with such lu other Partners as should be taken into the Contraft by Cu»u»a».

Sir Samuel Macklellan, upon his arrival in Scotland:

That, about a Twelvemonth after* Mr. Walpole gave to this Deponent a Note for Five hundred Guineas, signed by Mr. Montgomery;winch Mr. Walpole told

him had been left with him for this Deponent, by the Contractors for Forage in North Britain; which Note being made payable to Mr. Walpole, or Order, Mr.

Walpole did then indorse the Note with his own Name upon Delivery of it to this Deponent:

That this Deponent has received the Money due by the said Note from Mr. Montgomery, at several times; for which he gave his own Receipts, and in his own Name, at the several times of Payment; which Receipts, at the Payment of the last Sum, were cancelled; and a Discharge, or Receipt in full, was wrote upon the Back of Mr. Montgomery's Note, over Mr. Wal/wte's Name, that was before only a Blank Indorsement, which was done upon closing the Account betwixt Mr. -gomery, and this Deponent, as is usual upon the like Occasions.

That upon a Second Contraft, for the Year 17 jo, this Deponent received a Note of Mr. Montgomery's for Five hundred Pounds: That this Second Note is made like-wile payable to Mr. Walpole, or Order; and that this Deponent has received the greatest Part of the Money due thereon, although the same is not indorsed by Mr,

Walpole’, and that Mr. Montgomery has paid this Money, upon Receipts giveu in the Name, and for the Use, of this Deponent, upon distinct and different Papers; and not entered upon the Note, which is payable to Mr. Walpole, or Order; but not indorsed by him, or assigned to the Use of any Person:

And this Deponent does declare. That the several Sums of Money received by him, from the said Mr. Montgomery, upon the said Two Notes of Five hundred Guineas, and Five hundred Pounds, were received by him for his own sole Use and Benefit: And that he has not paid the said Sums, nor any part thereof, nor accounted for them; nor is under any Obligation or Agreement to pay or account for, the same or any Part of them, to any Person whatsoever, but that the same does, and is to remaih to his own foie Benefit and Advantage. Robert Mann,

Sir Gilbert Dolben reported from the Committee Address appointed to draw up an Address to be presented to her Hu*ien Majesty, upon her Majesty’s most gracious Message, to A ag*' this House, Yesterday, That they had drawn up an Address accordingly} which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as iblloweth; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, appear before your Majesty, with the greatest Satisfaction, to return our most humble Thanks for your Majesty's most gracious Message.

Your Majesty has, on all Occasions, shewn such a Tenderness and Regard to the Welfare of your People; and such a generous and disinterested Concern for the Support and Advantage of your Allies, in so many In fiances, during the Prosecution of the presentWar; that we have no Reason to doubt your Majesty’s Care of both, in a Treaty of Peace: However, we think our-selves obliged, with the greatest Gratitude, to acknow-, ledge your Majesty's Goodness and Condescension, in promising to communicate to your Parliament the Terms for a general Peace, before the same shall be concluded: And this, if any thing can, mult intirely silencethofe seditious Reports, That have been indijftri-ously and maliciously spread abroad, to the Dishonour of your Majesty, That afeparate Peace has been treated; which can have been raised only by some factious Incendiaries; who, to cover their own Disaffection to the present Establiftiroent and Administration, and such Designs as they have not dared publickly to own, endeavour to distraet your Subjects with unreasonable and groundless Distrusts and Jealousies.

Your Majesty’s Approbation of the Zeal your faithful Commons have already expressed forraifingtbe necessary Supplies, will engage them to continue their Application, and to give all possible Dispatch thereunto.

We are very sensible how much the Liberty of the Press is abused, by turning it into such a Licentioufnefe as is a just Reproach to the Nation; since not only false and Scandalous Libels are printed and published against your Majesty’s Government, but the most horrid Blaf-phemies against God and Religion: And we beg Leave humbly to assure your Majesty, That we will do our utmost to find out a Remedy equal to this Mischief, and that may effectually cure it.

Her Majesty thinks fit to inform the House, That in pursuance of an Act, intituled, An Act for granting to her Majesty several Duties on Coals, for building Fifty new Churches in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof; and other Purposes therein mentioned; flie issued her Commission, under the Great Seal of Great Britain, authorizing several Persons, to execute the Powers therein mentioned:

That her Majesty, finding, by the Report of the Commissioners, That they have not been able, within the Time limited, fully to answer the Purposes of the said Commission, earnestly recommends to her Parliament,

That the Time may be inlarged for effecting this Work; and such farther Powers may be given, as shall appear necessary, to render her Majesty’s pious Intentions more effectual.

The House proceeded, according to Order, to take into Consideration the Duplicate of the Report from the Commissioners for building Fifty new Churches in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs thereof; and also her Majesty’s most gracious Message to the House, Yesterday, relating the reto:

And the same were read;

And the said Duplicate of the Report is as followeth; viz.

To tire honourable the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled.

A Duplicate of the Report, or Certificate, made to her Majesty, by the Commissioners appointed by her Majesty, in pursuance of an Act of Parliament, intituled, An Act for granting to her Majesty several Duties upon Coals, for building Fifty new Churches in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof; and other Purposes therein mentioned:

Whereas, by your Majesty’s Commission, issued under the Great Seal of Great Britain, bearing Date the 21st Day of September One thousand Seven hundred and Eleven, in pursuance of an Act, intituled, An Act for granting to your Majesty several Duties on Coals, for building Fifty new Churches in and about the Cities of London and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof; and other Purposes therein mentioned; the Commissioners therein named are directed, authorized, and commanded, to inquire, and inform themselves, in what Parishes, in and about the Cities of London and Westminster', Fifty new Churches, except One for Greenwich, were most necessary to be built; and of proper Places, for the Sites of the respective new Churches; and also a Cemetery, or Church-yard, for each of the said Churches, for the Burial of Christian People, to be purchased; and also, what Chapels, in the respective Parishes aforesaid, are fit to be made Parish Churches; and to ascertain the several Houses, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments; and the Bounds and Limits, which may be fit to be made

distinct Parishes: And to inquire, and inform themselves, by the beftMeans they could, of the Value of such Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, and of the respective Estates and Interests therein, as they, or any Five or more of them, should think necessary to be be purchased for the said Sites and Cemeteries; and for the Houses for the Habitations of the respective Ministers: And that they, or any Five or more of them, do, on or before the Twenty-fourth Day of December One thousand Seven hundred and Eleven, report, or certify, to your Majesty, in Writing, under their Hands and Seals, such Matters and Things as shall appear to them upon their Inquiries aforesaid, with their Opinions thereupon; to the End such further Directions might be given thereupon as might be pursuant to your Majesty’s Intentions in the Premises:

In Obedience to your Majesty’s Commands, and in pursuance of the said Powers, your Commissioners have had frequent Meetings and Consultations; and have caused Schemes and Plans of the several Parishes, and of Sites for Churches, to be drawn and laid before them; the Delineation of which, by proper and skilful Persons, hath taken up much Time; and they have madediligent Inquiries, and informed themselves, by the best means they could, of the several Matters aforesaid: But they do, with all Humility, represent to your Majesty, That they have not, with their utmoftlndustry and Application been able, within the Time limited for the purposes aforesaid, to lay before your Majesty a Representation of all those Fasts which it is necessary for your Majesty to be fully informed in, in order to the putting in Execution your pious Intentions, for compleating a Work which tends so much to the Honour of God, to the spiritual Welfare of your Subjects, to thelntereftofiheEstablished Church, and to the Glory of your Majesty’s Reign: But, from what Prngress they have already made, they are humbly of Opinion, That if further Time were given them for the Purposes aforesaid, they should- then be able, fully and satisfactorily, to answer your Majesty’s Expectation:

And they do think it a Duty incumbent upon them, humbly to represent to your Majesty, That One great Obstruction they found in carrying on this pious and good Work was, the Want of Power to contract with the several Proprietors of Lands proper for Sites of Churches and Cemeteries, and for Houses for the Habitations of the respective Ministers: Which Defect of Power, the Commissioners do conceive, hath created a Backward-ness in several of the Proprietors, either to lay before the Commissioners their Titles, whereby it might appear what Estates and Interests the respective Proprietors had in the Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, fit for the Purposes aforesaid; or even so much as to treat with the Commissioners about the Sale and Purchase thereof.

All which Matters are, with the greatest Deference and Resignation, humbly submitted to your Majesty, for your further Directions therein:

In Witness whereof, your Majesty’s Commissioners havebereunto set their Hands and Seals, this Eighteenth Day of December in the Year of our Lord One thousand

Seven hundred and Eleven.

Die Mercurij, 1711.

Mr Cardonnel, being sworn, was a Iked, Whether there

are any Allowances, or Presents, made to the English General in the Low Countries by the Contractors for Bread, and Bread Waggons ? He answered, No, not that ever he heard of, till the late Noise of Sir Solomon de Medina's Evidence before this Commission.

The Question above was asked twice, and be repeated the same Answer.

He was also asked, on his Oath, Whether any Allowances, or Presents, had been made to any other of the Queen’s Subjects, on account of the said Contracts ? And he answered, That he himself had about Two hundred Pounds on each Contract, but would rather have been without any thing.

Translated out of French.

1 the underwritten. Book-keeper and Cashier of the late Messieurs Majhado and Pereira, deceased, Contractors General of Bread, for the EngliJIi and Dutch, during all the last War; and interested myself, with the late Monsieur Machado, in the Bread Contracts of this War, till the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Six, inclusive ;do hereby declare and attel\, That, during the whole Course of the last War, and of this present War, till the aforesaid Year 1706; I say, I do declare and affirm, That the Usage and Custom was, That the Contractors for Breaddidannually give a very Considerable

Vol. 17.

Present to the Generals commanding in Chief the Armies during the aforesaid time; and also to several General Officers of lefier Rank; which said Present, or Gratifications, were proportionable to the Strength and Number of the Troops that composed the Army to whom the Deliveries of Bread were made: And I do further attestand certify. That I have always heard, from the Persons that contracted for Bread in the First Campaigns made by King William, of glorious Memory, That the said Usage of making such Present, or Gratification, to the Generals commanding in Chief, was generally practised, and became, by long practice, a Right established in such a Manner, that the Contractors thought, that the Generals commanding in Chief might legally claim the same: In Wituefe whereof, I have sealed and signed these Presents, at the the

Twentieth Day of January 171a.

Jacob De Mercado, (L. S.)

I," Adrian VanThol, Notary Publick, admitted by the

Noble Court of Holland, residing at the , do

certify, That, on the Twentieth Day of January 1712, Mr. Jacob De Mercado did, in manner as above, sign the aforegoing Certificate, and confirm the same with his Seal, in the presence of Messieurs Matthias De , and Adolph Huijke, as Witnesses; which said Witnesses did affirm, before me the said Notary, That they do very well know him the said Mr. Mercado: In Testimony whereof, the said Witnesses, together with me the said Notary, have subscribed these Presents, with our own Hands, at the Hague, on the Day above written.

(L. S.) M.De Mele,

(L.S.) A. Huijke

Translated out of French.

The underwritten. Contractor or Purveyor General of Ammunition-Bread to the Troops of his Catholick Majesty, and of some of the Allies, daring the Space of Twenty-six Years, does hereby declare and certify. That, during that whole Time, he ever saw it practised to give the General a Sum of Money out of the Product of the Ammunition-Bread, upon including, in the Deliveries that were made, such Quantities as were designed for that Purpose, with others that related to the Service: And he doth further declare, That, at the Time his late Uncle, Don Joseph Del Cajlillo, was also Contractor or Purveyor of Ammunition-Bread, and Bread-Waggons, during the War of One thousand Six hundred Seventy-two, he, the Underwritten, did hear say, and saw it practised, that the General did receive a Present, or Gratification, in proportion to the annual Product of Ammunition-Bread, in Consideration of his constant Care: In Witness whereof, I have subscribed these Presents, at Brussels, the Fifteenth Day of January 1712.

Signed, Man. Cardofo.

Q- . S M. De Fonfeea,

Memorandum: The Body of English and Dutch which marched from Portugal into Spain, in 1706, and which has ever since continued upon that Service, is not included in this Lid on either Side.

Memorandum: notwithstanding the Reductions which have, from time to time, been made of the Queen’s Forces in Spain, the Supplies which have been yearly Cent thither have far exceeded such Reductions; so that there now remains in Spain, of English Troops, 24 Battalions, and 14 Squadrons; whereof 11 Squadrons, and Eight Battalions, were taken Prisoners at mega: And of the Auxiliaries in her Majesty’s Pay there are 37 Battalions, and 52 Squadrons, including 13 Battalions, and 18 Squadrons, of the King of Spain's own Troops, not inserted in the above Account, for which her Majesty pays a Subsidy.

Difference, on the Queen’s Side, 55 Battalions, and 52 Squadrons.

Translation of the Treaty between her Majesty and the States General, for securing the Succession to the Crown of Great Britain-, and for settling a Barrier for the States General against France; concluded at the Hague, the 29th of October 1709.

Her Majesty the Queen of Great Britain, and the Lords the Slates General of the United Provinces, having considered how much it concerns the Quiet and Security of their Kingdoms and States, and the Publick Tranquillity, to maintain and to secure, on one Side, the Succession to the Crown of Great Britain, in such manner as it is now established by the Laws of the Kingdom; and, on the other Side, That the States General of the United Proxunces should have a strong and

sufficient Barrier against France, and others, who would surprise or attack them; and her Majesty, and the said States General, apprehending, with just Reafoii, the Troubles and the Mischiefs which may happen with relation to this Succession, if at any time there (liould be any Person, or any Power, who should call it in question; and that the Countries and States of the said Lords the States General were not provided with such a Barrier: Forthefe Ileafons, her said Majesty the Queen of Great Britain (though in the Vigour of her Age, and enjoying a perfect Health, which God preserve for many Years), according to her usual Prudence and Piety, has thought fit to enter with the Lords the States General of the United Provinces into a particular Alliance and Confederacy; whereof the Publick Quiet and Tranquillity, and the preventing, by timely Measures, all the Events which might one Day or other occatton new Wars, are to be the principal End, and only Aim:

With this View it is that her Britannick Majesty, for adjusting certain Articles of a Treaty, which is additional to the Treaties and Alliances that (lie has already with* the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, has given her full Power to her Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Charles Viscount

Deputies to the Assembly of the said Lords the States General, on the Part, respectively, of the Provinces of Guelder, Holland and West Frizeland, Zeland, Utrecht, Frizeland, Overyfj'ell and Groningen and;

who, by virtue of their full Powers, hath agreed upon the following Articles:

I.

The Treaties of Peace, Friendship, Alliance, and Confederacy, between her Britannick Majesty and the States General of the United Provinces, are approved and confirmed by the present Treaty; and shall remain in their former Force and Virtue, as if they were insertectWord for Word.

IT.

The Succession to the Crown of England, having been settled by an Act of Parliament, passed the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, the Title of which is, An Act for the farther Limitation of the Crown, and better securing the Rights and Liberties of the Subject; and lately, in the Sixth Year of the Reign- of her present Majesty, this same Succession having been again established and confirmed by another Act, made for the greater Security of her Majesty’s Person and Government, and of the Succession to the Crown of Great Britain, &c. in the Line of the most Serene House of Hanover, and in the Person of the Princess Sophia, and of her Heirs, Successors, and Defendants, Male and Female, born or to be born; and no Power having any Right to oppose the Laws made to this Purpose by the Crown and Parliament of Great Britain: If itfliouldhappenneverthe-less, under any Pretence, or for any Cause whatever, Thatany Person, or any Power, or State, should pretend to call in question the Establishment which the Parliament has made of the aforesaid Succession in the moll Serene House of Hanover, to oppose the said Succession, to assist, or to favour, those who may oppose it directly or indirectly, by open War, or by fomenting Seditions and Conspiracies against her, or him, in favour of whom the Crown of Great Britain shall be settled, pursuant to the Acts aforesaid; the States General of the United Provinces engage and promise to assist and maintain in the said Succession her, or him, to whom it shall belong, by virtue of the said Acts of Parliament; to aflilt them in taking Post'eflion, if they have not already got it; and to oppose those who would disturb them in the taking such Post'eflion, or in the actual possession of the aforesaid Succession.

III.

Her said Majesty, and the States General, pursuant to the Fifth Article of the Alliance concluded between the Emperor, the late King of Great Britain, and the Isolds the States General, the 7th of September 1701, shall employ all their Forces to recover the rest of the Spanish L010 Countries.

IV.

And farther, they shall endeavour to conquer as many Vol. 17.

other Towns and Forts as they can, that they may serve as a Barrier, and Security, to the said Lords the States.

V.

And whereas, according to the Ninth Article of the said Alliance, it is to be agreed, among!! other Things, how, and in what manner, the States shall be secured by means of this Barrier; the Queen of Great Britain shall use her Endeavours to procure, that in the Treaty of Peace it may be agreed, that all the Spanish Low Countries, and what else may be found necessary, whether iri respect to Towns and Places conquered or not conquered, shall serve as a Barrier to the States.

VI.

That, to this End, their High Mightinesse may put and keep Garrison, change, augment, and diminish it, as they shall judge proper, in the Places following; namely, Neioport, Furnefe, with the Fort of Knocke, Ipres, Menin, the Town and Citadel of Lijle, Tour nay. and its Citadel, Conde, Valenciennes, and the Places which shall hereafter be conquered from; Mau-

beuge, Charleroy, Namur and its Citadel; Licre, Halle, to be fortified; the Forts of Perle, Philippe, Damme, the Castle of Gancland Dendermonde; the Fort of St. Donas,

being joined to the Fortifications of Sluice, and being entirely incorporated with it, shall remain, and be yielded, in Property to the States; the Fort of lloden-huyzen, on this Side Gand, shall be demolished.

VII.

The said Lords the States General may, in case of an apparent Attack, or War, put as many Troops as they shall think necessary into all the Towns, Places, and Forts, of the Spanish Low Countries, where the Usage of War shall require it.

VIII.

They may likewise fend into the Towns, Forts, and Places, where they shall have their Garrisons, without any Hinderance, and without paying any Duties, Provisions, warlike Ammunition, Arms and Artillery, Materials for the Fortifications, and all that shall be found convenient and necessary for the said Garrisons and Fortifications.

IX.

The said Lords the States General may also put in the Towns, Forts, and Places, of their Barrier, mentioned in the foregoing Sixth Article, where they shall have their Garrisons, such Governors and Commanders, Majors, and other Officers, as they shall think fit; who shall not be subject to any other Orders relating to the Security, and military Government, of the said Places, whatsoever they may be, or from whomsoever they may come, but only to those of their High Mightinesse, exclusive of all others; yet without Prejudice to the Rights and Privileges, as well ecclesiastical as political, of King Charles the Third.

X.

That, farthermore, the said Lords the States may fortify the said Towns, Places, and Forts belonging the reunto; and repair the Fortifications thereof, in such manner as they shall judge necessary; and, farther, they may do whatever shall be useful for their Defence.

XI.

The Lords the States General shall enjoy all the Revenues of the Towns, Places, Chattelenys, and their Dependencies, which they shall have for their Barrier, from France, whereof the Crown of Spain was not in Post'eflion at the Time of the Death of the late King Charles the Second; and, besides, a Million of Livres shall be settled, to be paid, of ^One hundred thousand Crowns every Three Months, out of the clearest Revenues of the Spanish Low Countries, which the said King was then in Post'eflion of: Both which are to serve for maintaining the Garrisons of the States, and providing for the Fortifications; as also the Magazines, and other necessary Expences, in the Towns and Places above mentioned: And, to the end that the Expences to be made may be supplied from the said Revenues, Endeavours shall be used for enlarging the Dependences, and Chattelenys, above mentioned, as much as

XII. General in the Possession of the said Barrier.

That no Town, Fort, Place, or Country, of the Spanish Low Countries, shall be yielded, transferred, or given, or descend, to the Crown of France, or to any one of the French Line; whether by virtue of any Gift, Sale, Exchange, Marriage Agreement, Inheritance, Succession by Will, or without Will nor by any Title, or in any other Manner whatsoever, shall they be put into the Power, or under the Authority, of the moil Christian King, or of any one of the French Line.

XIII.

And whereas the said Lords the States General, in pursuance of the Ninth Article of the said Alliance, are to make a Convention, or Treaty with King Charles the Third, for putting the States in a Condition of Safety, bymeansof the said Barrier; the Queen o Britain

will concur with her good Offices, that all that is above mentioned, relating to the Barrier of the States, may be inserted in the aforesaid Treaty or Convention; and that her said Majesty will continue her good Offices till the above-mentioned Convention between the States, and the said King Charles the Third, be concluded, agree-

ably to what is before mentioned: And that her Majesty will guarantee the said Treaty, or Convention.

XIV.

And, to the end that the said Lords the States may enjoy, from this present Time, as much as possible, a Barrier for the Spani/hLow Countries-,they shall be per-

mitted to put their Garrisons into the Towns already taken, and which may be taken before the Peace be concluded, and put in Execution: And in the mean while, the said King Charles the Third shall not enter into Possession of the said Spani/ Low Countries, neither in the whole nor in Part; and, during that Time, the Queen shall assist their High Mightinesse, in maintaining them in the enjoyment of the Revenues, and in finding the Million of Livres a Year, above mentioned.

XV.

And whereas their High Mightinesse havestipulated, by the Treaty of Munjler, in the Fourteenth Article, That the River Schelde, as also the Canals of Sas, Szoyn, and other Mouths of the Sea joining the reunto, should be kept lhut on the Side of the States;

And in the Fifteenth Article, That the shipsand Commodities going in, and coming out of, the Harbours of Flanders, shall be and remain charged with all such Im-posts. and other Duties, as are raised upon Commodities going and coming along the , and the

other Canals above mentioned:

The Queen of Great Britain promises and engages. That their High Mightinesse shall never be disturbed in their Right and Possession in that respect, neither directly nor indirectly, but that they shall continue fully to enjoy the fame; as also, that, in Prejudice of the said Treaty, the Commerce shall not be made more easy by the Sea Ports, than by the said Rivers, Canals, and Mouths of the Sea, on the Side of the States of the United Provinces, neither directly or indirectly.

And whereas, by the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Articles of the same Treaty of Munster, his Majesty the King of Spain is obliged to treat the Subjects of their High Mightinesse as favourably as the Subjects of Great Britain, and the Hans Towns, who were then the People most favourably treated: Her Britannick Majesty, and their High Mightinesse, promise likewise to take care, that the Subjects of Great Britain, and of their High Mightinesse, shall be treated in the Low Countries, as well as in all Spain, the Kingdoms and States belonging the reunto, equally, and, both the one and the other, as favourably as the Nations which are the most favoured.

XVI.

The said Queen, and States General, oblige them*

XVII.

After the Ratifications of this Treaty, a particular Convention shall be made of the Conditions, according to which the said Queen, and the said Lords the States General, will engage to furnish the Succours which shall be thought necessary, as well by Sea as by Land.

XVIII.

If her British Majesty, or the States General of the United Provinces, be attacked by siny one whatsoever, on account of this Convention, they shall mutually assist one another with all their Forces; and shall become Guarantees of the Execution of the said Convention.

XIX.

All the Kings, Princes, and States, that shall be willing to enter into this present Treaty, shall be invited and admitted into the same as soon as possible; particularly his Imperial Majesty, the Kings of Spain and Pntjjia, and the Elector of Hanover: And her Britannick Majesty, and the States General of the United

and each of them in particular, shall be permitted to require and invite those whom they shall think fit to require and invite, to enter into this Treaty, and to be Guarantees of its Execution.

XX.

And as Time has shewn the Omission that was made in the Treaty, signed at Ryswick, in the year 1697, between EnglSid&nd France, concerning the Right of the Succession of England, in the Person of her Majesty the Queen of Great Britain now reigning; and that, for want of having settled in that Treaty this indisputable Right of her Majesty, Fraitcerefufed to acknowledge her for Queen of Great Britain after the Death of the late King William the Third, of glorious Memdry: Hex Majesty the Queen of Great Britain, and the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, do agree, and oblige themselves, likewise, not to enter into any Negotiation, or Treaty of Peace, with France, before the Title of her Majesty to the Crown of Great Britain, asalfotheRight of Succession of the most Serene House of Hanover to the said Crown, in the Manner it is settled and established by the above mentioned Acts of Parliament, be fully acknowledged by France, as a Preliminary; and that Fram e has promised, at the same time, to remove out of its Dominions the Person who pretends to be King of Great Britain: And that no Negotiation, or formal Discussion of the Articles of the said Treaty of Peace, shall be entered into, but jointly, and at the same time, with the said Queen, or with her Ministers.

XXI.

Her Britannick Majesty, and the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, shall ratify and confirm all that is contained in the present Treaty, within the Space of Four Weeks, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing.

In Testimony whereof, the underwritten Amhaffador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of her Britannick Majesty, and the Deputies of the Lords the States General, have signed this present Treaty, and have affixed their Seals thereunto, at the Hague, the 29th of October in the Year 1709.
