the United Provinces, it 19 itipuluted, amongst other Things, That the Lords the States General shall have the entire Property and Sovereignty of the Upper Quarter of Guelder, according to the 52d Article of the Treaty of Munjisr, of the Year 1648; as also, that the GarrWous which are, or hereafter shall be, on the Part of the Lords the States General, in the Town of Hut/, the Citadel Of LiCgc, and in the Town of Bonne, shall remain there* till it shall be otherwise settled with his Imperial Majesty, and the Empire: And as the Barrier which has been this Day agreed to, in the principal Treaty for the mutual Guaranty between her British Majesty, and the Lords the States General, cannot give to the United Provinces the Security for which it is tftabfshed, unless it be well and closely formed, from one EikI to the other, and that the Communication thereof he well joined together; towards which the Upper Quarter of Guelder, and the Garrisons in the Citadel of Liege, Huy, and Bonne, are absolutely necess'ary; Experience having Thrice shewn, that France, Laving a Design to attack the United Provinces, has made Use of the Places above mentioned, in order to come at them, and to penetrate into the said Provinces:

That farther, in respect to the Equivalent for which the Tipper Quarter of Guelder is to be yielded to the United -Provinces, according to the 52d Article of the Treaty oUMiniJterabove mentioned, his Majesty King Charles-Vhc Tlii/d will be' much more gratified, and receive ^greater Advantages, in other Places, than that Equivalent can amount to: Wherefore, that the Lords the States General may have the entire Property and' Sovereignty of the Upper Quarter of j and that

the said Upper Quarter of Guelder may be yielded, in this manner, to the said Lords the States General, in the Convention, or Treaty, that they are to make with his Majesty Ring Charles the Third, according to the Thirteenth Article of the Treaty concluded this Day; as also, that their Garrisons in ihe Citadel of Liege, in that of Huy, and in Bonne, may remain there, until it be otherwise settled with his Imperial Majesty and the Empire; her Majesty the Queen of Great Britain engages and promises, by this separate Article, which shall have the same Force as if it was inserted in the principal Treaty, to make the same Efforts for this, as the has engaged to make for procuring to them the Barrier in trie Spanish Low Countries: In Testimony whereof, the underwritten Atnbaffador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary other British Majesty, and De puties *>tthe Lords the States General, have signed the present separate Article, and have affixed their Seals thereunto, at the Hague, the 29s li of October 1709.

Second separate Article.

WHEREAS the Lords the States General have rcprcl’euted, That, in Flanders, the Limits between Spanjh Flanders and that of the States are settled in' Vol. 17.

such manner, as that the Land belonging to the States ®amer , is extremely streightened; so that in some Places the 1

Territory of Spanish Flanders reaches to the Fortifications, and under the Cannon, of the Places, Towns, and Forts, of the States; which occasions many Inconve-nigneies; whereof an Example has been seen, a little before the Beginning of the present War, when a Fort was going to be built under the Cannon of the Sas de Gaud, on Pretence that it was upon the Territory of Spain: And as; for avoiding these and otherlnconve-niences, it is necessary that the Land of the States, on the Confines of Flanders, should be enlarged; and that thereby the Places, Towns, and Forts, should be better covered: Her Britannick Majesty, entering into the just Motives of the said Lords the States General, in this respect, promises and engages, by this separate Article, that, in the Convention the said Lords the States General are to make with his Majesty King Charles the Third, flie will assist them in having it agreed, that by yielding to the said Lords the States General the Property of an Extent of Land, necessary to obviate such like and other Inconveniences, their Limits in Flanders may be enlarged more conveniently for their Security; and those of the Spanish Flanders removed farther from their Towns, Places, and Forts; to the end that the same may not be so exposed for the future: I11 Testimony whereof, the underwritten Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of her British Majesty, and Deputies of the Lords the States General, have signed the present separate Articles, and have affixed their Seals thereunto, at the Hague, the 29th of October 1709.

A Petition of several Hackney Chairmen, on behalf Licensing of themselves, and the rest of the iinlicensed Hackney Hackney Chairmen usually employed within the Cities of London Chjirs-and Westminster, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth.

That by the late Settlement, there being only Two hundred Hackney Chairs licensed by Act of Parliament, the Petitioners are excluded their usual Work, whilst many of those who have obtained Licenses have loft off, or do not work themselves; but have either fold or let out their Licenses to Hire: *That the Petitioners, to their great Impoverishment, are forced out of their hard Labour to pay for the Hire thereof; and all of them cannot that way be supplied with a sufficient Number of such Licenses I That, by this means, the Petitioners Families, of some of them, are likely to be chargeable to their respective Parifltes: And praying a further Augmentation of the present Number of licensed Hackney Chairmen, or such other Relief as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider farther of the Supply granted to her Majesty: And that they he empowered to consider of the Ad, passed the last Session of Parliament., for licensing arid regulating Hackney Coadhes and Chairs; and for charging certain new Duties on ilamped Vellum, Parchment, and Paper, arid other Duties, for the Purposes therein mentioned; so far as the same relates to Hackney Chairmen.

A Petition of several Persons, on behalfof themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners and others, in 1708, paid into her Majesty’s Exchequer £.1,280,000 for the Purchase of Annuities of £.80,000 per Annum, for 99 Years, payable quarterly, from the 24th of June 170.8, upon Encouragement of an Act of Parliament for continuing One Half of the Subsidies of Tonage and Poundage, and other Duties upon Wine, and other Merchandizes imported, granted to the Crown, in the 12th Year of Ring Charles the lid; and for settling a Fund for Payment of Annuities, not exceeding £ 80,000 per Annum, to be sold, for raising a farther Supply to her Majesty, for the Year 1708: That the said Half Subsidies are, by former Acts, appropriated to otherUfes, until the lftof August 1712: That Provision was made in the said Act for the said quarterly Payments, till the 29th September 1711, out of the Monies anting by Sale of the said Annuities; but no Provision is made for the quarterly Payments already due, and to grow due before the said Half Subsidies are applicable to the said Annuities: And praying, That Provision may be made for those quarterly Payments which are unprovided for by the said Act.

And the Trauflations of the said Treaties are as follow; viz.

The King and Queen of Great having been

required, for above Two Months, by Messieurs the States General of the United Provine the Low Countries, to execute immediately the Treaty of the Third of March iGy-J-.made between the late King the

lid, and the said Lords the States General, by reason the same has now happened, That the most Christian King has declared War against them; their said Majesties, being willing to fliewpublickly the Sincerity and Affection which they have always had, and shall always have, for the said Lords the States General, have not onlythought it just to execute the said Treaty, according to its Tenor, but also to give them greater Marks of their cordial Friendship; and, to come so much the sooner to a good Peace, they have judged it proper to augment with a greater Number of Ships the Succours stipulated by the said Treaty: For this Purpose, and the better to agree in wlmt Manner they are to act at Sea, their said Majesties, and the said Lords the States General, have named Commissioners; to wit, on the Part of their Majesties, Daniel Earl of Nottingham, One of their Majesties Principal Secretaries of State, and One of their Privy Council; John Earl of Carbery, in Ireland, and Baron Vaughan in England, One of the Commissioners of the Admiralty; Am thurHerbert, Esquire, First Commissioner of the Admiralty, and one of their Majesties Privy Council; and Edward Rtf ill, Esquire, Treasurer of their Majesties Navy, and One of their Privy Council; and on the Parts of the said Lords the States General, the Sieurs Nicholas WitfenBurgermaster, Counsellor and Treasurer,

of the City of Amsterdam; William de Nassau, Baron of Cortegnc, Lord of Odick, Seyft, Diyberge, and Blicken-burg, Principal, and representing the Nobility in the Council, and in the Assembly of the States of Zeeland; and Everhard de Weede, Lord 6f Weede,

Ratclis, Lord Proprietor of the Town of Prelideut of the All’embly of the States of the Province

Treaty of of Utrecht, anti Deputy in the Assembly of the States 1689* &c. General. Which Commissioners and Deputies, after many Conferences, have settled, promised and adjusted, in the Name of their Majesties, and of the said Lords the States General, respectively, the following Articles;

1

That their Majesties shall put to Sea Fifty large Ships Of War} viz. One of the Second Rate, Seventeen of the

Third, and Two-and-thirty of the Fourth Rate; with Fifteen Frigates, and Eight Fire Ships; which Ships, Frigates and FireShips, shall have, together. Seventeen thousand Five hundred and Five effective Men for their Complement.

ir.

That the Lords the States General shall put to Sea, on their Side, Thirty large Ships of War; to wit, Eight which shall carry from Seventy to Eighty Guns, Seven Which shall carry from Sixty to Seventy Guns, and Fifteen from Fifty to Sixty Guns; besides which, the said Lords the States General shall also furnish Nine Frigates, and Four Fire Ships; which Ships, Frigates, and Fire Ships, shall have, together, for their Complement, Ten thousand Five hundred Seventy-two effective Men.

HI.

That their Majesties Fleet, and that of the said Lords the States General, shall put to Sea, and join together in such Place as shall he appointed by the King of Great Britain, as foou as possible.

IV.

That the Two Fleets of their Majesties, and the said Lords the States General, shall be divided into Three Squadrons; the Firstof which shall be com po fed of Fifty-great Ships, Six Frigates, and Eight FireShips, and shall be employed in the Mediteea; the Second shall be composed of Thirty great Ships, Eight Frigates, and Four Fire Ships, and shall be employed in the Sea, and in the Channel, unless it be otherwise regulated by the Consent of the Two Parties; and the Third, of Ten Frigates, which shall be employed from the Channel of Calais and Dover to Yarmouth, upon the Coast of England, and the Hie of IValcr upon the Coast of Zeland and the Two lad Squadrons shall mutually assist one another whenever any Occassion may require it.

V

Each of the said Squadrons shall be composed, Part of their Majesties Ships, and Part of those of the said I-ords the States General, in such proportion as may answer to the Number of Ships in each Fleet.

VI.

The First Squadron shall be abundantly furnished with all Sorts of Provisions, as well of Victuals, as for War, and the Sea Service, for One whole Year; and the Remains of what each Ship shall not be able to carry shall be put into Port Mahon, in the Isle of , or in

Port Ferraro, in that of Elba, or in such other Place as

the Admiral, with the Council of War, shall think the most proper: And the King of Spain, and the Great Duke of Tuscany, and the Republick of Genoua, fhn\[ be

required, on the Part of their Majesties, and that of the States General, to receive favourably in their Ports the Ships of the (hid Squadron, and give them all manner of good Reception: and the Two other Squadrons shall be also provided with Victuals, and other Necessaries, for One entire Year, or such time as shall be thought convenient for their doing most Service.

VII.

It has been agreed. That each of the said Squadrons shall be commanded, during this War, by the Admiral, or by the Officer commanding in Chief their Majesties Squadron.: which shall be observed also by the Detachments of each Squadron.

VIII.

The Council of War shall be composed of all the Flag Officers on each Side, and in equal Number; but, u-hen the Voices shall be equally divided, all the Captains of Ships of both Fleets or Squadrons shall be joined with them: of ail which laid Councils of War the Admiral, or

Commander in Chief, of the English Fleet or Squadron, shall be the PreGdent, and shall lit with the principal Officers and Captainsof their Majesties, each aCCording’to his Rank, oil the Right Side of the Table; and tike Admiral, or Commander in Chief, of the Fleet or Squadrott of the States General, shall fit with the principal Officers and Captains of the said States General, on the other Side of the Table, over-against those of their Majesties: And all the Affairs, of any Kind whatsoever, which lliafl be debated in the aforesaid Councils of War, or which shall be proposed therein, shall be determined by the Plura* lity of Voices; and atl that shall be so ordered, or resolved, shall be punctually executed, and without any Delay, in such manner as shall be directed.

When there shall beany Affair, or Can fe, which shall concern only the Officers, Soldiers, Seamen, or other Persons, who shall be in their Majesties Service, the said Affair, or Cause, shall be always judged and determined inaCouncil of War, which shall be composed of the Officers of their Majesties only; and likewise, when there shall be an Affair, or Cause, which shall concern only the Officers, Soldiers, Seamen, or other Persons, who shall be in the Service of the said Lord the States General, the said Affair, or Cause, shall be always judged or determined inaCouncil of War, which shall be composed of the Officers of the said Lords the States General.

X.

But if the Affair, or Cause, concerns the Officers, Soldiers, Seamen, or other Persons, of whatever Quality or Rank they are, who shall be in the Service of their Majesties, and of the said Lords the States General, or who shall be in any manner interested therein, one against another; in that Cafe, a Council of War, composed of the Officers of the Two Fleets, according to the Form prescribed in the 8th Article, shall take Cognizance of the whole Affair, that they may only judge and determine, what Party, or what Person, may be guilty, or ought to be punished; which Judgment having been passed the Council of War, composed of the Officers of their Majesties, if the Criminal is in their Service, or of those of the said Lords the States General, if the Criminal is in their Service, will cause him to be punished according to the Laws, Customs, and Instructiona, established or observed in such Cases by the Fleet which the Criminal shall belong to.

XI.

All the Prizes shall be divided between their Majesties, and the said Lords the States General, in proportion to the Number of Ships in each Fleet; viz. of Eight equal Parts, their Majesties shall have Five Parts, and the said Lords the States General shall have Three; which shall be always observed, though the said Prizes shall have been made by the Ships of their Majesties, without the Assistance of those of the said Lords the States General; or by the Ships of the said Lords the States General, without the Assistance of those of their Majesties.

XU.

In the CafeofPrizes taken by Ships of War, they shall be judged by the Court of Admiralty to which the Ship that shall have made the Prize shall be subject, whether (he be English or Dutch; and the Produce thereof shall be divided according to the Tenor of the preceding Article; but the Portion which shall be delivered to the Admiralty which shall not pass the Sentence, shall not be charged with profitable Fees for the Officers on both Sides, but only with the necessary Expences.

XIII.

And if the Prizes are made jointly by the Ships of the Two Parties, they shall be adjudged by the Court of Admiralty to which the ships that carry the greatest Number of Guns, and took the Prize, do belong.

XIV.

That their Majesties shall give Orders, That in all the Instructions to the Captains of their Ships of War, appointed, or to be appointed, to convoy the Merchant Ships to any place; and also i'ucit as shall go from tune

to time to the West Indies; an Article be inserted, enjoining them, very expressly, to protest, against the Insults or Attacks of any one whatsoever, the Merchant Ships belonging to the Subjects of the said Lords the States General, which shall steer the same Course as the said Ships of War, and desire to put themselves under their Protection: And that another Article shall be in* ferted therein, commanding also, very expressly, the said Captains, in case the Plantations, Colonies, or other Dominions whatsoever, which the said Lords the States General possess at present, or may possess hereafter, in the West Indies, want any Assistance to defend themselves against the Attacks or insults of their Enemies; that, as soon as they shall be required, they shall give all Help and Assistance for the Defence of the said Plantations, Colonies, or other Dominions, against all the Attacks or Insults aforesaid, as far as the State of the Plantations, Colonies, or other Dominions, of their Majesties, can afford it: And the said Lords the States General shall also direct, That in all the Instructions to the Captains of their Ships, appointed, or to be appointed, to convoy the Merchant Ships to any Place; and also such as shall go, from time to time, to the West Indies; like Articles be inserted, and very positive, as well in respect to the Protection which the said Captains shall give to the Merchant Ships belonging to the Subjects of their Majesties, as in reipeCl to the Succour and Assistance which they shall give for the Defence of the Plantations, Colonies, or other Dominions, which their Majesties possess at present, or which they may possess hereafter in the West Indies; all according to the Form and Manner above-mentioned.

XV.

This present Treaty shall be ratified by their Majesties, and the said Lords the States General; and the Ratifications shall be exchanged within the Space of Six Weeks; except a Treaty for an offensive and defensive Alliance between their Majesties, and the said Lords the States General, be concluded and signed before the Expiration of this Term, in which case, this present Treaty shall be comprehended and confirmed therein: In the mean time, the said Commissioners and Deputies have agreed, That all and singular the Articles of this Treaty shall not fail to be executed, punctually and faithfully, on each Side, in the same manner as if the Ratifications had been exchanged.

Done at Whitehall, the 20th of April 1680.

Whereas, since the Accession of the mostSerene Queen o (Great Britain to thelmperial Crown of these Realms, the High and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries have signified to her Majesty, by their Ambassadors Extraordinaries, the Desire they have to renew and confirm with the Queen the Treaties of Friendship, Alliance, and of Commerce, at present subsisting between the Crown of England, and the said Staties General, for the better maintaining and strengthening the present Friendship and good Correspondeuce between them, which is very agreeable to the Queen; and as her Majesty, and their High Mightinesse, have been obliged, as well by the unbounded Ambition of France, as by the very dangerous Union between that Kingdom and to enter into

a War, for hindering of the entire Ruin of the Liberty of Europe-, and as the said States General have declared,

That they are ready to enter into such Engagements with her Majesty, as shall be found necessary for the mutual Safety and Preservation of their Subjects, Countries, and States, and for reducing the most Christian King to a just and reasonable Peace; and the said States General having given Power to the Sienrs Frederick Baron of Reed, Lord of Lier, and William Van their Ambassadors Extraordinaries, to make and conclude such Treaties as shall be found necessary for the Ends above mentioned; and the Queen, being of the Vol. 17.

fame Opinion, and being willing to concur with them in so laudable a Design, has nominated, asCommissaries and Plenipotentiaries, on her Part, Sidney Lord Godot-phin. High Treasurer of England; Charles Duke of Somerset, President of the Privy Council; John Marquis of Normanby, Keeper of the Privy Seal; William Duke

of Devonjldre, Steward of her Household; Edward Earl of Jersey, Chamberlain of her Household; Thomas Earl of Pembroke and Montgo; Daniel Earl of Nottingham, her principal Secretary of State; Lawrence Earl of Rochester, her Lieutenant General and Governor of the Kingdom of Ireland; and Sir Charles Hedges Knight, her other Principal Secretary of State j the (kid Commissaries, and the said Ambassadors, after many Meetings and Conferences, have, by virtue of their respective Powers (Copies whereof are inserted at the End of these Presents), agreed, and concluded, what follows:

I.

That there shall be for the future, between the Queen of Great Britain, and her Successors, Kings or Queens of Great Britain, and their Kingdoms, on one Part, and the Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, on the other: and their States, Lands, and Subjects, reciprocally.; a sincere, firm, and perpetual Friendship, and good Correfpoudence, as well by Sea as by Land, in all Places whatever, as well in as out of Europe.

II.

And for the better securing the said Friendship, and good Correspondence, and removing all the Difficulties which may arise between the Two Parties, on any Pretence whatever, it is resolved and agreed between the said Queen of Great Britain, and the said Lords the States General, That all the Treaties of Peace, Alliance, Confederacy, Commerce, and Marine, hereafter mentioned, be approved and confirmed on both Sides, with the Explanations hereunto joined; viz.

The Treaty of Peace and Alliance, concluded at Breda the 54 July 1667:

The Treaty of Navigation and Commerce, concluded at the same Time and Place:

The Treaty of Navigation and Commerce, concluded at the Hague, the T7T February 1668:

The Treaty of Peace and Friendship, concluded at Westminster, the T*T February 167!:

The Treaty Marine, concluded at London, the First of October 1674; with a Declaration, explaining several Articles of the said Treaty, and of the Treaty Marine, of the T7T February 166 }-, concluded at the Hague, the December 1675:

Article for preventing, or accommodating, the Differences which may arise between the English and Dutch East India Companies, concluded at London, March 167-5-:

The Defensive League, concluded at Westminster, the 3d of March 167-J-:

The Treaty of Concert, for the Fleets of England and Holland, concluded at Whitehall, the 29th:

The Treaty of Alliance, concluded at the Hague, the 1 ith of November 1701:

As the said Treaties, and all and every the Articles thereof, are eflfe&ually approved and confirmed by this present Treaty, and are to remain in their first Force and Vigour, as if they were inserted herein. Word for Word, as far as they do not contradict or derogate the one from the other, or from this present Treaty: in such manner, that the Points and Matters stipulated by a frefiier Treaty shall be fulfilled in the Sense which they shall be agreed therein, without having regard to a Treaty more ancient.

III.

There shall be between her Majesty and her Successors, and the said Lords the States General, and their Subjects and Inhabitants, reciprocally,a strict Alliance, and sincere Confederacy, for the Maintenance and Preservation of themselves, mutually, in the Tranquillity, Peace, Friendship, and Neutrality, as well by Sea as by

Land;

2° Februarii. - 171

Land; fend in the Possession of all the Rights, Franchises and Liberties, which they enjoy, or ought to enjoy, or which they have or Audi acquire, by Treaties of Peace, Friendthip, and Neutrality, which have been made heretofore, or shall hereafter be made, jointly, and in common Concert with other Kings, Republicks, Princes and Cities, all which, however, within the Compass of Eurooe ouly.

IV.

And they likewise promise and engage to guarantee, reciprocally, not only all the Treaties which her Majesty, or her Predecessors, and the said Lords the States General, have already made with other Kings, Republicks, Princes, and States, which shall be exhibited on both Sides before the Exchange of the Ratifications; but also, -all those which they may hereafter make, jointly, and in common Concert; and to defend, assist, and preserve themselves reciprocally, in the Possession of the Lands, Cities, and Places, which do at present, or shall hereafter, belong, as well to her Majesty, and her Successors, Kings or Queens of Great B, as to the said Lords the States General, by the said Treaties, in whatever Part the said Lands, Towns, or Places, may be situated; in case that, as to what is above-mentioned, her Majesty, and tl e fa d States General, happen to be dif-turbed or attacked in any hostile Manner, or by an open War, by whom, or under what Pretence whatsoever; in such case, they shall govern themselves on both Sides, according to what is stipulated in the above-mentioned Treaty, concluded the 3d of March 167-f:

It shall be taken likewise, pro casu , not only

if either of the Allies shall be attacked, but also, if any of the Neighbours of the Parties make Preparations to attack, or threaten, any one of the Allies, either by an extraordinary Levy of Troops, Armament at Sea, or otherwise, in whatsoever manner it may be; provided that one of the said Allies, by a just Apprehension, be obliged to arm himself.

V.

And as the said most Serene Queen of Great Britain, and the said Lords the States, are at present in War against France and Spain 5 and that the said Queen, and the said States General, are under a reciprocal Obligation to help one another, and to maintain and preserve, mutually, their Countries and Subjects in their Pofifefflons, Immunities, and Liberties, as well of Navigation as Commerce, and other Rights whatever, as well by Sea as by Land, against all Kings, Princes, and States, and particularly against France and Spain: In order to he better able to obtain a just and reasonable Peace, which may restore the Repose and Tranquillity of Europe, it is agreed between the said most Serene Queen of Great Britain, and the said Lords the States General, That no Suspension of Arms, Truce, or Peace shall be made by either of the said Allies, with France or nor with any other King, Prince, or State, by whom either of the said Allies may be disturbed or attacked, but jointly, and in common Concert.

VI.

common Concert; and fartlicr, what has been stipulated by the Treaty of the Year 1701, above-mentioned, shall be exactly observed for the future.

VII.

It is further concluded and agreed, That the entire Quota Part of Men of War, which ought to be furnished . by her Majesty, and the States General, by virtue of the said Treaty of Concert for the Fleets of England and Holland, concluded at Whitehall, the 29th April 16S9, shall be adjusted every Year; and the Rendezvous of the Fleet shall be fixed yearly before the First Day of

December for the Yearenfuing; as likewise the Stations which the Ships ought to keep respectively: And in case her said Majesty, and the States General, do not make such Agreement before the First Day of December in any Year ensuing, it is concluded and agreed by these Presents, That the said Treaty of Concert for the Fleets shall be exactly observed for the next Year, ex-.cept the 4th,5th, 6th, and 7th Articles; which Articles, after the said First Day of December, may be changed or explained, according to what her said Majesty, and the said States General, shall judge necessary.

VIII.

It is further agreed, That when the States General shall think fit to lay an Embargo on Ships, in order to the more speedy equipping their Men of War, it shall not be permitted to demand the Fifth Seaman, or Money instead thereof, from anyShips belonging to the Subjects of her Majesty: And when any Man of War,' of either Nation, shall take under her Convoy Ships belonging to the Subjects of the other Nation, it is under-flood and concluded, That there shall not any Gratification or Reward be demanded by the Captain, or other Oilicer, of such Convoy, for the Service which he shall have done.

The present Treaty shall be ratified and confirmed by the most Serene Queen of Great and tire

Lords the States General; and Letters of Ratification shall be delivered on both Sides, in good and due Form, within the Space of Six Weeks, or sooner, if possible, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing: In Testimony whereof, the Commissioners of her Majesty, and the Ambassadors Extraordinary above-mentioned, by virtue of their respective Powers, have signed these Presents with their Hands, as usual, and thereto affixed the Seals of their Arms.

Done at Wcfimintlcr, the qth Day of June, 1703.

Mr. Ward, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for preventing the disturbing those of the Episcopal Communion in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland in the Exercise of their religious Worship, and in the Use of the Liturgy of the Church of England-, and for repealing the Act passed in the Parliament of Scotland, intituled, An Act against irregular Baptisms and Marriages; was committed; the Amendments they had made to the Bill, and had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one, as far as Clause B, the last Amendment by the Committee: And the same were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Clause B being read a Second time, That nothing in this present Act, or any other, contained, shall be construed to subject any Person or Persons who shall be onceconvift and punished for any Offence or Immorality, by the Judge or Judges Ordinary; and who for such Offence has given Satisfaction to the Church, Congregation, or Meeting House, where he or they resorts, be liable to any further Censure or Punishment for the same Offence, in any other Church, Congregation, or Meeting House, in whose Communion he or they are not; any Law or Custom to the contrary notwithstanding.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the same Amendment;

It passed in the Negative,

You 17.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That no Forfeiture, or Disability should be incurred by any Person by Excommunication, or Prosecution in order thereto, by the Church Judicatories in Scotland; and to prohibit all civil Magistrates from forcing any Person to obey such Summons, or Sentence when pronounced:

And the same was twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That every Minister and Preacher, as well of the established Church in Scotland, as of those of the Episcopal Communion, protected by this Act, should at some time, during the Exercise of Divine Service in such respective Congregation, pray in express Words for the Queen, the Princess Sophia, and all the Royal Family:

And the same was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up:

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

A nd other Amendments were made by the House to the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Mr. Conyers, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider of the State of the War, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the States General have been deficient in their Quotas for Sea Service, in proportion to the Number of Ships provided by her Majesty, some Years Two Thirds, and generally more than Half, of their Quota.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That towards the carrying on the War in Spain, in order to reduce that Monarchy to the House of Austria, neither the late Emperors, nor his present Imperial Majesty, have ever had any Forces on their own Account there, till the last Year; and then only a Regiment of Foot, confiding of 2,000 Men.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Forces supplied and paid by her Majesty for the carrying on the War in Spain, from the Year 1705, to the Year 1711, inclusive, amounted to 57,973 Men, besides 13 Battalions, and 18 Squadrons, for which her Majesty has paid a Subsidy to the Emperor.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Forces supplied by the States General for the Service in Spain, from the Year 1705, to the Year 1708, both inclusive, have amounted to no more than 12,200 Men; and that from the Year 1708, to this present time, they have sent thither no Forces at all.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That her Majesty has not only furnished her Proportion of 12,000 Men, according to the Treaty entered into for the Service of the War in Portugal, but has taken upon her the Emperor’s Proportion, by furnishing Two Thirds, when the States General only furnished One Third for that Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, by the Treaty with the King of Portugal, there was to be furnished 12,000 Foot, and 3,000 Horse, at his own Expence; and, in Consideration of a Subsidy to be paid him, 11,000 Foot, and 2,000 Horse, more; notwithstanding which it appears, That the King of Portugal did not furnish 13,000 Men in the Whole.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Thatfince the Year 1706, when the English and Dutch marched into Castile, and returned no more into Portugal, her Majesty has replaced more than her Share, according to her Proportion; and the States General have not had any Troops in Portugal.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, at the Beginning of this War, the Subsidies were paid in equal Proportions by her Majesty, and the States General; but her Majesty hasfince paid more than her Proportion, 3,155,000 Crowns.

Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Leflwithiell, in the County of Cornwall, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: "Where the Report, and Resolution, were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Robarts Esquire; and

also the Petition of the chief Magistrates and Assistants of the Borough of , in the County of Cornwall; complaining of an undue Return of Hugh Fortescue Esquire to serve for the said Borough:

That the Right of EleCiion was agreed to be in the Mayor, Six capital Burgesses, and 17 Assistants:

That the Petitioner’s Counsel alleged, the Assistants are to be annually chosen; which was denied by the Sitting Member’s Counsel:

That the Petitioners Counsel offered an ingrossed Parchment, as a Charter for LoJlwithieU; which, having neither Seed nor Date, was not admitted by the Com-inittee:

That the Petitioners Counsel produced a resolution of the House of Commons, the 20th of December 1709, in the then controverted Election for this Borough; When it was resolved, That the Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough is in the Mayor, and Six capital Burgesses, together with the i 7 Assistants annually chosen, and who had a Right to vote at the preceding Election of a Mayor.

That the Petitioners Counsel examined Witnesses; viz. Stephen Castile: "Who said. That about 40 Years ago, upon the Election of a Mayor, the after

Michaelmas Day, he was dismissed from being one of the Assistants: That the Town-people have always told him, the Mayor and Assistants are to be annually chosen: But that he was an Assistant above Six Years, and was elected but Once:

David Clenock said, He has known the Borough 25 or 26 Years: That the Assistants are chose, as the Mayor is chose, annually, upon Tuesday after Michaelmas Day; and that Alexander John, the present May or, has been Mayor Seven Years.

The Petitioners Counsel declared. That, having failed in their Evidence as to the Charter, on which they relied their Cafe, the Petitioners wTaved their Complaint, and would give the Committee no further Trouble.

' That the Committee came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Hugh Fortescue Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Lofwithiell, in the County of Cornwall.

The said Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That Hugh Fortescue Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Lojlwithiell, in the County of Cornwall.

That the Freemen vote in all Assemblies, and no Corporate Act can be done without them.

Sir Robert Davers reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Merchants trading to America was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which Report he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is followed); viz.

Upon the Petition of several Merchants trading to

America:

That the Committee having taken into Consideration the Petition of the said Merchants, who pray to be relieved against the Act, passed the last Session, for encouraging the Trade to Americ, which charges Prize Cocoa, which hath already paid her Majesty’s Customs in America, with the same Duties, upon its Importation in England, as in case it had not been Prize;

That it appeared to the Committee, by Mr.

Surveyor General of the Customs of North America, That a Spanish Ship, called St, X. De Burgo, upwards of 300 Tons, taken as Prize, and brought into New York, in September 1710, which had on board 250 Tons of Cocoa, and was entered at the Custom-house at New York, and paid f. 6,000 Custom at id. per Pound, and a 1 per Cent, upon the real Value:

And that he knows the Certificates that were produced to the Committee, and the Officers Hand Writing that signed them; and believes, Those Certificates are for Part of the said Cocoa that came out of the aforesaid Ship.

Mr. Wm. Hyde, Merchant, of South Carolina, likewise faith, That, when he was in Carolina, in 1710, there were Two Spanish Ships brought in as Prize, and condemned there, whose Ladings was chiefly Cocoa: the Name of the One was the San&a Cruize, Burthen about 250 Tons; the other was called the St.John, Burthen about 200 Tons; And that they paid between 5 and £. 6,000 Custom, in Specie, for the said Cocoa, at id. per Pound, and 2 % perCent. upon the Value: And believes.

That some of the Cocoa, now in her Majesty’s Ware-houses is Part of the Cocoa which came in those Two Ships to Carolina.

Mr Burchfield, and Mr. Hyde further declared, That

they knew the Hand of the Collector of her Majesty’s Customs at Carolina; and believe it to be the said Collector’s Hand that hath signed the Certificates which came from Carolina.

That it appeared to the Committee, by the Attorney General’s Opinion, that Prize Goods condemned in Great Britain, in the same Vessels as it wras taken in, are subject but to our owu Plantation Duties.

That an Instance also was given to the Committee, of Prize Cocoa entered at the Custom-house at London which was taken 'mo. French Ship, by the Leghorn Gaily, since the passing of the Act the last Session, which paid the Plantation Duty only; being but a Moiety of what the Petitioners are now obliged to pay by the said Act.

That the Petitioners also produced a Copy of the Commissioners of the Customs Report to the Lord High Treasurer; and a Copy of the Attorney General’s Opinion; withaCopy, of the Lord Treasurer’s Warrant to the Commissioners of the Customs, for the Landing of such Prize Cocoa as is now imported; and directing the same to be put into Warehouses, until the Petitioners could apply to Parliament for Relife.

And a Debate arising in the House upon the said Report;

Ordered, That the Debate be adjourned until this Day Sevennight.

Extract of her Majesty’s Instructions to the Duke of Marlborough and the I-ord Viscount Townshend, dated the ad Day of May 1709.

Whereas, by our particular Instructions to yon John Duke of Marlborough, bearing Date the a lit Day of March 1704, you were, among other Things, to declare to the Pensionary of Holland, and such others of the States General as you should judge proper, for our Service, that it was our Opinion, that no Negotiation of Peace should be entered upon withjFra«ce till the Preli-xninaries were first adjusted between us and the States General: In pursuance of which, we did set forth several Matters of the highest Consequence to us and our Realms; and did infill, that they should be agreed to, as Preliminaries, previous to any Treaty of Peace: And, at the same time you the said John Duke of Marlborough were directed, in our Name, to represent to the Pensionary, and other Members of the States as might be proper, how desirous we were. That such farther Preliminaries should be adjusted, as should be requisite for the Security and Interest of the States, and, as far

X as

Bairier

Treaty.

78 130 Februarii. A. 1711.

as far as was possible, of the rest of the Allies: And, particularly, you were to propose, That without Loss of 'time, a sufficient Barrier for Holland should be settled; for the maintaining of which we were willing to become Guarantee; not doubting, in like manner, but that the States would be Guarantees for the Succession to the Crown of Great Britain in the Protestant Line: And these our Instructions having been communicated to the Pensionary, and some others of the States; and they having sent over a Project of a Treaty for the Security of the said Succession, and also for securing a sufficient Barrier for Holland; which we having considered, and agreed to, with such Alterations as are reasonable; we canuot doubt but they will give Satisfaction j and are firmly persuaded, that this Treaty, so desirable for the mutual interest of both Nations, will be speedily concluded: Yon, therefore, the said John Duke of Marlborough, and Charles Viscount as soon

as you have received these our Instructions, are to repair, with all possible Diligence, to the Hague; and, upon your arrival there, you are to communicate to the Pensionary, and such others as may be convenient and necessary, how far we have concurred with the Project lately sent over, by agreeing to a sufficient Barrier, and providing for the Interest and Security of our own, and the Dominions of the States General:

And, for the greater Extent and Strength of the intended Barrier, you are likewise hereby directed to infill. That the Towns and Forts of Fumes, Knoque, Vines, Menin, Lille, Tour nay, Conde, Valenciennes, and Mau-beuge, be, at a Treaty of Peace, yielded up, and delivered by France, to Charles the Third, King of to be garrisoned irt such manner as shall be agreed on by the Treaty concerning the said Barrier, to be forthwith made and concluded between us and the States General.

Copy of her Majesty’s private and additional Instruction to the Duke of Marlborough, and the Lord Viscount Townshend, dated the id 709.

Whereas it is expected, that several Towns, now belonging to and in the Hands of ,iliould be

given up and yielded by the Treaty of Peace, to be garrisoned by the Forces of the States General, for the Security of their Barrier: If, therefore, the Revenues of such Towns, their Dependencies and Territories, so delivered up, and garrisoned, be not found sufficient to answer the necessary Expences to be made for that Service; in such same you have Liberty to consent to the adding such further Sum or Sums as shall be thought requisite and reasonable for that Purpose, out of the Incomes and Revenues arising, in general, from the Spanish Low Countries.

Extrafls of Letters from Mr. Boyle, to my Lord Townshend, concerning the Barrier Treaty.

1709.

As to what your Excellency writes in your Letters, of the td and 5th, of the Pensionary’s Opinion concerning the Difficulty there will be to procure the Consent of the several Members of the States to the Article in the Treaty about the Barrier, by which they are obliged to carry on the War till the whole Monarchy is restored; I mull acquaint you. That her Majesty takes it to be a Matter of such great Consequence, as well as Nicety, That llie has not thought fit to make any sudden Determination upon it; but has ordered the Lords of the Cabinet Council to meet, and consider of that Matter; so that, for the present, your Excellency cannot expect any answer to that point.

15»li 1709.

It is very probable, That if the States think it likely that the Treaty with France may soon be renewed, they will be more easy in agreeing to the Treaty about the Barrier, as it now Hands: But if, on the contrary, you find the Pensionary impatient to have her Majesty’s Answer to his Objection to that Article, which concerns the Restitution of the whole Monarchy, and

their Engagements to that end; in that Cafe, and not otherwise, the Lords thiiik your Excellency may pro-17

pose this Expedient, as from yonrself, That the Treaty should be signed as it is now drawn; but, because they feern to fear in Holland, that the Article above mentioned may oblige them to continue the War, in all Events, longer than they are willing or able to do, there may be a secret Article added, by which it shall be agreed, That the Treaty shall be in force but for One Year, except what is llipulated for the Barrier, and the Guaranty of the Snecession; and that to remain perpetual: If this Proposition is approved, your Excellency may offer to fuggell it here, in Expectation of her Majesty’s Pleasure upon it.

1709.

I find that your Excellency thinks it of the last Conseqtience to her Majesty’s Service, That no time should be loft in removing the Difficulties that have hindered the Conclusion of the Treaty for the Barrier; especially, since something which relates to Peace, as your Excellency expresses it, is in agitation, and that the expedient proposed will not be consented to: The Queen has taken this Affair into her most serious Consideration, and has commanded me to acquaint you, That, in regard to the present Circumstances and Dispositions of the People in Holland, and the Difficulty there will be in obtaining the Consent of all the Provinces to some of the Articles in that Treaty, her Majesty is disposed to agree, That nothing shall be made Part of it, but what relates to the Succession, and the Barrier; and her Majesty has no Difficulty in complying with the States in that Point, from any Opposition that may be made to it, either by the Emperor, or King of Spain: But as your Excellency has represented the ill Consequencesof not giving immediate Satisfaction to the Dutch in this Point; so it ought to be considered, on the other hand, what effeCl this Compliance of her Majesty is like to produce in Holland; and whether it may not be apprehended, That, when they have full Satisfaction in relation to their own Security, they will have less Regard to the Interest and Influence of England j and be more ready to precipitate a Peace with France, upon such Terms as may not be of equal Security and Advantage to the rest of the Allies as to themselves: Upon this Account, her Majesty thinks it reasonable to expect, That, before you impart these her Sentiments and Apprehensions to the Pensionary, or any other, your Excellency should give her Majesty your Opinion, how far she may depend upon the Steadiness of the Dutch, after (he has gratified them in what they most desire; and whether, from the bed Information you can get, you think the States will adhere to all the material Articles contained in the Preliminary Treaty, whenever the Negotiations of Peace shall be renewed.

ill November 1709.

The Copy of the Barrier Treaty, with your Excellency’s Letter of the iftlnstant, which accompanied it, has been read to her Majesty; and is referred to the Lords of the Committee of Council, to be considered, and compared with former Draughts, and Inllruc-tions upon that Occasion; and the Observations and Reasons contained in your Excellency’s Letter, cannot fail to have great Weight at the Meeting of the Lords, which is appointed for Thursday, in order to make their Report to the Queen on Sunday next; which is as much Dispatch as the Nature of an Affair of such Importance can admit: In the mean time, your Excellency may assure the Pensionary of her Majesty’s Inclination and Readiness, upon this and all other Occasions, to shew the greatest Marks of her friendship to the States: And you will acquaint him, at the same lime. That no Return from them can be more grateful to her Majesty, at this time, than their speedy and vigorous Resolutions, in agreeing to the State of the War the next 1 ear.

The Lords of the Council attended her Majesty this Night, and fat so late upon the Consideration of the Treaty signed by your Excellency, That I have only lime to inform you, before the going away of the Post, That her Majesty has determined to ratify it; and I am ordered to prepare the Ratification for Her Majesty’s Signing, which shall be sent over by a Messenger as soon as possible: Only the separate Article which concerns the Upper Quarter of Guelder, &c. will not be ratified.

The Treaty for the Succession, and the Barrier, which yonr Excellency lately signed, and sent over hither, having been laid before the Lords of the Council, to whom the Queen had referred it; their Lordships could not but take Notice of several Alterations and new Matters in il, which were not contained in the Counter-Project, or the lustructions your Excellency had received upon it: And their Lordships having reported their Observations to the Queen last at a Committee of Council, her Majesty was pleased to take that whole Business into her Consideration; and reflecting, that since your Excellency had signed the Treater, the States could not but expert, and conclude, that itmuft meet with her Majesty’s Approbation; and that, they having sent it, of course, to their several Provinces for their Consent, and received, the fame, in order to the Ratification, there could be no Hopes of their receding from what they had so solemnly done; but that our infilling on Alterations mull necessarily occasion the breaking off entirely this Treaty for the Guarantee of the Protestant Succession to the Crown of Great and settling a Barrier for the Security of the States General, which are Points of too great Importance to be hazarded at this Juncture; when Coldness, Jealousies, and Misunderstandings, between her Majesty and the States, might be of the last ill Consequence; especially, when some Steps have been lately taken, which seem to tend towards renewing the Negotiations of Peace, and finishing our great Work, which has been carried on so many Years, with such vast Expence of Blood and Treasure: For these Ileafons her Majesty ordered the Treaty to he ratified, notwithstanding some material Objections that were made to several Parts of it: And 1 accordingly fend your Excellency, herewith, by a Messenger express, her Majesty’s Ratifications of the Treaty, and of One of the separate Articles: And you will please to let the Pensionary know, at the same time that von will make him sensible that her Majesty had many weighty Reasonsto havesuspendedherRatification of this Treaty. That her earned Desire to preserve and establish a most lading Amity, and entire Confidence, with the States, prevailed over all other Objections: And as her Majesty cannot but think this to be a mostsignal Proof of her Eriendship; so (lie has Reason to expect, at the Treaty of Peace, that, besideswhatyour Excellency mentioned in yours, of the iftlnstant, N. S. concerning the Pretei.fions of Great Britain in the West Indies, the States will readily and vigorously concur in obtaining such other Advantages from France for her Subjects, as are suitable to her just Demands; particularly in relation toa more beneficial trade with that Kingdom. Vol. 17.

As to the first separate Article concerning the Upper Barrier Guelder, and the Garrisons in Huy, the Citadel of Liege, and Bon ;her Majesty could not but observe, That it is much enlarged, and very different from what her Majesty was willing to undertake by that Article, as settled in the Counter-Project: And though, as your Excellency fays, the several Particulars are already contained in the Preliminary Articles; yet that is so far from being thought an Argument to induce her Majesty to agree to it, as Part of the Barrier Treaty, That her Majesty thinks the States may very well rest satisfied with the Security of what has been stipulated by the Preliminaries, without obliging her Majesty to enter into separate Engagements on those Points; since there is as much Reason to expert, that her Majesty Aiould treat anew upon all the other Articles contained in the Preliminaries, as upon those Particulars; besides, that they seem to be of such a Nature, as by this unnecessary Precaution, only to increase Disgusts, and give a Handle to Misunderstandings, among some of the Allies.

Your Excellency is undoubtedly very sensible of the great Uneasiness the King of Prussia expressed upon that Head; and you know the Answer which was returned, in her Majesty’s Name, to Monsieur Repre-

sentations; to which this new and strong Engagement, without any the least Regard had to that King’s Pretentions, would appear to be so contradictory, that her Majesty cannot think the States will infill on her Compliance, especially in this nice and important Conjuncture; when the Situation of Affairs in the North, as well as the War against France, seem to require, that that Prince ihouhl rather be managed with a due Ten-demefs and Indulgence, than (hocked with an unfea-sonable Repetition of what has already disgusted him so much: Neither does her Majesty think it proper to engage herself further, at present, in that other Part, wherein the Emperor, and the Empire, are chiefly concerned; and which may give Offence to the neighbouring Princes, if he should promise the same Efforts in that Matier, as for the Barrier against France itfelfj Upon these Considerations, her Majesty did not think fit to ratify this separate Article: But, perhaps, your Excellency wilt not judge it proper to explain all this to the Pensionary, nor to say any more upon it, than.

That it being contained in the Preliminary Treaty, it is neither necessary, or proper, for her Majesty to enter into a particular Engagement on that Head.

26 November, 1709.

The Messenger I sent over muftbewith you by this time; and upon the Receipt of your Excellency’s Answer to my Letter, which he carried with him, of the 18th, her Majesty will signify her Pleasure to you in Form, upon the Point in Dispute: But it is proper for your Excellency to know before hand, That her Majesty will, at last, ratify the separate Article, rather than break with the States at this Juncture, or give them any Handle to fruftraie our Endeavours for obtaining a safe and lading Peace; though nothing can be more unreasonable and anjuftifiable than such menacing Insinuations: And your Excellency may let the Pensionary know, that you don’t at all doubt, that when her Majesty is informed, that they have that separate Article so much at Heart, and that it is so absolutely necessary for the Security of their State, the will not refuse, upon their further Representations, to rarity it: But this is not to be said, unless you apprehend some ill Consequences from the Refusal that has hitherto been made of ratifying that Article.

In mine of the 29th pail, to Mr. Secretary , I acquainted him, That I had signed the Barrier Treaty, and that it should be trail faulted to England by this Vo^ 17.

In my Conferences with the Committee of Secret Affairs, to adjust the Differences between the Two Projects, and to settle the Articles to our mutual Satisfaction, I found. That in case they (liquid prevail upon their Towns to leave out Ostend in the Barrier, they very earnestly infilled upon having a Garrison in dermonde; it being of such Consequence to their Fron-tiers, as well for its Strength as Situation, that, without it, their Garrisons in the other Towns in Flanders would , be a very insufficientSecurity; that (liould France, by Treachery or Surprize, get. the Possession of that Place with a good Body of Troops, which they would never want upon Occasion, they would become Mailers of the Scheld, cutolf the Communication of this Country with their Garrisons, and bring the States into the greateil Danger, before any effectual Measures could be taken to oppose them; ami the general DispolitionofT'VaHderj to the Interdt of France, and Averlion to the Dutch, might give the French such an Opportunity, as was seen by the Conspiracy last Year in Ghent-, 011 which Occasion, they observed, That 1 he Citadel of that Town m as of little Service to them: And they further urged.

That their having only a Garrison in could have no Iniluence upon the Trade, in the Low Countries: And, indeed, I fee no Objection against making that Town One for their Barrier; being convinced, upon Inquiry, that there could be no Danger from thence of any Prejudice, or Relifaint upon our Trade in Flanders;especialiy since they have, agreed

to have out OJiend, which is the Key of our direct.

Commerce with those Countries: For, besides that moll, of the Goods imported there are forwarded from Ghent, upon the causewray to Brtijfclls, - without being trans-. ported to Dendermonde, it is to be observed, that when the Commodities have once paid the lloyal Duties, or Customs, at OJiend, they are fiee for the other Towns in Flanders, and consequently at Dendermonde; And,

all civil Policy, Rights, and Privileges, being, by the gt i 1 Article of the Treaty, expressly saved to the King of Spain, even in the Towns where the States are to have Garrisons, the Dutch, by virtue of their military Power, can no more obstruct the Trade at th;.n at Ghent, Maun, Lijle, or in any other Tow ns; any Attempts of that Nature, in all Places, being equally a direct and open Infringement of the present Treaty: And since it is stipulated, in the 15th Article,

That the Trade which palles through the Sea Ports in Flanders, as well as through the Canals and Mouths of the Rivers on the Side of the United Provinces, shall be all charged with the same Duties and Impolisj and that the Subjects of her Majesty, and of the States, thall have equal Favour and Treatment on that Account; 1 hope, such a mutual Security, and good Underfianding in the difficult Point of Commerce is thereby established between the Two Nations, that her Majesty will not dif-approveofiny having contented, in the Sixth Article,

That the States ilia.11 have a Garrison in Dendermonde, and in some other Towns and Forts, not mentioned in our Project; most of them being pursuant to niy In-ftrnftions, and none of them of any other Use than to make the Barrier strong and sufficient.

Th? 14 th Article in our Project, being judged to be of ro manner of Importance, was agreed to be left out of the Treaty.

The x 5th Article was proposed by the Deputies, as-the Terms by which they were authorized to consent to the leaving Ostend out of the Barrier; which the Pensionary communicated to ine privately, before we met to adjust the Articles; and laid. He hoped we should now conclude this great and necessary Work: As soon as I had read it, I told him, I was ready to give my Consent to it, so far as it related to the Loiv Countries; but in case they iuiilted to extend it to all the Spanish Dominions, I then mull desire, on the Part of the Queen, that the States would engage to join their Endeavours with her Majesty, at a Treaty of Peace, that the Subjects of England and Holland should be upon the same Foot, and have the same Advantages of Commerce with France: To which he answered, That they desired nothing in this Article but what they had already a Right to by the Treaty of Munjler; it being the re stipulated, That the Subjects of the States should have the same Privileges and Benefit of Trade as were granted to the Subjects of Great Britain, and to the Anfeatick Towns, who were, at that Time, the Nations most favoured by Spain; and that it was not to be imagined, that King Charles would, in Violation of former Treaties, and in Return for all the Expence they have been at for his Support, attempt to put this People upon worse Terms of a Trade to his Dominions than they had formerly enjoyed; and that, as he was persuaded her Majesty did not intend to do any thing m their Prejudice, in that Affair, he hoped, that the Engagements in this Article being reciprocal, as to the Queen and the States, and the Trade of Britain to the Low Countries so fiilly secured by it, I would make no further Difficulties: That the States had never opposed our making any advantageous Treaty of Commerce with France, nor stipulated any thing with that Crown to exclude us from it; but should I infill to have that Part of the Article relating to the Trade to the whole Spanish Dominions left out, or what 1 proposed, on the Part of her Majesty, in regard to our Commerce with France, inserted, it would not only confirm this People here in the Jealousies they have entertained, of there being some private Transactions between her Majesty and the King of to their Prejudice, but also, new Obstructions beingraised, make them despair of ever seeing a happy Conclusion of thisTreaty: And in the Close of his Discourse, he told me, with a great deal of Concern, That he had been at greater Pains, and taken mor6 upon iiim, to bring this Matter of Ostend to bear among the Provinces, than he had ever done on any other Occasion; and therefore hoped I would not only agree to this Article, but also loie no time, with them, in figtiing a Treaty so absolutely necessary for the Security of both Nations, and which would be a Foundation of a lading Friendship and Confidence between them. I finding it impossible to make the States depart from this Point; and since Count has

owned to me. That he had assured the Pensionary, in King Charles's Name, That the Dutch should have the fatne Benefit of Trade to the Spanish Dominions, as her Majesty’s Subjects; and I being persuaded, that the immediate Dispatch of this weighty Affair would be of singular Service, at this Juncture, when their State of

War is to be settled, to llrengthen the Party that is best affected to the Interest of the Queen, and of her Allies, and to encourage them to take vigorous Measures for the next Campaign; as well as, that her Majesty is disposed to gratify this State in their having a sufficient Barrier for the preservation of Flanders, against the Power of France-, I thought it fit, for the Queen’s Service, to defer the Conclusion of this Treaty no longer.

As to the separate Article; That is no more than what was stipulated, in their behalf, in the Preliminary Articles.

At the Signing of the Treaty, I told the Deputies, That her Majesty expected more favourable Conditions, in regard to the West Indies, at the Renewal of the Negotiations for Peace, than what was agreed in the last; in which (he hoped they would give their Assistance; And I particularly mentioned, That France should renounce their Right to that Part of St. they

formerly possessed, and make an entire Reditu tion of Hud/on’s Bay: U pon which, they unanimousty gave me their Assurances of their hearty Endeavours to serve her Majesty in these Points; and added, That they would contribute their utmost, on all Occasions, to improve the Amity and Union established by this Treaty between the two Nations.

An Extract of a Letter from Lord Townshend, to Mr. Boyle, concerning the Barrier Treaty, dated at the Hague, the 26 th of November, N. S. 1709.

I have received the Favour of Yours, of the 8th and nth Instant; and am under very great Concern to find, that the Lords of the Council are of Opinion, That there are many Particulars in the Treaty of the Barrier, and some of great Moment, which differ very much from the Counter Project approved of in England: I am very feniible, that, in some Particulars, the Treaty does differ from the Counter Project; but I was in hopes there had been none of any Moment, but what were justified, either by that, or my Instructions; in one or the other of which, all the Towns and Forts, except Dendennonde, Charleroy., Fort St. , and Fort

Philippe. are specified.

In relation to Dendermonde, I can add nothing to what I laid in mine of the ift Instant: And, as fi»r

C.harleroy, its Situation seems to make it of as much Consequence to the Barrier, as most of the Towns named in the Treaty; and therefore, since the States were to have Garrisons in all the exposed Places from Newport a8 far as Namur, I did not apprehend why they might not have one in Charleroy: As to the Two Forts, the States being, in their own Right, in Possession of Eclvfe, to which Fort Donas is already annexed; and being by the Project to have Damme; and being likewise, in their own Right, in Possession of Lib, with a Mortgage upon Fort Mary; and being by the Project to have Fort Perle; I did not think the Addition of Fort St. Donas, and Fort Philippe, capable of being attended with ill Consequeuces.

As to the 15th Article, so much as it relates to the Trade of the whole Spanish Dominions, I mult own to be foreign to the Treaty; and likewise, that the States have all along desired, if not insisted. That the Treaty now in Question should be confined to the Guaranty of ourSuccession, and the Security of their Barrier; which I objected as a Reason against it to the Pensionary, at first when he (bowed it me; but he (till infilling to have it inserted, I then desired, as I acquainted you in mine of the ill Instant, that the like Advantages might be stipulated to England, in relation to the Commerce with France: I am fully persuaded, that nothing of this Nature was ever intended to be inserted in the Treaty, till one of the King of Spain's Ministers here had informed them, of her Majesty’s having some time since concluded a Treaty of Commerce with his Mailer: Neither would I have ever consented to this Part of the Article, could I have thought there was any Hopes of her Majesty’s preserving the good Effects of this Treaty to her own Subjects, exclufire of 19 all

-Februariu

*9

ioAnn. 14° — 150 —

ell others, after such a step taken by one of the King of Spain's Ministers here; and the Declaration which Count Sinxendorff told me he had made to the Pen-

fionary, by the King of Spain's Orders, That his Majesty always intended the States should be upon an equal foot with us, in point of Trade to all his Dominions; especially, considering that the King of Spain, even after he comes to be settled in the entire Possession of the Spani/hMonarchy, will still have so much Need of

the Friendship and support of this State; which he can never hope to purchase, but by establishing their Trade upon as favourable Terms as that of any other Nation whatsoever: These Keafons induced me to think, that there could accrue no real Advantage to her Majesty, and her Subjects, from my infilling upon leaving out those Words; but, on the contrary, that my not consenting might, at this critical Juncture, bave increased and inflamed the Jealousies conceived here upon that point; and have made the chief Trading Town % who have hitherto been the most zealous supporters of the War, join with those who have been, all along for accepting of a Peace on any Terms; which, added to the Difficulties this State is under for railing Money might have driven them into separate Measures with France, or at lead into a precipitated Peace: Besides, if one may judge of the Dispositions of the Court of Barcelona by the Behaviour of their Ministers, there is Rea-, son to think they were never heartily disposed to the Performance of that Treaty; otherwise they could not have been guilty of such imprudence, as, by discovering it at this time, to have endangered the creating. Jealousies between her Majesty and the States; upon whose Friendship and Union, their Hopes of obtaining the whole Spanish Monarchy do so evidently depend: And if that should be the Cafe, I submit it, whether it be not most for her Majesty’s Service, by joining with the States in this Particular, to ensure the Performance of this Treaty, or any other that shall be thought necessary for the Benefit of our Trade, excluGve of the French, or any other Nation whatsoever.

As to what is contained in the separate Article, it is no more than what her Majesty, the Emperor, and the King of Spain, have consented to in the Preliminary. Treaty: And therefore, though there was no mention, neither in the Project, nor my Instructions, of any thing relating to Bonne, Huy, and Liege; yet I thought I

might safely venture to consent to it, especially since the Foundation of their demanding this Article is so apparently true, that, for want of some such Provision, the French have. Three Times successively, attempted to bring the War into this Country, through those Places: and that there is no Probability of their being better defended for the future, but by the Method taken in the Treaty: There is the same Reason for that Part of this Article W'hich relates to Guelderland-, that being likewise-stipulated in the Preliminary Treaty: And it being said in the separate Article of the Project, That the Queen should use her Endeavours to have the Affairs of Guelder settled to the mutpal Satisfaction of the States ,-and King of Spain; and he having already consented to it in the Preliminary Treaty; I thqught all Difficulties upon that Head were entirely removed.

Upon tlje Whole,. I could not judge it for her Majesty’s Service, at a time when we were labouring to keep this People steady, to carrying on the War against France, and recovering the whole M°tiarpl,y Of Spain, to giye them the least Jealoqfy, that her Majesty was not disposed to afford them her Assistance, in procuring to them Advantages which so nearly concerned their Safety, and had been already fiipulated to them by the Preliminary Treaty.

I cannot perceive any other Particulars of Moment ia which die Treaty varies from the Project, except in the Addition to the 14th Article; by which the States are entitled to the Revenues of the Barrier Towns, and the Million which is to be raised annually before the Peace; And this I should not have ,con feu ted to, but that the Pepfipnary, and Deputies for foreign Affairs,

Vp L. 17.

assured me, That the States never intended to make, use of this Concession towards raising the Revenues; which was at present impracticable; they heing less than what are necessary to defray the civil Expences, and the Charges of the Body of Troops which is at present in the Pay of that Country; and that it was inserted only in order to induce King Charles the foonet to comply with the Convention which is desired: Thft Pensionary gave the Duke of Marlborough the like Alfu ranees, in relation to this Article, w hile he was at the Hague.

The Deposition of Sir David about the

Forage Contract in North Britain.

Sir David Dalrymple, being sworn, deposed, That in April 1709, as he thinks, he made a Proposal to Sir Samuel Macklellan, That Sir Alexander Murray his Son-in-law, should be admitted a Partner into the ContraCfc for foraging the Troops in North Britain; and that# being at London when the Design for his said Son-in-law came first into his Thoughts, he did make the said Proposal without waiting to communicate it to his said Son-in-law; but that he acquainted him with it afterwards; and his said Son-in-law did speak to Campbell, and as the Deponent has heard, to Sir Samuel McLellan, to have a Declaration in Writing, and to be employed; and was acquainted with all that pad in the said Matter; and the Deponent did, by written Warrant from Sir Alexander, transact with John , afterSir-SamHe/’s.

Death, for £.200.

That he does not remember any body was present when he first made this Proposal; nor can he be positive, that any particular Person was present at any other lime when he difeourfed Sir Samuel concerning the Terms of the said ContraCl; but does remember, that he spoke to the said Sir Samuel about it in a Coffee House, and, as this Deponent thinks, at Old Man's, when there were several Persons fitting at the Table, but this Deponent cannot now call to mind who they were; but that he understood his Son-in-law was to have been admitted into an equal Share with Sir Samuel himself; till Sir

Samuel afterwards at Edinburgh, in August 1709, endea-

voured to persuade the Deponent, that he had not infilled to have an equal Share with him the said Sir Samuel, for Sir Alexander Murray, but at inofl for a Tenth; and that the said Sir Samuel pretended he never designed more than a Fourteenth; but offered to purchase Sir Alexander's Interest, whatever it was, and to give Two hundred Pounds Sterling for it:

That Sir Samuel, on his Death Bed, took an Obligation from Mr. John Campbell; and that for Help to his

Memory, and clearing the Matter, this Deponent took John Campbell's Affidavits before Two Juliices of the Peace at Edinburgh concerning that Obligation, Sir Alexander Murray's Letter of Commission to the Deponent above mentioned, and the receiving the Money in Sir Alexander's Name.

And faith. That Sir Samuel MLelldn died, to the bell of the Deponent’s Remembrance, on the 27th or 28th of September 1709, or about that time; and that

Mr. John Montgomery's Deposition touching the Two hundred Pounds paid Sir David Dalrymple on the Forage Contract.

Mr. John Montgomery, being sworn, depofeth, That being informed by Sir Samuel McLellan, before lie went into Scotland in 1709, That Sir David Dalrymple, and his Lady proposed. That her Son Sir Alexander Murray should be assumed a Partner in the Forage Contract, he, the Deponent, declined it, as being a young Gentleman, and unacquainted with Business: Whereupon, forae few Days after. Sir Samuel told him. That he had made an Agreement with Sir David Dalrymple, and his Lady, That Sir Alexander Murray, instead of being admitted a Sharer in the said Contract, should have Two hundred Pounds, or Two hundred Guineas, out of the Profits of the said Contract, if they proved considerable.

Mr. John Montgomerie’s Deposition touching the One hundred Guineas given by the Forage Contractors to the Earl of Leven.

That when he formerly deposed, That a Hundred Guineas was given by the Contractors of Forage to the Earl of Leven, as Commander in Chief in Scotland, for regulating of the Troops there, he did no-ways mean. That the Earl of Leven was thereby to be influenced to dispose of the Troops at such Places as would be prejudicial to the Service of the Government, and advantageous to the Contractors; nor that ever any such Bargain was proposed, or made thereanent, to the belt of this Deponent's Knowledge.

John Montgomerie.

Deposition of William Livingston Esquire, touching an Allowance of One hundred Guineas to the Commander in Chief in North Britain by the Commissioners for Forage.

William Livingston, Esquire, maketh Oath, That several Years before the Union, he had known the General or Commander in Chief in Scotland to have received Forage for his Horses from the Commissaries of the Army out of their Magazines: That, in the Year 1693, when the Deponent was concerned in the Forage Contracts himself, there was 100 Guineas given to my Lord Tiviot, then Commander in Chief; and, in the Year 1697, when the Deponent was likewise one of the Commissaries, the Keeper of their Magazines delivered Forage to the General’s Servants for his Horses, which he, and the rest of the Commissaries, allowed of; and, therefore, that no Money was given that Year:

And farther maketh Oath, That there was a Stop.-page made of so much out of the Pound of the Pay of the General, as well as other Officers and Soldiers, towards the defraying the Expences of foraging the Troops, so far as I do remember.

He farther depofeth. That the Commissaries gave my Lord Tiviot a Present of One hundred Guineas, in Expectation that they should have his Favour and Countenance; and that he often addressed the General to quarter the Troops in some Places, where Forage was easy and

plentiful

io Ann. 19’ — 20

plentiful; which the General complied with, being an Advantage to the Troops, and bo Detriment to the Government.

Wm. Livingston.

Mr. Freman, according to Order, reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the City of Carlisle, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report, and Resolu-lution, were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Samuel Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir James Mounldgue Knight, to serve for the City of Carlisle:

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and Freemen, resident or not resident;

That it was also agreed. That the Sons of Freemen, born after their Fathers Freedom, and Persons serving Seven Years within the City, have a Rigid; to be made free.

That the Petitioner’s Counsel objected to 155 of the Sitting Member’s Voters:

That it appeared, That 41 of the Voters in this Election were admitted to Freedom after the Tejle of the Writ; viz. 32 upon the ad Day of October 1710; and Nine others upon the 7th of the same Month: And that of those 41, One voted for the Petitioner only: Eight for the Petitioner and Sitting Member; and the rest for the Sitting Member only:

That upon the said 2d of October, Three others, who had been disfranchised, were restored, and they voted for the Sitting Member:

Four others, who had been disfranchised, were objected to, for that they were restored just before the Tejle of the Writ; viz. the 21st of September 1710: One of these Four voted for the Silting Member only; and the other Three for the Petitioner and Sitting Member.
