That the Petitioners Counsel infilled* That by Act of 35th of Henry the Eighth, for Knights and Burgesses in Wales, concerning the Payment of their Fees and Wages; all the Cities and Boroughs in Wales, not find* ing Burgesses for the Parliament themselves, are to be contributory to the Wages of the Burgesses to Parliament for the Shire Towns; and are to have Notice, by the Mayors, Bailiffs, and other head Officers of the Shire Towns* or by one of them, of the Elections to Parliament; in which Elections they are to vote as the Burgesses of the Shire Towns used:

The Wiston Burgesses were come to destroy their Bights and Privileges, but he would {land by the Corporation of Pembrook with his Life and Fortune; and thereupon the Wiston Burgesses were said to be Enemies; and the Mob went up and down, and huzzaed at the Houses into which those Burgesses were got, to avoid the Danger of this Tumult; but no Mischief happened: That the Wiston Burgesses who came to Pembrook to vote, as aforesaid, were 239 in Number: The Mob declared they would knock them of the Head if they came to the Poll; and Guards were set against them at the Hall Stairs; upon which, the Wiston Burgesses went to the Castle Green at P, and were there called over, by a List of their Names, and they declared, one by one, they would vote for the Petitioner; And then the Mayor of Wiston went to the Poll, and there tendered that Lift to the Mayor of , and acquainted him it was a List of the Wiston Burgesses, who were there ready to vote for the Petitioner: and desired they might be admitted to the Poll: but the Mayor of Pembrook rejected the Lift, and declared, He would not admit a Wiston Burgess to vote there.

That the additional Forces of Ten thousand Men, which were taken into her Majesty’s Service in the Year 1703, be continued for the Year 1712.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a farther number of additional Forces in the Low Countries be continued for the Service of the Year 1712, not exceeding Fifteen thousand One hundred Seventy-eight Men; upon condition, That the States General do agree to add to such additional Forces the Proportion of Three-fifths to Two-fifths.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Eight hundred Eighty-six thousand Two hundred Twenty-three Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to her Majesty, for maintaining the said Forty thousand Men, for the Service of the Year 1712.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Seventy-seven thousand Five hundred and Eleven Pounds Three Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to her Majesty for maintaining the said Ten thousand additional Forces, for the Service of the Year 1712.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That so much Money as now is, or before the First Day of August 1712 shall be, deficient, to complete the Quarterly Payments of the Annuities, amounting to Eighty thousand Pounds per Annum purchased upon an Act of the Sixth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, and charged upon the Half Subsidies of Tonage and Poundage, to arise by several Acts therein mentioned; be supplied, and made good.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That so much as is, or shall be, deficient, to complete the Quarterly Payments of the Annuities, amounting to Forty thousand Pounds per Annum; purchased upon another Act of the Sixth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, and thereby charged upon several Overplus-monies therein mentioned; be all'o supplied, and made good, from time to time.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Fifty Pounds per Annum, be added to the Fund settled by an Act of the last Session of Parliament; whereby, amongst other things, a Rent of Ten Shillings a Year is payable upon licensing Hackney Chairs, towards the Payment of the Principal and Interest Monies therein mentioned.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said additional Sum, not exceeding Fifty Pounds per Annum, be raised during the Continuance of the said Act.

Mr. Secretary St. John acquainted the House, That he had received her Majesty's Command to communicate to this House a Proposition made to her Majesty by Prince Eugene of Savoy, in the Name of the Emperor* for the Support of the War in; viz.

His Imperial Majesty judges, that Forty thousand Men will be sufficient for this Service; and that the whole Expence of the War in may amount to

Four millions of Crowns: Towards which, his Imperial Majesty offers to make up the Troops which he has in that Country to Thirty thousand Men, and to take One million of Crowns upon himself.

Mr. Manley, according to Order, reported from the

Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for recruiting her Majesty’s Land Forces, and Marines, for the Service of the Year 1712, was committed, the Amendments they had directed him to report to the House, which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That whereas Persons were often wrongfully lifted, and delivered to the Officers, for Soldiers not being within the Description of the" A&; that therefore the Receivers and CoIlt6lors, directed to pay the several Sums therein mentioned, should not pay the same in less than Six Weeks Time after such delivering over, as aforesaid: And that the Commissioners have Power, upon better Information, to certify to the Secretary at War, that such Person or Persons was or were not within the Description of the Act; and the Secretary at War have Power thereupon to discharge such Person or Persons, on Payment of the Money expended on Account of hisor theirbeing lifted, not exceeding Twenty Shillings; provided such Certificate be signed within Six Weeks after such delivering over, as aforesaid:

And the same was twice read', with Blanks; which were filled up;

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Rfpresenta- Sir Thomas I I dinner reported from the Committee, to Siat.0"/11* "horn it was referred to draw up a Representation to be tte War wade to her Majesty, that they had drawn up the fame.

accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where it was twice read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutifnl and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, having nothing so much at Heart as to enable your Majesty to bring this long and expensive War to an honourable and happy Conclusion, have taken it into our moll ferions Consideration, how the necessary Supplies to be provided by us may be bell applied, and the common Cause may, in the most effectual manner, be carried on by the united Force of the whole Confederacy: We have thought ourselves obliged, in Duty to your Majesty, and in Discharge of the Trail reposed in us, to inquire into the true State of the War in all its Parts: We have examined what Stipulations have been entered into between your Majesty and your Allies; and bowfar such Engagements have, on each Side, been made good: We have considered the different Interests which the Confederates have in the Success of this War; and the different Shares they have contributed to its Support: We have, with our utmost Care and Diligence, endea-Voi. 17.

voured to discover the Nature, Extent, and Charge of it; R«p»fe»w-to the end, that, by comparing the Weight thereof with our.own Strength, wemight adapt the one to the other in y,e such measure, as neither to continueyour Majesty's Subjects under a heavier Burden than in Reason and Justice they ought to bear; nor deceive your Majesty, your Allies, and ourselves, by undertaking more than the Nation, in its present Circumstances, is able to perform.

Your Majesty has been graciously pleased, upon our bumble Applications, to order such Materials to be laid before us, as havefurnished us with the necessary Information upon the Particulars we have inquired into:

And when we shall have laid before your Majesty our Observations and humble Advice, upon this Subject, we promise to ourselves this happy Fruit from it; That, if your Majesty’s generous and good Purposes for the procuring a safe and lasting Peace should, through the Ob-ftinacy of the Enemy, or by any other Means, be unhappily defeated, a true Knowledge and Understanding of the past Conduct of the War, will be the bell Foundation for a more frugal and equal Management of it for the time to come.

In order to take the more perfectView of what we proposed; and that we might be able to set the Whole before your Majesty in a true Light; we have thought it necessary to go back to the Beginning of the War; and beg Leave to observe the Motives and Reasons upon which his late Majesty King William engaged first in it: The Treaty of the grand Alliance explains those Reasons to be, for the supporting the Pretensions of his Imperial Majesty, when aft ually engaged in a War with th King, who had usurped the entire SpanijhMonarchy for

his Grandson the Duke of Anjou; and for the assisting the States General, who, by the Loss of their Barrier*against France, were then in the fame, or a more dangerous Condition then if they wereactually invaded: As these were the justand necessary Motives for undertaking this War: so the Ends proposed to be obtained by it were equally wife and honourable: For, as they are set forth in the Eighth Article of the same Treaty, they appear to have been, the procuring an equitable and reasonable Satisfaction to his Imperial Majesty, and sufficient Securities for the Dominions, Provinces, Navigation, and Commerce, of the King of Great Britain, and the States General; the making effectual Provision, That the Two Kingdoms of France and Spain should never be united under llie same Government; and, particularly, that the French should never get into the Possession of the Spanifk West Indies, or be permitted to fail thither, upon the

Account of Traffick, under any Pretence whatsoever; and, lastly, the securing to the Subjects of the King of Great Britain, and the States General, all the same Pri-

vileges, and Rights of Commerce throughout the whole Dominions of Spain, as they enjoyed before the Death o (Charles the Second, King of Spain, by virtue of any Treaty, Agreement, Custom, or any other way whatsoever: For the obtaining these Ends, the Three confederated Powers engaged toaffiftone another with their whole Force, according to such Proportions as should be specified in a particular Convention afterwards to be made for that Purpose: We do not find, that any such Convention was ever ratified; but it appears, that there was an Agreement concluded, which, by common Consent was under flood to behind ing upon each Party respectively; and according to which, the Proportions of Great Britain were, from the Beginning, regulated and founded: The Terms of that Agreement were, That, for the Service at Laud, his Imperial Majesty should furnish Ninety thou-fantl Men; the King of Great Britain, Forty thousand; and the States General, One hundred and Two thousand; of which there were Forty-two thousand intended to supply their Garrisons, and Sixty thousaudto aft against the common Enemy in the Field: And, with regard to the Operations of the War at Sea, they were agreed to be performed jointly by Great Britain and the States General; the Quota of Ships to be furnished for that Service being, Five-eighths on the Part of Great,

and Three-eighths on the Part of the States General.

Upon

Repreftnta-tion on the State of the War.

120 i° Martii. J. mi i.

Upon this Foot the War began in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Two; at which time the whole yearly Expence of it to England amounted to Three mil* lions Seven hundred and Six thousand Four hundred and Ninety-four Pounds; a very great Charge, as it was then thought by your Majesty’s Subjects, after the short Interval of Ease they had enjoyed from the Burthen of the former War; but yet a very moderate Proportion, in Gimparifon with the Load which hath since been laid upon them; for it appears by Estimates given in to your Commons, that the Sums necessary to carry on the Service for this present Year, in the same manner as it was performed the last Year, amount to more than Six millions Nine hundred Sixty thousand Pounds, besides Interest, for the Publick Debt, and the Deficiencies accruing the last Year; which Two Articles require One million One hundred and Forty-three thousand Pounds more; so that the whole Demands upon your Commons are arisen to more than Eight millions for the present annual Supply: We know your Majesty’s tender Regard for the Welfare of your People will make it uneasy to you to hear of so great a Pressure, as tin’s, upon them; and as we are assured it fully convinces your Majesty of the Necessity of our present Inquiry; so we beg leave to representto you, from what Causes, and by what Steps, this immense Charge appears to have grown upon us.

The Service at Sea, as it hath been very large and extensive in itself, so it hath been carried on, through the whole Course of the War, in a manner highly disadvantageous to your Majesty, and your Kingdom: For the Necessity of Affairs requiring that great Fleets should be fitted out every Year, as well for the maintaining a Superiority in the Mediterranean, as for opposing any Force which the Enemy might prepare, either at Dunkirk, or in the Ports of West France; your Majesty’s example, and Readiness, in fitting out your Proportion of Ships for all Parts of that Service, have been so far from prevailing with the States General to keep Pace with you, that they have been deficient every Year, to a great Degree, in proportion to what your Majesty hath fur-nillied; sometimes no less than Two-thirds, and generally more than half of their Quota; From hence your Majesty has been obliged, for the preventingDifappoint-ments in the most pressing Services, to supply those Deficiencies by additional Reinforcements of your own Ships: Nor hath the Angle Increase of such a Charge been the only ill Consequence that attended it: for, by this means, the Debt of the Navy hath been enhanced, so that the Discounts arising upon the Credit of it have affected all other Parts of the Service; From the same Cause, your Majesty’s Ships of War have been forced, in greater Nnmbers, to continue in remote Seas, and at unseasonable Times of the Year, to the great Damage and Decay of the British Navy: This also hath been the Occasion, that your Majesty hath been straitened in your Convoys for Trade; your Coasts have been exposed, for want of a sufficient Number of Cruisers to guard them; and you have been disabled from annoying the Enemy in their most beneficial Commerce with the West Indies, from whence they have received those vast Supplies of Treasure, without which they could not have supported the Expences of this War.

That Part of the War which hath been carried on in Flanders, was at first immediately necessary to the Security of the States General, and hath since brought them great Acquisitions both of Revenue and Dominion: Yet, even there, the original Proportions have been departed from; and, during the Course of the War, have been sinking, by Degrees, on the Part of Holland, so that, in this last Year, we find the Number in which they fell lliort of their Three-fifths to your Majesty’s Two-fifths, to have been Twenty thousand Eight hundred and Thirty-seven men: We are not unmindful, that in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Three, a Treaty was made between the Two Nations, for a joint Augmentation of Twenty thousand Men; wherein the Proportions were varied, and England consented to take

Half upon itself: But it having been annexed, as an express Condition, to the Grant of the said Augmentation in Parliament, That the States General should prohibit all Trade and Commerce with France; and that Condition having not been performed by them; the Commons think it reasonable.That the First Rule, of Three toTvvo, ought to have taken Place again, as well in that, as in other subsequent Augmentations; more especially, when they consider that the Revenues of those rich Provinces which have been conquered, would, if they were duly applied, maintain a great Number of new additional Forces against the common Enemy; notwithstanding which the States General have raised none upon that Account, but make use of those fresh Supplies of Money only to ease themselves in the Charge of their first established Quota.

As in the Progress of the War in Flanders a Dispro* portion was soon created to the Prejudice of England, so the very Beginning of the War in Portugal brought an unequal share of Burthen upon us: For although the Emperor, and the States General, were equally Parties with your Majesty in the Treaty with the King of gal;yet the Emperor neither furnishing his Third Part of the Troops and Subsidies stipulated for; nor the Dutch consenting to take an equal Share of his Imperial Majesty’s Deleft upon themselves; your Majesty hath been obliged to furnish Two-thirds of the entire Expence' created by that Service: Nor has the Inequality flopped there; for ever since the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Six, when the Englishand Dutch Forces march-. edoutofPnftwga/into Castile, the States General have entirely abandoned the War in Portugal, and left your Majesty to prosecute it, singly, at your own Charge: which you have accordingly done, by replacing a greater Number of Troops there than, even at first, you took upon you to provide: At the same time your Majesty’s generous Endeavours for the Support and Defence of the King of Portugal have been but ill seconded br that Prince himselt; for, notwithstanding that, by his Treaty, he had obliged himselfto furnish Twelve thousand Foot, and Three thousand Horse, upon his own Account; besides Eleven thousand Foot, and Two thousand Horse more, in Consideration of a Subsidy paid him, yet, according to the best Information your Commons can procure, it appears, that he hath scarce, at any time, furnished Thirteen thousand Men in the Whole.

In Spain, the War hath been yet more unequal and burthensome to your Majesty than any other Branch of it: For, being commenced without any Treaty whatsoever, the Allies havealmost wholly declined taking any Part of it upon themselves: A small Body of English and Dutch Troops were lent thither, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Five; not as being thought sufficient to support a regular War, or to make the Conquest of so large a Country; but with a View only of assisting the Spaniards to let King Charles upon the Throne, occasioned by the great Assurances which were given of their Inclinations to the House of Austria: But this Expectation failing, England was insensibly drawn into an established War, under all the Disadvantages of the Distance of the Place, and the feeble Efforts of the other Allies: The Account we have to lay before your Majesty upon this Head is. That although this Undertaking was entered upon at the particular and earnest Requestof the Imperial Court; and for a Cause of no less Importance and Concern to them than the reducing the Spanish Monarchy to the House of Austria; yet neither the late Emperors, nor his present Imperial Majesty, have ever had any Forces there on their own Account, till the last Year; and then only One Regiment of Foot, consisting of Two thousand Men; Though the States General have contributed something more to this Service, yet their Share also hath been inconsiderable; for in the Space of Four Years, from One thousand Seven hundred and Five, to One thousand Seven hundred and Eight, both inclufne, all the Forces they have sent into that Country have not exceeded

appears to have been only superior to that of any one Ally, but even eqnal to that of the whole Confederacy; your Commons naturally inclined to hope, that they should find Care had been taken of securing some particular Advantages to Britain in the Terms of a future Peace, such as might afford a Prospect of making the Nation Amends in time for that imroenfeTreafure which hath been expended;and those heavy Debts which have been contracted in the Course osso long and burdensome a War: This reasonable Expectation could no way have been better answered, than by some Provision made for the further Security, and the greater Invprovement, of the Commerce of Great Britain: But we find ourselves so very far disappointed in these Hopes, that in a Treaty not long since concluded between your Majesty and the States General, underColour ofa mutual Guaranteegiven lor Two Poiuts of the greatest Importance to both Nations, the Succession, and the Barrier; it appears, the Interest of Great Britain hath been not only neglected, but iacrificed; and that several Articlesin the said Treaty are destructive to the Trade and Welfare of this Kingdom; and therefore, highly dithonourable to your Majesty.

Your Commons observe, in the First Place, That several Towns and Places are, by virtue of this Treaty, to beput into the Hands of the States General; particularly Nieuport, Dendermonde, and the Castle of; which

can in ooSenfe be looked upon as Part ofa Barrier against France; but, being the Keys of the Netherlands towards Britain, must make the Trade of your Majesty’s Subjects in those Parts precarious^md, whenever the States think fit, totally exclude them from it: The pretended Necessity of putting these Places into the Hands of the States peneral, in order to fecqre to them a Communication with their Barrier, must appear vain and groundless; for the Sovereigntyof the Low Countries being not to remain to an Enemy, but to a Friend, and an Ally, that Communication must be always secure and uninterrupted; besides, that in case of a Rupture, or any Attack, the States have full Liberty allowed them to take Possession of all the Spani/k Netherlands, and therefore needed no

particular Stipulation for the Towns above mentioned.

Having taken Notice of this Concession made to the States General, for seizing upon the whole Ten Provinces; we cannot but observe to your Majesty, That in the manner this Article is framed, it is another dangerous Circumstance which attends this Treaty: For had such a Provision been confined to the same of an apparent Attack from France only, the avowed Design of this Treaty had been fulfilled; and your Majesty’s Instructions to your Ambassador bad been purmed: But this necessary RestriClion hath been omitted; and the same Liberty is granted to the States to take Possession of all the Netherlands, whenever they shall think themselves attacked by any other neighbouring Nation, as when they shall be in danger from France; so that if it should at any time happen, which your Commons are very unwilling to suppose, that they should quarrel even with your Majesty, the Riches, Strength, and advantageous Situation, of these Countries, may be made use of against yourfejf; without whofs generous and powerful A Alliance they had never been conquered.

To return to those ill Consequenceswhich relateto the Trade of your Kingdoms; we beg Leave to observe to your Majesty, That though this Treaty revives, and renders your Majesty a Patty to the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Articles of the Treaty of by virtue of

which, the Impositions upon all Goods and Merchan-difes brought into the SpanijliLow Countries by the Sea,

are to equal those laid on Goods and Merchandises imported by the Sdield, and the Canals oiSafs and Swyn, and other Mouths of the Sea adjoining; yet no Care is taken to preserve that Equality upon the Exportation of those Goods out of the Spanijli Provinces, into those Countries and Places, which, by virtue of this Treaty, are to be in the Possession of the States: The Consequence of which must in time be, and your Commons are informed that in some Instances it has already proved to be the Cafe, that Impositions upon Goods

A. 1711.

carried into those Countries and Places by the Subjects of the States General will be taken off, whilst those upon the Goods imported by your Majesty’s Subjects remain; by which means, Great Britain will entirely lose this most beneficial Branch of Trade, which it hath been in all Ages possessed of, even from the time when those Countries were governed by the House of Burgundy, one of the most ancient, as well as the most useful, Allies to the Crown of England.

With regard to the other Dominions and Territories of Spain; your Majesty’s Subjects have always been distinguished in their Commerce with them; and, both by ancient Treaties, and an uninterrupted Custom, have enjoyed greater Privileges and Immunities of Trade, then either the Hollanders, or any other Nation whatsoever: And that wife and excellent Treaty of the grand Alliance provides effectually for the Security and Continuance of these valuable Privileges to Britain, in such a manner, as that each Nation might be left at the End of the War upon the same Foot as it flood at the Commencement of it: But this Treaty we now complain of, instead of confirming your Subjects Rights, surrenders and destroys them: for although by the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Articles of the Treaty of Munjler, made between his Catholick Majesty and the States General, all Advantages of Trade are (iipulated for, and granted to, the Hollanders, equal to what the English enjoyed; yet, the Crown of England not being a Party to that Treaty, the Subjects of England have never submitted to those Articles of it; nor even the Spaniards themselves ever observed them: But this Treaty revives those Articles in Prejudice of Great Britain, and makes your Majesty a Party to them; and even a Guarantee to the States General for Privileges against your own People.

In how deliberate and extraordinary a Manner your Majesty’s Ambassador consented to deprive your Subjects of their ancient Rights, and your Majesty of the Power of procuring to them any new Advantage, most evidently appears from his own Letters; which, by your Majesty’s Directions, have been laid before your Commons: For when Matters of Advantage to your Majesty, and to your Kingdoms, had been offered as proper to be made Parts of this Treaty, they were refused to be admitted by the States General, upon this Reason and Principle, That nothing foreign to the Guarantees of the Succession, and of the Barrier, should be mingled with, them: notwithstanding which, the States General had no fboner received Notice of a Treaty of Commerce concluded between your Majesty and the present Emperor, but they departed from the Rule proposed before, and infilled upon the Article of which your Commons now complain: Which Article your Majesty’s Ambassador allowed of, although equally foreign to the Succession, or the Barrier; and although he had, for that Reason, departed from other Articles which would have been for the Service of his oiyn Country.

We have forborn to trouble your Majesty with general Observations upon this Treaty, as it relates to and affects the Empire, and other Parts of Europe: The Mif-chiefs which arise from it to Great Britain are what only we have presumed humbly to represent to you: As they are very evident, and very great; and as it appears, that the Lord Viscount Townshend had not any Orders or Authority for concluding several of those Articles which are most prejudicial to your Majesty’s Subjects; we have thought we could do no less than declare your said Ambassador, who negotiated and ligned, and all others who advised the Ratifying of, this Treaty, Ene» mies to your Majesty, and to your Kingdom.

Upon these faithful Informations, and Advices from, your Commons, we assure ourselves, your Majesty, in your great Goodness to your People, will refeue them, from those Evils, which the private Counsels of ill-de-signing Men have exposed them to; and that, in your great Wisdom, you will find feme Means for the explain-, ing and amending the several Articles of this Treaty, fe as that they may coufift with theluterest of Great Britain,

Note, This Duty was voted in March, but did not commence until the 24th June following; during which Interval, all that could be was wrought into Wares, those not being chargeable with any Part of the Duty: and the Stock in Hand being, by the Act for granting the said Duties, charged with Half only; the Produce on that Article is less than it otherwise would have been by the Su n of£.15,789; and by the made Wares, wrought up in the Three Months, as above, and not charged with Duty, at lead the Suin of £.20,000: The Officers of Excise were made use of to affiit in taking Stock in Hand; the several Duties already under their Care rendering it impracticable to concern them any further without great Loss, and running the greater Revenues into Confusion: And as for the Duty on Houses, we found that Revenue, the last Year, in so unsettled a Condition, that those Officers could not be applied to the Duty upon Hides upon its first Establishment; but most of them are now instructed; and several of them employed, in making Surveys: And we hope, after a Settlement of the said Duty on Houses, and One Year’s View of the Duty on Hides, Sic. we may be able to Ieffen the said Charge of Management considerably.

Ways Mr. Conyers, according to Order, reported from the and Means. Committee of the whole House, who were to consider farther of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted toher Majesty, the Resolul ions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty be laid upon all Silks, Callicoes. Linens, and Stuffs, of what Kind soever, which shall be printed, flaiued, or painted, in Great; except Stuffs

made of Woollen, or whereof the greatest Part in Value shall be Woollen.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty upon all Silks so to be printed, stained, or painted, be after the Rate of Six Pence for every Yard in Length, reckoning Half a Yard for the Breadth; and in that Proportion /or wider or narrower Silks.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty on Callicoes to be so printed, stained, or painted, be after the Rate of Four Pence for every

V«t. 17.

Yard in Length, reckoning a Yard wide; and in that Proportion.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Duly upon all other Linen, and Stuffs, except before excepted, to be so printed, painted, or stained, be after the Rate of 2d. for every Yard in Length; and in that Proportion for greater or leller Quantities.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Duties be granted for the Term of Thirty-two Years.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That One Half of the said Rates be charged upon any Stock of the said Commodities, now in the Hands of Drapers, or other Traders for Sale, either by Wholesale Or Retail.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Duty be laid on all Bricks, Tiles, Slate, and Lime, made within the Limits of the Weekly Bills of Mortality, or brought into the fame; whether the said Bricks, Tiles, and Lime, be made or brought for Sale, or not for Sale.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Duty be laid on all Stones which shall be brought within the Limits of the Weekly Bills of Mortality, to be used in Building or Paving.

fiefolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Duty be after the Rate of Three Shillings per Thousand upon the said Bricks.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Duty be after the Rate of Four Shillings per Thousand upon the plain Tiles.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Duty be after the Rate of Two Shillings per Quarter upon the said Lime.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Duty be after the Rate of Six Shillings per Thousand upon all Pan Tiles, Ridge Tiles, and Gutter Tiles.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Duty be after the Rate of Three Shillings per Hundred upon all Paving Tiles of Twelve Inches square; and proportionably for a greater or lesser Size.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Duty be after the Rate of Four Shillings per Thousand upon all Slate to be used for Covering of Houses.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Duty upon Stone be after the Rate of Two Shillings per Ton, as well upon the unwrought Stone to be used in Building, as upon all Stone to be used in Paving.

The First, Second, and Third, of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The Fourth of the said Resolutions being, read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out " 2rf." and inserting " id.

And the Question being put, That " id." stand Part of the said Resolution;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the said Duty upon all other Linen, and Stuffs, except before excepted, to be so printed, painted, or stained, be after the Rate of id. for every Yard in Length; and in that Proportion for greater or leller Quantities.

The rest of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Freman reported from the Committee of Privi-

leges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Boroughs of Anstruther Easter, Anstruther Wester, Creall, and Kil

renity, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the said Report and Resolution were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Major-General George Hamilton, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir John Anjlruther Baronet, to serve for the Burghs of Pittemceem, Anstruther Anjlru-

ther Wester, Creall, and Kilrennie:

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Five’Commissioners for the D drift: of Burghs aforesaid.

That the Commissioners for Creall and voted for the Petitioner; the Commissioners for ther Easter, and Anjlruther IVvoted for the fitting Member.

That the Questions were, Whether Mr. Wm. Watson, who voted for the Petitioner; or Mr. Wm. Bell, who voted for the fitting Member, was the legal Commissioner for the Burgh of Pitfenweem; and whether the Commissioner for Anjlruther Wester had a good Vote: That the Town Counsel of Pittenweem who elected the Commissioner for that Burgh, confided of 16; Seven of which voted for Mr. Watson, and the other Nine for Mr. Bell.

That the Petitioner's Counftl objected against Patrick Mertoun, Robert Alexander, and William -Jon, Three of the Voters for Mr. Bell.

And they also objected against Mr. Bell himself; and produced a Protect made against him, and his Voters, at the Election of the Commissioner for Pittemceem, the 20th of October 1710, by Sir Alexander and

offered to call Witnesses to the Fasts alleged in that Protect:

But that was not admitted, nor the Protect read at the Committee; in regard it did not appear. That Sir Alexander Areskine had any Right to vote, protect, or be present at that Election:

That it appeared by the Minutes of the Election to Parliament, which was at Pittemceem, the 27th Day of October 1710, That the Laird of Bellfour, Commissioner for Killrenny, then protested, and adhered to his Pro-

teds, as follow; viz.

id, That Mr. Bell could have noVote in choosing a Representative for these Burghs, to the ensuing' Parliament, in regard there was, at the pretended Election of him to be Elector for Pittemceem, a valid Protefiation taken against him, that he could neither elect, nor be elected; and further, in regard there was likewise valid Protedations taken against the Plurality of his Voters; whereupon he took instruments: And, id, That John Lyell, the Commissioner for Anjlruther Wester, could have noVote in this Election; be-enufe, before he, or any of the present Bailies of Anstruther Wester, would accept of their Offices, my Lord Anjlruther did promise to pay, either the "Whole, or a good Part, of the Debt of the Town, providing the y voted for his Son Sir John, at the ensuing Elections; and so they have no free Vote:

Lyell protested the contrary, and adhered to hi«; Protest.

That the Petitioner’s Counsel called,

Vol. 17.

Mr. Johh Pittulock:Who said, That some Days before the Election, Mr. Lyell told him. He was elected Commissioner for Anstruther Wester, upon Condition that he would vote for the Lord Son; and

that the Lord Anjlruther had promised to pay the Town Debt, if they chose One that voted for his Son; but the Witness said, He did not know, nor hear from Lyell, that any Money was paid.

That the Petitioner’s Counsel infilled.

That, by the 6th Act of the 9th Session of King William's First Parliament, Anno 1701, for preventing wrongous imprisonment, the Pains for such Iropri-foument are; Forfeiture of a sum of Money, Lois of Office, and Incapacity of publick Trust:

And they produced an Extract from the Books of the Lords of Council and Session at Edinburgh, whereby it appears, That an action was commenced, and Summons raised there, and an Act, and Letters of Diligence, for adducing Witnesses, in order to prove her Allea-geance, were obtained by Jannett Horseburgh against , the said William Bell, for wrongous Imprisonment of her forae Years ago, upon the alleged Crime of Witchcraft; and that the said William depending the said Action, did, by a Declaration in Writing, under his Hand, dated the 14 th Day of January 1710, attested by Two Witnesses, and registered in the said Books, the 22d Day of January 1712, acknowledge the said wrongous Imprisonment, and made her Satisfaction for the fame.

And the Petitioner’s Counsel infilled;

That the said Declaration, or Acknowledgment, bpj ing registered as aforesaid, did amount to a Conviction of the said Offence; and that, therefore, the said William Bell was incapable of being a Commissioner to vote in this Election.

That the Sitting Member’s Counsel infilled.

That the Petitioner had not invalidated this Election; nor any of the Voters:

That Balfow's Protect, against Bell, being in general Terms only, is illegal and void:

That Bell's Commission to vote is not an Office within the Act for preventing wrongous Imprisonment:

That the Disability upon this Act incurs only upon-a legal Conviction, for wrongously detaining in Prison after Liberation; and that the Action and Process pre-ferive, if not pursued within Three Years after the last Day of the Imprisonment.

They also infilled upon the Act of Pardon pa fled since the said Imprisonment: And that the Commissionr to Mr. Bell, being under the Common Seal, and signed by the Bailies and Clerk of the Burgh of,

was the only, legal Commission for that Burgh.

That it appeared by the Minutes of the Election*, That the Commissioner for Anjlruther Easter protested, that .\Ir. Watson's Commission, subscribed by fume of the Counsellors of Pittenweem, was not according ta the Plan appointed by Law; wanting both the Subscription of the Town Clerk, and Seal of the said Burgh; and that the Subscribers thereof should be liable to the Penalties contained in the Acts of Burrows., That the Petitioner’s Counsel infilled, That Mr. Watson was elected by Majority of good Votes, and waa therefore the legal Commissioner; and that the Seal, or Town Clerk’s Eland, is not uecessary to the Commission.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee

came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir John Anjlruther Baronet, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Burghs of Pittenweem, Anjlruther Eajicr, Anjlruther

Creall, and Killrenny, in the County of Fife.

Mr. Freman reported from the Committee of Privi-

leges and Elections, the Matter as it appeared to them, upon the Petition of William Treene senior, Joseph Mayo senior, Joseph Mayo junior, William and

James Mayo, in behalf of themselves, and others, Members of the Company of Fullers, and Freemen; and of Ralph Whitehead, Thomas Clerk, Richard Henry

Clarke and Thomas Craner, in behalfof themselves, and many Scores ofother Freemen of the City of;

and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report and Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of William Treene senior, Joseph Mayo senior, Joseph May junior, Wm. Pilkington, and James Mayo, in behalf of themselves, and others. Members of the Company of Fullers, and Freemen; and of Ralph Whitehead, Thomas Clarke, Richard Nicklin, Henry Clarke, and Thomas Craner, in behalf of themselves, and many Scores of other Freemen of the City o( Coventry; complaining of their

being debarred, by the Sheriffs, of their undoubted Right of voting at the Election to Parliament, the 18th of October into: And praying. That their Right in voting may be ascertained to them; and Reparation made for the Injury they have sustained, in being denied the fame:

That the Committee haveexamined the Matter of that Petition; and heard Counsel for the Petitioners, and for the late Sheriffs of Coventry, thereupon. That the Petitioners Counsel examined Witnesses; viz. John Whadcock, and Tho. Wright: Who fa id. That the Fullers Company, as appears by their Books, have been incorporated above Two hundred Years: They have two Seats in St. Michael’s Church in the City of Coventry; they pay to Church and Poor in the City, though they live out of it; have always enjoyed all Privileges which are peculiar to the Freemen of that City only; and have voted in all Elections to Parliament for 20 Years pall, and never were objected to till within Three Years last:

That several of the Fullers Company live, with their Families, in the City, and have Shops there, which none but Freemen are permitted to have; they generally live without the City, for Convfcniency of the Water used in their Trade, but were never, upon that Account, objected to, or refused any Privilege of Freemen, or denied to vote, till 1708.

That above 60 Persons at a time have often come from London, and been permitted to vote without Objection; and the Petitioners were refused by the Sheriffs at the late Election.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions»

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Members of the Company of Fullers, of the City of Coventry, being Freemen, not receiving Alms, or weekly Charity, have a Right to vote in the Elections of Members to serve in Parliament for the said City.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Freemen of the City of Coventry, as do not receive Alms, or weekly Charity, and have served Seven Years Apprenticeship within the said City, or the Suburbs thereof, have a Right to vote in the Elections of Members to serve in Parliament for the said City.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Freman reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them,

touching the Election for the City of Edinburgh, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place , and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report and Resolution were read; and are as follow, viz.

Upon the Petition of Henry Hamilton Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir Patrick Johnson to serve for the City of Edinburgh:

That the Petitioner’s Counsel infilled, That, according to the fundamental Constitution of the City of Edinburgh, the Sitting Member is incapable of fitting in this Parliament, in regard he is a Merchant, and served for the said City in the last Parliament: For that, by a Decreet Arbitral, made by Arbitrators, and confirmed by Kin g James the First, as Umpire, Anno 1583, for determining all Differences between the Merchants and Craftsmen of the said City, the Magistracy of the said City was given to the Merchants; and it was finally settled, That the Two Members to serve in Parliament for that City should always be, one a Merchant, and the other a Craftsman:

That this Decreet was registred in the Books of Coun-cil at Edinburgh; was ratified by the Parliament there; and so obtained the Force of a Law, and became the fundamental Conllitntion of that City; and, as such, was always observed till the Union of the two Kingdoms:

That, by the Union, the Rights and Privileges of the Royal Boroughs in Scotland, as they then were, are to re-

main entire after the Union, and notwithstanding thereof; and only One Member is to be sent for Edinburgh:

And, therefore, they infilled, That in regard the Merchants and Tradesmen of the said City were, before the Union, dillinftly represented, they oughtftilito be distinctly represented, by electing a Merchant, and a Tradesman, by Turns.

That the Sitting Member’s Counsel admitted the Constitution of Edinburgh before the Union was as the Petitioner’s Counsel alleged: But insisted. That by the Act of Union, the Confutations of the Royal Boroughs, as to their Elections to Parliament, are altered; and other Burghs are to elect a Commissioner in the manner then in Use: and they are to elect by Turns: But Edinburgh is excepted; and the Election there, which is to be but of One Member only, is left free, and the Voters at Liberty to choose who they please.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Sir Patrick Johnson is duly elected a Member to serve in this present Parliament for the City of burgh.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

ANNE R.

to grant Leases of the Estateof the said Duke, and Sets for getting Copper and other Ore and Minerals therein; and for rendering valid and effectual several such Grants or Sets, already made; was committed. Mr. Secretary St. John reported to the House, That their Address, of the 14 th Instant, returning her Majesty the Thanks of this House for her Majesty’s most gracious Message, relating to the completing a Church at Roterdam, had been laid before her Majesty: And also, that their Addresses, the same Day, for Accounts of the Debt of the Navy, Victualling, Transports, and Ordnance, from Christmas 1710 to Lady-day 1711; and of the One million Five hundred thousand Pounds, granted the last Session of Parliament, for the Service of the War in Spain and Portugal; and for an Estimate of the Charge of the Navy, Ordnance, Victualling, and for Transport Service, for the Year 1711; had been presented to her Majesty; and that (he had been pleased to direct the proper Officers to prepare the said Accounts, according to the Desires of this House.

Mr. Secretary St.John also acquainted the House, Th at

he was commanded byher Majesty to acquaint this House, That, pursuant to their Address of the last Session her Majesty had given Directions for taking care of the Settlements in Africa, for the Preservation of the Trade thither; which the hoped would be preferred accordingly; and that her Majesty had been pleased to direct the State of that Trade to be laid before her; which had been done by the Commissioners of Trade: And that he was commanded by her Majesty to lay before the House a Representation, and several Papers, relating the reunto:

And he presented the same to the House,

And the Titles of the said Represention, and other Papers, were read; and are as follow;

Representation from the Council of Trade concerning the Settlement of the Trade to Africa:

Copy of the Answer of the separate Traders to Africa to the Queries sent them by the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations:

Copy of some additional Proposals from the separate Traders touching the Maintenance of the African Settlements:

Copy of a Letter from the separate Traders containing an Account of their Stock, and Proposals for managing the Trade to Africa in a regulated Company:

Copy of some farther Proposals from the separate Traders to Africa relating to the Trade thither:

Copy of the Account of the Ten per Cent. Duty paid by the separate Traders for maintaining the African Settlements in Three Years of Peace, and in the Two last Years of War:

Rules and Provisions proposed by the separate Traders as necessary for the better carrying on, improving, and increasing, the Trade to Africa:

Names of Fifty-six Ships of separate Traders loft between 1707 and 1711:

Extract of the Minutes of the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations relating to the Trade to Africa:

Copy of the Company’s Observations upon Three Queries sent by the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations to the separate Traders:

Copy of a Memorial from the Royal African Company, setting forth the absolute Necessity of a Joint Stock for carrying on the Trade to Africa:

Particular Valuation of the Company’s Forts, Cattles, and Factories, in Africa:

Copy of an Account of the annual Charge of the Company’s Forts and Settlements in Africa:

Copy of an Account of Eight Years Exports of the African Company, and Eight Years Exports of the separate Traders.

Ordered, That the said Representation, and other Papers relating the reunto, be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider farther of the Trade to Africa.

The said Representation, and other Papers relating the reunto, are bound up with the other Papers of this Session.

And the said Reports were read, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; and agreed unto by the House.

The said Reports, and Resolution, are as follow;

At the Committee appointed to consider the Report of the Commissioners appointed to examine how, to whom, and for what, Colonel John Rice disposed of£.11,420 17 s. in Army Debentures; That the Committee find, by an Act made in the 4th Year of her Majesty’s Reign, there was granted unto Colonel John Rice the Sum of 1,410 17 6d.

for Horses, Arms, and Accoutrements, and Arrears of Pay due to him; and, accordingly, received the said Sum in Army Debentures:

That the Committee do also find, That, by an Act made in the 5th Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled An Act for obliging Colonel John Rice to account for Debentures granted to him, Complaint was made. That he, the said Colonel Rice had not paid to the Officers and Soldiers of his Regiment the Sum of £.11,420 17 6d.

as was alleged by the said Rice-, but had, in order to obtain the said Act, fraudulently procured Releases from them for the Pay of their several Troops aforesaid, upon Assurances by him given, That he would pay the Sums for which such Releases were given, when he should have received the same from the Parliament; but the said John Rice had not paid the same:

Whereupon it is by the said last mentioned Act enacted, That the said John Rice shall be charged and chargeable in her Majesty’s Court of Exchequer with the Sum of £.11,420 17 s.6d.; and shall account for the same according to the Course of the Exchequer, as if the Monies had been issued to him by way of Imprest, or upon Account, for the Services of the Army:

It further enacts, That such Charge against the said John Rice shall be taken and reputed as a Debt, by Obligation or Specialty, of the Nature of a Statute Staple taken or acknowleged to the Use of her Majesty, accord-Vol. 17.

ing to the Statute mdde in the 33d Year of King Henry Col. Rice'* the VUIth, to oblige the said John Rice to answer in debenture*.0 Account for the said £. 11,420 17$.; and that the said Debentures, so made out to the said John which are remaining in his Hands, or of any other Person in Trust for him, and in which he hath still any Property, or Equity of Redemption; and also all other Effects in Money, Bills, Notes, Lands, Tenements,

Woods, Hereditaments, Goods, or Chattels; or any other Estate, real or personal, in England or Ireland, for which he hath disposed of any of the said Debentures, either in his own Name, or in the Name of any Person in Trust for him, or of which he is to receive the Benefit; except such Debentures touching which other Provision is made in the said Act; is by the said Act veiled in her Majesty:

In which Act there is a Proviso, That nothing in the said Act shall takeaway the Right or Title of any Person to any of the said Debentures, which have been, before the ill of March 1706, really, and bought or

taken as Security for Money lent to the said John Rice, by any other Person, having the Possession thereof, who shall fend an Account to the said Commissioners at any time before the ill of August 1707:

The said Act further provides, That where it shall appear, that any Monies have been really, and bonafde\ent upon Security of the said Debentures, the same Commissioners shall pay and satisfy such Money so lent by any Person, who shall make such Discovery thereof, and all Interest due for the fame; whereby such Debentures, or the Residue thereof, as shall be unfold, may remain to her Majesty, for the Purposes aforesaid: And in case such Sale shall not be made, and the Debt, and Interest due thereon, paid thereout, on or before the ill October 1707, the Persons having such Debentures in Security may, at any time after, fell the same to any Purchaser, and pay themselves their Principal and Interest:

That the Practice of the Custmn-house Officers in difiiguishing the said Metals appeared, by the said Report, to be thus; viz.

Battery, is raised Kettles or Pans; and is only accounted such when the Mark of the Hammer is apparent on it.

Metal prepared, is black Pans or Kettles, not having the Mark of the Hammer: And,

Black Lattin, is round Bottoms, and Folds of thin Brass.

And the Committee having furamoned Mr. Hard* tvick, and other Land Surveyors of the Customs, to attend them; and being asked, If they knew that Battery had been entered as Metals prepared? Mr. Hardwick said, That he had known Battery was once entered as Metal prepared; and then ’twas (lopped and re-entered: And all the Officers agreed, That they never heard of any Ingots or Lumps of Brass imported as Metal prepared, in their Time, though Hardwick has been an Officer there aibout 30 Years.

Then the Petitioners proceeded to prove the Allegations of their Petitions; and produced several Sorts of black Lattin, Metal prepared, and Battery; and' called several Witnesses to prove the Goodness of their Manufactures; viz.

Leonard Fitz/iue: Who said, He wrought in Copper and Brass for Years: That there is not better Brass than what is made in England, and all made of Materials, enough to supply the whole Kingdom; and is generally better than what is imported from Holland:

As to the aforesaid Certificate, Mr. Appleby owned the Seizing of the Fat; but that he knew nothing of any Battery contained in it, and his Invoice did not mention any such thing: And the Commissioners of the Customs, being satisfied that lie was a fair Trader and meant no Fraud, and his Correspondent not knowing the re was a higher Duty on it, excused the Mistake, upon making the Officers a Gratuity; and that he compounded with them for Fifteen Guineas.

The House being acquainted. That Mr. Brifcoe. the Messenger attending the Great Seal, attended, according to the Order of Saturday last;

He was called in; and, at the Bar, examined what was become of the Writ for electing a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of King's Lynn, in the County of Norfolk: He acquainted the House, That the Writ was tealed the 10th Inilant; and that, Upon the Becommendation of some Gentlemen, who said they knew one Mr. Cremer an Attorney of that Country, to be a very honell Man, and a Man of Bttfinels, who was going down, he delivered the Writ to him the 12th Inilant; who promised to deliver the same to the Sheriff the 17 th; and that it was not intended to be delivered sooner, to avoid the Consulion of having the At sizes and the Election together: That Mr. Cremer had acquainted him, by Letter, That he was to inquire for the High Sheriff at Nonoich, but that he was gone into Cambridgeshire; and that the Under Sheriff was gone into Suffolk: He confessed. That Mr. Cremer was not the Sheriff’s Deputy; that he did not take any Receipt from him for the Writ, as he does not from those he intrulls to deliver Writs to Sheriffs, who are to take Receipts themselves from the Sheriffs.

' And Mr. Brifcoe being withdrawn;

The First Section of the Act of Parliament of the 7th and 8th Year of his late Majesty, for the farther regulating Elections of Members to serve in Parliament; and for the preventing irregular Proceedings of Sheriffs, and other Officers, in the eleding and returning such Members; were read: And also that Part of the Journal of the 2d December 1704, as related to Mr. in another Cafe, was read.

Resolved, That Mr. Robert Brifcoe, having received the Writ for eleding a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of King's Lynn, in the County of Norfolk;and having not delivered the same to the pro-

per Officer; is guilty of a Neglect of his Duty, in Prejudice of the said Borough, and of the Right of Elections.

Mr. Farrar, reported from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider of the Trade to Africa, the llesolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read iu his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clcik’s Table: W here the same were read; and are as follow';

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Trade to Africa ought to be free to all Iter Majesty’s Subjects of Great Britain, and the Plantations, in a regulated Company.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the preferring, better carryingon, and improving, the Trade to Africa, it is necessary, that Forts and Settlements he maintained, and enlarged, on that Coalt.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Charge of maintaining the said Forts and Settlements be borne out of the said Trade.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Thai it is necessary the Contracts already made with the Natives be maintained, and other Alliances from time to time made for the Enlargement of the Trade to Africa.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Plantations ought to he supplied with sufficient Quantities of Negroes at reasonable Rates.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a considerable Stock is necessary for the carrying on the Trade to Africa to the bed Advantage of her Majesty’s Subjects, and for preserving and improving the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is necessary an Export of One hundred thousand Pounds at k-ail, in Merchandise, be annually made from Great Britain to Africa.

The tirll Six of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The lait of the said Resolutions, being read a Second time;

And the Question being put. That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution;

It passed in the Negative.

The House proceeded to take into Considerationthe Norwich Amendment made by the Lords to the Bill, intituled, Workhcafev. An Act for erecting a Workhouse in the City and County of the City of Norxoich, for the better employing and maintaining the Poor there:

And the same was twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and is as follows; viz.

" Provided, That nothing in this Act contained shall " extend, or be construed to extend, to charge all or any of the present Members of the Walloon, or French,

and Dutch, Congregations in the said City of Norwichand County of the fame, or such Aliens who

" who shall hereafter become Members of the said Congregations, with any Payment or Payments, Sum or Sums of Money, for or towards the building, erect ing,

"repairing, or amending, the Work-house or Work- houses intended to be erected and built by virtue of " this Act; nor to the Railing or Paying of any Sum " or Sums of Money for or towards the Maintenance or " Relief of the Poor of any Parish in the said City and " County of the City of Norxoich, other than and except " to the Poor of the respective Parishes where they respectively dwell; and that for and in respect only of . " the House or Houses, and Ground they dwell in and " occupy, in such respective Parishes.

" Provided nevertheless, That the said Members of " the Walloon, or French, and Dutch, Congregations,

from time to time, for ever hereafter, do, with other " their Stocks, Estates, and Values, provide for and maintain the Poor of their own respective Congregations, as hath been heretofore accustomed; so that " such Poor do not, or shall not, be or become chargeable to the respective Parishes where they dwell in the said City and County."

Ordered, That Mr. Ferrier do carry the Bill to the Lords, and acquaint them. That this House hath agreed to the said Amendment.

Mr. Medlycot, according to Order, reported from the' fJough*’' Committee, to whom the Petition of Sir William Douglas, Lieutenant General of her Majesty’s Forces, was <*u* referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee; having examined into the Allegations contained in the said Petition, do find, That by an Act, made in the Sixth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for the further directing the Payment of the Equivalent, it is, amongst other things, enacted.

That the Judges shall, by publick Proclamation at the Market Crofs&l Edinburgh, intimate to all Parties within or without the Kingdom havinglnterest in any of the publick Debts of Scotlandbefore the Union, and having Right by the said Art of Parliament to claim, to compear, by themselves, or their (awful Procurators or Attornies, before the said Judges, at any time within Six Months, at Edinburgh, and there to exhibit their Claims and Instructions; declaring. That the Accounts hereby, and by the aforesaid Act of Parliament of Scotland, appointed to be made, shall be made up only of such Claims as shall be presented to them within the said time; and the Commissioners of the Equivalent impowered to pay these only who shall be contained in the said general Account; that the said Judges shall proceed without Loss of Time, or Delay whatsoever, to the making up the aforesaid Accounts, according to the Claims and Instructions duly presented and verified; and the general Accounts being fomade, an authentic Copy of the fame, subscribed by the said Judges of the Exchequer, shall be delivered to the Commissioners of the Equivalent, and Certificates shall be granted to each of the several Parries of such Article of the said general Account as does concern them 3 which Certificate shall be signed, and shall contain the Name of the Party to whom the Debt was originally due; the Sum payable, with the Lift, Civil or Military, upon which the same is charged; and the Class and Order of Preference of such Debt, according to the said Act; and shall be alsignable and transferable by Indorsement.

It further enacts. That such Persons as shall happen to omit to compear, and make good their laid Claims, before the said Judges of the Exchequer, within the Time to be by them appointed; and shall thereby lose the Benefit of being placed upon the said First general Account, according to which only the said Commissioners of Equivalent are by that Act impowered to make Payment; shall neverthelessbe allowed to compear, by themselves or others, within One Year after Elapfing of the said First Day; and there to exhibit, and make good, before them, their respective Claims; which Claims, fa made good, shall be by the said Judges of the Exchequer admitted and formed into One Second general Account, without Distinction or Order of Preference whatsoever, to be by them signed, and delivered to the Commissioners of Equivalent; as also shall grant Certificates transferable by Indorsement, and in the same Manner and Form as those upon the First general Account are directed, payable by the Commissioners of Equivalent, next and immediately after the whole Debts due upon the First Two general Accounts are paid.

An' ACCOUNT of forne extraordinary Charges of the War, for which no Provision hath

by Parliament; viz.

For the extraordinary Allowance of green and dry Forage for the several Regiments of Dragoons quartered in North Britain, between the 22d December 1710 and the 23d 1711

That, by an A6l of the zzd of King Charles the lid, their Church was included in the 51 Churches to be rebuilt out of the Duties charged upon Coals: That the said Churches have all since been finished, except this of St. Mary Woolno/h’s: That, by the Opinion of able Surveyors, the East and West Ends, South Side, and Tower, of the Petitioners Church, are become very ruinous; and feme Part thereof, though the weakest beams have been supported, has fallen in: That many whole Families, for fear of the Danger, absent themselves from divine Service: That the Petitioners are informed, there will arise, by the Duties laid on Coals for rebuilding the Cathedral of Paul, a Surplusage more than necessary to complete the same: And praying. The said Return of the Commissioners of Customs, upon the Petition of Thomas Brooke and John Hellier, is as followeth; viz.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament affetnbled.

THE Return of the Commissioners of the Customs to an Order of this honourable House, of the 19th ult. on a Petition of Thomas Broolc and John Hellier, of London, Merchants; directing the said Commissioners to state the Fast; with their Opinion thereupon.

The Commissioners, in Obedience to the said Order, humbly acquaint this honourable House, That, having examined the Allegations of the said Petition, they do find, That the Petitioners did import coiiliderable Quantities of Wine, for which they had an Allowance °f£.8 per Cent, out of the Impost Duty, by virtue of the Act i° Jac. 2, as Merchants Importers:

But it appearing to the Commissioners, by the publick Advertisements, as well as by the Acknowledgment of the Petitioners, That they fold great Quantities of Wine by Retail, having publick Cellars and Houses for that Purpose; the Commissioners font for the Petitioners, and demanded the said £.8 per Cent, to be paid by them as Retailers; which they have accordingly complied with; and still continue to pay the Customs in this Port for their Wine, without the said Allowance being made to them.

The Commissioners humbly represent to this honourable House, That the said Act of Parliament declares. That all Importers, not being Vintners or Retailers, who are thereby obliged to pay ready Money for that whole Duty, are to be allowed and abated £.8 per Cent. in Consideration of any Defeat or Damage that may happen, by the Wines lying longer on the Importers Hands, or by real'on of other Accidents, upon the Importers making Oath, before the proper Officers of the Customs, that the same are imported byway of Merchandise, and with Intent to fell again; which is the Method made use of on the Entries of Wines imported.

As to what the Petitioners allege. That other Merchants, although they do retail Wines, yet have this Allowance of £.& per Cent, made to them; the Commissioners humbly olfer, That they have been, and are now, under lirift Inquiry, to find out this Abuse to the Revenue, in order to the Prol'ecution of the several Persons concerned therein, according to Law.

The Commissioners further humbly represent, That, finding the said Brooke and Hellier had imported several Quantities of Wines into Yarmouth, PortJ'moulh, and other Out Ports, they directed the Officers of the Customs to demand the Retail Duties for the fame; which the Petitioners refused to pay, alleging. That though they retailed Wines in London, yet they fold the Wine they imported into the Out Ports by Wholesale: Whereupon the Commissioners, to strengthen their own Opinion ordered their Solicitor to attend Mr. Attorney General for his Advice on the Cafe, which he has given in the following Words:

" I am of Opinion, B. and II. retailing Wines in " London, are thereby Retailers there; and, being so, " they are Retailers every where, within the Words of " the Act, i# Jac. referred to: For, being a Retailer, * while he is so, it matters not whether he retails, or "intends to retail, all the Wines he imports; but " must be considered as to all the Wines he imports as a Retailer."

As to what the Petitioners propose, to be relieved by a Clause in an Act of Parliament to be made. That they may pay the Duties upon their own Oath, as Merchants, fur Inch Wine as they shall fell by Wholesale; and as Retailers for such as they shall retail; the Commissioners humbly acquaint this honourable House, That they cannot think the same reasonable; because the Law, as it pow stands, seems to have been made in favour of the Vot. 17.

Merchants Importers, who are obliged to keep great Stocks by them, and would thereby be drove out of their Trade: For that the Vintners, who fell by Retail, do often fell also by Wholesale; and, consequently, might pretend to the same Privilege; which would elude the Intent of the Law: But the Commissioners are humbly of Opinion, it will conduce more to the Equality of Trade, and answer better what the Petitioners desire.

That where any Person has entered, or shall enter, his Wine* upon Oath, as a Merchant, and afterwards retail the fame; instead of making the Fast Perjury, as is proposed by the Petitioners; in that Cafe, over and above the Penalty already enjoined by Law, they be subject to such further penal Sum as shall be thought proper; one Moiety whereof to be for the Use of the Queen; the other for the Informer, or the Person that shall sue for the same:

Which is humbly submitted to the Consideration of this honourable House.

J. Stanley,

Custom-house, M. Prior,

London, nth April 1712. J. Bridges,

Robert IVm.son,

E. Gibbon,

Jo.

The said Report is as follows; viz.

To the Right honourable Robert Earl of Oxford and Earl Mortimer, Lord High Treasurer of Great Britain.

May it please your Lordship,

In obedience to your Lordship’s Order of Reference, of the 6th of September last, upon Two Representations relating to the Royal Hospital, and Out Pensioners, of Chelsea College; One from Mr. , by Directions

from the Right honourable Mr. How, Paymaster of the Guards and Garrisons, and Treasurer of the said Hospital, consisting of the several Heads following:

I ft, That the present great Expence of the disabled Invalids, who are sent from Abroad, and by her Majesty’s Establishment are entitled to several Allowances as OwtPensioners, according to the Condition in which they

*9

served, is not to be borne by the Poundage, and Days Pay, deducted from the Establishment of the Guards, Garrisons, Sc. the greatest Part thereof being expended for the annual Support of the Royal Hospital at,

and the necessary Charges payable out of that Fund: adly, That there’s no-other certain Provision for the Out Pensioners; many of whom are very moving Ob-jeQs of Companion; and, if not subsisted, must be exposed to perish, to the Discouragement of the Service: 3dly, That, by a State made of the full Deductions upon the present Year’s Establishment, with the Charge of the Hospital, to 24th June 1711, it appears, there will not be sufficient to pay all the Demands to that time, and subsist the Out Pensioners farther than the 24th of April last:

4thly, That, by the nearest Estimate which can at present be made, there will be wanting the Sum of £.35,800 to clear the Hospital, and carry on the Subsistence of the Out Pensioners, to 24th of next:

5thly, That, thereupon, he proposes a Demand may be laid before the Parliament, who the last Year gave the Sum of £.15,392. 17 s. at that time wanted* not only to grant a sufficient Sum to supply what shall appear wanting for the present Year; but likewise fix a Fund for the Support of the said Charge; which, during the War, is daily increasing:

6thly, That, till such Provision can be made, in case no Money can be issued for this Service, beyond the Poundage, and Days Pay, he desires to know, whether he may continue to pay the necessary Sums for the Support of the Royal Hospital, and Out Pensioners, out of any Money in his Hands, on Account of the Forces, till the same can be made good out of such Fund as shall be given for this Service; or whether he shall not issue any Money for the Support of the Hospital, and-Subsistence of the Out Pensioners, exceeding the Poundage," and Days Pay, of the Establishment under his Care.

The other Representation, being from the Governor and Deputy Governor of the said Hospital, imports, Thut pursuant to your Lordship’s Commands of the 25th July last, they humbly laid before your Lordship;

1 ft. A Copy of the Establishment of the Hospital: -2dly, A Lift of the Out Pensioners belonging thereto; the Pay tiiey are allowed; the Time of their Admittance; and the Regiments from whence they are certified ns Invalids:

3dly, There are some whom they have not an Account of the Time of their Admittance, or from what Regiments they came, beingbefore they were appointed CoBMnissioners; butfince that, the Account is as per-fest as can be prepared:

4thly, They take Notice, That, observing the daily Increase of the Invalids, the private Gentlemen of the Horse Guards, and the Corporals of Horse, have received Six Pence per diem per Man, and the Light Horsemen Three Pence per diem per Man, less than the Establishment directs:

All which having been referred to us by your Lord* ship, with Directions to inform ourselves, in the bell man* ner we can, of the Conditions and Qualifications of those named in the said Book; and of the Methods used in procuring Persons to be entertained as Out Pensioners; and to report to your Lordship a State of the whole Matter; with what Observations shall occur to us on such Examinations and Inquiries; and our Opinions thereupon;

We find the Monies paid over to the Use of the Hospital-by the Paymasters of the Forces abroad, out of the Days Pay of the Forces under their Care, to amount but to£. 13,369 in Seven Years, from 1703 to 1709, inclusive; besides a Sum of 4,000, being the Surplus of the Bounty-money given, by the Parliament, to the Forces who were at the Battle of And that nothing has been answered to the said Hospital by the Paymaster of the said Forces abroad; notwithstanding the Queen’s Warrants in the several Establishments of the 40,000 Men, directthe Poundage to be applied to Payment of Exchequer Fees, to Hospital, to the

Charge of the Paymaster General’s Office, and to such other Uses as her Majesty shall judge necessary: Which Distribution being limited to such Proportions as her Majesty, by her Warrants, shall direct; we find no Sums upon that Head paid over for the Use of the Hospital, though the Poundage of the Forces under the said Paymaster's Care amounts to above £. 54,000per Annum.; out of which, the Poundage of the Forces in Flanders amounts to about £. 23,000.

We cannot but observe the Difficulties which Mr. Howe hath lain under to support the Charge of the said Hospital; which would have been very greatly indebted, had he not procured from time to time the several Sums following, in Aid of the Charge of the said Hospital over and above his Deductions from the Forces under his Care, and the Days Pay of the English Forces upon the foreign Establishment; viz.

In 1703, from the Exchequer, £. 550, and, out of the Money impressed to £. s. d.

Upon the Whole, we agree with the Memorial, That the present great Expence of the disabled Invalids, who are generally sent from abroad, is not to be borne by the Poundage, and Days Pay, of the Guards and Garrisons, flfc. they being already about Six or Seven Months in Arrear, and will probably be about Eight or Nine Months in Arrear by Christmas next: Wherefore, we humbly propose, That such Sums of Money, which might have been applied to the Use of the Hospital, out of the Poundage of the English Forces acting in Conjunction with those of her Majesty’s Allies, and which shall remain still unapplied, be directed by Warrant to be paid to Mr. Howe lbrthe Use aforesaid: and what such Part of the Poundage abroad, together with *9

Mr. Howe's Poundage and Days Pay may fall short of £. 58,000 at Christmas next. Application be made to Parliament for such Deficiency; and, from henceforward, what shall be found wanting over and above what comes from Mr. Howe's Office, and what your Lordship may think fit to direct from what is deducted from the Forces abroad, to make up such Deficiency, may he likewise applied for to the Parliament, according to the exacteft Estimate that can be made.

And we further humbly propose to your Lordship’s Consideration, whether Mr. Howe may not be directed to apply such Savings, as shall at any time happen, and are not otherwise disposed of, to the Use of the said Hospital: And, in regard that the Out Pensioners are so many Months in Arrear, and their Credit funk in their several Quarters, so that many of them are thrown into Gaol; as well as many People, who have given them Credit have been obliged to Leave their Dwellings; and others, under Apprehensions of the like Fate, from an Opinion, that the Out Pensioners may be discontinued; we humbly submit it to your Lordship, whether an immediate Order should not be given to Mr. Hozve, to advance the said Pensioners feme Months Pay; which, for the Reasons above, we think would not only be a feasonable Relief, but a Means to procure them fresh Credit in their Quarters, till fuel) time as Application may be made to Parliament in their behalf.

Rut whatever Method should be taken to provide lor the growing Charge, we humbly observe to your Lordship, That the whole Hospital Expence being likely to get up by Christmas next, to £. 58,222 os. 11 d. whereof the Out Pensioners will probably amount to £.36,882 15$. 8 d.care is to be taken how such an Expence,

which may continue in a great Degree several Years after the Conclusion of a Peace, shall be borne, when the Poundage, and Days Pay, of the Guards and Garrisons, may pollibly be the only Fund for that Service.

All which is humbly submitted.
