A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Orlcbar and Mr. Dormer:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for Sale of the Manors of North Court and in the

Parish of Swingfeld, in the County of Kent, Part of

the Estate of Richard Gomeldoit Esquire, for discharging Incumbrances: To which they desire the Concurrence of this House. Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill intituled, An Act for making the River Avon, in the Counties of and Goucester, navigable from the City of Bath to or near Hanham's Mills, without Amendment Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to give farther Time for inrolling such Leases, granted from the Crown, as have not been inrolled within the respective Times therein limited; and for making the Pleading of Deeds of Bargain and Sale inrolled, and of Fee-farm Rents, more easy; without Amendment. Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for completing a Chapel of Ease in the Lower Town of Deal, in the County of Kent, by a Duty on waterborne Coals' to be brought into the said Town, without Amendment. Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the reviving and continuing several Acts therein mentioned, for the preventing Mischiefs which may happen by Fire; for building and repairing County Gaols; for exempting Apothecaries from serving Parish and Ward Offices, and serving upon Juries; and relating to the Returning of Jurors; without Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Petition of John Pomfey, James and Philip

Freake, on behalfof themselves, audthe rest of the Own-ers of the Ships Duke and D, lately arrived from the South Seas, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That in the Bill for collecting the Duties to Greenwich Hospital there is a Clause added, That, in case.. any Dispute or Controversy touching the Agency for Officers and Seamen, that then such Person only shall be Agent as shall be adjudged by the High Court of Admiralty to be lawfully appointed by the major Part of the Officers, and by the major Part of the Seamen, on their behalfs: That there has been several Controversies for the Agency for the Officers and Seamen of the said Ships: That the Petitioners are informed the said Clause will subject their Agreements to the Court of Admiralty, whereas they ought to be determined at Law-: And praying to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Clause.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

That there shall be paid by the Treasurer of her Majesty’s Navy, upon Bills to be made out, by the Commissioners of the Navy, to the Officers, Seamen, and others, on board such of her Majesty’s Ships of War, or Privateers, taking any Ship of War, or Privateer, from the Enemy, Five Pounds for every Man; be it therefore enacted, That so much of the said Act as relates to taking away or barring the aforesaid Admiralty Rights, and so much of the said Act as relates to the giving the said Bounty-money of Five Pounds per Head, as aforesaid, from and after the 29th Day of 712,

shall be, and is hereby, repealed; anything in the said Act contained to the contrary in any ways notwithstanding:

A Petition of the Pasteboard-makers, in and about the City of London, relating to the Bill for laying certain Duties upon Paper, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners understanding, that this honourable House have resolved to bring in a Bill for laying certain Duties upon the several Sorts of Papers made in this Kingdom, and imported hither from beyond the Seas: and the Petitioners having no other Dependence for the Maintenance of their Families, but their aforesaid Trades of making Paste-boards, whereof great Quantities are made in this Kingdom, and also imported from Holland, called Mill-boards; which, being wrought up in the Mill to the thickness of those Pasteboards made by the Petitioners, do not come under the Denomination of any of the Sorts of Paper liable to pay the Duties aforesaid; and her Majesty's Revenue, intended by the said Duties, greatly impaired; and the Consumption of Paper will be leffeued Fifty thousand Reams yearly: And whereas.

Aprilis. A. 1712.

formerly, all Boxes, called Pasteboard Boxes, were made of Paper, now intended to be subjected to the said Duties, those Boxes have been, of late Years, made of Wood, imported into this Kingdom, called Scaloboard, which hinders the Consumption of vail Quantities of Paper: And praying that a proportionable Duty may be laid upon Millboards; and that those Boxes; called Pasteboard Boxes, may be made only of Pasteboards made of Paper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider farther of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

Mr. Conyers, according to Order, reported from the Ways Committee of the whole House, who were to consider and Mean*, farther of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read; and are as followeth; viz.

1. Resolved,

aa° Aprilisi

Ways i. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

*nd Means. That, towards raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, certain Stamp Duties shall be laid upon Vellom, Parchment, and Paper, whereupon shall be ingrossed, written, registered, or entered, several Matters and Things, not heretofore charged with any Stamp Duties.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said new Duties, for every Piece of Vellom, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed, or written, any Surrender of, or Admittance to, any Copyhold Land, or Tenement, within that Part of Great Britain called

Wales, and Berwick upon Tweed; or any Grant, or Lease, by Copy of Court-roll, or any other Copy of the Court-roll, of any Honor, or Manor, within the same Part of Great Britain; be the Sum of Two Shillings and Three Pence Sterling.

3. Rejulved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said new Duty, for every Piece of Vellom, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed, written, or registered, any Mandate, Precept, Process, Libel, Allegation, Plea, Reply, Duply, Affidavit, Interrogatory, Deposition, Order, Decret, Sentence, or other Act judicial. Writ or Proceeding, of or in any Court or Session, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland; or any Copy of the fame, or any of them, whether the same be the Act of such Court, or of any of the Parties; be the Sum of Five Pence Sterling.

4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said new Duty, for every Piece of Vellom, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed, written, or registered, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, any Writ or Instrument, whereby to demise, lease, tack, enfeoff, pledge, gage, hypothecat, convey, settle, assure, assign, or transfer, any Manor, Lordship, House, Land, or Tenement, or other real or personal Estate, be the Sum of Five Pence Sterling.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said new Duty, for every Sheet, or Piece of Vellom, or Parchment, or Sheet, or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed, written, or registered, any Admission of any Advocate, Prodlor, Writer to the Signet, or other Member of the College of Justice, or into any other Society, or Body Politick or Corporate, Burgh, Stewartry, or other Guild, within that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, be the Sum of Twenty Pence Sterling.

6. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said new Duty, for every Piece of Vellom, or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed, or written, any Rule, Order, Judg-ment, or Act, not already charged with any Stamp Duty, of any Ecclesiastical Court, Court of Admiralty, or any Court of Law, or Equity, in Great Britain, be the Sum of Thirteen Pence sterling.

7. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That where more than One of any of the Matters or Things aforesaid shall be. ingrossed, written, entered, or registered, upon One Piece of Vellom, Parchment, or Paper, that then the said respective Duties be charged on every one of such Matters and Things.

8. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That over and above the present Duties, a farther Duty of Two Shillings and Three Pence be laid upon every Piece of Vellom, Parchment, or Paper, upon which shall be written any Transfer of Stock, in any Company, Society, or Corporation in Great Britain.

9. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty be laid upon all Pamphlets, and Newspapers, printed or written.

10. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty be One Peny on every Angle Half Sheet, printed or written.

11. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Twelve Pence be charged for every Advertisement in any printed Paper.

1 z. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Pence be laid upon every whole Sheet of any Pamphlet, or Newspaper, printed or written.

13. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That the aforesaid Duties upon all ft imped Vellom, Parchment, and Paper, be granted to her Majesty for the Term of Thirty-two Years.

14. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty be laid upon all Stock in Hand of Cards, and Dice, that has not already paid the former Duty thereon.

15. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty be Six Pence per Pack ou Cards, and Five Shillings a Pair for Dice.

16. Resolved, Th&tit is the Opinioivof this Committee, That a farther Duty be laid upon all Pasteboards, Millboards, and Scaleboards, made in Great Britain, or imported into the fame.

rj. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said farther Duty on the said Commodities imported, be after the Rate of Thirty Cent, ad valorem; and upon those made in Great Britain, after the Rate of Twenty per Cent, ad valorem.

18. Rc/olved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said farther Duties be granted to her Majesty for the Term of Thirty-two Years.

Mr. Bracebridge reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Thomas Brooke and John Merchants, was referred, the Matter, as it appealed to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read; and is as followeth;

That the Committee, to whom the Consideration of the Petition of Thomas Brook and Hellier Merchants, was referred, as also the Return from the Commissioners of the Customs thereupon, having examined the Allegations of the said Petition, and heard the Evidence produced by the Petitioners for proving thereof, do find, That the Petitioners have imported large Quantities of Portugal Wines, and fold the greatest Part thereof, as Merchants, by Wholesale; but, to prevent the late Combination of the Vintners, and the great Abuses of the Wine Trade, were obliged to fell some of their Wines by Retail, in several Parts of the Cities of Lon-, don and Westminster; and were afterwards compelled, by the Officers of the Customs, to pay, as Retailers, for all the other Wines they have imported and sold as Merchants, and by Wholesale; and particularly in the Port of Yarmouth, where they never offered to retail any Wines at all: That the Petitioners were thereby set upon a different Foot of Trade from other Merchants, who evaded the Acts of Parliament, by taking the Oaths, so as to gain a Discount of Eight per Cent; and afterwards retailed their Wines; which Practices were proved to the Committee to be made use of by the generality of the Wine Merchants, by the Testimony and Confession of several Wine Coopers, and their Servants.

The Committee, being desirous to know what Retail Duties had been paid upon Wines, for Seven Years past, and by whom, ordered such an Account to be laid before them; which was done by Mr. Charles Mein, the Exa-

miner of Wine Duties; whereby it appeared, That, from Lady-day 1705 to Lady-day 1712, there were but Four Persons, besides Brook and Hellier, that had paid any Retail Duties, and those Persons paid but for 21 Tons, and 103 Gall, in the said Seven Years; and Brook and Hellier, in Five Months, viz. from the 22d August to the iqth October last, paid Retail Duties, for 169 Pons, and 187 Gallons.

The Committee, taking the whole Matter into Consideration, came to the several Resolutions following; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That several Persons, who have imported their Wines as Merchants, and thereby had the Allowance of Eight Pounds per Cent, have afterwards retailed their Wines, contrary to the Meaning of the Act that ordered that Allowance.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That every Person felling any less Quantity of Wine than Ten Gallons, or in any Calk, or Vessel, containing any less Quantity than Ten Gallons, oilier than such Wine as shall be fold in the same Calks, or Vessels, in which it was imported, shall be deemed a Retailer.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That every Person importing Wine, by way of Merchandize, and to be sold by Wholesale, that afterwards retails any Wines, shall forfeit 40 s for every Gallon of Wine so retailed, and after the same Rate for every greater or Idler Quantity; one Moiety thereof to her Majesty, and the other Moiety to the Informer who shall prosecute for the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Wine Coopers ought to be excluded from having the Benefit of Eight Pound per Cent, upon Importation of Wines, as well as Vintners and Retailers.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That every Person importing Wines into any Port of Great Britain, not being a Vintner, Wine Cooper, or Retailer, within the same Port, or County wherein such Port is situate, shall not be deemed a Retailer, as to such Wine; but shall have an Allowance of Eight Pounds per Cent, upon his making Oath, That such Wine is imported by way of Merchandize, and to be sold by Wholesale, and not by Retail.

Rejoined, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners ought to have an Allowance of Eight Pounds per Cent, lor such Wines, which they have imported to be sold by Wholesale, in such Out-ports where they have not retailed any Wines, upon their making Oath thereof; and for which they have not already had that Allowance.

Ordered, That the said Report be re-committed to the same Committee.

The Depositions, Copy of a Discharge, and Letter, are as follows; viz.

The honourable William Cockran, Esquire, being sworn, deposed. That, being in Copartnership, 1 170-f, with Mr. Stezvart and others, he was commis-honed by them to come up to London, and dispose of Wines, Brandies, and other Goods, for the Copartners; for which they promised to pay him his Charges: That he was likewise commissioned to solicit Payment of the Salt Debentures from the Government: That, having disposed of these Goods, and solicited the Payment of the Debentures, which afterwards was allowed in Parliament, when he returned to Scotland, he claimed Three hundred Pounds for his Charges; which his Partners allowed him; but that there was no previous Bargain, whereby he was obliged to allow them any Gratification out of the Debentures: That the £.195 charged upon him in the Report of the Commissioners of Accounts, was obtained by his Partners, without hisKnow-lege; and that, directly or indirectly, he never received it; but it was paid in to Mr. Garden and Mr. Cummin: That he was at first unwilling to sign a Receipt for it, because it looked too much like Publick Money; but his Partners at last prevailed with him to do them that Favour, since thereby they would get that Sum of Money.

Jurat' 2 May 1712. W. Coekran.

George Yeaman, Esquire, being sworn, deposed, That he was one of the Committee for distributing the Money allowed by the Proprietors of the Flesh and Fish Debentures for Gratifications, and Expences in obtaining the Act of Parliament for paying the said Debentures: That the Committee allowed to William Cochran, of Kilmaronock, Esquire, £.195: That the

Deponent was against giving him that Money, as having no CommifRon from the Committee of the Royal Boroughs} but the Committee, in general, thought him instrumental in obtaining the said Act} and thereupon allowed him that Sum: And Mr. James Cuming, Merchant in Edinburgh, told this Deponent, That the said Mr. Cochran had prevailed with the Tories to consent to the said Act: And this Deponent understood, that the said £.195 was for the said Mr. Cochran's own Use, for his Service aforesaid} But Mr. Cuming told the Committee, That he, and some of his Partners in Trade, had given Mr. Cochran a Commission to go to London, and be assisting in procuring the Act of Parliament for pay-

Drumlangrig, 14th April 1712.

Gentlemen,

1 had the Honour of Yours the 8th April ', wherein you desire to know at what time the Account of the Twenty thousand Pounds was given in to the Earl of Godolphin: To the bell of my Knowledge, it was in the End of the Year 1707, during the Sitting of the Parliament: Sir David Nairne, then Secretary Deputy for Scotland, laid all the Vouchers before the Earl of Godolphin } whereof I gave a distiuft and particular Account of every Article in my lait Letter; That I had the Duke of Queenjberrie's Order for the Paying of the Money}

and had also Precepts from the Treasury of Scotland in favours of the particular Persons that received the Money: As to the £.12,325 which was paid to the Duke of Queensberry, the same was paid back again by Sir

David Nairne to the Earl of Godolphin, or his Order: Sir Darn'd can give you full Satisfaction in this Affair: The Money was received by the Duke ol out of the Equivalent in Scotland; and, to my Knowledge, there was no more paid back of the Twenty thousand Pounds, that was remitted to except the foresaid Sum of £.12,325: This, to the best of my Knowledge, is all the information I can give in this Matter. I no sooner received Yours, but I dispatch an Express with an Answer. I am, with great Duty and Respect,

Right honourable,

Your moll humble Servant, Glofcow.

Clause O being read a Second time, That, in Consideration of the Duty paid by virtue of the Act on Soap made use of in the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom, there shall, from and after the Five-and-twentieth Day of December 1712, for and during the

Remainder of the mid Term of Thirty-two Years, be paid, upon the Exportation of Blankets, Duffields, Ruggs, Frize, and Bays, after the Rate of One Shilling on every Hundred Weigiit of the said Goods so exported; and upon the Exportation of Cloth* Cloth Ralhes, Kirfies, and Half Thicks, after the Rate of Two Shillings on every Hundred Weight of the said Goods so exported; and upon the Exportation of Serges, Says, Perpetuanas, Shalloons, Stuffs, and all other Sorts of Draperies made of Wool only, after the Rate of Three Shillings on every Hundred Weight of the said Goods so exported; and upon the Exportation of Worsted Stockings, made of Wool only, after the Rate of Four Shillings on every Hundred Weight of Worsted Stockings so exported; and so in proportion for any greater or lesser Quantity of the said Woollen Goods so exported respectively; and that the Collector, or Chief Officers, of the Port where the said Goods shall be exported, shall forthwith give to the Exporter thereof a Certificate, or Debenture, expressing the true Weight and Quality of the said Goode so exported, or shipped for Exportation; which Certificate, or Debenture, being produced to the Collector, or other Officer, appointed to receive the said Duty on Soap, in thfe said County, or Place, where the said Goods were exported, or shipped for Exportation, he is hereby required to pay the Drawback or Duty herein before directed, respectively, to be paid; and in case the said Collector, or any other Officer, shall not have Money in his or their Hands to pay the same, then the Commissioners appointed for the executing that Part of this Act relating to the Soap Duty are hereby required to pay the same out of the Duty on Soap arising by the said Act; that there shall be paid by the Exporter of the said Goods, for every Certificate, or Debenture, relating to the said Drawback, over and above the Stamp Duties, the Sum of One Shilling, and no more; ami if any Officer, or Persons, shall at any time exact or take any more than the said Sum of One Shilling, as aforesaid, he. or they, so offending, shall forfeit ana Iple his or their Employments respectively; and be incapable of serving her Majesty, her Heirs and Sucedlorsy for the Term of Three Yea is, after the said Forfeiture;

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, That any Person or Persons, who shall export any Soap to any foreign Parts, shall or may make Proof, upon Oath, or by such Affirmation, respectively, as aforesaid, That the Duty of such Soap hath been paid, or secured, according to this Act; which Oath, or Affirmation, the Collector who received the said Duty is hereby required and impowered to administer; and thereupon the said Customer, or Collector of the said Port of Exportation, shall give to the Exporter thereof a Debenture, expressing the true Kinds and Quantities of the Soap so exported; and, the Exportation thereof being certified by the Searcher, upon the said Debenture, the Collector appointed to receive the said Duties upon Soap in such County or Place, where the said Soap was exported, upon producing the said Debenture so certified to him, shall forthwith pay the Duties, which shall have been received upon this Act, for the Soap so exported, to the Persons or Agents so exporting the fame; and if such Collector shall not have Money in his Hands to pay any such Debenture, then the respective Commissioners for the said Duties of Soap are hereby required to pay, or cause to be paid, the said Debenture, out of any Duties upon Soap arising by this Act; or if the Duty of such Soap, so exported, were only secured, and shall remain unpaid, then the same shall be discharged upon the Securities for the fame:

Hotchinfon’* A Petition of John Hulchinfon was presented to the Time House, and read: setting forth, That the Petitioner

Movement, having invented, and brought into Practice, a portable Movement to measure Time; which, instead of the several cross Motions, hollow Wheels with Teeth, parallel to their Axes, used in former Movements, hath all the Axes parallel and straight; all the Wheels, the Plates, and the Balance, parallel and flat; all the Teeth straight in the Lines of the Diameters of the Wheels; the Axes, or Spindle, of the Balance, moved by two Wheels alternately, and traversing equal Distance in equal Timle, without Pause, in such lort, that none of its moving Parts can move nearer to, or farther from, each other; whereby, in the Opinion of the greatest Mathematicians, and the best Judges of such Movements, it is capable of moving more equal!v, and less liable be

Vol. 17-

disturbed by external Motion ;To that it may be, of great Use to the Publick for finding the Longitude, and in several other respects: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill, or Clause, to secure these inventions, and the Improvements therein, to the Petitioner, by such Powers, and for such Term of Time, as to Justice and Wisdom shall seem meet.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the Representation of the Lords Commissiont rs of Trade and Plantations to her Majesty, touching the Distribution of the Money allowed, by a late Act of Parliament, to such Proprietors as should resettle at Nevis and Si. Christopher's.

And the said Representation was read; and is as fol-Ioweth; viz.

To the Queen’s most Excellent Majesty.

May it please your Majesty,

By a Clause, in an Act, passed last Session of Parliament, for licensing and regulating Hackney Coaches, fife, the Sum of One hundred and three thousand and Three Pounds Eleven Shillings and Four Pence is to be distributed to and amongst such Proprietors and Inhabitants only of the Islands of Nevis and St. Christopher's, who have resettled, or shall resettle, their Plantations in the same islands respectively: And that your Majesty *s Commissioners for Trade and Plantations are to cause a proportionable Part of the said Sum for every one of the said Proprietors and Inhabitants, who suffered by a late Invasion of the French, and who have resettled, or shall resettle, their Plantations in the said Islands, according as the Loss sustained by every such Proprietor and Inhabitant shall appear, by the Return of a Commission for that Purpose formerly issued, to be carefully computed and adjulled: And that her Majesty’s said Commissioners for Trade and Plantations do, on or before the 25th December 1711, make forth Debentures for the said proportionable Sums, as will more fully appear by the annexed Copy of the aforesaid Clause:

Upon Consideration of which Clause, and the Execution thereof, several Difficulties did arise:

First, It is not determined by the Clause what shall be deemed a Re-settlement; or when such as have not already resettled shall be obliged to do the fame; or in \vhat manner such Obligation shall be entered into: Secondly, For that the Clause hath restrained the Bounty intended, to such Inhabitants and Proprietors only who should resettle their Plantations; and cou-sequently excludes all that had not Plantations to re-, settle; whereas, in the Returns of the Losses sustained, there appears to be considerable Numbers of Persons who had no Plantations; such as Merchants, Shopkeepers, and other Dealers and Inhabitants:

Whereupon, we advised with your Majesty's Attorney and Solicitor General, who agree with us, That it is proper to lay these Matters before the House of Commons, that the said Sufferers may apply for an Explanation of the said Clause; and for enlarging the Time of their making Proof accordingly:

And the House of Commons having, on the 7th last, humbly addressed your Majesty, That an Account be laid before their House, the Beginning of the next Session of Parliament, of the Distribution intended to be made of the Debentures directed to be delivered by the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations, for Relief of the Sufferers in the Islands of Nevis and St. Christopher's,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion bf this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to her Majesty, farther Duties be laid upon all Callicoes and Muffins, and all Dimities, and other white Manufactures of Cotton, and upon alt Coffee, Tea, and Drugs, Dyeing Drugs excepted, which shall be imported into Great Britain, over and above all Duties already chargeable on the said Commodities, or any of them.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said farther Duties upon Collicoes, Muffins, Dimities, and other white Manufactures of Cotton imported, be after the Rate of Ten per Cent, ad,

to be ascertained by the Sale at the Candle.

Refbkoed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said farther Duty upon Coffee imported be after the Rate of Twelve Pence per Pound Weight avoirdupois.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said farther Duty upon Tea imported be after the Rate of Two Shillings for every such Pound Weight imported from any Places within the Limits of the Charter' granted to the East India Company; and Five Shillings for every such Pound Weight of Tea imported from any other Places.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said farther Duties upon Drugs imported, except as aforesaid, be after the Rate of Twenty per Cent. as they are valued in the Books of Rates.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said farther Duties be granted to her Majesty for the Term of Thirty-two Years.

Mr. Conyers reported from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider farther of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’sTable; where they were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That towards raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, a Duty to be laid upon all Starch made in Great Britain, or imported into the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty upon all foreign Starch imported be after the Rate oflwo Pence per Pound Weight Avoir-dupoife, over and above the present Duties payable upon the Importation thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty upon all Starch made in Great Britain be after the Rate of One Peny per Pound Weight avoirdupois.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That all Stock of Starch, in the Hands of any Persons trading or dealing therein for Sale, be chargeable with the like Duties.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, further Duties be laid upon all Coffee, Tea, and Drugs, Dyeing Drugs excepted, which shall be imported into Great Britain, over and above all Duties chargeable on

the said Commodities, or any of them.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said fqrther Duties upon Drugs imported, except Dyeing Drugs, be after the Rate of 20per as they are valued in the Book of Rates.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said further Duties upon Coffee, Tea, and Drugs, be granted to her Majesty for the Term of 32 Years.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Stock of Cpfffee, Tea, and Drugs, except as aforesaid, in the Hands of Persons trading or dealing therein for Sale, be chargeable with the like Duties.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That towards railing the Supply granted to her Majesty, Certain additional Rates or Duties be laid upon all Hides and Skips, and Pieces of Hides and Skins, and upon all Vellomand Parchment, to be imported intoGm?/ Britain, or to be tanned, tawed, or dressed, within the same, to be paid, over and above all Duties already charged or chargeable upon the same Commodities, respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty upon Deer-skins imported, being dressed in Oil or Allum, or otherwise perfectly dressed, be after the Rate of Three Pence for every Pound Weight avoirdupois.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Additional Duty upon all Loftiee, Buffalo, Elke, or any other H.ides dressed in Oil, to be imported Us aforesaid, be after the Rate of Five Pence for every such Pound Weight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional D.uty upon all Russia Hides, to be imported as aforesaid, be after the Rate of One Peny for every such Pound Weight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty upon all other tanned Hides, and tapped CalfTskins, to be imported as aforesaid, be after the Rate of Two Pence for every such Pound Weight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the faift additional Duty upon all Hides of Horses, Mares, or Geldings, to be imported as aforesaid, being dressed in Allumand Salt, or Meal, or otherwise tawed, be after the Rate of One Shilling per Hjde.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty upon all Hides of Steers, Cows, and other Hides; those of Horses, Mares, and Geldings, excepted; being tawed and imported as aforesaid, be after tue Rate of One Shilling Six Pence for, every Hide.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That the said, additional Duties upon all Calf-ikins and, Kipps to be imported, bein® tawed as aforesaid, be after the Rate of One Peny Halfpenny for every Pound Weiglut avoirdupois.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duties upon all Slink Calf-lkins to be imported, being dressed with the Hair on, be after the Rale of one Peny for every such Pound Weight; and upon all Slink Calf-lkins to be imported, being dressed without the Hair, and for all Dog-skins to be imported, being so dressed, be after the Rate of One Halfpeny for every such Pound Weight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty for all Skins called Cordi-vants to be imported, be Eight Shillings for every Dozen, and after that Rate.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty upon all other Goat-steins, not usually called Cordivants, to be imported, being dressed in Oil, or with Allum, Salt, Meal, or otherwise dressed, be after the Rate of Six Pence for every Pound WeightAvoirdupoise.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty for and upon all Kid-lkins to be imported, being dressed or undressed, or not perfectly dressed, be after the Rate of Sixpence for every Dozen: And, if any of the said Kid-lkins shall be dressed after Importation* the said additional Duty is not to be paid for the same, upon the drefting them in Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty for and upon all imported Sheep-lkins, dressed in Oil, be One Shilling Six Pence per Dozen; and for all imported Lamb-lkins, drefiediU-Oil, be One Shilling per Dozen; and for all imported Sheep-lkins and Lamb-lkins, tanned. Nine Pence per Dozen; and for all imported Sheep-lkins, and Lamb-lkins, tawed, Six Pence per Dozen; and in proportion to those Rates, for greater or lesser Numbers or Quantities of such Sheep-lkins and Lamb-lkins, respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty nponall Hides and Skins, and Pieces of Hides and Skins, to be imported as aforesaid, being tanned, tawed or dressed, and not before particularly charged; and for and upon all Wares made into Manufactures of Leather, or any Manufacture whereof the most valuable Part shall be Leather; be after the Rate of Fifteen Pounds for every One hundred Pounds of the true and real Value thereof, to be affirmed upon the Oath of the Importer.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Rates upon the said imported Commodities be paid by the Importers thereof, respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty to be laid on all Hides, of what Kind soever, to be tanned in Great Britain, be One Halfpeny per Pound Weight avoirdupois* and after that Rate.

Resolved, That it is the Opinon of this Committee, That the said additional Duty to be laid upon all Calve-Ikins, Kipps, Hog-lkins, and Dog-lkins, tanned in Great Britain, be after the Rate of One Halfpeny for every such Pound Weight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty to be laid upon all Goat-skins tanned with Shomack, or otherwise, in Great Britain, to resemble Spanish Leather, be after the Rate of Three Pence for- every such Pound Weight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said additional Duty to be laid upon all Sheep-lkins tanned for Roans, being after the nature of Spanish Leather, in Great Britain, be after the Rate of One Peny for every such Pound Weight.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,. That the said additional Duty to be laid on all Sheep-lkins and Lamb-lkins, to be tanned for Glovers and Bafiis, within Great Britain, he after the Rate of One Peny for every such Pound Weight.

That the Petitioners have acquired several Forts and Settlements, and Privilegesin the East Indies, which are absolutely necessary for the carrying on of their Trade, and are a greatSecurity to the British Interest in those Parts; and which cost the Petitioners very great Sums of Money; That by an Act of Parliament, made in the Sixth Year of her present Majesty’s Reign, the Petitioners Fund, granted them as a Security for Three millions two hundred thousand Pounds, which they advanced to the Publick, is redeemable at any time, upon Three Years Notice, after the 25th of 1726; and;

upon the Redemption thereof, the Petitioners Capacity of Trading, and Corporation Capacity itself, is to be determined: That by virtue of Forts and Settlements, the Dutch East India Company have securerl to themselves the foie Trade in all the Spices, except Pepper, of which they have also the greatest Part; and have made many Attempts to engross the Residue, and particularly of late on the Coast of Mallabar: That if the Dutch could engross the foie Trade of Pepper, they might fell it at the like extravagant Prices with other Spices; and, it being a bulky Commodity, it would greatly enlarge their Navigation: That, by reason of the

A Petit ion of the Aldermen, Stewards, and Company of Tanners, in the City of Chefi was presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That, notwithstanding the good Law now in Force against the engrossing of Oaken Bark, without which the Petitioners cannot exercise their Trade, the Petitioners find themselves much aggrieved by the late Exportation of great Quantities of Oaken Bark from England and Wales into Ireland-, by

reason whereof the u fual I mportation of raw Hides from Ireland into England, to be manufactured here; and the Exportation of Engl jh tanned Leather into foreign Parts; and, byConsequence, the Duties payable to her Majesty for fuel) Leather manufactured here; and the Customs for fuel) Importation and Exportation respectively; are very considerably lessened: And the Petitioners, by reason of the Scarcity of Oaken Bark in these Parts, labour

under very great Difficulties and Discoaragement in the Exercise of their said Trade; which will ltill be more sensible, in case of any Increase of the Duties upon Hides: And praying, that some Provision may be made,' whereby to prevent the future Exportation of Oaken Bark out of Great Britain.

A Petition of Nicholas Churchman, 'Fanner, M after of the Company of Tanners in the City of , and [Falter Chapman, Thomas Warren and John Scott, of the fame, Tanners, on behalf of themselves, and other the Tanners in and about the said City, was presented to the House, and read; felting forth. That the People up-

on the having our English Bark imported thither, have, for the most Part, declined to fend their raw Hides to England, and keep and tan the same at home with our Bark; and, through the Cheapness of their Leather, and paying no Duty, as is done in England, have drawn great Numbers of our Merchants, and of foreign Ships, to buy up their Cargoes of Leather in Ireland for foreign Markets; and are in a fairWay toengrofs the whole Tan Leather Trade: That such Exportation of our Bark doth tend very much to the lowering the Price of English Hides and Bark here, in regard that, England producing more Hides than our Home Consumption of Leather takes off, the Overplus is now left upon Hand, for want of our Merchants, and foreign Ships, taking the same off for foreign Markets, as they used to do before such Exportation of Bark j and by diverting, for that Purpose, t o Ireland, which they did not ule to do before; and, such Overplus thereby tying upon Hand in England, the Tanners in England do not drive half the Trade in Tanning, that they' used, before such Exportation, to do; which hath already occasioned the Fail-ling of the Price of Bark here, no leis than about Fifteen Shillings per Ton; as also a consideralde Fall in the Price 6f our Hides: That, by the Ruin or Decay of the said Trade, there will, in all Likelihood, be a consideralde Deficiency in the Tax lately laid upon Leather: That, on the contrary, the not Exporting of our Bark to Ireland, will recover and keep the Tanning Trade here; and tend very much to advance it, by regaining the Merchants, and foreign Ships, to buy their Cargoes of Leather here, for foreign Markets: And praying, That a Stop may be put to the farther Exportation of English Bark.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for laying several Duties upon Hides, Skins, Vellom, Parchment, Starch, Coffee, Tea, Drugs, Gilt and Silver Wire, and Policies of Insurance, to raise ayearly Fund, for Satisfaction of Orders to the Contributors of a farther Sum, of One million Eight hundred thousand Pounds, towards her Majesty’s Supply', is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do receive a Clause to prohibit the Importation of Gold and Silver Thread, Lace, and Fringe, and other Works made thereof j and of all Gold and Silver wrought up with Silks.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do receive a Clause to prohibit the Use of Lime, Alabaster, Stone, Plaster of Paris, Chalk, Whiteing, and Marble-dust, in making Powder for Hair.

Then t he Hou fe resolved itself into the said Committee.

Sir Gilbert Dolben reported from the Committee of Publication the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of of Libels, that Part of her Majesty’s Message to this House, the 17th of January last, which relates to the great Licence taken in publishing false and scandalous Libels, the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’sTable: Where they were read; and are as follow j viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee

That the great Liberty taken in printing and publishing false, scandalous, and impious, Libels, creates Division among her Majesty’s Subjects; tends to the Disturbance of the publick Peace, to the Increase of Immorality, Profaneness, and Irreligion; and is highly prejudicial to her Majesty, and her Government.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Want of a due Regulation of the Press is a great Occasion of the said Mischief.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Printing Prefies be registered, with the Name* of the Owners, and their Places of Abode.

Resolveed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That to every Book, Pamphlet, and Paper, which shall be printed, there be set the Name, and the Place of Abode, of the Author, Printer, and Publisher, thereof Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That no Bookseller, or other Person, shall fell or disperse any Book, Pamphlet, or Paper, to which the Name, and Place of Abode, of the Author, Printer, and Publisher, shall not be set.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Reib-lutions: And that Sir Gilbert , Sir Thomas

Powys, Mr. Attorney General, Mr. Conyers, and Mr, Hungerford, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The Order being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for laying several Duties upon Hides, Skins, Vellom, Parchment, Starch, Coffee, Tea, Drugs, Gilt and Silver Wire, *and Policies of Insurance, to raise ayearly Fund, for Satisfaction of Orders to the Contributors of a farther Sum, of One million Eight hundred thousand Pounds, towards her Majesty’s Supply;

Ordered, That it be an Inllruftion to the said Committee, That they do receive a Clause to explain the Act lately passed, for laying Duties upon Soap, and oth( r things therein mentioned, in such manner that the Makers of hard Cake Soap shall not be obliged to put the fame, upon making thereof, into Calks of such Gage as are prescribed by the Act last mentioned for the Makers of soft Soap.

Ordered, That it bean Inllruftion to the said Committee, That they do receive a Clause for preventing the setting up, or continuing, unlawful Lotteries j and the new invented Offices of Insurances on Marriages, Births, and other Contingencies; and the Offices or Contrivances set up under the Denominations of Sales of Numbers, Gloves, Fans, Pictures, or the like, upon Pretence of improving small Sums of Money; as being prejudicial to Trade and tending to defraud her Majesty’s Subjects.

A Petition of several Curriers, in behalf of themfel ves, and many others, in relation to the Exportation of Hides or Skins ready curried, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by an Act of Parliament, passed last Session, for laying a Duty upon Hides and Skins, it is, amongst other things, enacted, That rough or un-

1712.

dressed Hides and Skins are intitled to a Drawback upon their Exportation; but no Provision is made for allowing any Drawback upon Hides or Skins that are dressed or curried, upon their Exportation; which puts the Petitioners upon a worse Foot than any Branch of the Leather Trade; and is a great Prejudice to the Trade of this Kingdom in general, by reason, whilst Hides or Skins, dressed or curried, could go abroad upon the same Foot as other Goods, few or none rough or undressed Skins were lent; so the whole Manufacturing of the said Skins was preserved to this Kingdom; which, if dressed or curried Skins are not to be intitled to a Drawback, it will be the Ruin of that Trade: And praying, That Hides and Skins, dressed or curried, may be intitled to a Draw-. back upon their Exportation.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for laying several Duties uponHides, Skins,

Vellom, Parchment, Starch, Coffee, Tea, Drugs, Gilt and Silver Wire, and Policies of Insurance, to raise a-yearly Fund, for Satisfaction of Orders to the Contributors of a farther Sum, of One million Eight hundred thousand Pounds, towards her Majesty’s Supply.

A Petition of the Spanish Leather-dressers, Tanners,

Curriers, and other Persons concerned in Working and Dressing of Leather, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners lie under very great Difencouragementsfinee the laying on the Duties upon Leather, by reason of the divers Sorts of Things as are made use of for the upper Parts or Outsides of Shoes, instead of Leather; inso much that there are Abundance of ordinary, flight, Shoes made: That no Leather at all is used in the Upper Part or Outsides; to the great Prejudice of her Majesty’s Revenue; and, if not timely remedied, may prove very injurious to the Leather Trade of this Kingdom: And praying. That a Restraint may be put upon the making of Upper Parts or Outsides of Shoes of any thing but Leather, or Silk, or Sattin, or Velvet, or Lace, to prevent the aforesaid Mischiefs that will otherwise happen.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for laying several Duties upon Hides,

Skins, Vellom, Parchment, Starch, Coffee, Tea, Drugs,

Gilt and Silver Wire, and Policies of Insurance, to raise a yearly Fund, for Satisfaction of Orders to the Contributors of a farther Sum, of One million Eight hundred thousand Pounds, towards her Majesty’s Supply, is committed.

Then the House resolved itself into a Committee.

And that, afterwards, her Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses: Which being Tong, and to prevent any Mistake in reporting the fame, he had desired, and obtained, a Copy thereof; which be read; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

THE making Peace and War is the undoubted Prerogative of the Crown: Yet. such is the just Confidence I place in you, that, at the Opening of this Session, I acquainted you, That a Negotiation for a general Peace was begun; and afterwards, by Messages, I promised to communicate to you the Terms of Peace, before the same should be concluded.

In pursuance of that Promise, I now come to let you knpw upon what Terms a general Peace may be made.

I need not mention the Difficulties which arise from the very Nature of this Affair; and it is but too apparent, that these Difficulties have been increased by other Obstructions, artfully contrived to hinder this great and good Work.

Nothing, however, has moved me from steadily pursuing, in the First place, the true Interest of my own Kingdoms; and I have not omitted any thing which might procure to all our Allies what is due to them by Treaties, and what is necessary for their Security.

The Afl’uring of the Protestant Succession, as by Law established, in the House of Hanover, to these Kingdoms,

being what I have nearest at Heart, particular Care is taken not only to have that acknowledged in thestrong-eft Terms, but to have an additional Security, by the Removal of that Person out of the Dominions of France, who has pretended to disturb this Settlement.

The Apprehension that Spain and the Indies, might be united to France, was the chief Inducement to begin this War; and the effectual Preventing of such an Union was the Principle I laid down at the Commencement of this Treaty.

Former Examples, and the late Negotiations, sufficiently lliow how difficult it is to find Means to accom-plilli this Work. I would not content myself with such as are speculative, or depend on Treaties only: J infilled on what is solid, and to have at hand the Power of executing what should be agreed.

I can therefore now tell you, That , at last, Is

brought to oiler, That the Duke of Anjou shall, for himself, and his Dcfcendants, renounce for ever all Claim to the Crown of France: And, that this important Article may be exposed to no Hazard, the Performance is to accompany the Promile.

At the same time, the Succession to the Crown Of IS

A. 1712.

France is to be declared, after the present Dauphin, and his Sons, to be in the Duke of Berry, and his Sons; In the Duke of Orleans, and his Sons; and so on to the rest Of the House of Bourbon.

As to Spain and the Indies; the Succession to those Dominions, after the Duke of Anjou, and his Children, is to defeend to such Prince as shall be agreed upon at the Treaty; forever excluding the rest of the House of Bourbon.

For confirming the Renunciations and Settlements before mentioned, it it farther offered, That they shall be ratified in the most strong and solemn manner, both in France and Spain; and that those Kingdoms, as well as all the other Powers engaged in the present War, shall be Guarantees to the fame.

The Nature of this Proposal is such, that it executes itself: The Interest of Spain is, to Support it; and in France, the Persons to whom that Succession is to belong, will be ready and powerful enough to vindicate their own Right.

France and Spain are now more effectually divided than ever: And thus, by the Blessing of God, will a real Balance of Power be fixed in Europe, and remain liable to as few Accidents as human Affairs can be exempted from.

A Treaty of Commerce between these Kingdoms and France has been entered upon; but the excessive Duties laid on feme Goods, and the Prohibitions of others, make it impossible to finish th’13 Work so soon as were to be desired: Care is, however, taken to establish a Method of settling this Matter: And, in the mean time, Provision is made, that the same Privileges and Advantages as shall be granted to any other Nation by France, shall be granted, in like manner, to us.

The Division of the Island of St. between

us and the French having been the Cause of great Inconveniency and Damage to my Subjects, I have demanded to have an absolute Cession made to me of that whole Istand; and France agrees to this demand.

Our Interest is so deeply concerned in the Trade of North America, that I have used my utmost Endeavours to adjust that Article in the most beneficial manner: France consents to restore to us the whole Bay and Straits of Hudson\to deliver up the Island of r±

land, with Placentia; and to make an absolute Celfion of Annapolis, with the rest of Nova Scotia or Accadic.

The safety of our Home Trade will be better provided for by the Demolition of Dunkirk.

Our Mediterranean Trade, and the British Interest and Influence in those Parts, will be secured by the Possession of Gibraltar and Port Malion, with the whole Island of Minorca, Which are offered to remain in my Hands.

The Trade to Spain, and to the West Indies, may, in general, be settled as it was in the time of the tafe King of Spain, Charles the Second; and a particular Provision be made, That all Advantages, Rights, or Privileges, which have been granted, or which may hereafter be granted, by Spain, to any other Nation, shall be, in like manner, granted to the Subjects of Great Britain.

But the Part which we have borne in the Prosecution of this War, intilling us to some Distinction in the Terms of Peace; I have infilled, and obtained, Thai; the Afliento, or Contract, for furnishing the Spanish West Indies with Negroes, shall be made with us for the Term of Thirty Years, in the same manner as it has been enjoyed by the French for Ten Years past.

I have not taken upon me to determine the Interests of our Confederates: These must be adjusted in the Congress at Utrecht; where my bell Endeavours shall be employed, as they have hitherto constantly been, to procure to every one of them all just and reasonable Satisfaction: I11 the mean time, I think it proper to acquaint you, That France offers to make the Rhine the Barrier of the Empire; to yield Brifac, the Fort of Kehl and Landau; and to rafe all the Fortresses, both on the other Side of the Rhine, and in that River.

The filtered of the States General, with respect to Commerce, are agreed to, as they have been demanded by their own Ministers; with the Exception only of foms very few Species of Merchandizes j and the entire Barrier, as demanded by the States, in 1709, from France, except Two or Three Places, at most.

As to tlu-fe Exceptions, several Expedients are proposed; and I make no Doubt, but this Barrier may be

to settled, as to render that Republick perfectly secure against any Enterprize on the Part of France-, which is the Foundation of all my Engagements upon this Head will) the States.

The Demands of Portugal depending Oh the Disposition of Spain; and that Article having been long in Dispute; it has not yet been possible to make any considerable Progress therein: But my Plenipotentiaries will now have an Opportunity to assist that King in his Pretensions.

Those of the King of Prussia are such as, I hope, will admit of little Difficulty on the Part of; and my

ntmost Endeavours thall not be wanting to procure all 1 am able to so good an Ally.

The Difference between the Barrier demanded for the Duke of Savoy in 1709, and the Offers now made by France, is very inconsiderable; but, that Prince having so signally distinguished himself in the Service of the common Cause, I am endeavouring to procure for him still farther Advantages.

France has con Tented, that the Elector Palatine shall continue his present Rank among the Electors, and remain in Possession of the Upper Palatinate.

The Electoral Dignity is likewise acknowledged in the House of Hanover, according to the Article inserted, at that Prince’s Desire, in mv Demands.

And, as to the rest of the Allies, I make no Doubt of being able to secure their several Interests.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have now communicated to you not only the Terms of Peace, which may, by the future Treaty, be obtained for my own Subjects, but likewise the Proposals of France for satisfyingOuf Allies.

The former are such as I have Reason to to

make my People some Amends for that great and Unequal Burden, which they have lain under through the whole Course of this War; and I am willing to hope, that none of our Confederates, and especiafly those to whom lb great Accefiions of Dominion and Power are to accrue by this Peace, WiTl envy Britain her Share in the Glory and Advantage of it.

The latter are not yet so perfectly acffePfred as a little more time might have rendered them; but, the Season of the Year making it necessary to put an End to this Session, I resolved no longer to defer couHnuBiearing these Matters to you.

I can make no doubt but you ate all fully persuaded, that nothing wifi be neglected, on my Part, in the Progress of this Negotiation, to bring the Peace to an happy and speedy Issue; and I depend oh your entire Confidence in me, and your chearful Concurrence with me.

A Petition of the united Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by virtue of an Act of Parliament, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of the late King William the Third, intituled, An Act for raising a Sum, not exceeding Two Millions, upon a Fund for Payment of Annuities, after the Rate of Eight Pounds per Cent.per Annum; and for settling the Trade to the East Indies, several Persons did subscribe and pay in the said Two Millions; and, among others, Mr. John Powell fdb'scribed, and paid in, £.3,700, but refused to come into the Joint Stock of the said Company, which he might have done by Direction of the said Act, as most of the rest did: That, by the said Act, no Person was to trade, or licence any others to trade, to the said East Indies, for a greater Value than their said Subscription amounted to, under the Penalty in the Act mentioned: That Mr. Powell did, for divers Years, either enter, or license others to enter, and shipout, the Amount of his said Subfcrplion; and, for other Years, did make Entries thereof, but neglected to ship out the fame, notwithstanding the Direction of the said Act: That, at any time, on Three Years Notice, after the 49th September 1711; and on Repayment, by Parliament of the Money, or capital Stock, advanced by the several Subscribers, or those entitled thereto; and all the Arrears of the Annuities belonging to the fame; the Benefit of Trade given by virtue of the said Act Should cease and determine; That by an Act, made in the Sixth Year of her present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for alluring to the English Company trading to the East Indies, on Account of tire united Stock,

a longer time in the Fund and Trade therein mentioned; and for raising thereby the Sum of £.1,200,000 for carrying on the War, and other her Majesty’s Occasions; the Petitioners were knpowered, at any time after the 49th September 1711, to give Notice, on the Royal Exchange, London, of their Intention to repay the Subscribers, who did not unite their Stock and Fund with the Petitioners, the Sums by them subscribed, at the End of Three Years, after such Notice, with all Arrears of the yearly Fund: and the Petitioners gave the said Mr. Powell Notice accordingly; That the Petitioners under and a Bill is brought into this honourable House, intituled, a Bill for the Relief of the said Mr. John Poicell; the Intent whereof, as the Petitioners humbly conceive, is, to enable him to trade, contrary to the said Two Acts of Parliament, and in Prejudice to the Petitioners, who have advanced, besides the Two millions, Twelve hundred thousand Pounds more, without Interest, for the foie Liberty of the said Trade; and the Petitioners, by the last Act, and pursuant to their Conti-aft, having Right to pay off the separate Traders, as therein is mentioned; the said Mr. Powell, and one Mr. Ruffed, being now the only separate Traders; and yet, by the prel’ent Bill, the Petitioners Right and Agreement, purchased for so valuable a Consideration, is endeavoured to be set aside, and avoided: And praying to be heard by. their Counsel.

Ordered, That the Petitioners be heard by their Counsel, at the Bar of this House, again!! the said Bill, upon the Second Reading thereof: And that M r. Poicell be then also heard, by his Counsel, for the fame.

Mr. Manley, her Majesty’s Surveyor General, made Place where his Report to the House, pursuant to the Order of the Journal?,^. Third Instant:

And the same was read; and is as follows;

To the honourable House of Commons of Gredt

Britain.

In pursuance of an Order of this honourable House, of the Third of June instant, One thousand seven hundred and Twelve; whereby I am to consider of a more convenient Place, nearer the House to be set apart for keeping the Journals, Records, and other Papers belonging to the House, in the Custody of the Clerk; the Places where they now are being found very strait and inconvenient, ftnee the great Additions made to them, of late Years, by the constant annual and long;

Sessions of Parliament;

I have viewed the Places adjoining to, or near, the House of Commons, which I thought might be useful for the Purpose aforesaid; And that which, in my opinion, will be most convenient, is that Part of the Old Palace of Westminster, which is over the Passage from the House of Commons, leading into the Court of Request; the same being a large Room, with a Partition in it, frequently used for a Committee Room to the House, and other Rooms adjoining, which are called the Queen’s Chambers or Court; and, by the Nearneik of their Situation, to the House, may, at small Expence, have a Communication with it: These Rooms are of little Use at present; nor have they been, for many Years, of any Service to the Crown; So that it is to be humbly hoped her Majesty, upon the Application of this honourable House, may he graciously pleased to direct the same for the Accommodation thereof, and to be fitted up accordingly,

J.Manley, Supervisor General.

June the 13th, 1712.

And the House being moved, That an humble Application may be made to her Majesty, That lhe would be pleased to direct the said Rooms may be fitted up, and set apart, accordingly;

The Lord Willoughby acquainted the House, from the Lord Great Chamberlain, That, he having utiderstood Mr. Manley had viewed the said Rooms, in order to

MR. Speaker reported, That he, with the House, did attend her Majesty, at her) Palace of St. James’s, on Thursday, and humbly presented to her Majesty the Refointion of the House of Tueftlay last: To which her Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer; viz.

Gentlemen,

I return you hearty Thanks for this Resolution, which is very becoming you, who truly represent-all my Commons.

You have shewn yourselves honest Afferters of the Monarchy, zealous Defenders of the Constitution, and real Friends to the Protestant Succession.

What I have said and done is sufficient to satisfy any Person who is in earnell for the Succession, as by Law established, in the House of Hanover; that I need not be put in mind of doing any thing which may contribute to render that Succession secure.

And that afterwards her Majesty was pleased to make amost gracious Speech to both Houses: And, to prevent: any Mistake, he had obtained a Copy thereof; which he read; and is as followeth viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen.

The TH E lait Time I was here I spoke so folly, and after*

Speech. war(js received from both Houses such satisfactory Addresses, that there remains little more for me to say at the Closeof thisMeeting of Parliament, but to repeat my hearty Thanks for your late solemn Assurances: They will give me Strength to strugglewith any Difficulties which may yet be raised; and I hope, that -neither they who envy the making a good Peace, nor who think it theirlnterest to continue the War, will be able to defeat our joint Endeavours for the Honour and Advantage of Britain, and the Security of all our Allies. Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

At the same time that I thank }’ou moil kindly for the Supplies you have chearfully granted, I cannot but let you know my Satisfaction in the near View I have of a Peace; since it will, in some measure, recompense my Subjects for their vail Expences, and also lighten that heavy Burthen they have borne during the War.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

You have expressed how sensible you are of the Advantage and Security which accrue to Britain, and our Allies, by the Terms proposed for a Peace; and I need not mention to you the Mischiefs which mull follow the breaking off this Treaty: OurBurthens would be, at lead, continued, if not increased; the present Opportunity would be irrecoverably loll of Britain's establishing a real Balance of Power in and improvingour own

Commerce; and, if any One of our Allies should gain lbmething by such a Proceeding, the rest would suffer in the common Calamity: But I hope, by God’s Blefting, such fatal Designs will be disappointed.

You are now returning into your respective Countries; and I persuade myself, you will not be wanting in your Endeavours to obviate thcDefignsof any ill-minded Persons who may attempt to fow Sedition amongstmy Subjects; and, under specious Pretences, carry on Designs they dare not own.

1 hope at your next Meeting the re will be an Opportunity of perfecting what I have recommended to you, which you have left unfinithed in this Selfton.

I cannot conclude without alluring you. That nothing shall move me from lleadily pursuing the true Interest of so dutiful and affectiouate a People.

Adjournment/ And that afterwards the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal signified her Majesty’s Pleasure, That both Houses should forthwith severally adjourn until Tuesday the Eighth Day of July next.

By the QUEEN.

A PROCLAMATION.

ANNER.

WHEREAS our Parliament Hands prorogued to Tuesday the Thirteenth Day of January next; We, with the Advice of our Privy Council, publish and declare our Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Thirteenth Day of January next, be held, and fit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and Important

Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance accordingly, at Westminster the said Thirteenth Day of January next.

Given at our Court at Windsor, the Sixteenth Day of November 1712, and in the Eleventh Year of our Reign.

GOD save the Queen.

278 9# Aprilis 1713.

Th« Queen'* Mr. Speaker reported. That lie had, with the House, speech attended her Majesty in the House of Peers; and that

reported. her Majesty had been pleased to open this Session with

a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament, declaring the causes of calling this Meeting; and that, to prevent any Mistakes, he had desired and obtained a Copy thereof: Which he read > and is as follows; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I ended the last Session with my hearty Thanks for the solemn Assurances you had given me; by which I have been enabled to overcome the Difficulties contrived to obstruQ; the general Peace.

I have deferred opeuing the Session until now, being very defirotts to communicate to you, at your iirft Meeting; the Success of this important Affair: It is therefore with great Pleasure I tell you, the Treaty is signed, and in few Days the Ratifications will be exchanged.

The Negotiation has been drawn into so great a Length, that all our Allies have had sufficient Opportunity to adjuff their several Inter efts: Though the Publick Charge has been thereby much increased; yet I hope my People will be easy under it, since we have happily obtained the End we proposed.

What I have done for securing the Protestant Succession, and the perfect Friendship there is between me and the House of Hanover, may convince such as wish well to both, and desire the Quiet and Safety of their Country, how vain all Attempts are to divide us; and those who would make a Merit by separating our Interests will never attain their ill Ends.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

As great a Progress has been made in reducing the Publick Expence, as the Circumstances of Affairs would admit.

What Force may be necessary for securing our Commerce by Sea, and for Guards and Garisons, I leave intirely to my Parliament.

Make yourselves safe, and I shall be satisfied.

Next to the Protection of the Divine Providence, I depend upon the Loyalty and Affection of my People.

I want no other Guaranty.

I recommend tp your Care those brave Men, who have served well by Sea or Land this War, and cannot be employed in time of Peace.

1 mufi desire you to provide the Supplies you shall judge' requisite; and to give such Dispatch as may be necessary for your own Ease, and the Publick Service.

My Lords and Gentlemen, .

The-many Advantages I.have obtained for-my own Subjects have occasioned much Opposition, and long Delay, to this Peace.

It affords me great Satisfaction, that my People will: have it in their Power, by degrees, to repair what they have ftiffered.during so long and burdensome a War.

The Ealing of our foreign Trade, as far as is conliftent with national Credit, will deserve your Care:

And to think of proper Methods for improving and encouraging our Home Trade and Manufactures, particularly the Fishery; which may. be carried on to employ all our spai e Hands, ;and be a mighty Benefit even to theremoteft Parts of this Kingdom.

Several Matters were laid before you last Session, which the Weight and Multiplicity of other Business would not’permit you'to perfect: 1 hope you will take a proper Opportunity to give them due Consideration.

I cannot, however, but exprefiy mention my Dif-pleasureat the unparalleledLicentiousness in publilliing seditious and scandalous Libels.

The Impunity such Practices have met with has encouraged the blaspheming every thing sacred, and the propagating Opinions tending to the Overthrow of all Religion and Government: Prosecutions have been ordered; but it will require some new Law to put a Stop to this growing Evil; and your best Endeavours in your 4-efpeCUve Stations, to discourage it.

The impious PractTce of Duelling requires some speedy and effectual Remedy.

Now we are entering upon Peace Abroad, let me conjure you all to use your utraoft Endeavours for calming Mens Minds at Home; that the Arts of Peace may be cultivated.

Let not groundless Jealousies, contrived by aFaClion, and fomented by Party Rage, ell’ect that which our foreign Enemies could not.

I pray God to direct all your Confutations for his Glory, and the Welfare of my People.

Cfual Order*. Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against'.

Resolved, That in case it shall appear, any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, as a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respefit of his Evidence to be given to this House, or to any Committee thereof; or, direfilly or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemea-nor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before the House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of a County, to concern himself in the Elefilions of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he flia.ll fee, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Nine a Clock in the MomiUg to Three in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple-bar and Westminster-hall be kept free and open; and that no Obstructions be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

That the River Douglas, running from the Town of Wigan, in that County, to the River where ships of Burden come, may be made navigable: Thatalong the River Douglas, and its adjacent Parts, are many Pits of Coal, Delves of Stone and Slate, &c. the Land-carriage of which is not only very chargeable, but dangerous: That the making the said River Douglas navigable would advance the Manufactures, increase Trade, and open a Communication with several Places, to the Advantage thereof: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill for that Purpose.

Table: Where it was read; and is as follows $ viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave, with all Humility, to approach your Royal Person, with our unanimous Acknowledgments for all the Benefits we enjoy under your Majesty’s most auspicious Reign.

The many and great Successes which have attended your Majesty’s Arms had left nothing to be wished but such a Peace as might be conducted by your Councils; which now we have the Happiness to fceaccompliftied:

And as we are truly sensible of your Majesty’s gracious and generous Intentions in undertaking that great Work; so we have all possible Reafoh to admire your Steadi-ness in carrying it on, and overcoming the many Difficulties contrived to obstruct it: And it is with the highest Satisfaction we congratulate your Majesty upon the happy Conclusion of this Treaty; for we are so much convinced of your Majesty’s tender Regard to the Publick Welfare, and the many Instances of ybur Wisdom have taught us to have so perfect a Reliance upon it, that we cannot doubt but your Majesty hath procured all reafoiiable Satisfaction foryour Allies, and established the Interest of your own Kingdoms in such a manner, as to make us not only feoure lor the future, but a flourishing and a happy People.

Your

i2 Ann. 10° — -i i° Aprilis.

281

Your Majesty can give no higher Proof of the Care you take of Posterity, than by the Concern you are pleased to express for the Protestant Succession in the House of Hanover; upon which the future Happiness of this Kingdom so much depends: We hope and trust, that nothing will ever be able to interrupt the Friend-ship between your Majesty and that illustrious Family; since the wicked Designs of those who would endeavour to Separate your Interests must be too plain ever to succeed.

Your faithful Commons can never enough express the grateful Sense they have of the many gracious Assurances contained in your Majesty’s Speech: And after what your Majesty hath done to ease your Subjects of the heavy Burthen which before layupon them; and after your unparalleled Goodness in demanding nothing from them for the time to come, but what they themselves shall judge requisite for their own Safety; the belt Return they can make will be a ready and dutiful Compliance with every thing you have been pleased to recommend to them; and they cannot fail most chearfully to set about the providing the Supplies necessary for this Year’s Service. Your Majesty’s repeated Con-descensions mult in the strongeft manner engage the Hearts and Affections of all your Subjects to your Majesty: And we are satisfied we cannot more truly represent them, than by contributing our utmost Endeavours to make your lleign as prosperous, glorious, and easy to yourself, as it is beneficial and happy to your People.

Ordered, That the said Estimate be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider farther of the Supply granted to her Majesty.

The House being informed, That a Person attended Establishment from the Queen’s Remembrancer’s Office in Scotland: of Scotch

He was called in; and presented to the House, pur- Force* suant to their Address to her Majesty, Copies of the several Establishments that were made of the Forces in Scotland during the lad Peace.

And then he withdrew.

And the Title of the said Copies of the Establilli-ments was read.

Ordered, That the said Copies of the Establishments be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee of the whole House, who are to consider farther of the Supply granted to her Majesty.

The said Copies of the Establishments are bound up with the other Papers of this Session.

The Order of the Dry being read, for the House to s resolve itself into the said Committee;

Ordered, That it be an Inllruction to the said Committee, That they do consider what Number of Men may be necessary for a Summer and Winter Guard at Sea, for the Year 1713.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee of the whole House.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Conyers took the Chair of the Committee.

A Petition of divers Merchants of London, Traders Africa® to Africa, and thence to the Plantations, in behalf of Trade, themselves, and many others concerned in the said Trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by Encouragement, of the Act of Parliament, made in 1698, for laying open the Trade to Africa, the Petitioners have become great Adventurers in the said Trade, and have supported and enlarged the fame: That notwithstanding his honourable House was pleased, last Session, to repeat their former Resolution,

That the said Trade should be free and open, the African Company have threatened to sue the Petitioners:

That the Petitioners have many Ships fit only for the said Trade, and no other; which will be all loft, if the Petitioners be excluded the said Trade; to the Ruin of many Families: And praying, That the said Trade may be continued free and open to all her Majesty’s Subjects, and the Petitioners be relieved, as the House shall think fit.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Trade to Africa.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the ConGderation of the said Committee.
