The Serjeant at Arms attending this House being called upon, to give an Account, what had been done in relation to the Persons who were, the last Session, ordered to be taken into his Custody;

He acquainted the House, That theyhad all been either taken, or surrendered themselves, into his Custody; and that lie had received from them Satisfaction for his Fees; except John Haney, late Portreeve of the Borough of Tavistock, in the County of Devon-, and Henry Martin Esquire, late Bailift' of the Borough of Southwark.

And the Standing Order of the House, of the 4th Day of April 1707, being read;

Ordered, That John Harvey, late Portreeve of the Borough of Tavistock, in the County of Devon, be taken into

the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, he having not been taken, nor surrendered himself, and paid his Fees to the Serjeant; upon the several Commitments of this House, the Two former Session* of this Parliament, for his many corrupt and indirect Practices, in relation to the Election of Burgesses to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough.

Ordered, That Henry Martin Esquire, late Bailiff of the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surry, having absconded from Justice, when he was ordered, in the last Session of this Parliament, to be taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, for his arbitrary and illegal Proceedings in the Election of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough, in Breach of the Privilege of this House, and teuding to the Subversion of the Freedom of Elections; and having not been taken, nor surrendered himself, and given Satisfaction to the said Serjeant; be, for the said Offences, taken into the Custody of the said Serjeant.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee That a Supply be granted to her Majesty, for allowing Half Pay, for One Year, to the Several Officers who have Served well by Sea or Land in the lall War, and shall not be employed in Time of Peace.

A Petition of John Powel, of London, Merchant, was presented to the House, and read, setting forth. That, in 1698, the Petitioner advanced £.3,700 towards raif-iagTwo millions, on the Credit of an Act, whereby the Trade to the East Indies was for ever granted to the Contributors, redeemable by Parliament, on Payment of the said Two millions: That the Petitioner aid not enter into the Joint Stock; but traded separate; paying Five Pounds per Cent, on the gross Sale at the Candle to the Joint Stock Company: That the United Stock Company have since gained a further Term, upon advancing of £.1,200,000: That the Petitioner was, and is, willing to pay his Proportion of the same Sum: And when the Bill was brought in, whereby the Petitioner’s Stock was to be given to the United Company for One hundred Pounds per Cent, the Petitioner was not heard against the said Bill: That the Company have bought in all the separate Stock, except the Petitioner’s, and £.500 more: and the Petitioner has offered them his Stock, upon the same Terms; but they refuse it: And praying. j’.jf Pav r.f- Sir William JVi/ndham presented to the House, pur-

to their A«I«irels to her Majesty, a Copy of the Queen’s Orders and Rules to be obferVed in the Establishment of Half Pay:

And the Title thereof was read.

The said Orders and Rules are as follow; viz.

A NNER.

Whereas, upon the disbanding several of our Forces, we have thought fit, That Half Pay shall be allowed to the Commission Officers, who shall, by that means, be di (charged our Service, until they shall be again provided for therein; which it is our Royal Intention they shall be in the Fit ft Vacancies that may happen amongst our Forces that shall be kept on Foot, in Preference to all other Persons: We do, nevertheless, hereby declare our Pleasure, That, in order to the forming and settling the Establishment of Half Pay to the Officers, as aforesaid, the following Rules be duly observed:

1 ft. All Officers concerned are to produce their Commissions from us, or the Generals of our Armies, by which they are intitled to receive Half Pay, before they are entered upon the Lift thereof.

ad. The Allowance of Half Pay is to be made to such Commission Officers only, as are our Subjects: To which end, such Officers as may be Foreigners are to produce authentick Certificates of their Naturalization.

3. No Officer who has fold out of our Army, and, by that means, quitted our Service, shall be intitled to Half Pay.

4. No Officer having Two Ports in our Army shall be allowed the same in a double Capacity; and where any Officer shall have Two Commissions in our Service, the one intitling him to Pay, and the other to any ftlpe-rior Rank, his Half Pay shall be governed according to the Commission by which he receives Pay only, and not according to his other Commission* or Brevet.

5. We are further pleased to declare, That the said . Allowance of Half Pay to t lie Officers of the Regiments

already reduced shall commence from the 25th of March last; and such as are to be ditbanded, from the respective times of their Disbanding: And where it may happen, that any Officers, Prisoners, or others, of the Regiments already reduced, are not yet arrived from Spain,

tugal, or France, The Commencement of their Half Pay is to be regulated from the respective Times of their Arrival, or Exchange, as we shall hereafter think fit to direct.

Given at our Court at IVi this 30th Day of

July 1712, in the Eleventh Year of our Reign.

By her Majesty's Command,

Memd. It having been represented to her Majesty, That the Vote providing Half Pay for the reduced Officers, in the Year 1697, ran in these Words; " That Provision be made for giving HalfPayto the "Commission Officers, his Majfclly’Snatural-born " Subjects of England, of Horse, Dragoons, and "Foot, disbanded, or to be disbanded, till the said " Officers shall be fully paid and cleared, and olher- wife provided for j" her Majesty was pleased to direct, that Half Pay should be itfued to such as were (triftly her natural-born Subjects only, until this House should declare their Sense thereon.

Ordered, That the said Orders and Rules do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Sail Cloth A Petition of William Smith senior, Walter iiaatthifture. and Thomas Shefford, Merchants, in behalf of themselves and others, ManufacturersofSail Cloth in Britain, was presented to the House and read; setting forth, That the making of Sail Cloth in England is of great Benefit to the Nation, and employs many Thousands of Poor; and hath received due Encouragement by Acts of Parliament; but yet British Sail Cloth hath not the same Encouragement with foreign Sail Cloth; for that though it pays a Duty, yet, upon Exportation to the Plantations, it draws back moil of its Duty; whereas the British Flax pays a Duty equal to foreign Canvas, and when mannfactured, and exported, draws back nothing: That great Quantities of foreign Sail Cloth are daily imported, being made where little or no Duty is

Said for the Materials; whereby the said British lanufacture is greatly discouraged; and will be loft, unless some Encouragement be given: And praying such Encouragement for this useful Manufacture as shall be thought fit.

A Petition of the Merchants in London trading in Tobarc#

Tobacco, on behalf of themselves, and the Planters of Trade. Virginia and Maryland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Custom of Six Pence and One-third of a Peny per Pound on Tobacco is more than it can bear: That the planting of Tobacco in Europe so vastly increases, that the American Tobacco fells in foreign Markets for less than the Custom and Freight: These Discouragements have obliged several Merchants trading in Tobacco to leave it off; and forced many Planters upon Manufactures; inso much that some Counties in Virginia and Maryland make Shoes, Hats,

Linen, Woollen, fife, not only for their own, but for the Use of their Neighbours; others fow Corn, and fend great Quantities to several Parts of Europe: That the Petitioners are apprehensive their Bonds for Customs, dischargeable by Debentures, will be prosecuted before the Time allowed by Law for Exportation requires:

And praying the said Duty on Tobacco may be ldTeited; and such other Relief as shall be thought fit.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of the City Ditto,

of Bristol to Virginia and Maryland was presented to

the House, and read; setting forth, That the Trade to these Colonies daily diminishes, by the planting Tobacco in Europe, and the Discouragements Traders lie under, being obliged to pay the New Subsidy in Three Months, the additional Duty and One-third Subsidy in Nine Months; whereas Eighteen Months are allowed by Law for Exportation; and also the retaining Part of the Duty when exported; by which means, and by the heavy Duty lying thereon, our Tobacco is rendered dearer in foreign Parts: And praying. That the said Duties may be lessened* and Eighteen Months allowed for Payment thereof, and a Drawback of all Duties when exported; and such other Relief as shall seem meet.

Mr. Gonlfion reported from the Committee, to whom EndfWU the Petitions of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, IWd* and principal Inhabitants, of the Parishes of,

Edmonton, Tottenham, Hackney, Horn fey,

and Shoreditch, in the county of ; and of several Farmers, Waggoners, Pack Carriers, Stage Coarhmen, Carters, and Higglers, and others, that frequent and pass the Road, as well from and beyond End-field and Shoreditch; were re-committed; the Matter, as it appeared to them, and they had directed to be reported to the House, and their Resolutions thereupon; which lie read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report and Resolutions, were read; and are as follow; viz

That the Committee have met, pursuant to the Order of Re-commitment: And the Petitioners, to prove the Allegation of their Petition, both now and before, brought several Witnesses; viz.

Mr. William Daufon: Who said, That, in the Years 1(199 and 1700, he was Surveyor of the Highways in Hackney Parish; and, upon a Uriel Survey thereof, which took up 19 Days of his time; and represented the fad Condition the said Roads were in; ami particularly that Part of the High Road, mentioned in the Petition, in Hackney Parish; upon which, lie was deft red to go on with his Care of the Roads, under a Promise of Reimbursements; which he did, and had a Rate of per Pound given; and he collected more Monies thereon than any Surveyor had done there before him; and likewise can led more Work to be done to the Roads by the Statute; and

yet

i 2AnK. 4° Mali. 311

yet the Charge arose so high, that he was rated in proportion to 10 \d.in the Pound: IJe Paid, He believed a 6d. Rate was annually allowed for repairing the Roads, besides the Statute-work; and that is not sufficient for doing the fame:

That, when he was Surveyor, there was ?.8 Teams in Hackney Parish, and now not above 14 Teams; for that the final! Farms are turned into planting Potatoes, which they carry to Market in Panniers on Ilorfes, and not in Carts; and so not liable, to Statute-work: But that all the Teams did not only do their full Six Days Work, but several from Six to Ten Days; and several Farmers sent Two or Three Teams to the Service:

That the Generality of the Inhabitants at Hackney are Merchants, and others, who consist chiefly of personal Estates, who contribute to the repairing the Roads much beyond the Proportion of a Six Peny Rate, for the Purchasing of Ballad:

That if all the Surveyors had done as much since, as he did when he was Surveyor; which he supposes they did, because the Rates have been much the fame, he is satisfied the Roads could not be kept in Repair; because the Roads are in many Places lower than the adjacent Grounds on each Side; so that the Sewers cannot tarry off the Water:

That the High Road at Kingsland is full of Quick-sands; and cannot be secured, but by enlarging the Road there, and preserving it by Drains made of Brick: That upon the same Road, near Hackney, are several Springs, which cannot be secured without new Foundations made upon the Road there:

That upon the Ascent in the Road to and Descent therefrom, are several Quicksands, which cannot be remedied without extraordinary Brick-drains, and Bridges over them:

That Hackney Parish, upon a modest Computation, tare obliged to repair Six Miles and f of Roads in the Parish.

Mr. Tyson said. That he often rides from Hackney to Southgate, in Enfield Parish; and thinks a great Part of the High Road thither to be as bad as it is at Hackney, where it is so dangerous, that, when he rides to London, he is compelled for Safety to make a Way through his own Grounds to avoid the Road.

Mr. Hexteter said, That he knows the Road from Chejlonto Shoreditch to be in a very bad Condition; for that, as his Business calls him to Town Three times a Week, he has made it his Observation, that he has scarce come once this Winter but he has seen some Cart or Carriage overturned with the Lading, and sometimes several; and that he himself thinks, and is well assured, that Road cannot be repaired, and preserved, by Statute-work, because there will be extraordinary Drains and Bridges required to perform that Work, which cannot be done without extraordinary Means; and he knows of no Materials that lie contiguous to the Road, but what must be pufehafed for repairing the fame, and brought from some Distance.

Mr. Boulton said, That he knows the RoadinQuestion from Endfield to Shoreditch very well, and thinks it the

word Road about London, and has seen several Carts and Carriages overturned therein j and it is now become almost impassable, and cannot be repaired, and

much Jess be preferred without the Help of the Legifla-ture; the Roads being so much wore away in some Places, that they are lower than the adjacent G rounds; and therefore cannot be drained without cutting through such Grounds, and making good Foundations for that Purpose:

That from a Place called Ponders-end, in the said Road, for three Miles together, is as bad as any other Part of the Road; and that a Place called Duck-lane is so very dangerous, that upon a Computation made, Ten thousand Load of Gravel is not sufficient to repair it:

That he has been assisting at a Computation of the Charge of amending the High Road in Hackney Parish, about Three Miles; and found it could not be done under 21,000 Load of Gravel; 7,000 Load forward,

and 3,000 Load in Breadth, sufficient for Two Carriages to meet and pass by each other; which, at 3s. per Load, amounts to £.3,150; and that the remaining Part of the Road will require 14,000 Load more:

That he has known Hackney Parish have rated themselves 10 d.in the Pound for mending their Roads, and which was not sufficient for that Purpose; nor the same cannot be done without extraordinary Means of Drains and Bridges:

That he does not know what Fines and Issues have been applied to the Repair of the said Road; but knows that Six Pence in the Pound, at leal't, has been annually collected.

Mr. Stacey said. The Roads in Hackney Parish are bad} and believes there has been the Over-rates annually to repair the fame, which are about Seven Miles by Computation; but also believes the Statute-work, if fully performed, and a Six Peny Rate, would repair the said Roads; which Rate he believes will raise about £.200 a Year; for which Sum his Father undertook to supply the said Parish with Gravel from his Pits; and that his Pits are Two Miles, at lead, from the Road.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their said Petitions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayers of the said Petitions.

Robert Mitchel, Merchant, being sworn, depofeth,

That, he did receive 384. lor. 0 upon a Bill, made out by the Commissioners for Sick and Wounded, dated the 12th of March 1704., and assigned for Payment 27th

April 1706, for transporting Prisoners of War, between the 21 June 1704, and the 3d of following:

That William Churchill Esquire, One of the said Commissioners, recommended this Deponent to the rest of the Commissioners, as a proper Person to make this Contract: That, on making the said Contract, the said Mr. Churchill did agree with this Deponent to reserve Half the Profit for himself, or some other Person; but whether, this Deponent cannot say: That Mr. John Churchill Brother to the said William Churchill, tendered a Bond to this Deponent, to be accountable to him for Half the Profit so reserved, which he refused to sign; but looks upon himself, however, to be accountable for it: That he did employ Captain Robert Masters in some of the Voyages mentioned in the said Bill.

Rob. Michel.

Mr. John Pearce, being sworn, depofeth. That he contracted with the Commissioners for Sick and Wonnded, for transporting Prisoners of War, in February 170^, or thereabouts: That he has continued to carry on that Service to this time: That, when he first entered upon this Contraft, he agreed with William Churchill Esquire, One of the said Commissioners, that he should be a Sharer in the Profit and Loss arising from the same: That Two thousand Pounds was borrowed to carry on this Service, for which he and Mr. Churchill are bound: That this Deponent advanced to the said Mr. Churchill about Two hundred Pounds, which he intended as Part of his Share of the Profit, on this Account, if there appeared to be any, when the Money for Prisoners was remitted to this Deponent from France: But the Accounts are not yet made up.

Mr. Pearces Letter.

That, when 1 entered on the IVansport Business, it was entirely my tfwn Right, and under ito Obligation of Partnership; the French making then good Payment, enabled me to carry on the Service without being obliged to any Person for Money; but after some Years they entirely put a Stop to their Payments, and I found the Service wanted more Money to carry it on* than I was able to raise; I having agreed for is. 6d. for which others bad always Ten Shillings, I was forced to apply to my Brother for Assistance, who brought me firit in; and voluntarily promised to reimburse him by the Profits of the said Service, if any such should be, of otherwise, for his Kindness and Assistance in this Affair: And I, having formerly made use of his Money, when I was under him as Deputy Treasurer of the Ordnance, and at that time being incapable of repaying him, designed to reimburse him in this manner; and the mentioned in my Affidavit, tho’ intended by me as Part of such Money as should arise from the said Service, I never acquainted him with; there being great Sums dufe from France on that Account; and the State of the Profit or Loss could not pofliWy be made till the Remittances be procured, and the Debts owing on that Head are paid off.

Trade* -A Petition of the Royal African Company of England,

8 ' who by the Encouragement of an Act, passed the last Session of Parliament, are now united with all their Creditors, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Trade to Africa is not to be gained, or preferred, without Forts and Callles: That the Company have, at several times, raised a flock of above £. 400,000, and borrowed near 300,000 more to build those Forts and Callles: That they claim a legal Right in the Forts and Lands in Africa, under a Grant from the Crown; and hope, if their Property is denied, they shall have the like Tryal at Law as any other Subject is entitled to, to defend his Freehold: That the Bill now in the House, intituled, a Bill for establishing the Trade to Africa free and open to all her Majesty’s Subjects of Great Britain, tends to the utter Destruction of their Rights and Properties: And praying to be heard, by their Counsel, at the Bar of the House, against the said Bill, before the Second Reading thereof.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table.

Translation of a Treaty of Peace and Friendship between Great Britain and France.

WHEREAS it has pleased Almighty God, for the Glory of his Name, and for the universal Welfare, so to direct the Minds of Kings, for the healing now in his own time the Miseriesof the desolate World, That they are disposed towards one another with a mutual Desire of making Peace; Be it therefore known to all and singular whom it may concern, That, under this divine Guidance, themoll Sereneand modPotentPrincefsand L&dy, Anne, by the Grace of God, Queen of Great Britain, France, and Ireland; and the most Serene and moll Potent Princo

and Lord Lewis the XIVth, by the Grace of God, the moll Christian King; consulting as well the Advantage of their Subjects, as providing, as far as mortal Things will admit oh for the perpetualTranquillity of the whole Christian World; have resolved, at last, to put an End to the War which was unhappily kindled, and has been obstinately carried on above these Ten Years, being both cruel and destructive, by reason of the Frequency of Battles, and the Effusion of Christian Blood; And, for promoting this their Royal Purpose, of their own proper Motion, and from that paternal Care which they delight to use towards their own Subjects, and the Publick Weal of Chrijiendom, have nominated and appointed the most noble, illustrious, and excellent, Lords, their Royal Majesties respective Embassadors Extraordinary and Plenipotentiaries; viz.Her Sacred Royal Majesty of Great Britain, the Right Reverend John, by divine Permission, Bishop of Bristol, Keeper of the Privy Seal of England, One of her Royal Majesty’s Privy Council, Dean of Wind-for, and Regiiler of the most noble Order of the Garter; as also the most Noble, Illustrious, and Excellent, Lord, Thomas, Earl of Strafford, Viscount Wentworth, of Went-toorthfVoedhouse and Stainborough, Baron of Raby, One of her Royal Majesty’s Privy Council, her Atnbaffador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the High and Mighty ' Lords the States General of the United Netherlands, Colonel of her Majesty’s Regiment of Dragoons, Lieutenant General of her Majesty’s Armies, First Lord Comraiffioner of the Adm i ral ty of Great Britain an and

Martha! of France, Knight of the King's Orders, and Lieutenant General of the Dukedom of Burgundy; and Nicholas Mefnager, Knight of the King’s Order of St. Michel; and hath furnished the said Ambassadors Extraordinary with full and ample Power to treat, agree of.

Wherefore the aforesaid Ambassadors, after divers and important Consultations bad in the Congress held at tltrecht for that Purpose, baying at length overcome, without the Intervention of any Mediator, all thfe Obstacles which hindered the End of So wholsome a Design; and having invoked the Divine Affiiiance, That God would be pleased to preserve this their Work intire and in violated, and to prolong it to the latest Posterity; after having mutually coromuuicated, and duly exchanged, their full Powers; Copies whereof are inserted, Word for Word, at the End of this lostrument; they hare agreed on the reciprocal Conditions of Peace and Friendship between their above-mentiooed Majesties, and their People and Subjects as follows;

I.

That there be an universal perpetual Peace, and a true and sincere Friendship, between the most Serene and most Potent Princess Anne, Queen of Great and the most Serene and most Potent Prince Lewis the XIVth, the most Christian King, and their Heirs and Successors; as also the Kingdoms, States, and Subjects of both, as well without as within Europeand that the same l»e so sincerely and inviolably preserved and cultivated, That thcone do promotethelnterell, Honour, and Advantage, of the other; and that a faithful Neighbourhood on all Sides, and a secure Cultivating of Peace and Friendship, do daily flourish again, and increase.

II.

That all Enmities, Hodilities, Discords, and Wars, between the said Queen of Great , and the said

mod Chridian King, and their Subjects; doceafe, and be abolished; so that, on both Sides, they do wholly refrain and defid from all Plundering, Depredation, Harmdoing, Injuries, and Annoyance, whatsoever as well by Land as by Sea, and Fresh-waters, in all Parts of the World; and chiefly through all Tracts, Dominions, and Places of what Kind soever, of the Kingdoms, Countries, and Territories, of either Side.

III.

AH Offences, Injuries, Harms, and Damages, which the aforesaid Queen of Great and her Subjects,

or the aforesaid most Chridian King, and his Subjects, have differed, the one from the other, during this War, shall be buried in Oblivion; so that neither on Account, or under Pretence, thereof, or of any other thing, shall hereafter the Subjects of either do or give, cause, or suffer to be done or given, to the other, any Hodility, Enmity, Moledation, or Hindrance, by themselves, or by others, secretly or openly, directly or indirectly, under colour of Right, or by way of Fafr.

IV.

Furthermore, for adding a greater Strength to the Peace, which is redored, and to the faithful Friendship, which is never to be violated; and for cutting off all Occasions of Didrud, which might at any timeanfe from the established Right and Order of the Hereditary Succession to the Crown of Great Britain, and the Limitation thereof by the Laws of Great Britain, made and enacted in the Reigns of the late King William the Third, of glorious Memory, and of the present Queen, to the Offspring of the abovesaid Queen, and, in Default thereof, to themodSerene PrincessSopAia Dowager of BrunswickHanover, and her Heirs in the Protedant

Line of Hanover :That therefore the said Succession may

remain safe and secure, the most Christian King sincerely and solemnly acknowledges the abovesaid Limitation of the Succession to the Kingdom of Great Britain; and on the Faith and Word of a King, on the Pledge of his own and his Successors Honour, he does declare and engage, that he accepts and approves the fame, and that his Heirs and Successors do and shall accept and approve the same for ever: And, under the same Obligation of the Word and Honour of a King, the most Chridian

VI.

Whereas the most dedrtiftive Flame of War, which is to beextinguished by thisPeace, arose chiefly from hence. That the Sucurities and Liberties of Europe could by no means bear the Union of the Kingdoms of France and Spain, uuderOne and the same King: And whereas it has at length been brought to pass, by the Assistance of the Divine Power, that, at the most earned Indances of her Sacred Royal Majesty of Great , and with the Consent both of the most Chridian, and of the Catholick. King, this Evil should, in all times to come, be prevented by means of Renunciations drawn in the most effectual Form, and performed in the most solemn manner: The Tenor whereof is as follows:

Letters Patents by the King, which admit the Renunciation of the King of Spain to the Crown of France; and those of Mr. the Duke of , and of Mr. the Duke of Orleans, to the Crown of Spain.

LEWIS, by the Grace of God, King of France and Navarre, To all People present and to come, greeting: During the various Resolutions of a War, wherein we have fought only to maintain the Indice of the Rights of the King our most dear and most beloved Grandson, to the Monarchy of Spain, we have never ceased to desire Peace; the greated Succefies did not at all dazzle us, and the contrary Events, which the Hand of God made use of to try us, rather than to destroy u<^ did not give Birth to that Desire in us, but found it there; but the time marked out by Divine Providence for the Repose of Europe was not yet come: The distant Fear of seeing, one Day, our Crown and that of Spain, upon the Head of one and the same Prince did always make an equal Impression on the Powers which were united against us; and this Fear, which had been the principal Cause of the War, feemedalfo to lay an inlii-perabla Obstacle in the Way to Peace: At lad, after many

fruidefs Negotiations, God, being moved with the Sufferings and Groans of so many People, was pleased to open a surer Way to come at lb difficult a Peace: But, the same Alarms Hill subsisting, the First and principal Condition which was proposed to us by our most dear, and most beloved Sider, the Queen of Great , as

the essential and necessary Foundation of treating, was. That the King of Spain, our said Brother and Grandson, keeping the Monarchy of Spain, and of the Indies, Chon Id renounce, for himself, and his Defendants for ever, the Rights which his Birth might at any time give him, and them, to our Crown; that, on the other Hand, our most dear and most beloved Grandson the Duke of Berry, and our most dear and most beloved Nephew the-Duke of Orleans, should likewise renounce, for them* fe!ves, and for their Defendants, Male and Female for ever, their Rights to the Monarchy of Spain and the in* dies: Our said Sider caused it to be represented to us, That, without a formal and positive Assurance upon this point, which alone could be the Bond of Peace, Europe would never be at rest; all the Powers which share the same being equally persuaded, that it was for their general Intered, and for their common Security, to continue a War, whereof no one could foresee the End, rather than to be exposed to behold the same Prince become one Day Mader of Two Monarchies, so powerful as those ©£ France and Spain: But as this Prince Ik, whose indefatigable Zeal for re-establishing the general Tranquillity we cannot sufficiently praise, was sensible of all the Reluctancy we had to consent, that One of our Children, so worthy to inherit the Succedion of our Forefathers, should necessarily be excluded from it; if the Misfortunes wherewith it has pleased God to afflict us in our Family should moreover take from us, in the Person of the Dauphin, our most dear and most beloved Great Grandson, the only Remainder of those Princes, which cur Kingdom has so justly lamented with us; lhe entered into our Pain; and, after having jointly fought out gentle Means of securing the Peace, we agreed with our laid Siller to propose to the King of Spain other Dominions, inferior indeed to those which he possesses; yet the Value thereof would so much the more increase under his Reign, inasmuch as in that same he would j»reserve his Rights, and annex to our Crown a Part of the said Dominions, if he came one time or other to iucceed us: We employed, therefore, the dronged Rea-foBS to persuade him to accept this Alternative: We gave him to under and. That the Duty of his Birth was the First which he ought to confnlt; That he owed him-fols tp his House, and to his Country, before he was obliged to Spain; That, if he were wanting to his First Engagements, he would perhaps, one Day, in vain regret his having abandoned those Rights which he would be no more able to maintain: We added to these Rea* suns the personal Motives of Friendship, and of tender Love, which we thought likely to move him; the Pleasure we should have in seeing him from time to time sear us, and in passing forae Part of our Days with him, which we might promise ourselves from the Neighbourhood ol’the Dominions that were offered him; the Sa-tisfii&iou of instructing him ourselves concerning the State of our Affairs, and of relying upon him for the future; so (hat, if God should preserve to us the Dauphin, we could give our Kingdom, in the Person of the King onr Brother and Grandson, a Regent instructed in the Art of Government: And that if this Child, so precious to us, and to our Subjects, were also taken from us, we should at lead have the Consolation of leaving to our People a virtuous King, fit to govern them, and who would likewise annex to pur Crown very considerable Dominions: Our Indances, reiterated with all the Force, and with all the tender Affection, necessary to persuade a Son, who so justly deserves those Efforts which we made for preferring him to France, produced nothing but reiterated Refusals, on his Part, ever to abandon such brave and faithful Subjects; whose Zeal for him had been distingnished in those Conjunctures when his Throne seemed to he most shaken: So that, Vo*.. persisting, with an invincible firmness, in his First Treaties of Resolution; asserting likewise, it was more glorious, and more advantageous for our House, and for our Kingdom, than that which we pressed him to take; he declared, in the Meeting of the States of the Kingdom of Spain, assembled at Madrid for that Purpose, That, for obtaining a general Peace, and securing the Tranquillity of Europe by a Balance of Power, he, of his own proper Motion, of his own free Will, and without any Coudraint, renounced, for himself, for his Heirs, and Successors, for ever and ever, all Pretensions, Rights, and Titles, which he, or any of his Descendants, have at pre-. sent, or may have, at any time to come, whatsoever, to the Succession of our Crown: That he held for excluded therefrom, himself, his Children, Heirs, and Descendants, for ever: That he consented, for himself, and for them, that now, as well as then, his Right, and that of his Descendants, should pass over, and be transferred, to him among the Princes whom the Law of Succession, and the Order of Birth, calls or shall call, to inherit our Crown, in Default of our said Brother and Grandson the King of Spain, and of his Descendauts; as it is more amply specified in the Act of Renunciation, approved by the.

It is to this Law that we this Day sacrifice the Right of a Grandson, who is so dear to us; and, by the Price which the general Peace will cod our tender Love, we shall at lead have the Comfort of /hewing our Subjects, that, even at the Expence of our Blood, they will always keep the first Place in our Heart: For these Causes, and other Considerations us thereunto moving, after having seen in our Council the said Act of Renunciation of the King of Spain, our said Brother and Grandson, of the 5th of November' lad j as also the Acts of Renunciation which our said Grandson the Duke of Berry, and our said Nephew the Duke of Orleans, made reciprocally of their Right to the Crown of;

by separating, by the legal Means of my Renunciation, my Branch from the Royal Stem of France; and all the Branches of France, from the Stem of the Blood Royal of Spain; by taking care at the same time, in pursuance of the fundamental and perpetual Maxim, of the Balance of Power in Europe: That as this persuades, and juflifles, the avoiding, in all Cases imaginable, the Union of the Monarchy of France with that of Spain; the Inconvenience should likewise be provided against, that would be, if, in Default of my Issue, the same should happen, that this Monarchy should devolve again to the House of Aiifiria; whose Dominions and Dependencies, even without the Union of the Empire, would make it forrtiidable; That, by annulling all that shall be found to the contrary, it be established as a fundamental Law, as well the aforesaid Renuncia-' tions, as the perpetual Exclusion of the*House of from the Dominions of this Crown; and the Calling of that of Savoy to the Succession of these Kingdoms, iu Default, which God forbid, of the Issues of his Majesty; which the Kingdom, with the Approbation of his Majesty, does even now agree ta, as the Foundation whereon depends the greatest Good and Advantage of this Monarchy, so much pursued, favoured, and exalted, by the Royal Benevolence of his Majesty:

And the King our Lord having agreed to this unani-

mous and uniform Resolution and Representation of all the Knights Deputies in the Cortez of the Kingdom; be has been pleased, by his Royal Decree, of the 17th of this Month, to command it to be remitted to his Supreme Council, jointly with the Writing of Renuncia-. tion; ordaining. That the Tenor of the Law be forthwith formed, extended, and composed, with all the Cir-Cumliances of Clearness and Strength, for its more inviolable and perpetual observation.

Charles Son of France, Duke of Alenxon and Angoule/me, Viscount of Veand Lord of the Chatelanies of Coignac and To

all Kings, Princes, Commonwealths, Communities, and to all other Bodies, and private Persons, present and to come, be it known: All the Powers of Europe finding themselves almost ruined, on account of the present Wars, which have carried Desolation to the Frontiers, and into many other Parts of thericheft Monarchies, and other Dominions, it has been agreed in the Conferences Knd Treaties of Peace, which are negotiating with Great Britain, to establish an Equilibrium, and political Boundaries, between the Kingdoms, whereof the Interests have been, and are Hill, the fad Occasion of a bloody Dispute;-and to hold it for a fundamental Maxim, in order topreserve this Peace, that Provision ought to be pnade, that the Forces of these Kingdoms may not become formidable, nor (be able to cause any Jealously; which, it has been thought, cannot be settled more solidly, than by hindering them from extending themselves; and by keeping a certain Proportion; to the end that the Weaker, being united together, may defend themselves against the more Powerful, and support themselves respectively against their Equals.

For this Purpose, the King our moll honoured Lord and Grandfather, and the King of Spain, our most dear Brother, have agreed and concluded with the Queen of Great Britain, That reciprocal Renunciations shall be

made by all the Princes, both present and to come, of the Crown of France, and of that of Spain, of all Right*, which may appertain to each of them, to the Succession of the one or of the other Kingdom, by establishing an habitual Right to the Succession of the Crown of Spain in that Line which shall be made capable thereof, and declared immediate after that of the Vth,

King Philip shall renounce, for himself, and for all his Defendants, the Hopes of succeeding to the Crown of France-, that, on our Side, we shall renounce; in like manner, for us, and for our Defendants, the Crown of Spain; that the Duke of Orleans, our most dear Uncle* shall do the same thing j so that all the Lines of France, and of Spain, respectively and relatively, shall be excluded for ever, and by all kind of Ways, from all the Right which the Lines of France might have to the Crown of

Spain, and the Lines of Spain to the Crown of France j and, lastly, That Care shall be taken, that, under Pretence of the said Renunciations, or under any other Pretence whatsoever, the House of Atiftria may not make ufd of the Pretentions which it might have to the Succession of the Monarchy of Spain : Forasmuch as, by uniting this Monarchy to the Hereditary Countries and Dominions of that House, it would become formidable, even without the Union of the Empire, to the other Powers which are between both; and which would find themselves, as it were, surrounded; which would destroy the Equality that is establishing at present to secure, and strengthen, more perfectly, the Peace of Christendom; and to take away all manner of Jealously from the Powers of the North, and of the West* which is the End that is proposed by this political Equilibrium, by removing and excluding all these Branches, and calling to the

Crown of Spain, in Default of the Lines of King Philip the Vth our Brother, and of all his Children and Defendants, the House of the Duk^of Savoy, which defeends from the Infanta Catharina, Daughter of Philip the Second; it having been considered that in making the said House of Savoy succeed immediately in this manner, this Equality and Balance between the Three Powers may be fixed, as it were, in its Centre; without which it would be impossible to extinguish the Flame of War, which has been kindled, and is capable of destroying every thing.

The King’s Letters Patents of the Month of December 1700.

LEWIS, by the Grace of God, King of France and Navarte: To all present and to come, greeting: Thb Prdlperities which it has plerifed God to heap upon uS during the Course of our Reign, are so many Motives to us to apply ourselves, not only for the tirti£ present, but also for the future, to the Happiness and Trafl^uillity of the People, whereof Divide Providericif

has intruded to us the Government: His impenetrable Judgments let us only fee, That we ought not to place our Confidence, neither in our Forces, nor in the Extent of our Dominions, nor in a numerous Posterity; and that these Advantages, which we receive from his Goodness alone, have no other Solidity than what it pleases him to give tiiem: But as it is, however, his Will, That the Kings whom he chooses to lead his People should foresee, afar, the Events able to produce Disorders, and the most bloody Wars; that they should make use of the Lights which his Divine Wisdom pours upon them; we fulfil hisDesigns, when, in the Middle of the univer-fal Rejoicings of our Kingdom, we look upon, as a possible Thing, a fad Futurity; which we pray God to avert for ever: At the same time that we accept the Will of the late King of Spain, That our most dear and most beloved Son, the Dauphin, renounces his lawful Rights to that Crown, in Favour of his Second Son the Duke of Anjou, our most dear and most beloved Graudson, insti-tuted by the late King of Spain his universal Heir: That

this Prince, known at present by the Name of Philip the Vth, King of Spain, is ready to enter his Kingdom, and

to answerthe earned Willies of his new Subjects: This great Event does not hinder us from carrying our Views beyond the time present; and, when our Succession appears bed edahlished, we judge it to be, equally, the Duty of a King, and of a Father, to declare, for the future, ourWill conformably to the Sentiments which these Two Qualities inspire in us: Wherefore, being persuaded, that the King of Spain, our Grandson, will always preserve for us, for our House, for the Kingdom wherein he is born, the same Tenderness, and the same Seutiments, whereof he has given us so many Proofs, that his Example uniting his new Subjects to ours, is going to form a perpetual Amity, and the most perfect Correspondence between them; we should think, likewise. That we do him an Injudice, whereof we are incapable, and occasion an irreparable Prejudice to our Kingdom, if we should hereafter look upon, as a Stranger, a Prince, whom we grant to the unanimous Requests of the Nation:

For these Causes, and other great Confederations as hereunto moving, of our special Grace, full Power, and Royal Authority, we have resolved, declared, and ordained, and by these Presents, signed with our Hand, we do resolve, declare and ordain; we will, and it is ourPJeafure; That our most dear and most beloved Grandson, the King of Spain, do preserve, for ever, the Rights of his Birth, in the same manner, as ifhe made his actual Residence in our Kingdom: Wherefore, our most dear and most beloved only Son, the Dauphin, being the true and lawful Successor and Heir of our Crown, audof our Dominions; and, after him, our most dearand most beloved Grandson, the Duke of; if it

Now whereas it is provided and settled, by the preceding Renunciation, which is always to have the Force of a general, fundamental, and inviolable, Law, That at no time whatever, either the Catholick King himself, or any one of his Lineage, shall seek to obtain the Crown of France, or ascend the Throne thereof; and, by reciprocal Renunciations, on the Part of France, and by Settlements of the Hereditary Succession there, tending to the same Purpose, the Crowns of France and Spain are so divided and separated from each other, that the aforesaid Renunciations, and the other Tran factions relating thereto, remaining in Force, and being truly and faithfully observed, they can never be joined in one: Wherefore the most Serene Queen of Great Britain, and the most Serene the most Christian King, engage together, solemnly, and on their Royal Words, That nothing shall be ever done by them, or their Heirs and Successors, or allowed to be done by others, whereby the aforesaid Renunciations, and the other Transactions afore-mentioned, may not have their full Effect; but rather, on the contrary, their Royal Majesties, with joint Councils and Forces, will always sincerely take that Care, and use those Endeavours, that the said Foundations of the Publick Safety may remain unlhaken, and be preserved untouched, for ever.

Moreover, the most Christian King consents and engages, That he will not, for the Interest of his Subjects, hereafter endeavour to obtain, or accept of, any other Allowance of Navigation and Trade to and the.

Spanish Indies, than what was praflifed there in the Heign of the late King Charles the’.Second of Spain; qr than what shall likewise be fully given and granted, at the same time, to other Nations and People concerned in Trade.

VII.

That there be a free Use of Navigation and Commerce between the Subjects of both their Royal Majesties, ns it was formerly in time of Peace, and before the Declaration of this last War; and also, it is agreed and concluded by the Treaty of Commerce this Day made between the Two Nations.

VIII.

That the ordinary Distribution of Justice be revived, and open again, though the Kingdoms and Dominions of each of their Royal Majesties; so that it may be free for all the Subjects, on both Sides, to sue for and obtain their Rights, Pretensions, and Actions, according to the Laws, Constitutions, and Statutes, of each Kingdom,.

and most Potent Prince and Lord, the XIVth, by

the Grace of God, the most Christian King; sincethey-applied their Minds, by the Disposal of the Almighty, to the Study of Peace, have both been moved with an. earnest Desire to increase the Advantages of their Subjects

which are to arise therefrom, by a reciprocal Liberty of Navigation and Commerce; which ought to be as well the principal Fruit, as Establishment, of Peace: And, to that End, they most graciously gave Instructions to their Ambassadors Extraordinary, and Plenipotentiaries, going to the Congress at Utrecht, That they should employ their utmost Diligence and Care, both to re-establifo Peace, and to renew the former Treaties of Commerce, between the Two Nations; and to adapt them to the urefent State of Affairs; that isto say, her Sacred Royal Majesty of Great Britain, to the Right Reverend John,

by Divine Permifoon, Bifoop of Bristol, Keeper of the IVivy Seal of England, One of her Majesty’s Privy Council, Dean of Windsor, and Register of the motl Noble Order of the Garter; as also to the most Noble, IHuftrious, and Excellent, Lord, Thomas Earl of Strafford, Viscount Wentworth, of Wentworth Woodhouse &nd Stainborough, Baron of Raby, One of her Majesty’s Privy Council, her AmbafTador Extraordinary, and Plenipotentiary, to the H igh and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Netherlands, Colonel of her Majesty’s Regiment of Dragoons, Lieutenant General of her Armies, First Lord Commissioner of the Admiralty of Great Britain and Ireland, and Knight of the most noble Order of the Garter; and his Sacred Royal most Christian Majesty, to the most Noble, illustrious, and Excellent, Lords, Nicolas Marquis of Huxelles, Marfoal of France, Knight of the King’s Orders, and Lieutenant General of the Dukedom of Burgundy -, and Nicolas Mefnager, Knight of the King's Order of St. Michael: Whereupon the said Ambassadors, to the end that the so pious and wholsome Design of their Royal Majesties might attain the desired Effect, having had several Conferences upon that Affair; and having adjusted the principal Matters on both Sides, as far as they could in so foort a time; after having communicated to one another, and duly exchanged, the full Powers wherewith they were provided for this Purpose; Copies whereof are infer ted, Word for Word, at the End of this lustrument; agreed upon Articles of Navigation and Commerce, in Manner and Form, as follows:

I.

It is agreed and concluded between the most Serene and most Potent Queen of Great Britain, and the most Serene and most Potent the most Christian King, That there shall be a reciprocal, and entirely perfect. Liberty of Navigation and Commerce between the Subjects of each Part, through all and every the Kingdoms, States, Dominions, and Provinces, of their Royal Majesties, in Europe, concerning all and singular Kinds of Goods in those Places, and on those Conditions, and in such Manner and Form, as is settled and adjusted in the following Articles.

II.

But, That the Commerce and Friendfoip between the Subjects of the abovesaid Parties may be hereafter secure most free from ail Trouble and Molestation, it is agreed and concluded. That, if at any time, any ill Undemanding, and Breach of Friendfoip, or Rupture, should happen between the Crowns of their Royal Majesties (which God forbid), in such case the Term of Six Months shall be allowed, after the said Rupture, to the Subjects and Inhabitants on each Part, residing in the Dominions of the other, in which they themselves may retire, together with their Families, Goods, Merchandizes, and Effects, and carry them whithersoever they foall please; as like-wife, at the same time, the Selling and Disposing of their Goods, both moveable and immoveable, shall be allowed them freely, and without any Disturbance; and, in the mean time, their Goods, Effects, Wares, and Merchandizes, and particularly their Persons, foall not be detained or troubled by Arrest or Seizure; but rather, in the mean while, the Subjects on each Side shall have and enjoy good and speedy Justice; so that, during the said Space of Six Months they may be able to recover their Goods and Effects intruded as well to the Publick, os to private Persons.

nr.

It is likewise agreed and concluded, That the Subjects and Inhabitants of the Kingdoms, Provinces, and Dominions, of each of their Royal Majesties, foall exercise no Acts of Hostility and Violence against each other, neither by Sea, nor by Land, nor in Rivers, Streams, Ports, or Havens, under any Colour or Pretence whatsoever; so that the Subjects of either Party foall receive no Patent, Commission, or Inftrnftion, for arming, and acting at Sea, as Privateers, nor Letters of Reprisal, as they are called, from any Princes or States which are Enemies to one Side or the other; nor by virtue, or under Colour, of such Reprisals, Commissions, or Patents, foall they disturb, infeft, or any way prejudice or damage, the aforesaid Subjects and Inhabitants of the Queen of Great Britain, or of the most Christian King; neither foall they arm Ships in such manner as is above said, or go out to Sea therewith: To which End, as often as it is required by either Side, strict and express Prohibitions shall be renewed and publifoed in all the Regions, Dominions, and Territories, of each Party where-soever; that no one foall, in anywise, use such Com-. millions, or Letters of Reprisal, under the severest Pu-nifoment that can be inflicted on the Transgressoi-s, be-iides Rest it ut ion, and full Satisfaction, to be given to those to whom they have done any Damage; neither foall any Letters of Reprisal be hereafter granted, oa either Side, by the said Confederates, to the Detriment or Disadvantage of the Subjects of the other, except in such case only as Justice is denied, or delayed; to which Denial, or Delay, Credit shall not be given, unless the Petition of the Person who desires the said Letters of Reprisal be communicated to the Minister residing the re on the Part of the Prince against whole Subjects they are to be granted; that, within the Space of Four Months, or sooner, if it be possible, he may evince the contrary, or procure the Performance of what is due to Justice, ’

!V.

The Subjects and Inhabitants of each of the aforesaid Confederates foall have Liberty, freely and feenrely, without Licence or Passport, general or specia!,by Land, or by Sea, or any other Way, to go into the Kingdoms, Countries, Provinces, Lands, Islands, Cities, Villages, Towns, walled or unwalled, fortified or unfortified, Ports, Dominions, or Territories, whatsoever, of the other Confederate in Europe; there to enter and to return from thence; to abide there, or to pass through the fame; and, in the mean time, to buy and purchase, as they please, all things necessary for their Subsistence and Use: And they shall be treated with all mutual Kindnefa and Favour:

Provided however. That in all these Matters they behave and comport themselves conformably to the Law* and Statutes, and live and converse with each other friendly and peaceably, and keep up reciprocal Concord, by all Manner of good Understanding.

X.

The Duties on Tobacco imported into France, either in the Leaf, or prepared, shall be reduced, hereafter to the same moderate Rate as the said Tobacco of the Growth of any Country in Europe, of America, being brought into France, docs, or shall pay: The Subjects on both Sides shall all’o pay the same Duties in France, for the said Tobacco: There shall be, likewise, an equal Liberty of felling it: And the Subjects shall

have the same Laws as the Merchants of France themselves have and enjoy.

for every Ton, shall wholly eeafe, and be from henceforward annulled; in like manner, the Tax of Five Shillings Sterling, laid on French Ships, in Great Britain, for every Ton, shall cease; neither shall the fame, or any the like, Impositions, be laid hereafter on the Ships of the Subjects on either Side.

XII.

It is further agreed and concluded, That it shall be wholly free for all Merchants, Commanders of Ships, and other the Subjects of the Queen of Great Britain, in all Places of France, to manage their own Business themselves, or to -commit them to the Management of M homsoever they please 5 nor shall they be obliged to make nfe of any Interpreter, or Broker; nor to pay them any Salary, unless they choose to make nfe of them: Moreover, Masters of Ships shall not be obliged, in loading or unloading their Ships, to make life of those Workmen, either at Bourdeaux, or in any other Places, at maybe appointed by publick Authority for that Purpose; but it shall be intirely free for them to load or unload their Ships by themselves; or to make tile of such Persons in loading and unloading the fame, as they shall think fit, without the Payment of any Salary to any other whomsoever; neither shall they be forced to onload any Sort of Merchandizes, either into other Ships, or to receive them into their own; or to wait for their being loaded longer than they please; and all and every the Subjects of the most Christian King shall reciprocally have and enjoy the same Privileges and Liberty, in all Places, in Europe, Subject to the Dominion of Great Britain.

XIII.

It shall be wholly lawful and free for Merchants, and others, being Subjects, either to the Queen of Great Britain, or to the most Christian King, by Will, and any other Disposition, made, either during the time of Sickness, or at any other time before, or at the Paint of Death, to devise or give away their Merchandizes, Effects, Money, Debts belonging to them, and all moveable Goods which they have, or ought to have, at the lime of their Death, within the Dominions, and any other PI: ces, belonging to the Queen of Great Britain and to the most Christian King: Moreover, whether they die having made their Will, or intestate, their lawful Heirs and Executors, or Administrators, refilling in either of the Kingdoms, or coming from any oilier Part, although they be naturalized, fl, all free!v and quietly receive, and takePolieflion of, all the said Goods and Effects whatsoever, according to the Laws of Britain and France, respectively; in such manner, however, lhat the Wills, and Right of entering noon the Inheritances of Persons intestate, must be proved according to Law, as weil by tiic Subjects of the Queen of Great Britain, as by the Subjects of the most Christian

King, in those Places where each Person died, whether that may happen in Great Britain, or in France, any Law, Statute, Edict, Custom, or Droit d’ what-

ever, to the contrary notwithstanding.

XIV.

A Difpnte arising between any Commander of the Ships on both Sides, and his Seamen in any Port of the other Party, concerning Wages due to the said Seamen, or other Civil Causes, the Magistrate of the Place shall require no more from the Person accused, than that lie give to the Accuser, a Declaration, in Writing, witnessed by the Magistrate, whereby he shall be bound to answer that Matter, before a competent Judge, in his own Country; which being done, it shall not be lawful cither for the Seamen to desert their Ship, or to hinder the Commander from prosecuting his Voyage: It shall moreover be lawful for the Merchants on both Sides, in the Places of their Abode, or elsewhere, to keep Books of their Accounts and Affairs, as they shall think fit; and to have an Intercourse of Letters, in such Language or Idiom as they shall please, without any Molestation or search whatsoever: But if it should happen to be necessary for diem to produce their Books of Accounts, for deciding any Dispute and Controversy, in such case they shall be obliged to bring into Court the intire Books or Writings; but so as that the Judge may not have Liberty to inspect any other Articles in the said Books than such as shall relate to the Testimony or Authority in question, or such as shall be necessary to give Credit to the said Books: Neither shall it be lawful, under any Pretence, to take the said Books or Writings forcibly out of the Hands of the Owners, or to retain them; the same of Bankruptcy only excepted: Neither shall the said Subjects of the Queen of Great Britain be obliged to write their Accounts, Copies of Letters, Acts, or Instruments, relating to Trade, on stamped Paper; in French, Papier; except their Day

Book; which, that it may be produced as Evidence in any Law-suit, ought, according to the Laws which all Persons trading in France are to observe, to be fu!>-feribed, gratis, by the Judge, and signed with his own Hand.

XV.

It shall not be lawful for any foreign Privateers, not being Subjects of one, or of the other, of the Confederates, who have Commissions from any other Prince, or State, in Enmity with either Nation, to fit their Ships in the Ports of one, or the other, of the aforesaid Parties, to fell what they have taken, or in any other manner whatever to exchange either Ships, Merchandizes, or any other Ladings; neither shall they be allowed even to purchase Victuals, except such as shall be necessary for their going to the next Port of that Prince from whom they have Commissions.

XVI.

The Ships of both Parties being laden, failing along the Coast or Shores of the other; and being forced, by Storm, into the Havens or Ports, or coming to Land in any other manner; shall not be obliged, there, to unlade their Goods, or any Part thereof, or to pay any Duty, unless they do, of their own Accord, unlade their Goods there, or dispose of any Part of their Lading; but it may be lawful to take out of the Ship, and to fell, Leave being first obtained from those who have the Inspediou of Sea Affairs, a small Part of their Lading, for this End only, That Necessaries, either for the Refreshment, or Victualing, of the Ship, may be purchased; and, in that case, the whole Lading of the Ship shall not be subject to pay the Duties, but that small Part only which has been taken out, and fold.

XVII.

It shall be lawful for all and Angular the Subjects of the Queen of Great Britain, and of the most Christian King, to fail with their Ships, with all manner of Liberty and Security, no Distinction being made who are the Proprietors of the Merchandizes laden thereon, from any Port to the Places of those who are now, or shall be

XVIII.

This Liberty of Navigation and Commerce shall extend to all Kinds of Merchandizes; excepting those ©illy which follow in flic next Article, and which are signified by the Name of Contraband.

XIX.

Under this Name of contraband, or prohibited, Goods, shall be comprehended Arms, great Guns, Bombs with their Fufees, and other Things belonging to them, Fireball, Gunpowder, Match, Canuon-ball, Pikes, Swords, Lances, Spears, Halberds, Mortars, Petards, Granadues, Saltpetre,- Musquet, Musquet-ball, Helmets, Head pieces, Bieall-plates, Coats of Mail, and the like Kinds of Arms proper for arming Soldiers; Musquet-relts, Belts, Horses with their Furniture; and all other warlike Instruniciits whatever.

XX.

These Merchandizes which follow shall not be reckr ©ned among prohibited Goods; that is to say. All Sorts of Cloths, and all other Manufactures woven of any Wool, Flax, Silk, Colton, or any other Materials whatever; all kinds of Clothes, and wearing Apparel, together with the Species whereof they are used to be made; Gold and Silver, as well coined as uncoined; Tin, Iron, Lead, Copper, Brass, Coals; as also Wheat and Barley, and any other kind of Corn and rulfe; Tobacco; and likewise all manner of Spices; falttd and finoked Flesh, failed Filli, Cheese and Butter; Beer, Oils, Wines, Sugars, and all Sorts of Salt: and, in general, all Provisions, which serve for the Nourish-nient of Mankind, and the Sultenance of Life: Furthermore, all kinds of Cotton, Hemp, Flax, Tar, Pitch, Ropes, Cables, Sails, Sail-cloth, Anchors, and any Parts ©fAnchors; alfoShip-malls.Planks, Boards, and Beams, of what Trees soever; and all other tilings proper either for building or repairing Ships; and all other Goods whatever, which have not been worked into the Form of any Ir.flrument, or Tiling, prepared for War, by Land, or by Sea; shall not be reputed Contraband; much less such as have been already wrought, and made lip, for any other Use; all which shall wholly be reckoned among flee Goods; as likewise, all other Merchandizes and Things, which are not comprehended, and particularly mentioned, in the preceding Article; so that they may be Transported and carried, in tile freest manner, by the Subjects of both Confederates, even to Places belonging to an Enemy; such Towns, or Places, being only exempted, as are at that time belieged, blocked up round about, or invested.

To the end that all manner of Difienfious and Quar-

XXII.

The Ships of the Subjects and Inhabitants of both their mo ft serene Royal Majesties, coming to any of the Sea-coasts within the Dominions of either of the Confederates, but not willing to enter into Port; or, being entered, yet not being willing to shew, or to fell, the Cargoes of their Ships; shall not be obliged to give an Account of their Lading, unless they are suspected, upon sure Evidence, of carrying to the Enemies of the other Confederate, prohibited Goods, called Contraband.

XXIII.

And, in case of the said manifest Suspicion, the said Subjects and Inhabitants of the Dominions of both their most serene Royal Majesties shall be obliged to exhibit, in the Ports, their Passports and Certificates, in the manner before specified.

XXIV.

But in case the Ships of the Subjects and Inhabitants of both their most serene Royal Majesties, either on the Sea-coast, or on the high Seas, shall meet with the Men of War of the other, or with Privateers; the said Men of War, and Privateers, for preventing any Inconveniencies, are to remain out of Cannon-shot, and to fend their boats to the Merchant-ship which has been met with; and shall enter her with Two or Three Men only; to whom the Mailer, or Commander, of such Ship or Vessel, shall shew the Passports concerning the Property thereof, made out according to the Form annexed to this present Treaty; and the Ship which shall exhibit them, shall have free Passage; and it shall be wholly unlawful any way to molest, search, or compel her to quit her intended Course.

XXV.

But that Merchant-ship of the other Party, which intends to go to a Port at Enmity with the other Confederate, or concerning whose Voyage, and the Sort of Goods on board, there shall be just Suspicion, shall be obliged to exhibit, either on the high Seas, or in the Ports and Havens, not only her Passports, but her Certificates, expressing, that they are not of the Kinds of Goods prohibited, which are specified in the 19th Article.

XXVI.

But if one Party, on the exhibiting the abovesaid Certificates mentioning the Particulars of the Tilings on board, should discover any Goods of that Kind which are declared contraband, or prohibited, by the 19th Article of this Treaty, deligned for a Port subject to the Enemy of the other, it shall be unlawful to break up the Hatches of that Ship wherein the same shall happen to be found, whether lhe belong to the Subjects of Great Britain, or of France; to open the Cliefts, Packs, or Calks, therein; or to fell even the smalltft Parcel of Goods; unless the

XXVII.

On the contrary, it is agreed. That whatever shall be found to be laden by the Subjects and Inhabitants of either Party on any Ship belonging to the Enemy of the other, and his Subjects, the Whole, although it be of the Sort of prohibited Goods, may be confiscated, in the same manner as if it belonged to the Enemy himself; except those Goods and Merchandizes as were put on board such Ship before the Declaration of War, or even after such Declaration, if so be it were done within the Time and Limits following; that is to say, If they were put on board such Ship in any Port and Place, within the Space of Six Weeks after such Declaration, within the Bounds called the Naze, in Norway, and the Soundings; of Two Months, from the Soundings, to the City of Gibraltar; of Ten Weeks, in the Mediterranean Sea; and of Eight Months, in any other Country, or Place, in the V/brld: So that the Goods of the Subjects of either Prince, whether they be of the Nature of such as are prohibited, or otherwise, which, as is aforesaid, were put on board any Ship belonging to an Enemy, before the War, or after the Declaration of the Fame, within the Time and Limits abovesaid, shall no-ways be liable to confifeation; but shall well and truly be restored, without Delay, to the Proprietors demanding the same; but foas that, if the said Merchandizes be contraband, it shall not be any-ways lawful to carry them afterwards to the Port belonging to the Enemy.

XXVIII.

And that more abundant Care may be taken for the Security of the Subjects of both their most serene Royal Majesties, that they fulfer no Injury by the Men of War, or Privateers, of the other Party, all the Commanders of the Ships of the Queen of Great,

and of the most Christian King, and all their Subjects, shall be forbid doing any Injury or Damage to the other Side; and, if they act to the contrary, they shall be punished; and shall moreover be bound to make Satisfaction for all Damage, and the Interest thereof, by Reparation, under the Bond and Obligation of their Person and Goods.

XXIX.

For this Canfe, all Commanders of Privateers, before they receive their Patents, or special Commissions, shall hereafter be obliged to give, before a competent Judge, sufficient SeciSVity, by good Bail, who are Men able to pay, and have no Interest in the said Ship, and are each bound, in the Whole, for the Sum of^.1,500 Pounds Sterling, or 16,500 Livres Tournois; or, if such Ship be provided with above 150 Seamen, or Soldiers, for the Sum of £.3,000 Sterling, or 33,000 Livres Tournois; that they will make entire Satisfaction for any Damages and Injuries whatsoever, which they, or their Officers, or others in their Service, commit, during their Course at Sea, contrary to this present Treaty, or the Edicts of either of their most serene Royal Majesties, published by virtue thereof; under Penalty, likewise, of having their special Commissions, and Patents, revoked and annulled.

18

XXX.

Both their above-named Royal Majesties, being willing to shew a mutual, and equal, Favour, in all their Dominions, respectively, to the Subjects of each other, in the same manner as if they were their own Subjects, will give such Orders as shall be necessary and effectual, that Justice be administred concerning Prizes, in the Court of Admiralty, according to the Rule of Equity and Right, and the Articles of this Treaty, by Judges who are above all Suspicion, and who have no manner of Interest in the Cause in Dispute.

XXXI.

Whensoever the Ambassadors of each of their Royal Majesties above-named, and other their Ministers, having a publick Character, and residing in the Court of the other Prince, shall complain of the Unjustness of the Sentences which have been given; their Majesties, on each Side, shall take care, that the same be revised and re-examined in their respective Councils; that it may appear, whether the Directions and Provisions prescribed in this Treaty have been observed, and have had their due Effect: They shall, likewise, take care, that this Matter be effectually provided for, and that Right be done to every Complainant within the Space of Three Months: However, before or after Judgment, given, the Revition thereof still depending, for the Avoiding of all Damage, it shall not be lawful to fell the Goods in dispute, or to unlade them, unless with the Consent of the Persons concerned.

XXXII.

A Suit being commenced between the Captors of Prizes, on one Part, and the Reclaimers of the fame, on the other; and Sentence, or a Decree, being given in favour of the Reclaimer; that same Sentence, or Decree, Security being given, shall be put in Execution; the Appeal of the Captor to a superior Judge in anywise notwithstanding; which, however, is not to be observed when Judgment has been given against the Reclaimers.

XXXIII.

In case that either Ships of War, or Merchantmen, forced by Storm, or other Misfortune, be driven on Rocks or Shelves, on the Coasts of one or the other Party; and are there broken to pieces, and shipwreck-ed; whatever Part of the Ships or Tackling thereof, as also of the Goods and Merchandizes, shall be saved, or the Produce thereof shall be faithfully restored to the Proprietors, Reclaimers, or their Factors; paying only the Expences of preserving the fame, in such manner as a Regulation may be made, on both Sides, concerning the Salvage; saving, at the same time, the Right and Customs of each Nation: And both their most serene Royal Majesties will interpose their Authority, that such of their Subjects may be severely punished, who, in the like Accident, shall be guilty of Inhumanity.

XXXIV.

It shall be free for the Subjects of each Party to employ such Advocates, Attornies, Notaries, Solicitors, and Factors, as they shall think fit: To which End the said Advocates, and others above-mentioned, may be appointed by the ordinary Judges, if it be need, and the Judges be required thereunto.

xxxv.

And, That Commerce and Navigation may be more securely and freely followed, it is further agreed, That neither the Queen of Great Britain, nor the most Christian King, shall receive any Pirates and Robbers into any of their Ports, Havens, Cities, or Towns; neither shall they permit them to be received into Port, to be protected or assisted by any manner of Harbouring, or Support, by any the Subjects, or Inhabitants, of either of them; but they shall rather cause all such Pirates and Sea Robbers, or whoever shall receive, conceal, or assist, them, to be apprehended, and punished as they deserve, for a Terror and Example, to others: And all the Ships, Goods, or Merchandizes, being piratically taken by them, and brought into the Port of the Kingdom of either, as much as can be found, although they have, by

Sale,

Sale, been conveyed to others, shall be restored to the lawful Owners, or their Deputies, having Instruments of Delegation, and an Authority of Procuration for reclaiming the fame, and Indemnifation shall be made; proper Evidence being first given in the Court of Admiralty for proving the Property: And all Ships and Merchandizes, of what Nature soever, which can be rescued out of their Hands, on the High Sea, shall be brought into some Port of either Kingdom, and shall be delivered to the Custody of the Officers of that Port; with this Intention, That they be delivered entire to the true Proprietor, as soon as due and sufficient Proof shall have been made concerning the Property thereof.

XXXVI.

It shall be lawful as well for the Ships of War of both their most Serene Royal Majesties, as for Privateers, to carry whithersoever they please the Ships and Goods taken from their Enemies: Neither shall they beobliged to pay any tiling to the Officers of the Admiralty, or to any other Judges; nor shall the afore-mentioned Prizes, when they come to, and enter, the Ports of either of their most Serene Royal Majesties, be detained by Arrest: Neither shall Searchers, or other Officers of those Places, make Examination concerning them, or the Validity thereof: But, on the contrary, they shall have Liberty to hoist Sail at any time to depart, and to carry their Prizes to that Place which is mentioned in their Commission or Patent; which the Commanders of such Ships of War shall be obliged to shew: On the contrary, no Shelter or Refuge shall, in their said Ports, be given to such who have made Prize upon the Subjects of either of their Royal Majesties; and if, perchance, such Ships shall come in being forced by Stress of Weather, or the Danger of the Sea, particular Care shall be taken, as far as it is not repugnant to former Treaties with other Kings and States, that they go from thence, and retire elsewhere, as soon as possible.

XXXVII.

: Neither of their most Serene Royal Majesties shall f>ermit. That the Ship or Goods of the other be taken under the Coasts, and in the Ports or Rivers of their Dominions, by Ships of War, or others having Commission from any Prince, Commonwealth, or Town, whatsoever: And, in case such a thing should happen, both Parties shall use their Authority, and united Force, that the Damage sustained be made good.

XXXVIII.

If hereafter it shall happen, through inadvertency, or otherwise. That any Contraventions or Inconveniences on either Side should arise, concerning the Observation of this Treaty, the Friendship and good Intelligence shall not immediately thereupon be broke off; but this Treaty shall subsist in all its Force, and a proper Remedy for removing the Inconveniences shall be procured; as likewise Reparation of the Contraventions: And, if the Subjects of one, or the other, be found in Fault, they puly shall be severely punished and chastised.

XXXIX.

But if it shall appear. That a Captor made use of any Kind of Torture upon the Master of the Ship, the Ship’s Crew, or others who shall be on board any Ship belonging to the Subjects of the other Party; in such case, not only the Ship itself, together with the Persons, Merchandizes, and Goods whatsoever, shall be forthwith released, without any further Delay, and set entirely free; but also such as shall be found guilty of so great a Crime, as also the Accessaries thereunto, shall suffer the most severe Punishment suitable to their Crimes; which that it be done without any Respect of Persons, the Queen of Great Britain, and the most Christian King, do mutually engage to each other.
