Translation of an Act, declaring the Particulars referred, by the gth Article of the Treaty of Commerce and Navigation between Great Britain and France, to the Discussion of Commissioners.

BE it known unto all People, That whereas in the gth Article of the Treaty of Commerce concluded this Day between the most Serene Queen of Great Britain, and the most Serene the Christian King, by their Majesties AmbalTadois Extraordinary, and Plenipotentiaries, mention is made of some Heads of Matters, which, being proposed on the Part of Great Britain, have not, as yet, been mutually adjusted; and therefore it was thought fit to refer them to be difeufied and determined by Commissioners: We therefore, the under-written Ainbaffadors, that it may certainly appear what are those Heads of Matters, which are to be referred to Commissioners, have resolved to give a particular Account of them in this Writing, declaring, that they are the fame, and no other than what follow:

1.

No Manufactures of either Kingdom, and the Dominions belonging the reunto, shall be subject to be inspected and confiscated, under any Pretence of Fraud or Defect in making or working the m; or becadfe of any other Imperfection therein: But absolute Freedom shall be allowed to the Buyer, and the Seller, to bargain and agree for the same as they shall see good 3 any Law, Statute, Edict, Arrest, Privilege, Grant, or Custom, to the contrary notwithstanding.

II.

And for asmuch as a certain Usage, not confirmed by any Law, has obtained in several Towns of Great Britain, and of France; that is to say. That every one, for coming in, and going out, shall pay*a Kind of Tax, called, in English, Head-money; and in French, du Chef: It is concluded, That neither the fame, nor any other Duty, on that Account, shall any more be exacted:

III.

And the British Merchants shall not, hereafter, be forbidden to fell the said Tobacco to any Buyer whom they please, for which Purpose the letting out the Duties on the said Tobacco to Farmers, which has been hitherto practised, shall cease; neither fitall such Farming be used again hereafter.

IV.

The following same being only excepted; that is to say, where British Ships find! take up Merchandizes in one Port, and carry them to another Port, of;

in which Cafe, and in no other, the British Sul >j efts shall be obliged to pay the Duties abrogated and abolished by this Article, only in proportion to the Goods which they take in, and not according to the Bulk of the Ship.

V.

Whereas several Kinds of Goods, contained jn Calks, Vol. 17.

Chefis, 0fr Other Cafes, for Jvhifch the Butifes are paid by Tr«tMi et Weight, will be exported from, and -imported into, Peac* at France, by British Subjects: It is therefore agreed, that, Utr»ckv*«v in such Chfe, thfe aforesaid Duties shall be payable only according to the Weight of the Gobds themselves; but the Weight of the Caflcs, Chefls, dnd other Cafes whatever, shall be deduced in such manner, and in such Proportion, as has been hitherto in Use in,

and is still -nra&ifed.

VL

It is further agreed. That if any Mistake or Error shall on either Side be committed by any Master of Ship, his Interpreter or Factor, or by others employed by him, in making the Eritry or Declaration of the Goods on board his Ship; for such Defect, if so be a Fraud does not evidently appear, neither the Ship, nor the Lading thereof, shall be subject to be confiscated; but it shall be free for the Proprietors to have again such Goods as were omitted in the Entry or Declaration of the Mailer of the Ship; paying only the accustomed Duties, according to the Rates settled in the Books: Neither shall ' the Merchants, or the Master of the Ship, Iofe the said Goods, or suffer any other Punishment, if so be that the said Goods so omitted he not brought on Shore before the Declaration made, and the Customs paid for the same.

VII.

And whereas the Quality of the Ship, Master, and Goods, will sufficiently appear from such Passports and Certificates, it shall not be lawful for the Commanders of Men of War to exact; any other Verification, under any Title whatsoever: But if any Merchant Ship shall want such Passports or Certificates, then it may be examined by a proper Judge, but in such manner, as if it shall be found from other Proofs and Documents, that it does truly belong to the Subjects of either of the Confederates, and does not contain any prohibited Goods, designed to be carried to the Enemy of the other; it shall not be liable to Confiscation, but shall be released, together with its Cargo, in order to proceed on its Voyage* since it may often happen, that such Papers could not come to the Ship when she was setting Sail from any Port; or that they have been loft by some Chance or other; or that they have been taken away from the Ship:

And if, besides the Passports, and Certificates made according to the Form of this Treaty, other Passports and Certificates happen to be found in the Ship in another Form, and perhaps.according to the Prescription of Treaty made with others, no Pretence shall betaken from thence of detaining, or in anywise molefling, either the Ship, or Men, or Goods: If the Matter of the Ship named in the Passports be removed by Death, or any other Cause, and another be put in his Place, the PalFt ports shall nevertheless retain their Force; and the Ships and Goods laden thereon, shal^be secure.

VIII.

It shall further be provided on both Sides, and taken for a general Rule; That Ship and Goods, although they have remained in the Enemies Power for Four-and-twenty Hours, shall not therefore be elleemed as Capture, and be immediately made Prize; but if on other Accounts they ought to be restored, they mhy be reclaimed, and shall be given again to the Proprietors;

IX.

It shall be free for both their Royal Majesties, for the Advantage of their Subjects trading in the Kingdoms and Dominions of the other, to constitufte National Consuls of their own Subjects, who shall enjoy that Right and Liberty which belongs to them by reafori of the Exercise of their Funftion; but, as to the Places where such Consuls are to be appointed; both Sides shall afterwards agree between themselvfes:

Tran flat ion of an Act, explaining the general Terms of the 9th Article of the Treaty of Commerce and Navigation between Great Britain and re-

lating to the Four Species excepted out of the Tarffi of 1664.

BE it known unto all Men, That whereas in the 9th Article of the Treaty of Navigation and Commerce}

concluded the Day of lipir 1713, between the most SereneQueen of Great Britain, and the most Serene most Christian King, by the Ambassadors Extraordinary, and Plenipotentiaries, of their Majesties, certain Merchandizes, namely, Woollen Manufactures, Sugar, Salt, Fish, and what is produced from Whales, are excepted in general Words from the Rule of the Tariff made the 18th Day of the Month of September, in the Year 1664, in order to be afterwards referred to the Discussion of the Commissaries: To prevent therefore all Mistake and Ambiguity, which might perhaps arise from such general Terms; and to make it more evidently appear what particular Sort of Goods are to come under the Consideration of the aforesaid Commissaries; we the underwritten Ambassadors Extraordinary, and Plenipotentiaries, have declared by these Presents, and do declare. That the Exception of the above-mentioned Merchandizes is to be understood in the manner following:

X*

Whale, cut and prepared, the Fins and the Oils of Whale, shall pay, at all Places of Importation in the Kingdom, the Duties appointed by the Tariff of the 7th of December 1699.

II.

Cloth, Ratins, and Serges, shall be likewise subject to the Duties of the Tariff of the 7th of December 1699; and, in order to facilitate the Trade thereof, it shall be allowed to import them by St. Valery upon the , by Rouen, and by Bourdeaux, where these Goods shall be subject to Vilitation in the same manner as those which are made in the Kingdom.

III.

Salt Fish, in Barrel only, is to be imported into the Kingdom; and at the Ports of the Kingdom, Countries, and Territories, under the Dominion of the King, even at free Ports, the Duties of Landing, and of Consumption, shall be paid, which wereappointed before the Tariff of 1664; and, besides, 40 Livres per Last, consisting of V2 Barrels, weighing each 300 for the Duty of Entry; which Entry shall not be permitted but by St. Vallery upon the Somme, Rouen, Nantx, Libourne, and Bourdeaux and shall remain prohibited at all other Harbours or Ports, as well in the Ocean, as in the Mediterranean.

IV.

v Refined Sugar, in Loaf, or in Powder, White and Brown Candy, shall pay the Duties appointed by the Tariff of 1699.

Translation of a Treaty of Peace and Friendship between Great Britain and Spain.

Whereas it has pleased the Supreme Ruler of all Things, after a most grievous War, which for so many Years has ravaged almost the whole Christian World with Blood and Slaughter, of his Divine Clemency, to compose the Minds of the Princes engaged in the Dif-«5

[with his Titles] wish for nothing more heartily, and endeavour to obtain nothing with greater Earnestness, than that the ancient Bonds of Alliance and Friendship between the British and Spanish Nations should not only be renewed, but also more strongly knit together by fresh Engage-, ments of Amity and interest on both Sides, and transmitted inseparably to all Posterity; in order, at last to finish happily so who!Come, and so very desirable, a Work; they have nominated, on each Side, their Am-bafladors Extraordinary, and Plenipotentiaries, and have instructed them with sufficient Orders; that is to say, the Queen of Great Britain on her Part:

L

That there be a Christian universal Peace and a per* petual and true Friendship, between the most Serene and most Mighty Princess Anne, Queen of Great Britain, and the most Serene and most Mighty Prince Philip the Vth, Catholick King of Spain, and their Heirs and Successors; and also the Kingdoms, States, Dominions, and Provinces, of both Parties, wheresoever situated, and their Subjects; and that the same be so sincerely preserved and cultivated, that neither Party do, under any Colour whatever, endeavour to attempt any thing to the Destru6tio» or Detriment of the other; or yield any-Aid, by what Name soever it may be called, to those who attempt the fame, or who endeavour to do any Damage; neither may or ought they to help them by any means: On the contrary, their Royal Majesties shall, be obliged, the one to promote the Advantage, Honour, and interest, of the other; and to direct their Counsels to that End with all Care, that by mutual Proof of Friendship, the Peace, which is now made, may daily receive new Additions of Strength.

But whereas the War, which is so happily ended by this Peace, was at the Beginning undertaken, and was carried on for so many Years, with the utmost Force, at immense Charge, and with almost infinite Slaughter, because of the great Danger which threatened the Liberty and Safety of all Europe, by reason of the too dole Conjunction of the Kingdoms of Spain and France: And whereas, to take away all Unealiness and Sul'pieion concerning such a Conjunction out of the Minds of People, and to settle and establish the Peace and Tranquillity of Christendom by an equal Balance of Power, which is the belt and most solid Foundation of a mutual Friendship, and of a Concord, which will be lasting on all Sides; as well the Catholick King, as the most Christian King, have consented, that Care should be taken, by sufficient Precautions, that the Kingdoms of Spain and France should never come and be united under the same Dominion; and that one and the same Person should never become King of both Kingdoms: And, to this End, his Catholick Majesty has for himself, his Heirs and Successors, most solemnly renounced all manner of Right, Title, and Pretension, to the Crown of France, in the Form and Words following:

It is further agreed and concluded, as a general Rule, That all and singular the Subjects of each Kingdom shall, in all Countries and Places on both Sides, have and enjoy, at lead, the same Privileges, Liberties, and Immunities, as to all Duties, Impositions, or Customs, whatsoever, relating to Persons, Goods, and Merchandizes, Ships, Freight, Seamen, Navigation, and Commerce; and shall have the like Favour, in all things, as the Subjects of France, or any other foreign Nation, the most favoured, have, possess, and enjoy, or at any time hereafter may have, possess, or enjoy.

X,

The Catholick King does hereby, for himself, his Heirs and Successors, yield to the Crown of Great Britain, the full and entire Propriety of the Town and Castle of Gibraltar, together with the Port, Fortifications, and Forts, thereunto belonging; and he gives up the said Propriety, to be held and enjoyed, absolutely, with all manner of Right for ever, without any Exception or Impediment whatsoever: But, that Abuses and Frauds may be avoided by importing any Kinds of Goods, the Catholick King wills, and takes it to be understood, that the above-named Propriety be yielded to Great Britain, without any territorial Jurisdiction, and without any open Communication, by Land, with the Country round about: Yet, whereas the Communication, by Sea, with the Coast of Spain, may not, at all times, be safe or open, and thereby it may happen, that the Garison, and other Inhabitants, of Gibraltar, may be brought to great Straits; and as it is the Intention of the Catholick King, only, that fraudulent Importations of Goods should, as is abovesaid, be hindered by a Communication to the Landward; it is therefore provided, that, in such Cases, it may be lawful to purchase, for ready Money, in the neighbouring Territories of Spain, Provisions, and other things, necessary for the Use of the Garison, the Inhabitants, and the Ships, which lie in the Harbour: But if any Goods be found imported by Gibraltar, either by way of Barter for purchasing Provisions, or under any other Pretence, the same shall beconfifcated, and, Complaint being made thereof, those Persons who have acted contrary to the Faith of this Treaty shall be severely punished: And her Britannick Majesty, at the Request

XVII.

But ifit happen through Inadvertency, orlmprudence, or any other Cause, that any Subject of either of their aforesaid Royal Majesties do or commit any thing by Land, Sea, or on fresh Waters, in any Part of the World, whereby this present Treaty be not observed, or whereby any particular Article of the same hath not its Effect, thisPeace, and good Correspondence, between the Queen of Great Britain and the Catholick King shall not therefore be interrupted or broken; but shall remain in its former Strength, Force, and Vigour: And that Subject only shall be answerable for his own Fa&, and shall suffer such Punishment as is inflicted by Law, and according to the Prescriptions of the Law of Nations.

XVIII.

But if (which God forbid) the Disputes, which are composed, should at any time be renewed between their said Royal Majesties, and break out into open War, the Ships, Merchandizes, and Goods, both moveable and immoveable, of the Subjects, on both Sides, which shall be found to be and remain in the Ports and Dominions of the adverse Party, shall not be confiscated, or suffer any Damage; but the Space of Six Months, ort the one Part, and on the other, shall be granted to the said Subjects of each of their said Royal Majesties, in order to their felling the aforesaid Things, and any thing else belonging to their Effects; or carrying away and transporting the same from thence, whitbersoever they please, without any Molestation,

A Petition of the Merchants of the City of London trading to Italy, and other Parts of the in behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Italian Trade has always been deemed beneficial to the Kingdom, by taking otf yearly great Quantities of Fish, Copperas, Lead Ore, Tin, Lead, Pepper, Woollen Manufacture, Sic.; in Return of which is received from Italy about 2,000 Tuns of Wines, and the Remainder in useful Commodities, proper for our own Manufactures: That the Ad million of French Wines, paying the same Duty as those from Italy, will be an actual Prohibition of the latter; which, by Difference of Distance, must pay larger Freight, have greater Leakage, and other incident Charges, in proportion to the Distance: That it will also be a Discouragernent to Navigation, by reason Trade to France will be carried on with small Vessels; v'ho, even in proportion to the Burthen, will fail with Half the Men bbips for the Mediterranean are forced to carry: And praying, That, if any Alteration be made in the Duties on French Wines, it may be such only as may, in some measure, set the Italian Trade on an equal Footing with the Traders for France, in proportion to the First Cost of Wines, Difference of Risque, Freight, and other Charges.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to suspend, for Two Months, the Duties of Twenty-five Pounds per Tun on French Wines imported, is committed.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer presented to the Treaty House, pursuant to their Address to her Majesty, The ^Orllo-'< Treaty with Portugal, of the 27th of December 1703; , 3* and a Translation of it:

And the Tran flat ion was read; and is as followet h; viz. PETER, by the Grace of God, King of Portugal and the Algarves, on both Sides the Sea, in Africa;

Lord of Guinea, of the Conquest, Navigation, and Commerce, of Ethiopia, Arabia, Persia, and India, To all and Angular who shall fee these our Letters we make known, and declare, That, between our Plenipotentiary, Emmanuel TelPJius Silvias Marquis of One of

our Chief Gentlemen of the Bedchamber, and Counsellor of State, on our Part, and John Methuen, the Queen of Great Britain's Ambuffador Extraordinary to us, on the other, on the 27th December the lall Year,aTreaty was made and signed, in the following Words;

Whereas the Alliance, and lirirt Friendship, which fub-fists between the most Setene and Potent Princess, the Lady Anne, Queen of Great Britain, requires. That the Commerce between either Nation, of Portugal and Britain, may be encouraged as much as conveniently may be; and that her Sacred Royal Majesty-of Britain

ii Ann. ia° Mail. 349

has signified to his Sacred Royal Majesty of Portugal, by the most Excellent John Methuen Esquire, a Member of her Parliament of England, and her Ambassador Extraordinary in Portugal, That it would be very acceptable to her, if the Cloth, and other Woollen Manufactures, of Britain, might be admitted into Portugal, and their Prohibition taken off: In order to the treating of this Matter, their full Powers and Commands were given by his Sacred Royal Majesty of Portugal, to the most Excellent Lord Emanuel Marquis

of Allegrete, Count of Villar Major, of the Order of Knighthood of Chrifi, Commendary of St. John de grete and Trapc/cs de Soure, and in the College of the Avienfii, Commendary of St. "John de Moura and St. Mary de Albufeira, President of the Council of the

Treasury, One of the Chief Gentlemen of the Bedchamber, and Council of State, to his Sacred Royal Majesty of Portugal, and by her Sacred Royal Majesty of Great Britain, to the above-mentioned most Excellent Lord John Methuen; who, by virtue of the full Powers to them respectively granted, having maturely and carefully debated this Matter, agreed upon the following Articles relating the reunto:

Article ift.

The King of Portugal promises for himself and Successors, That Woolf n Cloths, and all other Woollen Mamifafltties, of Great Britain, shall, in all times, be permitted to be imported into Portugal, in the same manner as they were before they were prohibited by the Pragma!ick Sanctions; but nevertheless under the following Conditions:

Article 2d.

That is to say, That the Queen of Great Britain shall, in her own Name, and that of her Successors, promise. That the Wines of the Growth of shall, in all

times to come, be imported into Great Britain: so that, w hether there be Peace or War between the Kingdoms of Great Britain and France, no other Duty shall be laid, directly or indirectly, upon the said Wines, than what shall be laid upon the like Quantity or Measure of French Wine; a Third Part being deducted of the said Custom or Duty1 by whatever Sort of Vessels those Wines may be imported into Great Britain: That if at any time hereafter any Diminution shall be made of these Duties, in Derogation to this Agreement, it shall then be lawful for the King of Portugal again to prohibit the Woollen Manufactures of Great Britain. Article 3d.

The most Excellent Lords Plenipotentiaries do promise and undertake, That their above-named Mailers will ratify this Treaty; and that the Ratifications shall be exchanged in Two Months.

In WitnessandTeftimony whereof, I the Plenipotentiary of his Sacred Royal Majesty of Portugal have signed this Treaty with my Hand, and hereunto affixed my Seal of Arms: And the most Excellent Lord Plenipotentiary of her Sacred Royal Majesty of Great Britain, to avoid the Dispute there is about the Priority of Place between the Crowns of Portugal and Britain, has signed another of the same Tenor, those Alterations only being made that were proper upon this Account. Given at Lisbon, the 27th Day of December in the Year of our Lord One Thousand Seven hundred and Three.

(L. S.) The Marquis of Alegrete.

Which Treaty being by us maturely weighed and considered, we have approved all and Angular the Contents thereof; and the same have ratified and confirmed, as for ourselves, and our Heirs and Successors, we do approve and ratify the fame; promising and engaging, upon our Royal Word, That we will fulfil and observe the same fiucerely and faithfully; nor will we suffer any one to violate it, in the Whole, or in Part. In Witness whereof, we have ordered these Letters of Ratification to be made forth; which are subscribed with our Hand, and sealed with our Arms, at Lisbon, the 2d Day of May. a?1 Ci°ih Mr. Bertie reported from the Committee, to whom J Jnu d ure‘ the Petition of William Smith senior, Walter Stewart, and Thomas Shefford, in behalf of themselves, and other Manufacturers of Sail Cloth in Great Britain, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows;

That the Committee had, in pursuance of the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition, and find the same to be as follows; viz.

That by Two several Acts of Parliament; viz. 7° ct 8’* fVillielmillV1, Chapter the iotb. Sec. 14th; and 70

el l'c Willielmi III11, Cap. 39 % Seel. 2d; Encouragement was given for making the said Manufactures in England, by obliging the Commissioners of the Navy to give Preference to all such as should be found fit for that Service; allowing id. per Yard more than for foreign Sail Cloth, though of equal Goodness; and also, by permitting Englishi Sail Cloth to be exported Custom free.

That to prove great Quantities of Sail Cloth are made in Great Britain-, the great Number of Poor h employs; and the Goodness of it;

Captain Smith said, That he and his Son employed 5 or 6,ooood Persons in Middlesex, Berks, and -

shire, in making the said Manufacture, when in full Work: That the Commissioners of the Navy, in One Year, contracted for a8,ooood Pieces, or Bolts, of Sail Cloth, whereof Mr. Smith said he furnished u,ooood; and that to perform the whole Contract might employ above io, ooood Hands; the mere Manufacturing of each Piece, or Bolt, amounting to- upwards of 28r. and Freight of Flax to near 5:

That the Commissioners of the Navy have used our British Sari Cloth for many Years, pursuant to the said Acts, without any Complaint; and they have bought no foreign, except i,ooood Pieces, or Bolts, which were used for mending old Sails: That, foreign Canvas being 30 Inches broad, and oars bat 24, the Merchants generally make use thereof; and the Petitioners now make it of the same Goodness, and Breadth, as foreign Sail Cloth:

That, the War being now at an End, the Encouragement given by the said Acts is greatly diminished; and Mr. Smith said, that he has turned off Two-thirds of the Hands employed in the said Manufacture, for want of Work; and that it is likely to be wholly loft to this Nation, if not timely encouraged by Parliament.

That Foreigners can afford to make and sell their Sail Cloth cheaper here than the British Manufacturers, though of equal Goodness; for that Foreigners pay little or no Duty' for the Materials wherewith they make it.

That a Bolt of Foreign Sail Cloth pays but 3*. id. Duty upon Importation; and draws back about is. 6£rf.; and the Freight costs not above 5 per Piece: Whereas rood Weight of Flax, which will make a Bolt of English Sail Cloth, of 36 Yards, pays about 3s. id. Duty; Vol, 17.

draws back nothing on Exportation; and pays near 5;. Freight.

Mr. Samuel Holding, Merchant: That in February 1711, be fold Mr. Smith a whole Ship’s Lading of Flax, imported here at 4$. 1 id. perC. Weight: That, before the War, great Quantities of Our Woollen Manufactures were exported; the Returns Ivbereof Were mostly Flax: That -fds of the Flax imported has been used in making British Sail Cloth; but if Ehcouragement be not given thereto, there will not be One Third Of the inferior Sort of Flax imported.

Mr. Steioart and Mr. Rayner said, That North Britain employs about 5,000 Hands in making Sail Cloth, as they verily believe: and that great Quantities thereof are all'o made iti Kent, Lancashire, Somerfeshire, Dorsetshire, and other Counties of this Kingdom,

That the Commissioners of the Navy attended the Committee, and said, That, in pursuance of the said Acts of Parliament, they, for several Years, hate used the British Sail Cloth; and that their Officers have from time to time viewed it, and reported it fit for her Majesty’s Service: And although, when it was iu its Infancy, it did not give full Satisfaction; yet, since, the same has been greatly improved, and no Complaints have been made thereof.

And the said Answer was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Answer of the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations to an Order of the honourable the House of Commons:

In Obedience to an Order of this honourable House, of the 9th instant, directing us to lay before this House, the Representations made to this Board from the Merchants, and several Corporations, of Britain, in relation to Trade, while the Ger Treaty was depending, und afterwards; and also the Petitions and Memorials that have beeu lately laid before the said Commissioners, relating to the Trade of this Kingdom; and what Directions and Commands they have received from her Majesty thereupon;

We take Leave to inform this honourable House, That, in May 1709, the then Commissioners of Trade and Plantations were directed by the Earl of Sunderland, to consider of several Treaties of Commerce with France-, aii i to report to her Majesty which of them was moll

for the Advantage of Great Britain: They accordingly considered such Treaties, or Projects of Treaties, as they could procure: and ordered Letters to be writ to the mostconsiderable Merchants, and other Persons, for their Thoughts in Writing, what might be of Use, and for the Advantage of this Kingdom, in the framing a Treaty of Commerce with France, particularly in relation to the Duties laid upon our Manufactures and Goods there: In Answer whereunto, the Board received the several Memorials and Letters herewith laid before this honourable House; and numbered, 1. 2. 3.4. 5. 6. 7. 8. g. 10. 11.12. 13.14. 15. 16.

Upon the Consideration of all which Papers, the Project of a Treaty of Commerce with France was prepared, and in October 1709, sent to the Earl of Sunderland, with several other Papers relating the reunto; Copies whereof are herewith laid before this honourable House, and are numbered 17.

On the 26th April 1710, the Turkey Company communicated to the Board the Copy of a Petition from them to her Majesty; setting forth, That before the late War, they had Liberty to export great Quantities of Turkey Goods into France; which they were not allowed to do during the last Peace then on Foot....

such Provisions may be made as may restore so beneficial a Trade to this Kingdom: Whereupon they were acquainted, That in the Project of a Treaty of Commerce with France, Provision was made, that the Trade

from this Kingdom to France should be upon the same Foot as in 1664.

In December 1711, the Earl of Dartmouth referred to the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, by her Majesty’s Command, a Petition from the Turkey Company relating to what they desired might be done for them in a Treat}' of Commerce with France-, as also a Petition from the Hudson's Bay Company, praying that, at a Treaty of Peace, the French may be obliged to renounce all Right to the said Bay: Upon Consideration of which Petitions the Board reported. That their Desires were reasonable; as will more fully appear by the Papers, numbered, 20. 21. 22. 23. 24.

In March 1711, Mr. Secretary John, now Lord Viscount Bolingbroke, transmitted to us the Draught of

a Treaty Marine, and of Commerce, with France, for our Observations and Opinion upon it (No. 25.); Whereupon Letters were writ to several of the most considerable Merchants, and others, desiring them to consult with such others as they should think proper, and to let us have, as soon as possible, what they might have to offer in relation to the said Treaty; whereupon we received the several Memorials and Papers, numbered 26. 27. 28. 29. 30. 31. 32.

We also consulted some experienced Officers of the Customs, and several Merchants and Civilians, upon the said Treaty i and, on the 15th of April 1712, we returned to the Lord Bolingbroke the said Treaty, with our Observations thereupon: A Copy whereof is herewith laid before this honourable House, and numbered 33.

On the qthof January last, Mr. Onslow, Mr

and Mr. Harris, with some other Planters in the West Indies, attending us, a Memorial (No. 16), signed by several of them; setting forth, their Apprehensions, That Sugars, and other West India Commodities would be pro-

hibited in France, was read; Whereupon we asked them, Where they had their Information ? And they desired to be excused the naming of Persons: But, after some Discourse with them, they said. They had several Letters of it from Holland-, and that it was the common Discourse among the French here, and upon the Exchange: Upon which we acquainted them, That they might be satisfied her Majesty would not agree to any Treaty of Commerce with such Prohibitions: And we communicated to them some Restrictions to be made upon granting the Tariff of 1664 to the Dutch-, in which Sugar refined, in Loaf or otherwise, Sugar Candy White and Brown, was to pay the Duties mentioned in the Tariff of the 7th of December 1699: To which these Gentlemen replied, That if we were to be

.upon the same Foot as the Dutch, they were afraid, that that Article would affefr all our Sugars, except those from Jamaica; for, the Barbadoes and Leeward Islands Sugar being clayed, they would pass for refined, and do pay Custom here as such: And therefore they desired. That some Explanation might be made in favour of the Barbadoes and Leeward Islands Sugars: Whereupon we desired them to consider, Whether this Dispute did not relate to the Dutch more than to England; and Whether by stirring in that Matter they might not prejudice themselves: Upon which the said Merchants desired, that we would not do any thing on the said Memorial until they considered farther thereof; and they would attend us again, in a short time, with their Thoughts thereupon; but they never thought fit To todo.

Mefliiagps, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, of a greaterValue, and which lie more convenient, in the County of Norfolk, in lieu thereof; was committed; That they had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Contents to the Bill, except William Holland, Sir John Holland's Brother; touching whom the Committee, having presumptive Evidence that he was dead, had ordered the same to be reported specially to the House; which is as followeth; viz.

Thomas Hyde, who was a very intimate Friend and Acquaintance of Mr. Holland's did declare. That a Commission of Bankrupt having been issued out against the said Mr. Holland about 11 or 12 Years since, he thereupon absconded; and that, about Eight Years since, he sent over a Person to him, from Dublin, acquainting him. That he lay dangerously ill, and desired him to transact some Maiters relating to hisAffairs; and though the same would have been of great Consequence to him, as relating to his own private Interest, yet he has never heard from him since; and verily believes, That he is dead.

Mr. Nath. Prime and Mr. Two

other Witnesses, being likewise examined, laid, They were acquainted with the said Mr. Holland-, and though they have made Inquiry after him several times within these Nine Years', havingMatters of great Moment with him, could never hear of him; and verily believe he is dead:

And that the Committee had made several Amendments to the Bill; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossccl.

I never had any Acquaintance with, or personal Knowlege of, the Lord Wharton, or had ever spoken to him, till I was advised, by a Friend, to apply to him, by means of the Lady Lockhart, his Lordship’s Sifter; to whom I made my Proposition, and Promise of a Present, if, by her, I could be recommended to Lord Wharton her Brother, and by him to Lord Treasurer, to have Leave for Mr. John Earl, my Predecessor, to resign his Office to me: And, when I was by her Lndyship so recommended to Lord Wharton, her Lndyship told me, That his Lorrlship was very unwilling to meddle with any thing of that kind; and that I must not expect, that his Lordship would make any Steps in it, unless he found, by Lord Treasurer, that I was very capable and fit for the said Employment.

Whilst this Affair was thus transacting, the said Mr. John Earl died; upon which I told her Lady ship I could, and would, make her Ladyfiiip a better Present, if her Ladyship could prevail that I might succeed the said John Earl: Her Ladyship then gave me a Letter of Recommendation to Lord Wharton, who was then at Newmarket; and when I came there, and was introduced to Lord Treasurer, his Lordship was pleased to say, That for my own Sake, and my Father’s, and upon Lord Wharton's Recommendation, his Lordship was

willing to prefer me to that Employment.

When I had thus obtained his Lordship’s Promise, the Lord Wharton, being afterwards returned to Town, told me. That, for some lleafons, he did not think proper to put the Money into her Ladyship’s Hands; nor make the Bills payable to her; and directed me to put the Money into a Goldfinith’s Hands; which I did, and made the Notes payable to myself, and indorsed them; and afterwards delivered them to a Person his Lordship, who was then gone into the Country, by his Letter,'appointed to receive the same:

And I always apprehended, from what my Friend said.

And that Part of the said Report, which relates to the Earl of Wharton, was again read.

A Petition of the Merchants, Sugar-bakefs, and Dif- Duties on tillers, of the City of Bristol, in behalf of themselves *'rene!‘

SI J t* - _ , UroiJ.iai

and others, was presented to the House and read; letting forth. That the Materials made use of in diffilling Brandies in this Kingdom are of its own Growth, as Perry, Cyder, and Malt; or imported from its Pianta* tions, as coarse Sugar and Moloffes; by the vast Consumption whereof, Tillage and Husbandry are en» couraged; Navigation promoted; and many Families employed; That the Diliillery brings in a great Revenue to the Crown; every C. Wt. of Moloffes paying 8a. and every C. Wt. of Sugar ioj. besides Custom at Importation; Cyder, Perry, and Malt, also paying a large Duty, when diffilled, above the other Excise they are charged with: That the English Brandies excel some foreign, and are equally as wholesome, and but little inferior to French Brandies: That the consumingcoarfe Sugars, and Moloffes, enables the Sugar-bakers to make refined Sugars cheap, and to supply foreign Markets;

That if the Use of coarse Sugars be discouraged here, they will be exported to foreign Markets, there to be refined; and the Crown lose the Custom by Drawbacks, and the Excise also they would have paid, had they been diffilled: That, if any of the Duty be taken off foreign Brandies, it will destroy the Diffilling Trade of Great Britain, unless the Duties on home Brandies be proportionably abated; both which will prejudice her Majesty’s Revenue: And praying their same may be considered; and such Relief in the Premises, especially in preventing the running the Duty of foreign Brandies, as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir William Withers reported from the Committee, to Deficiency whom the Petition of the Proprietors of the Two mil- pu^"" lion Adventure for the Year 1712, was committed.

That they had examined the Matter: and had directed him to report the same to the House, as it appeared to them; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where it was read; and is a? followeth; viz.

That the Committee haying read the Clause in the Act of Parliament mentioned in the Petition to them referred, in an Act, passed in the Ninth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for liCenfing and regulating Hackney Coaches and Chairs; and for charging certain new Duties on stamped Vellora, Parchment, and Paper; and on Cards and Dice; and on the Exportation of Rock Salt for Ireland; and for securing the re* by, and by a weekly Payment out of the Poll Office, and by several other Duties on Hides and Skins, a yearly Fund of £186,670 for 32 Years, to be applied to the Satisfaction of such Orders as are therein mentioned, to the Contributors of any Sum, not exceeding Two millions, to be raised for carrying on the War, and other her Majesty's Occasions;

It appeared to them, from the said Clause, That so much of the Money arising from the Duties, Revenues, and Branches, thereby appointed, as should be brought into the Receipt of the Exchequer, should be computed and reckoned the yearly Fund of £186,670 in case the same would extend so far, for the Term of 32 Years, to be computed ftofti the 29th of September 1711, for paying off £2,602,200 Principal Money, and Interest at Six per Cent, per Annum: And that by the same Act it was Enacted, That in case the Monies by the said Act appointed should, at any time or times, appear to be so deficient, or low, in the Produce of the lame, as that, within any One Year, to be reckoned as aforesaid, the said Monies arising into the Exchequer, for all the Duties, Revenues, and Branches, as aforesaid, should not amount to so much as £ 186,6 70, then, and so often, so much as should be wanting to make up the said Fund,

And, the Petitioners having alleged, in their Petition, That the Money arising into the Exchequer, by the said Duties, Branches, and Revenues, in the Year ending the 29th September 1712, did fall short upwards of £.70,000 of the said Sum of £.186,670; the Committee did order Mr. Clayton, of the Exchequer, to attend them with an Account of what Money did arise into the Exchequer from the several Duties appropriated to the said Fund, before the 29th September 1712.

And it appeared to the Committee, from the Account brought before them, by the {hid Mr. , pursuant

to Order, and signed by him, That, at Michaelmas 1712, the Sum of £.136,354 17 s.i had been brought into the Exchequer upon the said several Duties, Branches, and Revenues; of which the Sum of £.11,902 155. 7d. was applied towards the Discharge of Principal Money, according to the Directions of the said Act, as having been brought into the Exchequer before Michaelmas 1711; and also the Sum of £.7,805 is. 3 was applied for paying the Charges of Management before Michaelmas 1712; and that the net Money, after the said Two last mentioned Sums deducted, which was applied towards the said Annuity of£. 186,670, due at Michaelmas 1712, was the Sum of £.116,646 igr. 9|d.; and that there was wanting, at Michaelmas 1712, of the Monies arising into the Exchequer for the said Duties, Branches, and Revenues, the Sum of £.70,023. 6s. i\d. to make up the said Annuity of £.186,670 due at Michaelmas 1712 aforesaid.

That the Committee further sent Orders to the several Offices to whose Care and Management the said several Duties are committed, to send to them their several Accounts of the gross and net Produce of the said several Duties, Revenues, and Branches, for the Year ending at Michaelmas 1712.

And that it appeared to the Committee, from the several Accounts brought before them, pursuant to Orders, That, computing the Deficiency of the said Fund of £. 186,670 from the net Produce of the said several Duties, Branches, and Revenues, the said Deficiency, at Michaelmas 1712, was the Sum of £.62,000.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled.

In Obedience to an Order of the 9th Instant, directing the Commissioners of the Customs to lay before this honourable House an Account of the Quantities of W ines and Brandies imported, annually, from the Year 1674, to this time; distinguishing the French Wines and Brandies, and those of other Countries; the said Commissioners gave immediate Directions to the proper Officers in London, and the Out Ports, to prepare the said Accounts: And the Officers of this Port having laid before this Board the following Accounts; the same are herewith humbly presented; -

1. An Account of the Quantities of Wines and Brandies imported into L for 22 Years, from Michaelmas 1674 to Michaelmas 1696: a. An Account of the Quantities of Wines and Brandies imported into London, and the Out Ports, for

16 Years and J, from Michaelmas 1696 to Christ-viasijn.

Mail. 1

The Commissioners crave Leave, hereupon, to acquaint this honourable House, That the Office of ln-spedor General being erected in the Year 1696, for extracting and keeping general Accounts of Imports and Exports in London, and the Out Ports, for the Information of the Publick; before which time it was found impracticable to make out such Accounts in any reasonable time; they have obtained from that Year a perfect Return to the Order of this honourable House, to Chrijhnas last; but that the Accounts for the Years preceding cannot be had from the Out ports; the Commissioners being informed, by several Answers already received. That many of the Books are wanting; the same having not been regularly delivered over on Deaths, or Removals of Officers, to the Persons who succeeded: But the Commissioners humbly take Leave to acquaint this honourable House, That from the general observations which have been made by the Officers of the Customs, the W ines brought into the Out Ports may bear a Proportion of about a Fourth Part to the Port of London:

Which is humbly fubrnitted to this honourable House.

Ordered, That the said Accounts do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

An ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act to enable William Harvey the elder, Esquire, and William Harvey, Esquire. his Son, to settle a Jointure, and

grant a Lease; and for vesting the Inheritance, after a Term of Five hundred Years, of Lands, in , in

Trullees, to -be ibid, for railing Portions for his Daughters, was read the First time.

fiefolved.That the Bill be read a Second time.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing, and punching, Robberies that shall be committed in Hpufes, was read a Second time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Bejblved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Tuesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House upon the said Rill.

Mr. Bertie reported from the Committee, to whom the several Petitions of the Merchants in London and Bristol, trading in Tobacco, on behalf of themselves, and the Planters of Virginia and Maryland, were referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards de-ivered it in at, the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee had, according to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and find the same to he as followeth, fife.

That the Commissioners of the Customs attended the Committee, and agreed; That Tobacco imported pays Six Pence and One-third of a Peny per Pound for Customs; and that the Merohants give Baud to pay the new Subsidy in Three Months, and the Additional, and One-third, Subsidy, in Nine Months; and that Eighteen Months are allowed, by Law, for Exportation, as set forth in the said Petitions:

That to proye the othqr Allegations of the Petitions;

Mr. Richard Perry, Merchant, said, That the high

Duties payable on Tobacco imported and fold in this Kingdom, are more than it can Tear: To prove which, he presented a List of 24 Bankrupts who had been of late Years considerable Merchants and Planters:

Thathimself, and others, must have been in the like Condition, if they had npt lessened their Trade ip Tobacco; for that it would have been impossible for them to have paid the Duties: And it appeared to the Committee, by 15 several Accounts produced, for the Years 1709, 10, 11, and 12, That our Virginia and Maryland Tobacco fells in foreign Markets; viz. in Holland and Spain, for less than the Customs, Freight, and Charges, amounts to, considerably, besides the prime Cqft in £hp Plantations:

That this has caused divers other Merchants utterly to leave off trading in Tobacco; so that that Trade, which was formerly carried on, and encouraged, here, by Merchants, is fallen into the.Hands of the Planters, who cannot-subsist by it; and consequently the Plantation Trade, and Navigation, of this Nation, will be very much lessened:

That the high Duties, and Freight on Tobacco, in the Reign of the late King /Pm. was one great Cause of lessening our Plantation Trade; for this put the Dutch upon planting vast Quantities of Tobacco; who can afford to fell it cheaper than the Petitioners by One-half, and supply those foreign Markets which the Petitioners formerly served; viz. Stockholm, Hamburgh, Bremen, and many other Places, and even the Hollanders themselves: And they now mix Three-fourths of their own Tobacco with One of ours in Rolls; though formerly it; was One-fourth of theirs to Three-fourths of her Majesty’s Plantations: And Mr. Perry said, He has now 1,800 Hogsheads of Tobacco on shore, and there are

now on board, in the River of Thames, above 6,000 Hogslieads, which, one with another, will not yield -so Jh.per Hogshead, after Customs, and other Charges,

.paid; though the Duties amount to above 120,000; And that he has lessened his Trade, by Two-thirds, for 10 Years last past; and must continue so to do, unless Encouragement be given.

That it appeared also to the Committee, by an Account delivered in by Mr. Gerard Raesfield, which he affirmed to be the bell Account he could get in those Parts, About Five Years since, of the yearly Growth of several Tobacco Plantations in Holland and Germany, viz.

} log (heads.

In the Province of Utrecht - - - 22,000

In Vehie, Gdderland, and County of Zutplien 24,700 In Oventfftl ----- - 16,500

In Cleeves, or Cleveland - - - - 9,000

In Germany ----- - 21,000

Amounting in all, to 93,800 Hogsheads j each Hogs? head containing 500 Pounds of Tobacco:

And that the Dutch vastly increased their Plantations, by reason of the great Duties on Tobacco here, in the Reign of King William; and fold their Tobacco at Five Guilders per C. Weight.

Mr. Linton laid, He ul'ed to employ above 300 poor PnrXons,-annually, -here, in rolling Tobacco; but the Hollanders have intirely gotten that Trade.

Mr. Tho. Cary said, That he traded in exporting Tobacco, for 25 Years, into Holland, , and up the

Bultick, totPe Value of,£. ioo, oco per Annum; but has now left it off, by reason the Dutch supply the foreign Market oheaper than the EngMerchants can afford it; and that he has great Quantities of Leaf Tobacco at Stockholm, and elsewhere, which he cannot dispose of but to considerable Loss.

That, to prove that Planters now make Woollen, Linen, and other Manufactures;

Mr. Doy/ey said, He is a Native of Virginia, and came from theuce but a Month ago: that he lived'on James River for Six Years: and that the Planters there have left off planting Tobacco, and apply themselves to the making of Shoes, Linen, planting Cotton, and making of Druggets, in Surry County; and tdipost every House has a Loom: And said, That Captain Boling loft f. 50 per Cent, in returning Tobacco hither.

Mr. Charles Chiswell, Merchant, said, He lived in Virginia and Maryland for above 10 Years last past; and came from thence about Six Mouths since: That iu Ten Counties they have left off planting Tobacco, and, instead thereof, fow Wheat and Rarlev, which they export to Lisbon, and other Places; and most Families now spin Linen, Woollen, and Cotton, and keep Sheep, who used to have none:

That the high Duties on Tobacco have caused the Decrease of the Plantation Trade; and has heard it generally said, That the Planters will lJiip no more for England; and, if the planters qould make but f. 3 per Hogshead, he believes they would rather turn their Hands to the Tobacco Trade than any other.

Mr. Micajah Pern/ produced 10 several Policies of Insurance, within Three Years last, for several Ships Lading of Wheat that was exported from Virginia, and other Places on that Continent, to Lisbon, and the Ma-deras\ and that their Corn is much better than our English Corn, and is bought there from 18 to is. 6d. per Bushel; and fells for more titan our Wheat

at Lisbon, and th e Maderas.

Mr. Tobias Bowles said, That about Nine Years since ;he was in Virginia; and then their Corn was better, harder, and heavier, than English Corn, and that little or none was then exported from the Plantations.

John Falkner said, That Virginia Corn will keep better than English; and that ’tis within Four or Fivg Years that Corn has been exported from the Plantations; and, as a Proof of its Goodness, lie said, they export it in Bulk from the Plantations, whereas the English Corn is exported in Bags.

Mr. Milner, Merchant, said, That himself, and

several

iaANN. ji°,

several other Importers of Tobacco, received threatening Letters from the Custom-hotife, that, if they did notdif-charge their Bonds given, payable at Three Months, and Nine Months, they would be put in Suit J although it had been the general Practice not to call for Payment of those Bonds until the time allowed, by Law* for Exportation, was expired: And Mr. Milner further said; That the hasty Exportation of 15 or 16,000, Hogsheads of Tobacco to Holland, within Three Months after Importation, to prevent Prosecution of the Three Months Bonds, did occasion the Selling thereof for less than the Freight, Custom, and Charges, besides the Prime Colt intirely loft.

That, in answer to this last Paragraph, the Commissioners of the Customs presented to the Committee their Report to the Lord Treasurer, of the 26th t)ay of March last, upon the Tobacco Merchants Represen-tation to the Lord Treasurer, touching the Hardships they lay under; and praying to be indulged, so far as that their Bonds for Customs might not be put in Suit till after the time allowed, by Law, for Exportation of their Tobaccoes, be expired; which Representation the Lord Treasurer referred to the said Commissioners, to consider well the Cafe, and report what was fit for his Lordship to do therein:

That, by the said Report, it appeared, That, on the 2ot h of February last, the Commissioners taking into Consideration the State of the Bonds in the Hands of their Receiver General, they gave him Order to call upon the Merchants tocleartheir Bonds; to the Intent ihey might have no Reason to complain of their Bonds being delivered over to the Solicitor, to be put in Suit without timely Notice: And that, on the 10th of March, the Receiver General wrote Lettejs to

the Tobacco Merchants accordingly; which might occasion the said Represen tat ion: But none of those Bonds have as yet been putin Suit, till the time for Exportation has been expired, utiless where the Circum-itances of the Debt required immediate Proeefs: And that, considering the Merchants have been always so far indulged, that their Bonds, though payable before the Emi of 18 Months, have not been prosecuted till the Expiration of that time, the Commissioners cou-ceived ;t a Hardship on the Trade to put the Laws in Execution at this time, by a vigorous Prosecution of the said Bonds as they become due: But that this In* diligence, being, in Strictness, not conformable to the several Laws granting the said Duties, the Merchants were only rtlieveable by Parliament:

And the Commissioners said, They thought it reason* able, and for the Ease of Trade, that the same time be given for Payment of the Duties upon Bonds, as is allowed for Exportation; and that Twelve Months are enough for both, as they conceive; and that *tis hard for the Merchants to pay Interest on their Bonds, and have none allowed them on their Debentures and Certificates.

That, in pursuance of the Instruction from this House to the Committee, That they do consider of Ways to secure the Duties of her Majesty’s Customs, and to prevent the Running of Tobacco, the Committee thought it proper to have the Assistance of the Commissioners of the Customs, and also of the Tobacco Merchants, therein; which they severally delivered to the Committee in Writing; and which the Committee have ordered to be presented to the House; viz.

To the .'honourable the Committee, to whdrti the Petition of the Merchants iu ,trading in

i The Commissioners of her Majesty’s Customs, in pur* fuan.ee of an Order of the honourable Committee, of the 8th Instant, do humbly lay before them the following Proposals; which they conceive may be necessary for the better securing her Majesty’s Customs, and preventing the Running of Tobacco:

That all Tobaccoes be landed in.....Days after

Importation, or the Report of the Ship; and that, on paying down the Half Subsidy, the same be put into proper Warehouses, under the Queen’s Locks:

That all damaged Tobacco, which the Merchant shall refuse to pay Duty for, be separated and destroyed:

That the Tobacco which shall be taken out of such Warehouses for Home-confuinption, within Months, shall pay the Remainder of the Duties, with

.....Discounts, to be computed in proportion from the time of the Entries, or on good Security for paying

the same in.....Months: And that all Tobacco for

Exportation be not delivered but of the said Warehouses, but in order to be forthwith exported; and upon Oath, and Security, not to be re-landed, Sic.: Nevertheless, if any Merchant shall, upon Entry, pay down all the Duties of the said Tobacco, the same shall be forthwith delivered to him, with a fitting Discount, as an Encouragement for so doing:

That all Tobacco remaining in such Warehouses, after ..... Months, shall be fold publickly, by Inch of Candle; the Produce to be applied, first, to Payment of the Duties; and the Overplus to be rendered to the Merchant:

That all Persons that flat or cut Tobacco stalks be liable to a Fine; and that all Mills, or other Engines, used in the flatting or cutting Tobacco (talks, be destroyed:

That Provision be made for a proper Encouragement for the exporting Cut or Roll Tobacco, upon due Proof of the Duties having been paid:

All n hich is humbly submitted.

Patent Officers of the Customs Proposal for securing the Duties on Tobacco.

May it please your Honours,

Having received your Minute, of the 8th Instant$ wherein we are to consider of Ways to secure the Duties, and prevent the Running, of Tobacco, and lay the same before the Board: wecraveLeavetoinformyou, That we doobserve the high Duties upon Tobacco have brought that Trade into few Hands; that a great many of them are already broke; and that most of those w ho remain dill in that Trade, are so embarrafied in great Debts to the Crown, for the Duties on Tobacco, that they areata Stand, and cannot go on therein; so that we cannot think of any better Way to preserve the Trade, and secure the Duties than if it were possible Ly lefi’ening the Duties; without which, we are afraid, the Importation of Tobacco will lessen yearly: As for Wa3-s to prevent the Running of Tobacco, that Information will better be given you by those Officers that are concerned in the landing and re-shipping Tobacco for Exportation:

All which is humbly submitted.

Dated, Custom-house, Chr. Towenfend,

The Answers of the Virginia Merchants to the Proposals of the honourable Commissioners of her Majesty’s Customs, laid before this honourable Committee on the X2th of May 1713.

In the Proposals of the honourable Commissioners of Customs, laid before this honourable Committee, it is proposed;

5 B " That

Tobacco

370 21

"That allTobaccocs be landed in..... Days after " Importation, or the Report of the Ship; and that, on paying down the Half Subsidy, the same be put into " proper Warehouses, under the Queen’s Locks

We humbly apprehend, That these Warehousesr are to be general and compuffive; if they are intended as ffach, we are of Opinion, that they will be found impracticable; and, in the Consequence, ruin this Trade:

It will be hard for the Merchant, upon Entry of his Goods, to pay down the Half Subsidy, and thereby be fabje&ed to pay Freight and Charges; and; at the same time; hare his Property locked' up; which will be attended'with the following Evils; viz.

Such Tobaccoes as are only forforeigwConfomption-mull, after landed, be sorted as the several Markets require; there being frequently different Sorts'in the' fttme Hogshead; and very often a great many damaged, which must of necessity be re-packed:

There are many Perl'ons who come from foreign Parts, and Merchants commissioned here, bay final! Parcels for' Exportation; which cannot be done without great Difficulty, if our Tobaccoes are kept under the Queen’s Locks;

For want of having our Tobacco within our Pbflfef- fions, to fort anddlfpose of it, as before-mentioned,' we must be obliged to export, in gross, our whole Parcels for Holland, &c.; whither the Buyers will naturally resort, to suit themselves with proper Parcels:

This Method of housing Tobacco will utterly destroy the Roll and Cutting Trade: Rolling requires a great Number of Hands, and very much Room: Besides, the Mystery, which every Manufacturer keeps as a Secret," to support himself and Family by, he will not expose to publick View, which cannot be avoided in these Warehouses: This will quite take away our manufacturing Tobacco, and, consequently, the Labour of many Thousands of Poor: Tobacco is very different in Quality, from any other Commodity which at present are under this Way of Warehousing; viz. Pepper, Coffee, TCa: Such Warehouses would oblige the Merchant to ‘ expose his Customers, and the Privacy of his Affairs; and give the Buyers a great Advantage, by knowing what Quantity of Tobacco remains in the Importers Hands; which is the Business of both Buyer and Seller to keep as a Secret:

No Merchant can possibly raise ready Money to clear his Tobacco out of the said Warehouses while the Duties remain thus high: Besides, all Merchants give large Credits when they lellthcir Tobacco; from SiX to Sixteen Months: And if, as the Commissioners propose, the Tobacco may be delivered the Merchant out of the Warehouses on giving Security, the Security may as well be taken at the time of the: Merchants Entry, without putting him to the Charge and Trouble of housing:

It’s intended. That all Tobacco taken out of these Warehouses shall not be capable of Exportation, and a Drawback; whereas all Merchants, when they have, for a whole Year’s Trade, fold all they can in this Kingdom, they must at lall clear their Warehouses of the ordinary Sort of Tobacco so left, by exporting it generally to Spain, &c. to make Snuff: If this be not allowed, some Merchants will, in Two or three Years Trade, have their Warehouses filled with ordinary Tobacco; and' their ready Money, which they have advanced to clear their Tobacco out of the Queen’s Warehouses, . will be effectually locked up in their own, without any Prospeet of turning it into Money to carry on their Trade.

It is proposed, by the Commissioners, " That all damaged Tobacco, which the Merchant flia.ll refuse " to pay Duty for, be separated and destroyed :"

This Proposition will be very difficult in the Execution: But if this honourable Committee shall think fit to make a Trial, we humbly desire, that it may be a temporary Law only, for Three Years; and that Provision be made, that the Merchants may have a Consideration for the Freight, and prime Cost, of their Tobacco so destroyed: As_to Stalks; if the Mills are prohibited to fiat them, and a reasonable Value given 21

Mail,

A. 1713.

by the Queen, on their Delivery to the Officers, to b* destroyed, it will effectually cure this Evil.

In Obedience to the Order of this honourable Committee, we hope we have herein artfwered the several Articles of the Commissioners of the Customs to your Honours Satisfaction: We cannot but conclude, this* Way of housing Tobacco, as they propose, is utterly impracticable; and will put a finishingStroke' to this Trade* and effectually'rivet the Planters in the feve--ral Manufactures wherein they have made so great a’ Progress:

For remedy whereof, we humbly propose;

First, That the Merchants Bonds for Payment of all the Duties on Tobacco, and' the time of Exportation, may commence from the Day of the Merchant’s Entry: That all the Duties on Tobacco, which, by Law, may be secured, be put into One Bond, payable Eighteen Months, which is the time allowed, by Law,' for Exportation:

That there be the same Allowance for Waftd and* Decay on all the final! Duties as is now, by Law, allowed on the Impost Duty:

That the Half Subsidy, or Halfpeny per Pound1 Weight, on Tobacco, now detained, may be also drawn-back on Exportation.

Unless these Indulgences be granted by Parliament; the greatest Part of the foreign Trade will be inevitably loft, and the Plantations rendered useless to tain-, which we humbly think is a national Concern, and hope may deserve the Consideration of this honourable Committee.

The Duties on Tobacco for the Home-consumption: are so vastly high, above Six times the Value, That the Planters have not, of late Years, been able, by its Produce, to clothe the Servants that made it: It is therefore humbly, hoped this present Parliament will lower the Duty:

If this be not granted, the Revenue will in this, as Experience (hews it has in Pepper, and aH other Cafes of the like Nature, annually decrease: For it is not possible to secure foexceflive a Duty on what is of so little Value in itself from fraudulent Practices, but by such oppressive Methods as will force the fair Merchant to quit a Trade, which can be carried on by none but Persons whose Morals and Fortunes are equally desperate.

This would be prevented by a moderate Duty, and undoubtedly bring more Money into the Exchequer; protect the fairTrader;cause the Planters toapply themselves, as formerly, ouly to making Tobacco; and very much increase the Navigation, as well as the Exports of Woollen, and other Manufactures, from Great Britain.

If damaged Tobacco and Stalks are destroyed, and these Indulgences granted, it wiU fake off the Temptation to all the Frauds practised, which the many good Lkws now in Force are, by Experience, found not able to prevent.

All which is humbly submitted.

May 16th, 1713.

A Petition of several Planters, Inhabitants of, and Merchants trading to, the Bland of Jamaica, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by a Clause in an Act, of the Sixth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of the Trade to America, such Duties were demanded on Prize Goods brought into the said Island, as often exceeded the Value of the Prize; and several Captors, their Agents, or Securities, were obliged to enter into Bonds with excessive Penalties: That these excessive Duties have been since taken off; and Proceedings on' such Bonds ordered to be staid: That though Penalty of such Bonds amount to £.54,830 there is no more due than £.9,043 os. id.current Money which,

when all Charges, with the Exchange, are deducted, amounts to about £.5,000 Sterling: That, though the Bonds were given at Jamaica, the greatest Part ofthofe Prize Goods have been imported into Great;

paid here so high a Duty, that they fold for but little more than those Duties, and the Charges, amounted to: That, if those Bonds be not remitted, it will be a Dif-couragemerrt to the Seafaring-men of the Island; and also a Prejudice to the Securities on such Bonds: And praying the Consideration of the House, and Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same to the House:

The humble Representation and Petition of the Bailiffs, Wardens, Assistants, and Commonalty, of the Trade, Art, and Mystery of Weavers, London, on behalf of themselves and Trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Silk Manufacture of this Kingdom is now about Twenty times as great as it was in 1664; and all Sorts of Black Silks for Hoods and Scarves, and all coloured Silks, Ribbands, Sic. made as good here, as in France, or any other Country: That as the Silk Manufacture increases, so does the Exportation of our Cloth, Serges, and other Woollen Manufactures, to Turkey and Italy; and the Return from those Parts are made in raw, and thrown, Silk: That, by the Treaty of Commerce with France, the free Importation of the like Manufactures from France into Great Britain are permitted: That, if there is no Provision made to encourage our own Manufacture of Silk, it will ruin our Trade, and many thousand Families; lessen the Consumption of our Wool, and lower the Value of Land: And praying the Consideration of the House; and that the Silk and Woollen Manufactures may not lie under too great Discouragement by . reason of the said Commerce.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Re/ohed, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, at Eleven of the Clock, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Bill for the better regulating the Elections of Members to serve in Parliament for that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Mr. Shackerly reported from the Committee, to whom

it was referred to consider what Laws are expired, or near expiring, and which of them are fit to be revived and continued, That they had considered the Matters to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place j and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read; and are as follow; viz.

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the A ft, made in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Years of the Reign of the late King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for the better Relief of the Poor of this Kingdom; which, except what related to the Corporations therein mentioned, and thereby constituted, was enacted to have Continuance until the 29th of May 1665, and from thence to the End of the First Session of the next Parliament; which Act, except as aforesaid, hath been, by several subsequent Acts, continued to several limited times, and is near expiring; and being found to Jie a very useful and necessary Law; be made perpetual.

a. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Tha t the Act, made in the Sixth Year of her present Majtw V*s Reign, intituled, An Act for the Importation of Coclu.^eal from any Ports in Spain during the present War, t'pd Six Months longer, be continued.

3. Refilveul That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Act, *n the Thirteenth and Fourteenth

Years of the Reign' the late King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for preventing of Theft and Rapine upon the Northern-Bor.'icis of England, and the several subsequent Acts for cont.’,ulinS the same having been

found very useful and necessary, and are near expiring, be made perpetual:

4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Third and Fourth Years of the Reign of her present Majesty, intituled, An Act for encouraging the Importation of Naval Stores from her Majesty’s Plantations in America which is near expiring; be continued.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, an Act, made in the Seventh and Eighth Years of the Reign of the late King William the Third, intituled, An Act, That the Solemn Affirmation and Declaration of the People called Quakers shall be accepted, instead of an Oath in the ufuat Form; which was Enacted to have Continnance for the Space of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the next Session of Parliament; which Act, by an Act, made in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Years of the Reign of the said late King William, was continued to be in force for and during the Term of Eleven Years, after the Determination of the said recited Act, and from thence to the End of the next Session of Parliament; which, said Act is near expiring; be continued.

6. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Clause in an Act, made in the Ninth and Tenth Years of the Reign of the late King William, intituled, An Act to settle the Trade to Africa (in the Words following; viz. And whereas by an Act of Parlia--ment, made in the Fifth and Sixth Years of the Reign of his present Majesty, and the late Queen among other things, it was Enacted, That no other Copper than what is made of English Ore, only, should be exported; which proving very prejudicial to the Trade of England, by enabling Foreigners to export Copper much cheaper than it can be carried from England: Be it Enacted, by the Authority aforesaid, That it shall and may- -be lawful to and for any of his Majesty’s Subjects to export from England all such' Copper Bars as hath or shall be imported into England from foreign Parts; and, upon Exportation, shall drawback all Duties, or vacate the Securities, saving the One-half of the old Subsidy, as is ufuul in other Commodities), being expired, be revived.

red, the Matter, as it appeared to him; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he reaid the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That it appeared to the said Committee, by an Extract of Minutes, containing an Address from the Governor, Council and Assembly, of Jamaica, dated the Twenty-seventh and Twenty-eighth of March One thousand Seven hundred and Ten, delivered to the Committee by Mr. Popple, Secretary to the Lords Commissioners of Trade and Plantations, That the Duties demanded on Prize Goods, by virtue of an Act, 6* Amite Regina, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of the Trade to America, often very much exceeded the Value of the Prize.

That it further appeared by the said Address, and the Instances annexed to it; and by the Examination of Richard Rigby Esquire, a Member of the Council in that Island, who had been present at the Examination of those Matters in Jamaica; That the Demand of those Duties had been a great Discouragement to that Colony: That the Sea-faring men had deserted in great Numbers; and were not likely to return, unless those Duties, and the Bonds entered into, were remitted.

That it also appeared to the Committee, 'That those Duties were taken off, for the timeenfuing, by aClause in an Act, 90 Anna Regina, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of Trade to America’, and all Proceedings upon the Bonds entered into were ordered to be flayed till the End of the then next Session of Parliament:

And by the Account of the Collector of Jamaica, delivered to the Committee by Mr. Carcqffe, Secretary to the Commiflxoners of Customs here, it appeared. That though the Penalty of the Bonds amounted to^.54,830, there was really due no more than. 9,043. oj. id. current Money of that Island.

That the said Richard Rigby, upon his Examination, further informed the Committee, That fmee the Act 9® Anna Regina, he knew some of the Agents had paid a Duty, laid by the Act of Assembly upon Prize Goods, which had always been laid for the Support of that Government, and which was confirmed by the aforesaid Act to be paid; and therefore had so muchless in their Hands now to answer the British Duties; which even at first had not been sufficient:

And that the Prize Goods brought into Jamaica, except Goods of Europe, were generally sent to Great Britain; where they paid a Duty, which, together with the Charges, very near amounted to the Value oflhem:

And that many of the Privateers belonging to afterwards carried their Prizes to New York, and other Parts, without returning to Jamaica: And the War being ended, hefpared, unless they were invited to return, by the Discharge of theie Bonds, many of them would turn Pirates; besides, that the Payment of them would not only prove a great Hardship to the Securities, by being answerable for more than they have, but also to

A Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, and Assistants, Commercial of the incorporate Company of Clothiers, in the City wlttL of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; ra* *" setting forth. That if the present Duties on French wrought Silks be lessened, it will be of evil Consequence to the Clothing Trade of this Nation; but more particularly to this City; by reason Worcesterwhite Cloths are chiefly sent to Turkey, from whence we have raw Silks iu Exchange: That if due Care be not taken to encourage the bringing in raw Silks to Great Britain as cheap as to other Nations, the Petitioners Trade mull of Necessity be ruined, and English Wool fink much in its Value, and many Thousands of poor Manufacturers: be undone: And praying the Relief and Protection of this honourable House; and that the Privileges and Advantages, which they formerly enjoyed, may be restored upon the same Duties that were settled by the Tarilf of 1664.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill to make effectual the 8th and yth Articles of the Treaty of Commerce between Great Britain and France, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Clothiers, concerned in the Woollen Ditto. Mamjfacture, of Troubridge, and adjacent Villages; of Froom, and adjacent Villages; and of; was

presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by a Treaty of Commerce between England and Portugal, the Duties in England are to be -j-d higher upon the Wines of France than those of Portugal; and that such Duties only are paid on the Woollen Manufactures of Great Britain in that Country: That great Quantities of Goods are yearly exported, and fold there, much more than the Value of the Wines, Oils, fife. imported thence; by which means many thousand Families are maintained, and a great Balance yearly coming to this Kingdom:

And that by a Law to reduce the Duties upon French Wines, fife, of France, as low as those of Portugal, or any Nation, might induce Portugal to prohibit, or lay a high Duty on, the Woollen Manufactures of Great Britain, to the utter Ruin of that Trade: That by a late Treaty of Commerce between her Majesty and the mostChristian King, that such a Law shall be first pasted as aforesaid, and that all Prohibitions laid upon French Goods by Parliament, since 18th September 1664, be taken off, France hath agreed to allow the Subjects of Great Britain to fell Cloths, Ratines, and Serges, subject to the Duties of the Tariff of 7th of December 1699; and, to facilitate the Trade thereof to import them by St.Valery, Rouen upon the Somme, and by Bourdeaux, only; where they shall be subject to Visitation, as those ‘ made in that Kingdom: By which Visitation the Petitioners are afraid their Officers will determine the Lengths, Breadths, fife, of our Cloths, according to their Model, and at any time to throw them into Water; which, with the Loss of the Market, and Charge of being manufactured anew by them, or the Petitioners fending their Sheermen over to finish them, would be a great Discouragement, and Prejudice to their Trade:

And, by the said Tariff, the Duty of every Piece of Spanish Cloth, of 25 Eils, is 55 Livres 10 Sols; which is a Fourth Part of the Price for which the finest Cloth can be made in Great Britain, and near Half the Value of the Middling Cloth; which amounts to a Prohibition, unless it could be made much cheaper in Great Britain than in France; That the Subjects of his most Christian Majesty are now arrived to a great Perfection in the Woollen Manufactures; so that they-pretend to make as good of every Sort in France as is made in Great Britain: That the finest Cloth is made entirely of Spanish Wool, without Mixture of English

Wool 7

392

4' Junii.

J. 1713.

Wool; and the French, by their Opportunities of Carriage by Longrone, Agredand other inland Passages

of Spain, may avoid paying the Cadorns; by which means they are likely to have their Wool

cheaper than her Majesty’s Subjects: That the Subjects of France have, of late Years, converted vast Tracts of Land to Sheep-walks; and, being supplied by the Ovvling Trade with our Wool, Wool is at a low Price in France, and their Materials cheap for all the Parts of the Woollen Manufacture: That the Hire of all Sorts of labour is not above Two-thirds of the Price that’s given in Great Britain: The Petitioners are of Opinion, That though coarse Wool were as dear again in France as Great Britain; yet, by the low Wages given in with their Advantage on the Price of Oil, Soap, and dyeing Goods, the whole Manufacture would be cheaper there than in Great; and that little or no

Quantity would be exported hence, or fold there, though the Duties of 55 Livres 10 Sols were taken off, and the same allowed to be sold in every Port of France, subject neither to Customs nor Visitation: And, by not passing such a Law as aforesaid, the Treaty with Portugal may still fubfill; when passing it may endanger the Petitioners Trade, with the Loss of the Exports of Woollen Manufactures there, without gaining an Equivalent; and at last be the Ruin of the Petitioners, and many Thousand Families maintained by the fame, and the Exports to Portugal: And praying such Relief in the Premises as to this honourable House shall feetn meet.
