those Duties amounting to a Prohibition: That the Exportation of our Woollen Manufactures to Portugal, Spain, and Italy, is of late very much increased; but fear will be exceedingly lessened, if not loft, should the Duties on French Wiues be reduced to an Equality with those of the aforesaid Places; apprehending it maybe a means of railing the Duties of our Manufactures there, or cause an intire Prohibition: That, by the Alliance between the Crowns of France and Spain, France hath gained greater Advantages in Trade than formerly they had; for thereby they import Spanish Wool on better Terms than the Subjects of this Kingdom; and export Spanish and other Cloths to Turkey in greater Quantities than formerly; and import, as the Produce thereof, raw Silk, which they manufacture in France-, which, if permitted to import their wrought Silks into England under easy Duties, will prove very defiruClive to the Turkey Trade, which takes off the greatest Part of our Cloths, and is the most beneficial Trade belonging to the Woollen Manufactures; and thereby many Thousand poor Families have and may be maintained, which otherwise mud become a Burthen to their respective Parishes; and will, consequently, fink the Value of Lands of England to a great Degree, and lessen the Price of Wool: And praying the Relief of the House in the Premises.

The House being informed. That the Commissioners of the Customs attended;

They were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House their Answers to the Three Orders of the 3d Instant: With,

An Account of the Exports from London to France, between Michaelmas 1668 and Michaelmas 1669: And, An Account of Goods imported from France into the Port of London, from the 19th oi October 1668, to the 20th of October 1669: And,.

Woollen Manufacture exported to Portugal, in Four Years, before the Year 1703: And,

An Account of the Quantities and Species of Goods exported from the Out Ports to France, from Michaelmas 1685 to Michaelmas 1686: And,

An Account of Goods imported into the Port of London from France, from Michaelmas 1685 to Michaelmas 1686: And,

An Account of the Quantities, and Species, of Goods imported into the Out Ports from France, from Michaelmas 1685 to Michaelmas 1686.

And then they withdrew.

And the Titles of the said Accounts were read.

The said Answers and Accounts are as follow; viz.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament affenibled;

The Return of the Commissioners of her Majesty’s Customs to Three Orders of this honourable House, dated the 3d Instant.

THE Commissioners, in Obedience to the First of the said Orders, humbly lay before this honourable House an Account of the Exports from the Port of London to France, between Michaelmas 1668 and Michaelmas 1669, N° 1: And also, the Imports from France to the Port of London, N* 2, from the 20 October 1668 to the 1 19 October 1669; except the Wines (the Books of Entries for Wines, for that time, being not to be found; and the Books for other Goods being deficient from Michaelmas 1668 to the 20th October following); according to the Entries in the Custom-house Books; prepared and certified by the proper Officers.

In Obedience to the Second Order, they humbly lay before this honourable House an Account of the Woollen

unit. 1713*

Manufactures entered to Portugal for Four Years before the Year 1703; distinguishing the Species and Quantities in the several Years, in the annexed Paper, N* 3.; as prepared and certified by the Inspector General of Exports and Imports: And,

In Obedience to the Third Order, the Commissioners humbly lay before this honourable House an Account of the Exports from England to France, from Michaelmas 1685 to Michaelmas 1686, contained in the Account

N* 4.; and the Imports from France, N° 5, during the same time; being the only Accounts the Officers had ready: As to the Accounts for the other Years, mentioned in the said Order; viz. 1687, and 1688; the Commissioners, upon Receipt thereof, gave Directions to the respective Officers to prepare them with all Expedition; and, as soon as the same can be perfected, the Commissioners will lay them before this honourable House.

Which is humbly submitted.

Custom-house, /. Stanley, Bridges,

London, 4* June 17131 Robert W,m.son, E. Gibbon.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Hiccocks and Mr. Lovibond:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for enabling Sir Charles Gresham Baronet, to raisetheSum of Five thousand Pounds, and Interest, and Maintenance, for Elizabeth the Daughter of his Brother, Sir Edward Gresham, Baronet, deceased; and to make Provision for his younger Children: T° which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for confirming Articles, and veiling the Manor of Kirby Underwood, in the County of Lincoln.and other Manors, Lands, and Hereditaments, thereby agreed to be sold, in Trustees, for discharging the Debts of Sir Brown-low Baronet, deceased, and his Daughters Portions; and other Purposes in the said Articles mentioned;, without Amendment. And,

The Lords have agreed to the Amendment, made by this House, to the Bill, intituled, An Act to enable William Harvey the elder, Esquire, and Esquire, his Son, to settle a Jointure, and grant a Lease, and for veiling the Inheritance, after a Term of Five hundred Years, of Lands, in , in Trustees,

to be sold, for raising Portions for his Daughters.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The Order being read, for the Second reading the Bill to: abolish Tryals by Angle Combat; and to prevent the impious Practice of Duelling; ,

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a Second time upon Saturday Morning next.

The Order being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for securing the Freedom of Parliaments, by limiting the Number of Officers in the House of Commons;

And the Question being put. That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair;

It passed in the Negative.

Resolved, That this House will, upon next,

at Twelve of the Clock, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

A Bill to make effectual the Eighth and Ninth Articles of the Treaty of Commerce and Navigation between Great Britain and France, was, according to Order, read a Second time.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put. That the Bill be committed;

The House divided.

The Yeas go forth.

Tellers for the Yeas, J }*«

Tellers for the Noes,| } *35

So it was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Tuesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

Ordered, That the several Petitions which have been presented to the House, relating to the said Bill, be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Petitioners be heard before the Committee, if they think fit; and that no more than Two Persons be heard upon any Petition.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thursday Morn" British ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of that Part of her Majesty’s Speech, which relates to the Encouragement and Improvement of the Fishery.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to Half Pay her Majesty, That the will be pleased to direct an Offic*r*> Estimate to be laid before this House of the Half Pay to be given to the Officers who have served Well by Land during the late War.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s moil honourable Privy Council.

Ordered, That all Committees, which were to fit this Committees. Afternoon, be adjourned.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

Ditto. A Petition of divers Planters, on behalf of themselves,

and others, who have Sugar Plantations in her Majesty’s Colonies, in America, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have per used the Bill, now depending, intituled, A Bill for establishing the Trade to Africa free and open to all her Majesty’s Subjects of Great Britain, and the Plantations: That no Supply of Negroes is provided for the Sugar Colonies, or any Stock obliged to be exported; and should the said Bill pass into a Law, to the Pleasure of some designing Persons, who would impose greatly on the Petitioners, and engross that Trade wholly to themselves, the Petitioners cannot depend on certain Supplies, unless from substantial Security, by a large Stock appropriated for that End; for want of which the Plantations will become uncultivated, and the Trade and Navigation from Great Britain be loft: And praying to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, upon the Third Reading of the said Bill.

iy.tto. A Petition of the Royal African Company was

presented to the House, and read; praying to be heard against the Bill for establishing the Trade to Africa free and open to all her Majesty’s Subjects of Great Britain, and the Plantations:

And the said Petition was, by Leave of the House, withdrawn.

A Petition of the Dyers, Cloth-WOrkers, Packers, Commercial Calenders, Setters, and others concerned in the WooIIen Treaty with Manufactures, in behalf of themselves, and many Thou-fond others, living in and about the City of London, was presented to the House and read; setting forth, That great Quantities of the Woollen Manufactures of this Kingdom have been annually exported to Portugal,

Italy, Turkey, the Levant and Spin time of Peace:

That it is notorious, that the Encouragement of late Years given to the importing into these Kingdoms the Product of those Countries, upon easier Terms than Goods of the some Kinds were suffered to be imported from France, has enabled them, in return, to take off such large Quantities of our Manufactures, which hereafter they cannot do, should the Duties on the Goods and Merchandizes brought from France be reduced equal with the Duties on Goods, Sc. of like Kind, imported from other Countries; and should all the Prohibitions on Merchandizes brought from thence, ina-posed since 1664, be repealed: That French Commodities have been tod much preferred here to the like of other Countries, when they were at higher Rates; and, if cheaper, will prejudice the Importation of other Wines; and that from thenceforwards raw Silks from Turkey and Italy will not bemanufactured in this Kingdom, whilst the French import their Silks ready manufactured; which will abolish the Manufactures of like Kind in Great Britain, and ruin the Exportation of Woollen Goods to those Parts: That, should the French obtain the Ibwering the Duties, and Repeal of the Prohibitions on their Goods and Merchandizes, they will engross the raw Silks, and dyeing Wares, from Turkey and Italy; and supply those foreign Markets with their Woollen Manufactures, which formerly were only supplied from Great Britain; to the Ruin of the said Manufactures: That at the same time the French demand the Lowering of the Duties, and Repeal on their Goods and Merchandizes, propose to continue higher Duties on the said Woollen Manufactures, and other Merchandizes, amounting almost to Prohibitions; and with a Design to improve their own Manufactures; to the Ruin of the Petitioners: And praying this House to continue and encourage them in this Kingdom, on such a Foot as may enable them to supply the Portuguese,

Spaniards, &c. with the Manufactures of this Kingdom, and advantageous to Great Britain.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to make effectual the Eighth and Ninth Articles of the Treaty of Commerce between Great Britain and France is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard thereupon, before the said Committee, if they think fit.

And the said Proposal and Resolution are as follow; viz.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled.

Whereas, in pnrfuuuce offeveral Arts of Parliament, Exchequer Bills, to the Amount of 2,500,000, and £. 400,000, have been made out, and issued, for her Majesty's Supply; and other quarterly Exchequer Bills have been, and may be, made out for Payment of the Interest, and Allowances for Circulation, upon the Bills for £. 2,500,000 and £. 400,000 first mentioned, until the Funds established by those Arts shall commence; all which B'l'.s, by the said Arts, were at first to be answered by the Governor and Company of the Bank o at such times only as they should pass through the Revenue: But the said Governor and Company afterwards, by an Art of the gth of her Majesty’s Reign, for the Con-siderations therein mentioned, are obliged to exchange all the said Bills for Money, from time totiuie, at Demand, whether such Bills should pass the Revenue or not:

Now the said Governor and Company of the Bank of England humbly propose, That for the Publick Supply this Year, if it shall be thought fit, to issue a ftnther Sum of Twelve hundred thousand Pouudsin Exchequer Bills; and that the Principal, together with the Interest thereof, at Twc-pence per Centum per Diem, and an Allowance of three Pounds/;er Centum in 1 eipert

thereof, for Circulation, to he answered quarterly, be charged upon the present Funds for Exchequerliills, in the like manner as is settled by the former Acts; and for paying off, and cancelling, the said lall-mentioned Bills, Yol . 17.

of £. 100,000, per Annum, for Ten Years, and a Year’s Notice, are willing to undertake, and be obliged, fronv the time of issuing any of the said further Bills for £. 1,200,000, to exchange for ready Money, all such of the said further Bills, and quarterly Bills to be made out, for the Interest thereof, and Allowance thereupon, as from time to time, and at all times, shall come to the Hands of any Person or Persons, and shall be demanded of the said Governor andt ompaay, to be exchanged for ready Money: But the said Governor and Company further humbly propose. By Order of the Court of Directors.

Mr. Conyers reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; Where they were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That, towards making the Duties for Goods and Merchandizes brought from France equal to the Duties payable for Goods and Merchandizes of tlielike Nature imported from any other Country it is

the Opinion of this Committee, That such and the like additional Impositionsupon several Sorts of Goods and Merchandizes, which were granted by an Act of Parliament in the Fourth Year of the Reign of their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, of blessed Memory, and are continued by several Acts of Parliament since made for the Uses and Purposes therein expressed, other than the particular Rate of 25 per Centum on French Goods, and the particular Duty on every Tun of French Wines thereby imposed, be charged and chargeable, for the like Uses and Purposes, upon all such of the said Goods and Merchandizes which shall be brought from France to Great , as by

the said Acts they are charged orehargeable upon Goods and Merchandiz, s of like Nature imported from other Countries in Europe.

Resolved, That, towards making the Duties for Goods and Merchandizes brought from equal to the Duties payable for Goods and Merchandizes of the like Nature imported from any other Country in Europe, it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Rate of Twenty-five Pounds per Centum, imposed by the said Acts on French Goods, be taken off, and be no longer payable.

Resolved, That, towards making the Duties for Goods and Merchandizes brought from France equal to .‘he Duties payable for Goods and Merchandizes of the like Nature imported from any other Country in Europe, it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Four Pounds per Tun, Part of the Duty of Eight Pounds per Tun, chargeable by the said Acts on French Wines, be abated; and that Four Pounds Tun, ^Remainder of the said Duty of Eight Pounds Tun, be continued, for the Uses and Purposes expressed in the said Acts, or such of them as are now in Force.

Resolved, That, towards making the Duties for Goods and Merchandizes brought from France equal to the Duties payable for Goods and Merchandizes of the like Nature imported from other Countries in Europe, it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in all Cases where, by general Words, in any Act or Acts of Parliament, made or passed during the Prohibitions of Trade and Commerce with France in the tjme of the late Wars, or any of them, any Duties of Customs or Excise, or any other Duties whatsoever, were imposed upon any foreign Goods or Merchandizes imported into Great Britain, for any Uses or Purposes whatsoever, the like Duties shall be understood to be due and payable, and shall be charged and chargeable, for the same Uses and Purposes, upon Goods and Merchandizes of tlielike Nature which shall be brought from into Britain,

as fully as the said Goods and Merchandizes from F> mice wo: Id have been charged or chargeable with those Duties, by the general Words of the said Acts, if there had been no such Prohibition of Trade or Commerce with France at the time of granting, or continuing, such Duties respectively.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That the said Resolutions be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to make effectual the Eighth and Ninth Articles of the Treaty of Commerce and Navigation between Great Britain and France, is committed; and that they do receive Clauses pursuant to the said Resolutions.

Mr. Oglethorp reported from the Committee, to

whom the Petition of Major General Henry dc Cort, Baron de Wales, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee having taken into Consideration the Petition of the Baron de Waif, and examined the Allegations therein contained, do find, That the Petitioner had the Honour to serve her Majesty as Colonel of a Regiment of Dragoons; and that he had a Commission, signed by the Duke of Marlborough, dated the First of January 170F, appointing the Petitioner a Brigadier General; and served two Years as such:

That by another Commission, under the Hands and Seals of the Earl of Orery, and Monsieur dated the First of January 1710, he was made a Major General; and served Two Years and Four Months, in that Quality.

That it appeared, by a Certificate signed byhisGrace the Duke of Ormond, That, in July 1712, when his Grace had received her Majesty’s Orders to separate her Troops, and those in her Majesty’s Pay, from such of the Allies as should refuse to agree to a Cessation of Arms with France; his Grace sent Orders to the Baron de Wales to be ready to join the Queen’s Troops, and march with the Regiment of Dragoons under his Com-Vol. 17.

liiand, when he should be required so to do i which Or* der the Petitioner readily obeyed: For which his Grace, together with the Earl of Strafford, according to the Instructions his Grace had received from the Secretary of State, did promise the Petitioner should be paid what should appear to be due to him from the Crown of Great Britain; and, as the Petitioner was appre-hensive he should, by following the Duke of Ormond's Orders, lose his Extraordinaries, which was by Agreement to be paid him by the States General, the said Duke promised the Petitioner further to use his Endeavours, that Reparation should he made the Petitioner for the Loss he should sustain by the Discharge of his Duty: The Petitioner obeying his Grace’s Orders, (he Deputies of the States General discharged the Petitioner from being Major General and stopped the Pay of his Extraordinaries:

That it also appeared, by a Certificate from the Pay Office, dated the 20th of May 1713, signed by Mr. William Sloper, That no Allowance had been made to

the Baron Wales, as General Officer, upon any Establishment in that Office; and that no Monies had been paid him from that Office, as such;

That the Petitioner, the Baron de did allege,

That, by his faithful Service to her Majesty, seeing himself deprived of all Hopes of ever being employed by the said Allies, he thought himself obliged to avoid their Resentment, and to seek for Refuge in England.

Ordered, That the Report do lie upon Table.

A Petition of Sir John Lambert Baronet, Samuel French Shepheard, and the Executors of the late Janies " "lf*.

David, was presented to the House, and read; setting c"ptu forth. That the Petitioners, in Augttjl 1708, bought of Henry Bray and John Bcxvden 23 Tuns, 1 Qr. of French Wines, at Penryne, taken by the Success Privateer of Guernsey, and condemned in the Court of Admiralty: That the Petitioners had Bills drawn on them by Peter Hill, their Agent, at Falmouth, to the Value of 1,050, payable to Receiver General of the Customs for the Duties of said Wines; whereof 20 Tuns, 3 Ilogf-heads, were ffiipped on board the Nero TopOi am, William Daire, Mailer, who failed from Falmouth, bound foi ^London, in October following, under Convoy of the

Dover and Sunderland-, but was taken by a French Privateer off of Beachy Head, in the Sight of the Sunderland, and carried into Calais-, where the Vessel and Wines were sold by the Privateer: That the Petitioners have applied to the Lord Treasurer of Great Britain, and been referred to the Commissioners of Customs:

That, the Duties being appropriated by Parliament, and the Law not providing for such Accidents, it was not in his Power to give them Relief; whereupon his Lordship ordered Prosecution against the Petitioners on the Bills of Exchange might be Hayed; whereby they might apply to Parliament for Relief: That by Act of Parliament, the Exporters of any Merchandize, for which the Duties have been paid, upon Proof the same were loft at Sea, or taken by the Enemy, are allowed to ftiip off the like Quantity, Custom-free; and the Petitioners conceive their same to be within the Equity of that Law: And praying, upon Payment of said Bills, they may be admitted to import as many French Wines,

Custom-free, as will amount to the Duties of those taken by the French.

The Lord Lumley reported from the Committee, to pi(ch and whom the Petition of the several Persons concerned in Tar mAm* the Making of Pitch and Tar from Roch or Roof Stone was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Petitioners, to prove the Allegations of

their Petition, called,

Mr. Robert Sand ford and Air. T Who

both said. That the said Pitch and Tar was made from a certain Stone, arising and growing in the Kingdom of Great Britain, called or known by the Name of Roch or Roof Stone; and that it hath cost the Proprietors, 1

within

i2 Ann.

421

within the Space of 20 Years, in bringing this great Undertaking to Perfection, near the Sum of Eight thousand Pounds:

And Mr. Sam!ford further said. That the Pitch

and Tar is much better than the foreign; he, having tifed of both Sorts, does find, that the Pitch far

exceeds the other in Duration; and, particularly, instances his using it upon a Ship of his own, Part being payed or pitched with the foreign Pitch, and the other Part with English Pitch, which he sent on a Voyage to Mount Sarrat, in the West Indies: and, at the Return of the said Ship to the Port of , it appeared, that

the foreign Pitch was consumed to Dirt; buttheEfl^-lish Pitch had so penetrated the Plank, that when the said Ship came to be breamed with Fire, in order to be r fitted, that it came out again with the Heat of the Fire: And the said Veil’d being a Second time payed, one Part with English Pitch, and the other with foreign, did proceed a Second Voyage to and, on her Return again to the Port of and being

hauled ashore to be refitted, the foreign Pitch was again turned to Dirt; and the Worm had bit her very much where the foreign Pitch lay; but the Pitch lay

fmoorh and firm, and little or no Worm at all had touched the Plank; and that it is also very useful, and exceeds the foreign, in pitching and tarring Weatherboards and Timber-boards, behaving often experienced it.

Mr. Wheeler said, He has been a Ship-carpenter about 40 Years, and of late Years hath used the English Pitch and Tar as well as the foreign; but finds the English to be more durable for preserving and keeping the Plunk, and far exceeds the foreign; and it is the bell that he ever used in his Life.

Mr. Jfauc Bennet, Purveyor to her Majesty’s Office of Ordnance, said, He had madeufe of the English Pitch for about two Years, on the Bottom, Sides, and Decks, of a Vessel, about 40 Tons; which has been employed in the River TIuimes and Midway-, and finds it keeps cleaner and longer than the foreign Pitch; and is allured, That if it be used upon a new Vell'el, before any other Pitch be laid on, being of an oily Substance, it will mightily preserve the Plank.

Mr. Peter Delamoll said, That he had, for 12 Years pall, very often used the English Stone Pitch, and have found it far exceed the foreign Pitch, by keeping Ships Bottoms clean and free from the Worm longer than any yet found out; being of a very imbibing Nature, and will not break and scale off, as foreign Pitch will do, if not mixed with Oil or Tar to soften it; but the,

without Mixture, fucks into the Plank, more than any other, and will continue clean, as well as fall, on the Ship’s Bottom, a whole West India Voyage, as he has often

experienced, by seeing it laid on himself, particularly on his Ships the Stowagel’rigot, the Hermitage, the London

Gaily, and the Be/Jy Brigantine; The two lad of which have used the said Trade Three or Four Years without sheathing, and very little worm-eaten; though fume Worms huck on the Outfideof the Pitch, but did not bite through; t he Be/Jy Brigantine went from London in 1712, payed with the said English Pitch, and lay Nine Months in Antcgoa, where the Worm eats mofl; and is now come home, the last Month, clean, and not eaten, except where the Bill of the Anchor scratched off a little of the Pitch from her bottom; her Anchor-stocks, which lay in the W ater, were notdone with it, being quite spoil-e<l by the Worm eating them, as may be now seen on board her in the River Thames: The first Experiment he made with it was on two Lime Hoys, one done with English, and the other with foreign; the English was clean at the Year’s End, but the foreign dirty and rotten: He further said. That he had a Shed, and Weather-boarding, done with the said English Pitch 15 or 16 Years since; and is Rill black, clean, and the Boards preferred from rotting, by the oily Part soaking into them.

That the said Pitch and Tar so made has been for many Years lall palt tried and experienced in many Parts of Ureal Britain, appeared to the Committee by Certi-

VOL. 17.

ficates under the Hands of several Merchants and others who have used the said Pitch and Tar, and likewise the foreign Pitch: and have found by Experience, that the English has been more lading than the foreign.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled;

The Return of the Commissioners of her Majesty’s Customs to the Orders of this honourable House, of the 10th Instant, directing the said Commissioners to lay before you the Scheme of Trade beween England and France, as entered in the Custom-house

Books, in the Y'ear 1674; and the Schemes and Computations they have in their Office of the said Trade, from Michaelmas 1668 to Michaelmas 1669.

The said Commissioners do humbly acquaint this honourable House, That they do find in a Book in their Secretary’s Office, commencing the gth September 1674, among Entries of divers Papers relating to different Matters, the Account hereafter mentioned, intituled,

" A Scheme of the Trade, as it is at present carried on " between England and France, &c." An exact Copy whereof, as certified by our Secretary, is herewith humbly laid before this honourable House:

But the Commissioners think it their Duty, humbly to observe. That the Account mentioned in the said Scheme, being from Michaelmas 1668 to Mich 1669, differs very much from the Account of that Y'ear, which was, by Order, laid before this honourable House, the 4th Instant, as far as the said Account could be compared with the Scheme; and therefore they humbly conclude,

That the said Sc heme could not be taken from the Custom-

By the Account above, your Lordships may perceive. That the Linen and Silk Manufactures, only, imported from France, amount to upwards of £. 800,000; and that the Manufactures of Wool and Silk exported from England thither, do not amount to £. 85,000; as also that all other Commodities of the Product and Manufacture of England exported into France, do not amount to £. 90,000 more; whereas the Wines, Brandies, and other Commodities, of the Product and Manufacture of France, imported into England, amount to upwards of £.320,000, besides an incredible Value of Toys, rich Apparel, Point Lace, S'c.; so that it is apparent, that the Exports of our native Commodities and Manufactures to France are less in Value by at least £.1,000,000 Sterling, than the native Commodities and Manufactures of France which we receive from thence: And, ifitpleafe your Lordships to reflect thereupon, your Lordships will easily discern the great Prejudice the English Nation have sustained, and the great Advantages the French have, and do daily make, by holding this Treaty in Suspense; this Nation being, upon the Matter, excluded Trade thither; while, in the meantime, the French enjoy all and as great Advantages as they can reasonably expect by any Treaty.

Memorial; and the Memorials, Petitions, Representations, Schemes of Trade, and Papers, relating thereto; aed the Representations to his late Majesty in 1697, in relation to the Commerce with France-, with the Memorials and Representations therein mentioned:

And the said Answer was read; and is as follows; viz.

Answer of the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations to au Order of the honourable the House of Commons, of the 10th Instant.

In obedience to an Order of this honourable House, requiring us to lay before this House the Memorial of Robert Meeres-, as likewise all Memorials, Petitions,

Representations, Schemes of Trade and Papers, relating the reunto, that are before us, concerning the Trade of England and France, between the Years 1664 and 1676; anil also the Representation made by the then Cora-miff oners of Trade and Plantations in 1697, in relation to the Commerce with France-, we take Leave to inform this House;

That, having searched our Books, we find no Memorial given in to the Board at any time by the forementioned Robert Mcers; and, having thereupon sent for him, he affirmed, That he never did deliver us* any.

We do lay before this House what we find in the Books in this Office between the Years 1664 and 1676, relating to the Trade between England and France -,viz.

Extract of the Minutes of the Lords of the Council, then a Committee for Trade and Plantations, from March 1675 to Jidy 1676:

Copies of Two Projects of a Treaty of Commerce with France, prepared in 1669:

The Copy of a Representation made by the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations to his late Majesty King William, in the Year 1697, upon the general State of the Trade of this Kingdom; in which are some Articles relating to the Trade with France:

As also, A Scheme of the Trade between England and France, dated the 29th of November 1674.

Which is most humbly submitted.

Guildford, Francis Gzyyn,

Phil. Meadows, T. Foley,

Robert Mention, J. Cotton.

Whitehall, June the 17th, 1713.

A Petition of the Clothiers, Combers, Weavers, and many Thousands concerned in the Woollen Manufactures, in and about the Town and Borough of Tavistock, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by the great Quantities of Wool of late carried out of this Kingdom, and Ireland to France, the French are enabled to make Serges, Cloths, Stull’s, Sic.and to fell them cheaper than the English can; and if not speedily prevented by Hopping the Exportation of all Wool, in such clandestine manner, will ruin the Woollen Trade in England: And praying That the Woollen Manufacture may be encouraged, both abroad and at home.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill be brought in to make the Laws more effectual for preventing the Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland to foreign Parts.

The Memorial is as follows; viz.

May it please your Lordships,

INQUIRY having been made, as said, by your Lordships Order, as several Places in the City of London, for Information of the Advantages, or Disadvantages, that may accrue to, or be fulfered by, this Kingdom, in granting to* the French King Cape Bralon, upon the Coall of Arcadia, and its Dependencies, by the present Treaty of Peace; we, as in Duty bound, for her Majesty’s and the Nation’s Service, and the Security of the Trade to all America, humbly prelume to lay before your Lordships a brief Account of some of the Disadvantages, and Prejudice, that probably will attend such Grant.

ill. The Place called Cape Bralon is not a small Point of Land, as the Name imports; but that, with the Country of Accadia, its Dependent, is of vast Extent; viz. 420 Miles in Length, and 120 Miles in Breadth; wherein are divers Harbours, which, both for Depth of Water, and commodious Entrance, are fit to receive in Security the Royal Navy of this Kingdom.

2d. The said Coast, and Entrance into those Harbours, are so well fortified by Nature, that they may, with a small Expence, be made almost impregnable;

Vo i. 17,

which, undoubtedly, the French King is well informed of, and was never yet found wanting to himself to secure and improve such Advantages as will accrue thereby.

3d. There is very good Fishing on the said Coast; where the Season begins earlier, and holds longer, than at Newfoundland, some say the whole Year; and the Fish is much brighter, better, more valuable, and earlier at all foreign Markets, than those of can

be; so that the French, by such Grant, would in a few Years intirely ruin, not only the Fishery of Newfoundland, but also of Nero England, which have a great Dependence on that Coast.

4. There is a considerable Trade on the said Coast for Furs, and other valuable Commodities; inso much that the French have laden on the said Coast about Ten Sail of Ships in a Year, befidcS what have been laden by her Majesty’s Subjects, which have also been very considerable Quantities.

5. The Advantages of making Oil on the Island of Cable, which have been made there in great Quantities,

will be loft, upon Pretence the said Bland is a Dependency of Cape Bralon; as to your Lordships may appear, by a briefSpecimen of the Usage which the Subjects of this Nation had from the French, during the last Peace; when the French Men of War, and Traders to that Place, would not suffer any of the Subjects of England to fish on the said Coast, nor upon any Banks or Shoals to the Northward or Eastward of Sable, but forced them away as far as the Isle of Shouls, which is above 480 Miles from Cape Bralon.

6. The said Coast is the only Place, in all America, as yet discovered, that produceth Coals; and upon that Coast they are so plenty, that Ships may lie close to the Place where they are, and load them.

We therefore humbly hope your Lordships will please duly to weigh, and rightly to represent to her Majesty, and her most honourable Privy Council, the unspeakable, and indeed incredible, Advantages that will accrue to France by such Grant; and consequently an irreparable Loss to the Crown and Subjects of this Nation in general, but more particularly to the Inhabitants of, and the Merchants and Traders to, Newfoundland and America:

For ifyour Lordships please to consider, That in same another War should happen between this Crown and France, which God forbid; and Cape and the

Coast of Accadia, which is so very fertile, and of so large an Extent, should be granted to France, and the Land peopled, manured, and cultivated, and the Harbours fortified; of what evil Consequence it might be to this Nation;

ill. As to the Fishery of Newfoundland, and Settlements of that Island, the French, bordering thereon, and having such commodious Harbours as may secure, support, and supply with Provisions, and Naval Stores, which are plenty in those Parts, may keep such Number of Ships there as ihey thall fee needful, wholly to prevent the Fishery, and destroy the Settlements, of that Bland, and, consequently, ruin the said Trade.

2d. The near Neighbourhood of the French to New England by Land, and of their Naval Force by Sea, will render the Navigation, not only to those Parts, but to all America, very hazardous and precarious.

3d. The French, by this means, will be capable of Applying the Indians, which in those Parts are generally in the French Interest, with Ammunition, SCc. so that, notwithstanding Peace with France, the said Indians will be thereby more capable to burn and ruin the Eastern Plantations of New; and the French

were never yet waning to encourage the fame.

4. The French may, with Ease, and great Expedition,

supply their Elands in the fVcJl with Stores and

Provisions; which are considerably increased in Number of Inhabitants; and have, even duringlhe lateWar, peo-pled and fortified the Island of , which borders

upon, and lies convenient for Trade with, the Coast of Crocoa; which, with the other Blands in their Possession, will render the Navigation of this Kingdom to those Parts - - - 5 R . not

Commercial Treaty with France.

And whereas the Trade to the Spanish is

Which is most humbly submitted.

Sir Tho. Hanmer reported from- the Committee, to whom it was referred to draw up an Address to her Majesty, That they had drawn up an Address- accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it ini at the Clerk’s Table: Where it was twice read; and is as follows;

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, having, at the Opening of this Session, congratulated your Majesty upon the Conclusion of a Peace, find ourselves now under equal Obligations of Duty to express our Thankfulness to your Majesty, since we have been acquainted with the Conditions and Terms of it; which by your great Wisdom have been procured, and by your gracious Condescension have been communicated to us: Your Majesty’s extensive Care hath not only provided for the Security, but the Honour, of your Kingdoms; and we should be wanting in our Concern for both, if tve should omit our just Acknowledgments for the particular Regards which your Majesty in this, as well as in other Instances, hath shewn to them.

The good Foundation your Majesty hath laid for the Interests of your People in Trade, by what you have done in the Treaty of Navigation and Commerce with France, gives us Hope9 of seeing it yet farther improved to the Advantage ofyonrKingdoms: And we make it our humble Request to your Majesty, That you will be pleased to appoint Commifliaries to treat with those of France, for the adjusting such Matters as are still necessary to be settled; and that you will give such Orders for the perfecting the said Treaty, and explaining the several Parts of it, that an entire Scheme of Trade may

be framed between Great Britain and France; which may fully answer, and make effectual, your Majesty’s gracious Intentions for the Good, and Welfare of your People.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committeein the said Address to be presented to her Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be prefeuted to her Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council do humbly know her Majesty’s Pleasure when the will be attended by this House.

A Petition of the Merchants, Importers, and Sail- Ditto, makers, of Holland Sail-cloth, common tv called Holland Duck, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That one Suit of Sails, riiade in the Dominions of the United Provinces, do more Service than Two Suits of any other Sail-cloth whatever; and that many Ships have been saved merelvbyStretigth of those Sails, when others.

Who have not had good Sails, haveperlflied at Sea: That English Sail-cloth, when once wet, lofesitsSubftanee and Colour; and the Dutch, by being wet, retains its Substance, and becomes brighter than before; and not One Ship in 20 or 30 cleared from Custom-house, London, ofe English Sail-cloth; and, if once, lcarce again: That the Dutch make such Sail-cloth of the Growth of their Country; that so good cannot be made of the Growth of any other: That the Importation of Duck

brings in a considerable Duty, yearly, to her Majesty’s Revenue; in lieU whereof great Quantities of our Manufactures are exported tU Holland, the Benefit whereof is well known to this Nation; the Duties on Importation of Holland's Duck is already very h-gh; and if burthened with a further Duty, as English Sail-cloth-makers request, it will totally rUin that Commodity; btfides, the Importation of Holland's Duck, as now imported, is as

beneficial to this Nation as the Dutch, not only tending to the Preservation of our Shipping, but promotes the Woollen Manufactures: That, some Years past, fds of the Old Subsidy, amounting to more than Part of the present Duty on Holland's Duck, was taken off as well from Holland's Duck, as all Holland and German Linens;

Which is evident the Duties on it were then too high:

And praying nothing m‘ay be done to discourage the Importation of Holland's Duck, by laying any further Duty upon it, being so benteficial a Branch of Trade to this Nation.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for the better Encouragement of the Making of Sail-cloth in Great Britain, be read a Second time.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That her Majesty having been waited on, humbly to know when the would please to be attended by this House, her Majesty had been pleased to appoint Tomorrow, at Six of the Clock in the Afternoon, at her Palace nt Kensington.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer also acquainted the House, That he had a Message from her Majesty lo deliver to this House, signed by her Majesty; and he presented the same to the House: And the same was read by Mr. Speaker: and is as followed);

A NNE R.

Her Majesty thinks fit to acquaint her loyal House of Commons with the Difficulties, which, in a particular manner, the lies under by the Debts contracted in her Civil Government, occasioned by several extraordinary Expences formerly incurred; to that her Majesty thinks lierself obliged, in Justice to many Creditors, to order an Estimate to be laid before this House of what was owing on the Civil List in the Year 1710.

Her Majesty hath used unexampled Parsimony to remove, if possible, this Burthen from lierself; but the granting away, and lefl’ening, some Part of her Revenue, by Parliament, has made that impracticable: Therefore her Majesty hopes, that this House of Commons, which, on all Occasions, has shewed themselves so well affected to her, will not be unwilling to impower her to raise such a Sum of Money, on the Civil List Funds, as may enable her to discharge the Debts, and settle the Expence to be regularly paid for the future.

Kensington,

June the 25th, 1713.

and read; setting forth, That, on a strict Inquiry and Report of a Committee this Session, before w hom attended the Commissioners of the Navy, Customs, Merchants, Importers of Hemp and Flax, and others, who employ many Thousands of the Poor of Great Leave was given for bringing in a Bill for the better Encouraging of Making of Sail-cloth in Great Britain: That several who are Factors for the Dutch, and Dealers in Holland's Duck, endeavour to delay the said Bill: That if the said Bill should not pass, the Petitioners, with their Vo I- 17.

Families, will be destitute of a Maintenance, and a great and growing Manufacture be loft to this Kingdom: That the Navy of Great Britain hath, for some Years past, been safely navigated with British Sail-cloth; and by Encouragement of the said Bill, the Merchant Ships of Great Britain may in time be furnished therewith; and what of late Years has employed 20,000 Poor, may in a short time employ Five times that Number: And praying. That such Endeavours against said Bill may not hinder the Pafiing thereof.

Aliens The House being informed, That One of the Alder-Goods. men of the City of London, and some of the Common Council, attended;

They were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House a Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council of the City of London; and the same was read; setting forth. That, by ancient Laws of this Kingdom, Aliens, and Merchants, Strangers, for all Merchandizes imported into this Realm, are liable to pay several Customs to her Majesty more than her own Subjects: That, for better securing said Customs, Laws have been made against Englishmens colouring the Goods of Aliens, and entering them in their Names in Custom-houseBooks; to prevent which, every Person, on Admis-. lion to the Freedom of this City, takes an Oath, not to colour Foreigners Goods under or in his own Name: That, of late Years, many naturalized Foreigners, and Unfreemen, notwithstanding the Acts to the contrary, not being under Oath, as Freemen are, have and do enter Goods of Aliens in their Names, to defraud her Majesty, and City, of those Customs, fife. payable by Aliens; to Decay of her Majesty’s Customs, and Revenues of this City: And praying. That all passing any Merchandize inwards may make an Oath, as shall be thought proper. That said Merchandizes don’t belong to any Alien, or, on Refusal, said Goods may be deemed Aliens Goods.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir Wm. Withers, Sir George Newland, Sir John Cafs, Mr. Recorder, and Mr. Vernon, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

of the Merchants upon Payment of the Duties upon Wine-bonds and Tobacco-bonds:

Sir George Newland reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Sir John Lambert Baronet, Samuel Shepheard, and the Executors of the late John

James David, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee have, in pursuance of the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition, and find the same to be as follows;

Mr. Henry Bray affirmed to the Committee, That, in April 1708, he sold to the Petitioner Mr. Samuel

Sheppard and Mr. John James David about 82 Hogsheads of French Clarets, which were taken by the Rammelly Gaily, of Guernsey, and condemned as Prize in her Majesty’s Court of Admiralty; and produced a Copy of the Bill of Parcels.

That the Petitioners produced Two Bills of Lading, dated the 23d of September 1708, for shipping 73 Hogs-heads and 15 Tierces of the said Wines, amounting to 20 Tuns and Three Hogsheads, on board the New at Falmouth, Mr. Wm. Dare, Mailer, with Convoy, for the Account of the Petitioners at London:

That the Petitioners also produced to the Committee Three several Letters from Mr. Peter Hill, their Agent at Falmouth, signifying. That he had drawn Bills on them, to the Value of £.1,050, payable to Mr. Fern, Receiver General of her Majesty’s Customs, for the Duties of the said Wines:

Vol. 17.

That, in October following, the said Dare failed- from Falmouth, on board the New Topsham, with the said Wines, under Convoy of her Majesty’s Ships the Dover and Sunderland-, but was taken off Beachy-head by a French Privateer, the Sunderland being very near, and carried into Calais, where he lay a Prisoner, as appears by his Letter from thence of the 22th October 1708:

And the Petitioners allured the Committee, That the said Vessel and Wines were fold, by the said Privateer, at Calais:

That the Petitioners applied themselves to the Lord Treasurer, to be relieved from Payment of their said Bills to Mr. Fern’, and thereupon his Lordship ordered all Proceedings at Law against them, on Account of the said Wines, to be flayed; and referred their same to the Commissioners of the Customs; who reported to hits Lordship, That they could only lament the Petitioners Misfortunes; doubting the y were not relievable by his Lordship; for that notwithstanding where English Goods shipped over Sea, having paid Culiom, happen to be loft in the Sea, or taken by the Enemy, the Merchant is allowed by Law, on due Proof of such Loss, to Chip off, in the same Port, Goods to the like Amount in Customs with those loft, free of Duty; yet there is no such Provision by Law, as to Goods inward:

That it appeared to the Committee, by a Clause in an Act of Parliament, 12 Car. Hd, Cap. 4®, Sec. 4®, That if any Goods or Merchandizes shall be taken by the Enemy, or Pirates, upon the Sea, or perished in any Ship, whereof the Subsidies, and other Duties, shall be duly paid, or agreed for; then such Merchant shall or may newly ship in the same Port, where the Goods and Merchandize were, or shall be, customed, so much other Goods or Merchandize as the same Goods or Merchandize are, or shall be, loft, as aforesaid, shall amount unto in Culiom, without paying for the same.

And the Petitioners produced, under the Hand of the present Attorney General, his Opinion upon their Cafe; That they can only be relieved by Parliament for the Duties of the Wines appropriated by Act of Parliament for the Use of the War; there not being a Provision by Parliament to make such Allowance as is prayed.

Ordered, That the Report do lie upon the Table until the Report be received from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for encouraging the Tobacco-trade; and for Ease of the Merchants upon Payment of the Duties upon Wine-bonds and Tobacco-bonds; was committed.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled* having nothing so justly at our Hearts as the Honour and Safety of your moll sacred Person, and Government, and the Security oftlie Protestant Succession, do crave Leave most thankfully to acknowledge the great Care which your Majesty, in Tenderness to your People, hath always taken toprevent the Pretender to your Crown from being in a Condition to disturb these Realms; and particularly by the late Treaty of Guaranty with the States General, and the Treaty of Peace between your Majesty and the French King; wherein, amongst other just and necessary Provisions, for the Security of the Protestant Succession, it is llipulaied, That the Pretender to your Majesty’s Crown shall not be suffered to reside in any of that King’s Dominions.

Your Majesty wifely infilled upon his Removal from that neighbouring Kingdom; and your faithful Commons are so fully convinced of the Necessity there is to remove him as far as possible, that they cannot but express to your Majesty their Apprehensions of the many Dangers which may accrue to your Majesty, and to your Kingdoms, from his residing in the Territories of the Duke of Lorrain.

We do, therefore, out of the highest Duty and Concern for the Preservation of your Royal Person, and the Quiet of your People, most humbly beseech your Majesty, That you will be pleased to use the moll speedy and pressing Inllances with the Duke of Lorrain, and with all other Princes and States in Amity or Correspondence with your Majesty, That tl toy will not, under any Pretext whatsoever, receive, or fuft’er to continue, within any of their Dominions, that Person who, in Defiance of your Majesty’s moll undoubted Title to the Crown, and the Settlement thereof on the illullrious House of Hanover, has afiumed the Title of King of these Realms: And ive farther beg Leave to allure your Majesty, That the Commons of Great Britain will, on all Occasions, to the utmost of their Power, flip-port your Majesty in such Steps as shall be necessary towards rendering those Instances effectual, and your Majesty safe and easy upon your Throne.

Refilled, Kdmine contradicente, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to her Majesty.

R(joined, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by the whole House.

Anno Septimo Anna: Regina, An Act passed, impowering Commissioners to treat and agree for suchLands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, as llin.ll be judged proper to be purchased, for the better fortifying Chatham, and Harwich; in pursuance whereof a Commission was issued, under the Great Seal, dated thei7th Day of June, in the Eighth Year of the Queen’s Reign, appointing Sir Richard OnflowSpeaker of the House of Commons, Marquis of Winchester, Lord Lord IVm. By a Second Act, Anno Octavo Anna Regina, intituled, An Act for vesting certain Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in Trustees, for fortifying and securing the Harbours an d Docks at Portsmouth, Chatham, and Harwich, it is Enacted, That it may be lawful for her Majesty to appoint Commissioners, under the Great Seal to determine all manner of Rights, Estates, and Interests, Controversies, Debates, and Questions, which should happen to arise between any Persons, relating to the Premises; as by the said Act does more at large appear:

In pursuance of the said Act, a Commission passed, under the Great Seal; but the Commissioners never have met; and nothing hath been done thereupon.

A Petition of the subscribed Proprietors of some Lands taken Lands and Tenements at Portsmouth, Chatham, and °Jt,1<lca' llarivich, which, by a late Act of Parliament, are veiled Dock-prds. in Trustees, for the Use ofher Majesty, for the better securing the Harbours and Docks at those Places, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, 8° Anna Regina, for veiling certain Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in Trustees, for better fortifying and securing the Harbours and Docks at Portsmouth, Chatham, and Harwich, the Petitioners Estates are vested in the Trustees therein named, for the Use of her Majesty, her Heirs, and Successors; which Act provides, That Proprietors be paid for said Lands, fife, as agreed by Commissioners appointed, or valued bya Jury at each Place where suchAgreement could not be made:

Pursuant to said Act, her Majesty was pleased to appoint Commissioners under Great Seal, to put in Execution said Act; and, as informed, a sufficient Sum was given into Treasury of the Ordnance, for said Uses; yet Proprietors remain unpaid for their Estates, vested as aforesaid, since ioif\ April 1710; the Commission for settling

the Interests and Rights of Proprietors is not executed; nor the Commissioners ever met thereupon: That several of Petitioners Tenants upon passing said Act, ex-pefting the Houses near the Docks and Magazines to be pulled down, began to leave the Estates; and Petitioners being diverted of their Power to make Leases, to assure Tenants of their Continuance, can neither keep the old, or get new, Tenants; but forced to pay Taxes for said Estates Handing empty: That several of said Houses are built on short Leases, renewable, some at Seven Years, on paying Fines, most of which belong to Persons employed in her Majesty’s Docks or Ships, or Widows, fife, of such; and those which are old Houses,

Handing empty, run much out of Repair; some Leases forfeited, and others run out; the Proprietors having no Reason to pay Fines to renew, or lay out Money to rebuild or repair the Estates; being valued by the Juries, according to the Condition they were then in, at low Rates; which, by the said Act, they are fixed down to: That, the Houses and Lands lying under such hard Circumstances, Proprietors can’t lett, or settle to any Uses; nor mortgage, though some for want thereof are under pinching Necessities: And praying Relief therein, to prevent the Ruin of many Families.

the House;'and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows;

That it appeared to the Committee, That, by an Act. of Parliament, passed in the 8th Year of her Majesty’s Reign, for veiling certain Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in Trullees, for the better fortifying and securing the Harbours and Docks aforesaid, That the Petitioners Estates are veiled in Trullees therein named, for the Use of her Majesty, her Heirs and Successors; which Act provides. That the Proprietors shall be paid for their said Lands and Tenements, as the same had been agreed for, by Commissioners appointed; or valued by a Jury, at each Place, where such Agreement could not be made.

That it further appeared to the Committee, That, pursuant to the said Act, her Majesty had been pleased to appoint Commissioners, under the Great Seal of Great Britain, to put the said A ft in Execution:

And that there is a sufficient Sum of Money given, raised; and paid, into the Treasury of the Ordnance, for the Uses aforesaid.

That it also appeared to the said Committee, That the Petitioners nevertheless remain unpaid for their Estates, so veiled as aforesaid, ever since the 10th of April 1710, by reason the Commission for the respective Rights and Interests of the Petitioners not having been executed, nor the Commissioners ever met thereupon.

That the Committee further proceeded to examine Evidence; and called,

Mr. James Dixon, One of the Proprietors of Port/-mouth: Who said, That he had a Brewhouse, Lands, and other Buildings, which was, by Jury, valued at £.4,000, and that, depending upon this Agreement, he fuiced and brought his Affairs to a Compliance with the publick Service; which caused him to lose thestrong Beer Trade belonging to the said Brewhouse, which was very considerable; and that the said Brewhouse and Utensils run daily' to Decay, for want of necessary Repairs; and that there are Two Mortgages of £.1,100 Principal, besides Interest, upon the said Premises; and that he is prosecuted, both in Law and Equity, for the fame, and forced to pray Time of the Court of Chancery, for the Payment thereof, until this Agreement is made good to him, to his great Cod and Charge; and is further threatened with an Execution.

/ He further said. That there are several other Instances of the like Nature at Portsm and particularly mentioned the same of one Mrs. , who has Mills there valued at £.2,000, which was left, by her deceased Husband, for her Four Maiden Daughters, who remain unprovided for till the said Money is paid.

Mr. Andrw Hates, One of the Proprietors of

said, His Estate, conlilling of divers Messuages, Tenements, and Gardens, thereto belonging; which he holds by Lease of the Church of Rochester, wherein the Term of about 20 Years was then to come; lying very near the Storehouses belonging to the Dock, were very much out of Repair; and accordingly valued, by Jury, for the Sum of £.1,069. 4 s.6 d.and, being tied down to the said Sum, is discouraged from repairing, and now become very ruinous; and, not having been able to give any Assurances to his then Tenants for any certain Term of Years, Part of the said Premises immediately after became empty, and ever since hath so remained; and hath, notwithstanding, been obliged to pay Taxes for the fame; and others his Tenants, who have continued in the said Premises, have and do refuse to pay him any Rent, by reason the Profits arising by the said Premises being, by the aforesaid Act, veiled in Trullees, for the Use of her Majesty, is thereby disabled to distrain for the growing Rents.

Mr. Thomas Rogers, another of the Proprietors of

Chatham, said. That his Estate is valued, by the Jury, at £.2,554. 2 s.6 d.and is all in, Land, lying near the Dock-yard at Chatham, which is a considerable Distance from the Town; and he had lately, before the passing the said Act, laid out a Piece of Ground there for Build-Vot. 17.

ing; and there were several Streets began to be built there, containing above 100 Houses, by several Persons that purchasedthe Lands of him; but when the aforesaid A ft of Parliament parted, wherein there is a Clause that forbids the erecting any more private Buildings upon that Land, a full Hop was made to the carrying on his Improvements, whereby the said Streets remain not peifefted; and he is Sufferer more than £.1,000.

Mrs. Alice Tetvfon, and Mrs. Warren, Daughter of one Mrs. Rofeiocll, Two other Proprietors of Chatham, said, That their respective Estates, confiding of Houses and Tenements, lying near the Dock at Chatham, which they held by Lease from the Dean and Chapter, being both valued by the Jury; the'former at £.484. is.iSd. and the latter at £.772. 6r. 6d. and being respectively mortgaged, and daily in Expectation of receiving their Purchase-money; which hitherto having not been paid, the Mortgagees daily threaten to’prosecute them for the said Money; and the said Estates being all the Subsistence they have for themselves, and numerous Families, having many Children, are reduced to a deplorable Condition; and the said Dean and Chapter are pressing them to renew the said Leases; and, not complying, may take Advantage thereof.

And the Committee was further informed, That there were a great many more Instances of the like nature; and that divers other Proprietors, by reason of Poverty in not receiving their Purchase-money, were not in a Condition to give their Attendance here, in order to obtain Relief.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, That lhe will be pleased to direct a new Survey to be made of such of the Lands and Tenements as are necessary for the Fortifications at Portsmouth, Chatham, and Harwich, that are now in being, or for the Service of the Navy, or for the Victualing thereof, that they may be paid for; and also to enquire what Damages have been sufferedby the Owners of other Lands, that are not so necessary for the said Uses and Services, that Satisfaction may be made for the fame; and that her Majesty will be pleased to direct her Commissioners to proceed in the execution of their Commission for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s mOft honourable Privy Council.

Ordered, That Mr. Pytls have Leave to make a Motion; it being pall Two a Clock.

And he moved accordingly, Thatan humble Address may be presented to her Majesty, That flie will be pleased to issue her Royal Proclamation, requiring a due and strict Execution of the Laws against Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland to foreign Parts; and humbly to desire her Majesty, That the will be pleased to give such Reward, as her Majesty in her Wisdom shall think fit, to such Persons as shall discover any Exportation thereof.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, That lhe will be pleased to issue her Royal Proclamation, requiring a due and strict Execution of the Laws against Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland to foreign Parts; and humbly to desire ber Majesty, That lhe will be pleased to give such Reward, as her Majesty in her Wisdom shall think fit, to such Persons as shall discover any Exportation thereof.

By the QUEEN.

A PROCLAMATION

For dissolving this present Parliament, and declaring the speedy calling another.

ANNE R.

WHEREAS we have thought fit, by and with the Advice of our Privy Council, to dissolve this present Parliament, which now Hands prorogued to Friday the Eight-and-twentieth Day of this inllant August: We do, for that End, publish this our Royal ^Proclamation; and do hereby difiblve the said Parliament accordingly: And the Lords Spiritual and Vo 1. 17.

Temporal; and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and Commissioners for Shires and Barghs of the House of Commons; are discharged from their Meeting on Friday the said Eight-and-twentieth Day of this instant August. And we, being resolved to meet our People, and have their Advice, in Parliament, do hereby make known to all our loving Subjects, That we will speedily call a new Parliament.

Given at our Court at Hampton he Eighth Day

of August 1713, in the Twelfth Year of our Reign.

GOD save the Queen.

By the QUEEN.

A PROCLAMATION Per calling a new Parliament.

ANNE R.

WHEREAS by our royal Proclamation, bearing Date the Eighth Day of this Month of August, we did difiolve the Tall Parliament, and declared our Intentions of speedily calling a new one: We do accordingly hereby further declare, that with the Ad-

vice of our Privy Council, we have this Day given Order to our Chancellor of Great. , to issue out Writs, in due Form, for the calling a new Parliament; which Writs are to bear Tejle the Eighteenth day of this Inllant August, and to be returnable on Thursday the Twelfth Day of November next following.

Given at our Court at Wind, the Seventeenth Day of August 1713, in the Twelfth Year of our Reign.

GOD save the Queen.

By the QUEEN.

A PROCLAMATION For proroguing the Parliament ANNER.

WHEREAS we have caused our Writs to be issued for the Calling of a Parliament to meet and be.holden. at Westminster, on the Twelfth

Day of November next following; We, by the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall be prorogued, on the said Twelfth Day of November, to Thursday the Tenth

Day of December next ensuing: And we have given Order to our Chancellor of Great Britain to prepare a Writ Patent, under our Great Seal, for proroguing the same accordingly: And we do hereby further declare, That convenient Notice shall be given, by Proclamation, of the Time when the said Parliament shall be holden, and fit, for the Dispatch of Business; to the end that the Members of both Houses may order their Affairs accordingly.

Given at our Court at Windsor, the Eighteenth Day of October 1713, in the Twelfth Year of our Reign.

GOD save the Queen.

By the QUEEN.

A PROCLAMATION.

ANNE R.

WHEREAS our Parliament, which we called to meet at Westminster, on the 12th Day

of November last, Hands prorogued to Tuesday the Twelfth Day of this Instant January: We, with the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby publilli and declare, That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said Twelfth Day of this instant,

to Tuesday the Sixteenth Day of February next: And we have given Order to our Chancellor of Britain

to prepare a Writ Patent, under our Great Seal, for proroguing the same accordingly: And we do further hereby declare our Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Sixteenth Day of , be held,

and fit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and impor- ’ tant Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance accordingly, at on the said

Sixteenth Day of February.

Given at our Court at Windsor, the Third Day of January 1713, in the 12 th Tear of our Reign.

GOD save the Queen,

After which the Lord Chancellor said;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

r

We have it in Command from her Majesty to let you know. That her Majesty will, as soon as the Members of both Houses shall be sworn, in Person, declare to you the Causes of her calling this Parliament: And, it being necessary a Speaker of the House of Commons should be first chosen, it is her Majesty’s Pleasure, That you. Gentlemen of the House of Commons, repair to the Place where yon are to fit; and then to proved to the Choice of some proper Person to be your Speaker: And that you present such Person whom you shall lb choose here on Thursdaynext, at Twelve a Clock, for her Majesty’s Royal Approbation.

And the House being returned;

Sir Arthur Kay Baronet, One of the Knights of the Shire for the County of York, acquainted the House, That her Majesty had directed them to proceed to the Choice of a Speaker:

That lie conceived a Person fitted for that high Troll must be one of great Temper, who would hear with Candour, what every Gentleman had to offer for the Service of her Majesty, and the Publick: That, he ought to be a Person unquestionably true to the Interest of the Church of England, upon which the safety of the State depends: And, as he took this Opportunity to express his Satisfaction in the Choice of the Iaft Speaker, who would ever be an Honour to those who chose him, and whole conduCl. ought to convince the World, That nothing can more effectually make this Kingdom safe, than the same Principles; so, to succeed that honourable Gentleman.

We took Leave to propose another of the like Character, v> hose sincere Adherence to our Constitutions, whose Affection to the House of , whose Con-

duct, Integrity, and Ability, were so well known, that he needed only take Leave to propose him: And he named Sir Thomas Hanmer.

After which the Lord ScudamKnight of the Shire

A. 1713.

for the County of Hereford, (kid, That he could add nothing to that Gentleman’s Character; and therefore fhoilld only second tire Motion, That Sir Thomas -mer be Speaker.

Then Mr. Thotopjbn, Mr. Onslow, and Mr. Steely federally spoke, and agreed in the same Motion.

Whereupon Sir Thomas Hanmer stood up, in his Place; and acknowledged the Obligation he had to those Gentlemen who had thought him worthy to be mentioned upon that Occasion; bnt said. He was sure, there were many Others present, with whom he had had the HonOtir to fit in former Parliaments, who could witness for him, botar unequal he was to such Undertaking: -That, it was true, he had been a Member of the House long enough to have qualified himself better for the Service of it; but the Experience he had got served only to deter him, by making him sensible of the great Difficulties which attended the Chair, without giving him Improvements sufficient for it:

That he had always found the Duty of a private Member to be nice and difficult enough; but the Mistakesof a single Person could be of little Consequence to the Publick; whereus, in the Service of the Chair, it was necessary to bring proportionable Abilities, as well as honest Intentions; other wise the Bnfiness, both of the Queen and Kingdom, would suffer by it:

That it would be a great Concern to him to be the Occasion of any Impediment or Prcjudicete the Publick Affhirs by those Imperfections which it would not be in his Power to help; and therefore he desired the House would think of calling some other Gentleman to the Chair, of better Abilities, to answer the Expectations which they ought justly to have from him whom they should appoint to serve them in that Station.

But the House unanimoutly called upon him, To the Chair:

Whereupon,

Sir Arthur Kay and the Lord . took him

out of his Place, and led him up the House from the Bar to the Chair:

Where, upon the Steps, he said, It was not yet too late for Gentlemen to alter their Resolution; and begged Leave to repeat his just Excuses, and to assure them, that no one ever came so near the Chair who was so little qualified to do the Duty of it; and therefore he hoped they would consult their own Honour and Service, by turning their Thoughts to a better Choice: But the House cried, No, no.

Whereupon he took the Chair, and laid. Though the House would not allow of his Excafe, he hoped they weald be pleased to permit him to intercede with her Majesty to command them to proceed to another Election.

The Members Cried, No, no.

And then the Mace was laid upon the Table.

After which,

Mr. Secretary Bromley said. He congratulated the House and the Publick, for the good Choice they had made of one who brought with him Abilities, not only to fill, but to adorn, the Chair:

That he understood it was her Majesty’s Pleasure, the House should present their Speaker on Thursday; and therefore moved to adjourn till Thursday Morning next.

And then the House, accordingly, adjourned till Thursday Morning next. Nine a Clock.
