Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorised b7 virtue of her Majesty’s Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker elect, with the House, went up to the House of Peers:

And some of the Lords Commissioners being seated upon a Form, between the Throne and the Wool-sacks, Mr. Speaker el eft spake to the Effect following} viz.

My Lords,

The Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, of Great Britain, assembled in Parliament, by virtue of her Majesty’s Writ, and directed, by her Royal Command, to proceed to the Choice of a Speaker, have call their first lially Nomination upon One the most unworthy of their Number; commanding me to present myself to her Majesty, as the Person they have hitherto thought of calling to that Service.

It is an Honour, and a Duty, which no good Subject ought to decline, who could hope so to acquit himself in that Station as to be inllrumental to the Publick Service, and to the great Ends of her Majesty’s Government: But the Trust is so important, and the Talk so difficult, that none should presume to undertake it, without Abilities sufficient for the due Discharge of it.

The many Imperfections 1 am conscious of in myself make me justly apprehend the great Prejudice which the Business of Parliament would receive from my weakPer-formances, in a Station upon which the good Dispatch of it does very much depend: And therefore, from this unad vised Step of the House of Commons (which I hope is the only one they will be guilty of), I mult make my humble Appeal to the Throne, the last Resort of Justice; where the Errors of all inferior Judgments are reversed: And I desire, with all Duty, to offer my Petition to her Majesty, That, for her own Service and Satisfaction, for the better Success of those arduous and urgent Affairs which have induced her to call this Parliament, and for the Honour of the House of Commons, the will be pleased to order them to re-consider this their Resolution, and to come again, prepared to present some other Person to her Majesty more worthy of their Choice, and of her Royal Acceptance and Approbation.

Whereupon the Lord Chancellor said j

Sir Thomas IIdinner.

She Queen could expect no less from an House of Commons composed of so many dutiful and affectionate Subjects, whose Interest in their Country is an unquestionable Pledge of their true Concern for it, than the Choice of a Person for their Speaker equally qualified for that important Trull, by a just Regard for her Prerogative, and an hearty Zeal for the Welfare of her People,

The commands us. Sir, to tell you. That on both these Accounts their Choice of you to be their Speaker is acceptable to her; and, therefore, that Ihe approves and confirms it.

After which Sir Thomas H replied;

My Lords,

Whatever other Failings belong to me, there shall be no Defect in my Obedience to her Majesty, and since lhe is graciously pleased to think me worthy of these Commands, it is my Duty to endeavour to make myself as little unworthy of them as I can:

The Sincerity of my Intentions, and my Zeal for her Majesty’s and the Publick Service, will be lure to guard me from all wilful Errors: And as I rely upon her Majesty ’s grealGoodness for the pardoning my involuntary Mistakes; so I will comfort myself yet further with this Hope, that the Wants and Imperfections of one of the meanest of her Subjects can never be of Moment enough to interrupt thefignal Prosperity of her Reign, or do any eoniidcrable Prejudice to the Publick Affairs, whilst her great Wisdom presides and watches over them.

Under these Encouragements, I will, with all Diligence, and according to the best of my Abilities, apply VOL. 17.

myself to the Discharge of this great Trull; and I shall account myself happy, if, in so publick a Post, I may be able to give any more open and apparent Proofs of that Loyalty and Fidelity to her Majesty’s Person and Government, and that Love and Value for the Conliitution and Liberties of this Kingdom, which in my private Station, as a Subject, and an , I have al-

ways proposed to myself as the Rule of my Actions.

In pursuance therefore of my Duty, and as the First Act of that Trust which I am commanded to undertake, I beg Leave, by way of humble Petition to her Majesty, in the Name of the Commons of Great Britain, to lay Claim to all their ancient and accustomed Rights, Privileges, and Immunities; particularly,

That for their better Attendance upon the Publick Service, they, and their necessary Servants, may be free, in their Persons and Estates, from all Arrests, Suits, and Moleflations:

That they may be allowed Freedom of Speech in their Debates:

That, upon all Occurrences of Moment, and at times convenient to her Majesty, lhe will be pleased to vouch-safe them Accel’s to her Royal Person:

And that all their Proceedings may be free from Misconstruction, and receive the most favourable Interpretation.

Then the Lord Chancellor said;

Mr. Speaker,

We are commanded by her Majesty to allure you of her Support in the Discharge of your Duty; and to let you know, That her Majesty’s graciouflypleased to grant to the House of Commons all the Privileges you alk in their Name, as fully as they have been at any time granted by her Majesty, or any ofherRoyalPredecessors.

The House being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House having attended in the House of Peers, he had obeyed their Commands, in presenting himself to her Majesty, as their Speaker; To which her Majesty had been pleased to signify her Content, by her Commissioners; and, in so doing, had given a great Proof of her gracious Inclinations to agree in every thing with the House, by confirming a Choice which lhe could have no other Reason to approve, but because they had made it:

That there was now no longer any room for him to decline the Service: He was therefore obliged to apply himself to the Performance of it, according to the bell of his Abilities; and he hoped he might promise himself that just Indulgence from the House, that they would pardon his many Failings in the Execution of so great a Trust, since they had not thought fit to allow them as Excuses for his not undertaking it:

That he would allure the House of so much, That they should find no other Faults to exercise their Forgive-ness upon, but such only as were natural and uaavoidable to him; for, as far as his Judgment would serve to guide him, he should prefer the doing his Duty in that Place to all other Considerations; and no Views or Motives what foe ver should draw him from a Uriel Fidelity to the Trust they had reposed in him, and a perfect Regard to the Honour of the House, and the publick Interests of those whom they represented:

That he requested the Assistance of all Gent!emen, and especially those who were more experienced than himself, for preserving the established Rules and Orders of the House; upon, which not only the Dignity of their Proceedings, but the necessary Dispatch of their Buff-ness, did depend: That nothing should be wanting on his Part, as far as he could contribute to it: And that he was persuaded. That his sincere Endeavours to do the most acceptable Service he could, would be the bell Return of Thanks he could make for the undeserved Honour they had conferred upon him.

porting it, he had obtained a Copy thereof; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have much Satisfaction in being able, at the opening this Parliament, to tell you, That the Ratifications of the Treaties of Peace, and of Commerce, with Spain, are exchanged ;by which my Subjects will'have greater Opportunities than ever to improve and extend their Trade: Many Advantages formerly en joyed by Connivance, and procured by fuel) Methods as made a Dif-tinClion between one ^/'//////Merchant and another, are now settled by Treaty, and an equal Rule is established.

It has pleased God to bless my Endeavours to obtain an honourable and advantageous Peace for my own People, and for the greatcll Part of my Allies: Nothing which 1 can do shall be wanting to render it universal: And I persuade myself, that, with your hearty Concurrence, my Interposition may at lad prove effectual to complete the Settlement of Europe.

In the mean while, I congratulate with my own Subjects, That they are delivered from a consuming Land War; and entered on a Peace, the good E flee is whereof nothing but intestine Divisions can cbliruct.

It was the Glory of the W’ifod and great eft of my Predecessors to hold the Balance of; and to

keep it equal, by calling in their Weight, as Necessity required: By this Conduct, they enriched the Kingdom, and rendered themselves dreadful to their Enemies, and usefulto their Friends: I have proceeded on the same Principle; and I doubt not but my Successors will follow' these Examples.

Our Situation points out to us our true Intered; for this Country can flourish only by Trade; and willvbe most formidable by the right Application of our Naval Force.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered such Accounts to be prepared, and laid before you, as willlhew you, at the Conclusion of the War, the true State of vourCondition; whereby you will be better able to judge what Aids are necessary: And I only ask of you Supplies for the currentService of the Year; and for the Diieharge of such Debts as you shall find, on Examination, to bejudand reasonable.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Joy which has been generally expressed on my Recovery from my late Indisposition, and on my coming to this City, I edeem as a Return to that tender Adection which I have always had for my People.

I vvifli that effectual Care had been taken, as I have often desired, to suppress those seditious Papers, and faflious Rumours, by which designing Men have been able to fink Credit, and the Innocent have suffered.

There are some who have arrived to that Height of Malice as to insinuate, that the Protedant Succession in the House of Hanover is in Danger under my Government.

Those who go about thus to didract the Minds of Men with imaginary Dangers, can only mean to didurb the present Tranquillity, and to bring real Mif-chiefs upon us.

After all I have done to secure ourReligion, and your Liberties, and to transmit both safe to Poderity, I cannot mention these Proceedings without some Degree of Warmth; and I mud hope, you will all agree with me, That Attempts to weaken my Authority, or to render the Possession of the Crown tmeafv to me, can never be proper Means to drengthen the Protedant Succession.

I have done, and shall continue to do, my bed for the Good of all my Subjects: Let it be your Endeavour, as it shall be mine, to unite our Differences, not by relaxing from the dricted Adherence to our Conditution in Church and State, but by observing the Lawsyourselves, and enforcing a due Obedience to them in others.

A long War has not only impoverished the Publick, however some particular Men may have been Gainers by it, but has also greatly affected Government itfolf.

Let it bo your Care so to improve the prel-nt

Mr. Gore reported from the Committee, who were appointed, upon Tuesday last, to dravv up an Address, to be presented to her Majesty, That they had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz*

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, do, with all Humility, return our sincere and hearty Thanks for your Majesty’s most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We beg Leave to assure your Majesty, That as nothing could be more afflicting to your People than the Indisposition of the bed of Sovereigns, so nothing has ever been an Occasion of greater Joy and Satisfaction to them than your Majesty’s late happy Recovery.

We congratulate your Majesty on the Conclusion of the Treaties of Peace and Commerce with Spain, whereby your Majesty is pleased to declare, That you have procured new Benefits to your Subjects: But your Royal Care hath not been confined to your own People; it hath been extended to all your Allies: And your Majesty’s Goodnefsmuft be for everadmired, That, notwithstanding any Discouragements you may have met with, you are pleased still to continue your Endeavours to make the Peace universal, and thereby to complete the Settlement of Europe: And your faithful Vol. 17.

Commons will never be wanting in an hearty Concurrence to assist your Majesty in all such Measures as your Majesty shall judge proper to finish a Design, so great and so glorious.

Your Commons will, with all Cheerfulness, grant such Supplies as are necessary for the current Service, and for the Discharge of such Debts as are just and reasonable:

They can never sufficiently express the Sense they have of their Happiness, in being delivered from the Calamities of a consuming War: They will therefore, in Duty to your Majesty, and in Justice to those they represent, do all that is in their Power, that the good Effects of Peace may not be obstructed by any intestine Divisions:

They will, as far as in them lies, dilappoint the Designs of malicious and unreasonable Men: They will, on all Occasions shew their just Abhorrence of the licentious'

Practices, in publishing scandalous Papers, and spreading seditious Rumours: And, as your Commons will always fhpport and maintain the Protestant Succession in the House of Hanover, they cannot but be astonished at the' malicious Insinuations of any, who would fugged that Succession to be in Danger under your Majesty’s moll nufpicious Government: For when we consider* that it is secured by the greatest Obligations, ciVII and sacred; by A els of Parliament, Oaths, and Treaties; we cannot but declare our entire Acqpiefcence in these Securities; and mud look upon such Insinuations to be groundless in themselves, and affronting to your Majesty, and your Government:' ,

And your Majesty may depend. That your loyal Commons will never be prevailed on by any Pretences whatsoever to countenance Attempts that may tend to weaken your Majesty’s Authority, and to render the Possessiouof the Crowu uneasy to you; which can only proceed from the Rage of a disappointed Fa&ion, and the Spirit of Rebellion.

The said Address being read a Second time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to her Majesty,;

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s moil honourable Privy Council do humbly know her Majesty’s Pleasure when ihe will be attended by this House.

Mr. Speaker reported, That he, with the House, did Answer t. Yesterday attend her Majesty, and presented to Iter Ad<lrei* their humble Address: To which her Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer;

Gentlemen,

This Address is so dutiful, and expresses so fully the Sense of my loyal Subjects, that I esteem it a Proof of the good Choice they have made of you to represent them.

I give

12 Ann, 6° 4

I give you my hearty Thanks for it.

The Confidence you have in my Afieftion; the Abhorrence you declare of the malicious Infmuations of the Protestant Successionbeing in Danger under my Government., and your Acquiescence in the present Securities for it, are very suitable Returns for the tender Regard I have always had for what concerns my People;

and will most effectually, by the Blessing of God, unite

the Minds of my Subjects, and disappoint the Defigus of those who would disturb the present Tranquillity.

Members Mr. Frcman ,according to Order, reported from the committee who were to consider of the Act, of the 9th Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for securing the Freedom of Parliaments, by the farther qualifying the Members to fit in the House of Commons, the Kesolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read; and are as follow; viz.

lft. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, notwithstanding the Oath taken by any Candidate at or after any Election, his Qualification may be afterwards examined into.

2d. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Person whoseQualification is expressly objected to in any Petition relating to his Election, shall, within Fifteen Days after the Petition read, give to the Clerk of the House of Commons a Paper, signed by himself, containing a Rental or Particular of the Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, whereby he makes out his Qualification; of which any Person concerned may have a Copy.

3d. Resolved,'\'\\at it is the Opinionof this Committee, That of such Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, whereof the Party hath not been in Possession for Three Years before the Election, he shall also insert in the same Paper, from what Person, and by what Conveyance or Act in Law, he claims or derives the fame; and also the Confi-derat ion, if any, paid; and the Names and Places of Abode of the Witnesses to such Conveyance and Payment.

4th. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, if a Sitting Member shall think fit to question the Qualification of a Petitioner, he shall, within 15 Days after the Petition read, leave Notice thereof, in Writing, with the Clerk of the House of Commons; the Petitioner shall, in such Case, within 15 Days after such Notice, leave with the said Clerk of the House the like Account, in Writing, of his Qualification as is required from a Sitting Member.

The Firfi, Second, and Third Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The Fourth Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by inserting, after " Commons," the Word " and

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon,

agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That, if a Sitting Member shall think fit to question the Qualification of a Petitioner, he shall, within Fifteen Days after the Petition read, leave Notice thereof, in Writing, with the Clerk of the House of Commons; and the Petitioner shall, in such Case, within Fifteen Days after such Notice, leave with the said Clerk of the House the like Account, in Writing, of his Qualification as is required Irom a Sitting Member.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Act, of the Ninth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for securing the Freedom of Parliaments, by the farther qualifying the Members to fit in the House of Commons;

Resolved, That this House will, To-rnorrow Morning, resolve itself into the said Committee.

Sir Edward Knatchbull reported from the Committee, Exporting to whom it was referred to consider of proper Heads for Wocl-a Bill for the more effectual preventing the Running of Wool, That they had prepared proper Heads for that Purpose: which they haddirested him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read; and are as follows;

Refolded, That the Register, or Entry, of all unwrought Wool, be made throughout the whole Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland.

Refolded, That all Permits, or Sufferances, whereby any unwrought Wool is removed, be extended to all the Persons that shall buy it, or to whose Use it shall be delivered.

Refolded, That all Persons receiving any unwrought Wool do give a Receipt for the fame; that it may be traced through the several Hands till the same be fully manufactured.

Refolded, That upon Information of any Quantity of unwrought Wool, or Woollen Yarn, that is run, any J uftiees of the Peace of the County shall have '

Power to summons the Party, and, upon Conviction, to levy a Penalty upon his Goods and Chattels; out of which thelnformer. Aider, and Assister, is to be rewarded.

Refolded, That all Persons removing Wool at any time, except between Sun and Sun, shall be liable to the Penalty, and be deemed Runners of Wool.

Refolded, That all Persons have Power to seize the

Person or Persons, as well as the Wool, of such who shall remove it in the Night time.

Refolded, That not above Men shall be

allowed to travel with any Waggon, Cart, or other Carriage, of Wool; and not above Men to

Horses, loaded with Wool: And if such Person or Persons be found armed, to be deemed Runner or Runners of Wool, and be liable to the same Penalties.

Refolded, That every Custom-house Officer, or others concerned in the Execution of this Act, shall be obliged to grant a Permit, or Sufferance, when demanded.

Refolded, That every Custom-house Officer, or others concerned in the Execution of this Act, shall be obliged todischarge his Book from the Entry, upon the Sufferance granted.

Refolded, That every Custom-house Officer, or others concerned in the Execution of this Act, who, upon Information, shall refuse or neglect to apprehend the Person or Persons of those who shall be concerned in Running of Wool, shall suffer the Penalty of

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Chetxoynd reported from the Committee appoint- Highway ed to inquire into the Management and Application Trufi*. of all Sums of Money which have been collected for repairing any particular Highways, by virtue of any Act of Parliament passed since her Majesty’s Accession to the Crown, That they had considered the Matter touching the Act, made in the 9th Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highway between Hockley and Dunstable, in the County of Bedford; and that it appeared to the Committee, That the yearly Receipt, taken at a Medium, of the Three Years, amounts to £240; and that there has been expended, more than received, on the Highway near £.1,000 by reason of the great Distance of Materials; and that the Committee had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk's Table: Where they were read j and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, for the effectual Repairing of the abovesaid Road, it will be necessary that a Duty be laid upon single Horses travelling that Road, which at present pay nothing.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Power be given to the Commissioners, for putting the said Act in execution, to oblige the Inhabitants of the several Parishes, within which this Road lies, to perform Three Days Work, upon the said Road, of the Six Days they are obliged to by the Statutes of this Realm for the Repairing Highways, at the Direction of the Surveyor thereof, appointed by the said Commissioners.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, upon the said Resolutions: And that Sir Pincent Charnock, Mr. Harvey, Mr. Chettoynd, and Mr. Chapman, do prepare, and

bring in, the fame.

I have likwife annexed a State of the Third Branch of their Demand, being for an Arrear of their Gratification-money, from the Year 1703 to the Year 1713, amounting to One hundred Twenty-five thousand Four hundred Gilders: according to the Allowances made to the Troops of Hanover: But, since this Arrear is of To long Standing, I beg Leave to be particular, in the Stating thereof: These Troops are a Moiety of the Holjiein Troops, who entered into the Service of her Majesty and the States General, in the Year 1703; and, by the 4th Article of their Treaty, dated the 15th March, 1703, N. S. they are to enjoy the same Waggon-money, Recruits, and other Gratifications, which the Troops of Hanover enjoyed; and the Troops of Hanover are to enjoy, without Exception, the same Gratifications, Profits, Douceurs, and Advantages, which the States give to their own Troops.

It appears, by the Duke of s Warrant

to Charles Fox Esquire, Paymaster General of her Majesty’s Forces, dated the 13th March 1704, That the Sum of 200,000 Gilders was directed to be paid to the Baron de Bothmar, and S' Killingraf, in full for Recruits, and all other extraordinary Expences and Claims, from the Hanover Troops, from the time of their entering Into the Service, to the end of the Year 1704; which Money was accordingly issued: And though there is no particular State how the same arises, being a certain Sum agreed to be paid, pursuant to the

Fifth Article of the Convention, for the said Troops, dated the 30th December 1704; yet it appears by the said Article, that the same was for the ordinary Recruits, as well as those of Action; all other Extraordinaries for the said Troops being adjusted in the respective Treaties, and the Money made payable every. Forty-two Days, with their ordinary Pay.

In the Treaty for the Year 1705, and in all other fub-sequent Treaties the Gratification-money, being/. 700 Gilders for each Troop, and /. 800 Gilders for each Company of Foot, was likewise included, amounting to f 75,600 Gilders a Year, and made payable with their ordinary Pay; in Consideration whereof, the said Troops quitted their Claim and Pretensions to any Douceur, or other Extraordinaries, w’hich the States General might hereafter allow to their own Troops, except for such Men and Horses as should be loft in Action:

But it does not appear, upon examining (he several Accounts of Extraordinaries, made up for the Holjiein Troops, that they have ever been allowed more than f. 100 Gilders a Year for each Troop of Dragoons, and /. 200 Gilders a Year for each Company of Foot, as a Douceur towards recruiting, except for Men and Horses loll in Action; and that has likewise been allowed to the Troops of Hanover, over and above the aforesaid Gratification-money.

Count Vandemath likewise produced a Certificate

from Mr. Slingelandt, Secretary to the Council of State of the United Provinces; whereby it appears, that the States have paid, from the Beginning of the late War, f. 800 Gilders a Year to each Troop of Dragoons, and Company of Foot, of their own National Troops, for their Gratification-money; which is /. 100 Gilders a Year to each Troop of Dragoons, more than is allowed to the Hanover Troops, or demanded by the Troops of Holjiein; but this Allowance being never made but in the time of War, I have deducted /. Eleven thousand Four hundred Gilders, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Thirteen; and then the Demand on this Head amounts but to One hundred and fourteen thousand Gilders.

All which is most humbly submitted to your Lordship.

Whitehall,

the 31st December 1713.

Henry Watkins.

llefolxed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Three Pence Farthing per Pound, Part of the Drawback onTobacco, to be exported from Great Britain for Ireland, be taken off.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Diminution of the Drawback do take Effect upon all Tobacco exported for Ireland after the 24th Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Thirteen; and continue until the additional Duty of §{d. per Pound upon Tobacco in Ireland, expiring on the said 24th Day of March, be re-granted.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out the Word " barthing

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That Three Pence per Pound, Part of the Drawback on Tobacco to be exported from Great Britain lor Ireland, be taken off.

The Second Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Petition of John Powell, of London, Merchant* was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Old East India Company, trading in a Joint Stock, being thought prejudicial to the Nation, a free Trade to the East Indies was, in the Year 1698, granted by Act of Parliament for ever, to all Persons contributing towards railing the Sum of Two Millions, for the Service of the Crown of England, and settling the Trade to the East Indies, subject to Determination, upon Repayment of said Sum of TwcMillions, unto the respective Contributors thereof on Three Years Notice, alter Michaelmas 1711: That the Petitioner, depending his Right to such Trade, being equal with others, would be preserved to him equally with thefameRight to others, did, on Credit of the said Act, advance £. 3,700 towards the said £. a,000,000 and was thereupon incorporated, with the other Contributors, into a general Society for such free Trade: Nevertheless, after passing the said Act, a Joint Stock Company was again set up; but your Petitioner, relying on the said Act, continued in the said Society; and, by Authority of the said Act, had Right to trade for the yearly Sum he advanced; and did so do, till the Two Companies being united, by their excessive Power, did deny him his Right to trade, notwithstanding the separate Traders have paid the Crown very great Sums for Customs, and considerableSums to the Company, upon the gross Sale of the Candle, and have employed many Vol. 17*

Aprilis. 529

Ships, to the great Encouragement of the Merchants and Traders of Great Britain: That, about Six Years since, the said united Stock Company obtained alongej Term of Years, upon advancing £. 1,200,000: Before the Proposal of such Sum the Petitioner did' petition the Commons for Continuance of his Trade, on paying his Proportion of any Sum to be advanced; and when the Bill was brought in, by which his Capital Stock, and Trade, were to be taken from him, and given to the united Company, he did again petition for the Preservation of his Property, to be heard, by Coun-fel, against such Matters of the said Bill as related to his Right; but was not heard; and the said Bill passed: That, under colour of a Clause in such Act, the said Company do now pretend to deprive the Petitioner of hisRight to trade; and to take from him, at next, his said original Stock, and Trade, at the Price of £. 100 only, for each £. 100 Capital Stock, without regard to the great Worth thereof; and have accordingly given him Notice thereof in Writing: And praying to be relieved against the said East India Company, with respect to his Right of pall and future Trade to the East Indies, according to the said Act of Parliament, on which he and others advanced the said £.2,000,000; and that such his Right, equally established, may be preserved and confirmed, with the said other Contributors Right to the said Trade; the Petitioner offering to

f»ay his full Proportion of any Sum advanced by the aid Company, or which shall hereafter be advanced for the Service of her Majesty’s Government; and to pay Interest for his Prpportion of the £. 1,200,000 from the time the Company paid the same; and to be relieved.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of this House, have taken into Consideration, and examined, the several Heads of the Ordinary Estimate of the Navy for the Year 1714: And, under the First General Head of Allowances granted by her Majesty to the Lords Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of G real Britain; and lo the principal Officers and Commissioners of her Majesty’s Navy, which Head amounting, in the Whole, to the Sum of £.30,616 6s. 5 d;

That the Committee did observe, that there is a Charge of £.7,000, for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain 1 and that in their humble £. d.

Opinion the Sum of £.5,000 would be a sufficient Allowance for the executing the said Office; so that there may be deducted in that Article - - - 2,000 — —

That the Committeedid further observe,

That over and above the Sum of £.2,000, charged for the Treasurer of the Navy’s Salary, there is charged, for Fourteen Commissioners of the Navy, £.7.000, and that, in their Opinion, £.5,000 would be a sufficient Allowance for that Service; so that there may be deducted out ofthofe Articles 2,000 — — That the Committee did also observe an Article of £.400, for the House-rent of Five Commissioners, that have not Dwelling at the N avy Office; and are of Opinion, that there may be deducted out of that Art icle 320 — — That the Committee then proceeded to take into Consideration the Second General Head of the said Estimate, relating to superannuated Sea Officers, which amounts to £.11,186 i8*. 8 d.But, being informed, that it was an usual Article in the Ordinary Estimate of the Navy, found no Occasion to make any Remarks upon it.

That they then considered the 3d general Head of Pensions and Allowances, amounting to £.6,610 12 s. 6dAnd it appearing to them to be an Allowance to such Persons as have served well, or the Widows, Children, or Families, of such who had lost their Livesinthe Service, they only made the Observations following; viz.

The said Account, and Copies of the said Letters, are as follow; viz.

Her Majesty, in a very-pressing Manner, made her Instances to the Court of for the Removal of

the Pretender from Lorrain, as being the most effectual Measure to attain that End.

LTpon the Address from this House, her Majesty repeated the same to that Court: And her Majesty having no Minister residing at Lorrain, the Minister of that Prince was spoke to here, as were his Ministers in the several Courts where her Majesty has Ministers residing.

Some time after, the Minister of Lorrain at the Hague sent an Answer to the Lord Bishop of London; and has since communicated a Letter to him he received from his Master on this Subject; in which it is represented, that the Pretender came to Bar, upon the pressing Instances of his Most Christian Majesty; that he came publickly thither, being a neutral Country, where any Person might be; and that the Emperor gave him a passport, with this Restriction, not to depart from thence: The Queen, thereupon, renewed her Instances to the Court of France; and expects to hear the Pre-Vo l. 17.

A Petition of the Adventurers, and Fishermen, of the Duties on Town of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, Salu concerned in the Island and North Sea Fishings, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Fishings employ great Numbers of Vessels, from this and other Ports of this Kingdom, and is a Nursery for Seamen: That Encouragement has always been given to this Trade; and, by an Act of the Fourth of her Majesty, Provision was made, That Island and North Sea Fish might be imported, though salted with Salt that had not paid Excise; That the greatest Part of the Salt used has been bought in Scotland, and no Excise paid; but, by the 8th Article of Union, Part of the Excise paid it rEnglandwill, after May-day next, be paid for Salt made in Scotland-, and that the Salt-makers in Scotland, taking Advantage of the approaching Duty, have already raised the Price of Salt proportionable to the said Duty; so that no Place remains in Great Britain, where Salt can be had Excise-free; and consequently these advantageous Trades will he ruined:

And praying Leave to take Salt at or any

other Port in Great Britain, Excise-free, for the Service of the North Sea and IslandTrade, under Caution to secure the Revenue on Salt.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Supply granted to her Majesty.

Sir Gilbert Dolben, according to Order, reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Manner of signing the Petition of James Berry Earl of -mrre, in the Kingdom of Ireland, complaining of an undue Election for the Borough of Wiggan, in the County of Lancaster; which Report he read in his Place; and

afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to their Instruction. from the House, have inquired into the Manner of signing the said Petition:

And the Committee examined Edward Harvey Esquire, who delivered the Petition; and also the Petitioner, the Earl of Barrymore.

Mr. Harvey said. He received the Petition from the Petitioner the Earl of Barrymore, at Wardley, as he was coming to London: That his Lord ship desired him to consult with his Friends in Town, whether it was according to the Methods of the House; and, if he found it to be so, his Lordship gave him Authority to set his Name to it; and desire him to deliver it; which he did accordingly: That if he had found it not according to the Methods of the House, he was to fend it back for his Lordship to sign: And said, That the Petition delivered is the very individual Paper which he received from his Lordship.

The Earl of Barrymore, being examined, confirmed what Mr. Harvey had said; and declared, he owned the Petition delivered, and is ready to proceed upon it.

The Committee did not inquire into the Manner of signing the said Petition by Mr. Bridgman-, there being an Order of the House, whereby the Committee is discharged from proceeding upon that Part of the Petition, which relates to the said Mr. Bridgman.

Mr. Conyers, according to Order, reported from the Committee who were to consider further of the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’sTable: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding^.498,085. ioj. be granted to her Majesty, to make good, for the Services of the Navy, the like Sum, which, in the Year commencing from Christmas 1713, is to be paid by the Treasurer of

the Navy, by quarterly Payments, to the South Sea Company, pursuant to the Act of Parliament in that behalf.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Number of Men to be allowed for Guards and Garisons in Great Britain, and for Jerfy and Guernsey,

for the Year 1714, be 8,23a Men; Commission and Non-commission Officers, and the Two Independent Companies in North Britain, included.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, That the will be pleased to order an Account of the present State and Condition of the Navy to be laid before this House.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by fuel) Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s moll honourable Privy Council.

Resolved-, Nemine coritradicente, That this House will, upon Tomorrow Sevennight, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the State of the Nation, with regard to the Protestant Succession.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to her Majesty, That (he will be pleased to direfit, That the Letter from the Qishop of London to the Baron de Begue Minister of the Duke of Lorrain to the States General, concerning the Removal of the Pretender from the Dominions of the Duke of Lorbe laid before this House.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to her Majesty by such Members of this House as are of her Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

The Baron Le Bcgue's Answer to a Letter from the Bishop of London, November 9th, 1713.

My Lord,

I have this Morning received the Letter your Excellence did me the Honour to write to me the 8th Instant; which I will fend Tomorrow to his ltoyal Highness; and, as soon as I know his Intentions, I wilt not fail to acquaint you with them; begging you, my Lord, in the mean time, to remember, that, when the Chevalier de St. George came to reside at Bar, I had Orders to tell you, that his Royal Highness, My Matter, would not have given Refuge to that Prince but upon the pressing I nuances which were made to him by the Court of France; which even engaged his Royal Highness to solicit Passports, as well from the Imperial Court, as also from the States General of the United Provinces, for the Security of the Chevalier: At present, my Lord, I do not know whether those Instances which you mention have been repeated; nor whether my Master is at Liberty to oblige a Prince to go out of his Dominions, who was received there only at the Solicitation of the most Christian King. This is, my Lord, what I submit to your Excellency’s Prudence; to whom I have the Honour to be, with all possible Respect,

My Lord,

Your most humble, and Most obedient Servant,

J. Le Begue.

Copy of a Letter from his Royal Highness of

to the Baron Jje Begue, his Minister at the Hague,

bearing Date the 17th November 1713.

This Morning I received your Letter of the nth Instant, together with that which the Bishop of wrote to you from Utrecht, the 8 th of this Month; and also the Copy of your Answer to him, which I approve of I own I was surprised at the Demand which the Bishop of Bristol makes, from the Queen of Great Britain: And my Intention is, that you should say for Answer to that Minister, That, having nothing more at my Heart than to preserve to myself the Favour and good Graces of the Queen, I will omit no Opportunity 21 to

13 Ann. 8° — 9°

to deserve them: But ns to the Demand which is made me, to oblige the Chevalier to go out of

my Dominions, I could make no other An fiver, but that, will) the Knowledge and Acquiescence of all Europe, he came to relide in my Dominions, in which any body might relide, it being a neutral Country: That even the Emperor had given him a Passport to come and relide there; with this Restriction nevertheless, not . to go out of it; and that I have no other Answer to make; hoping that these Reafous being found good, the Bishop of Bristol will continue his Friendship to me; and, through his good Offices with the Queen, maintain to me the Honour of her Protection, which is all that I moll passionately wish. This is an Answer to yours.

Leopold.

Utrecht, 8° November 1713.

Sir,

- I shall with Pleasure lay hold on all Opportunities

that shall offer, to shew you my Respects, and to make you Returns for the Friend ship you expressed for me during your Stay at Utrecht: It is now by Order of

her Majesty, the Queen of Great Britain, whom I have the Honour to serve, that I acquaint you, her Majesty, finding the Pretender to her Crown is not yet gone out of the Territories of his moll Serene Highness the Duke your Master, notwithstanding the repeated Instances which have been made for that Purpose, has commanded me to desire \ou will represent to his Highness the Dangers which may be apprehended to her ... Majesty, and her Kingdoms, as also to the Protestant Succession, in case the said Person continue to flay any longer in.his Dominions; and how inconsist-ent such Protection will be with the Friendship and

good Correspondence that is between her Majesty and his Highness: When I have the Honour to meet you,

I shall explain this Matter to you further, and remind you of the Addresses lately made to her Majesty, by her Parliament, and of other Considerations, which, (

> am persuaded, are sufficiently known to you; which,

being represented to his Highness by a Minister of so much Credit, and so well inclined, as the Baron Le Begue, cannot fail to have the desired Effect, that the Pretender may not be permitted to flay any longer in the Dominions of the Duke your Master.

I am,

Jolt.

Sir Win.Withers reported from the Committee, to

whom the Petition of the Merchants, Drapers, and other Dealers, in Mixt or Medley Broad-cloths, was referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read; and the Report, and Resolutions, are as follow; viz.

That, upon Examination of the Allegations thereof, found. That by an Act, passed in the 10th Year of her Majesty’s Reign, it is enacted, That all Mixt or Medley Broad-cloth, to be made after the 24th Day of June 1712, shall be measured at the Fulling-mill, by the Master, Owners or other Ofccupier, thereof upon Oath; who is also to rivet a Seal of Lead on every such Cloth, and to seal, and llamp, in Figures, the Length and Breadth of the fame; which is to be and remain the only Rule of Payment for all and every Buyer or Buyers whatsoever, to accept the said Cloths, subject to a Penalty of 20 s.for any and every Refusal:

Whereby, through lack of Knowledge in some Owners or Occupiers of such Mills, or extraordinary Covetouf-ness in the Clothiers who employ them, it happens that these Mixt or Medley Cloths frequently come into the Petitioners Hands, short in Measure, both in Length and Breadth, of what is fixed and stampt on the Seal of the said Owners or Occupiers of the Mills; as appeared by several of the said Cloths, produced before the Committee; the false Measurement whereof was attelied by various Witnesses, who had measured the fame.

That itappearedto the Committee, That the Clothiers lie under a Penalty of 20s. only, if after any Mixt or Medley Broad-cloth is fully wet, leased and stamped, he, the said Clothier, shall stretch or lirain any inch Cloth, above One Yard in 20 in Length, or above One Nail of a Yard in Breadth; which Penalty, the Petition^ ers alleged, is no-ways adequate to the Offence; besides, that the Manner of recovering thereof renders the Law ineffectual; for that no Forfeiture is to be paid, unless

!ihe Offender be duly convicted before such Cloths be old, or exposed to Sale.

And that upon Consideration of the whole Matter, the Committee canoe to the following Resolutions; viz. Rejoiced, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

2S

That the Petitioners have 'fully -proved the Allegations of the said Petition.

Resolved, That it 'is theiOpinion of this Committee,

That the said recited Act subjects 'the 'Mill-man, who mills or fulls any Mbat or Medley 'Broad-oldfhs, to no Penalty -in case he makes false Measure, although his Measure is 60 be a Rule of Payment for every fudh Cloth to the Buyer: And likewise -no Penalty lies upon the'Ciothier.ifqr any Fraud put‘upon the Buyer, by brs overstraining the said Cloths, in Length and Breadth, unless the same be discovered before they are fold, or exposed'to Sale.

Resolved,^at it is the'Opinion Of‘this Committee,

That the House be moved, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to-explam and amend the said recited Act.

Ordered, That Leave be given to 'bring hi a BiN to explain and amend an Act; passed in the Tenth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for regulating, improving, and encouraging, the Wpollen Manufacture of Mixt or Medley Broad-cloths; and for the better Payment of the Poor employed therein; and that Sir Wm. Withers, Sir Richard Hoar, Sir William locke, and Mr. London, do prepare, and bring in the fame.

This short Account of the pfefent State of the feveril Treaties of her Majesty, and her Allies, with France and Spain, shews how little is wanting, in comparifou with what has been already done, to render the Peace at last universal; as it would have been along time ago, had not continual Obstructions been thrown in the Way of this great Work at its Beginning, and in every Step of its Progress.

France havingcomplained of the Manner of Treating when former Attempts were made to set a Negotiation for a general Peace on Foot; and having, for that Reason, refused to make any hew Overtures to the States General; her Majesty received, in the Month of 1711, a Proposal from the most Christian King, which she immediately communicated, by her Ambassador, to the Ministers of Holland;a(l\ir'mgthem, that, in making

Peace, as in making War, she would aft in perfect Concert with the States: The Dutch Ministers, in Return to this Mark of her Majesty’s Confidence in them, and Friendship for their Republick, having expressed themselves to be weary of the War, heartily ddirous of Peace, and ready to join in any Method her Majesty should think proper to obtain it, gave their Opinion, That the Overture made by France was too general: that it was necessary the Queen should make the French explain themselves more particularly; and that, till they had done so, it was not proper to take any Concert with the rest of the Allies:

As soon as her Majesty received this Answer from the Hague, she insisted that the French should be more direct and particular in their Overtures: and that they should form a distinct Project of such a Peace as they were willing to conclude: No Time was loft in carrying this

Negotiation forward; and the utnioft Care was taken, according to the Defife of the Ministers in Holland, whom her Majesty had consulted, to preserve the Secret: But the dilatory Method of Treating, which in those Circumstances was unavoidable, and other Accidents to which Transtftions of this Kind muftbe always exposed, were the Ofcoafions that nothing more satisfactory than the first Propositions which France had made could be obtained till the End of September 1711,

On the First of October the Queen’s Instructions were given to the Earl of Strafford to repair, with all possible Diligence, to Holland, to acquaint the Ministers of the States with all that had been done, in consequence of what they had, in the Month of May, desired; and to communicate to them the Propositions signed by Monsieur MefnagerFour Days before; to wit

the 27th of September-, which her Majesty looked Opon to include, in their general Expressions, all the particular Demands proper to be made in the Course of the Negotiation; and to be a sufficient Foundation whereupon to open the Conferences: The Earl of Strafford was, at the same time, instructed to assure the Ministers of Holland, That her Majesty was determined to accept of no Advantage, herself, repugnant to their Interests; nor of any Peace, unless they had all reasonable Satisfaction as to their Barrier,*as to their Trade, and in every other respect: He was likewise to exhort them to join with her Majesty in promoting the strictest Union among all the Confederates, as the only means to carry the Negotiation successfully forward; and Communications and Afluranees of the same Nature were, at the same tim« given to the other Allies.

Before these Orders could be executed, and even before the last Overtures had been made on the Part of France, or it could pbflibly be known what had been t ran failed, the whole Confederacy was industrioully alarmed; Jealousies were every-tvhere sown; and, even in Britain, the most licentious Clamours were raised against her Majesty’s Proceedings.

This Behaviourmuft appear very extraordinary, when besides what is above mentioned, it shall be considered, th’at the receiving a M inifter from France by her Majesty, which was urged as the Reasonof the Apprehensions of the Allies, and which wras the only one they pretended to give, was no more than what the Dutch, and, there was Ground to believe, others of the Confederates, had several times done; and that the Person sent hither was the same ^lonfxcutMefnager, who, a Year or Two before, had Iain concealed in Holland for many Weeks; and had treated, during that time, with the chief Ministers of that Republick.

The fatal Consequersces which the lead Appearance of Disunion amongst the Allies would necessarily produce, began then to be felt; and her Majesty found herself obliged to let the Imperialists, and the Dutch, know, that the French might have been brought to explain themselves further than they did, had it not been for the extraordinary Uneafmefs, Impatience, and Jealously, which, upon the First Appearance of taking any Measures towards Peace, discovered themselves among the Allies.

From thence are all the Obstructions to the Peace to be dated; and to those Obstructions alone such Points as seem to fall short of the Expectations of any of the Parties concerned are to be attributed: The Queen fore-saw that nothing would be left undone to force the Negotiation out of her Hands, as well by those who were against any Peace at all, as by those w ho feared, that her Majesty being at the Head of the Negotiation, more Advantages might accrue to Great Britain than they were willing to allow; and, therefore, the Confederacy which formed itself in Oppofttion to what the Queen had undertaken, instead of inclining her Majesty to alter her Conduct, became the strongest Real'on imaginable to continue it: Things were already brought to that Ext remity, that there was no middle between a steady Pursuit of the true Interest of Great Britain, in the First Place, and abandoning ourselves to be disposed of, in

Soou after the Earl of Straff Departure to Holland, Monsieur Buys arrived here, with the Character of Envoy from the Stales General: When a Minister of this Consequence was sent, Hopes were immediately conceived, that all Jealousies might be cured, and a perfect Harmony he created between the Queen and the States; after which an Union with the other Allies would necessarily follow; and, the whole Confederacy entering, as one Man into the Congress, the Sincerity of the French would have been soon tried; and the Possibility, or Impossibility, of obtaining a good Peace, soon decided.

In order to this End, her Majesty’s Servants were instru£ied and impowered to settle with this Minister such Disputes as related to the reciprocal Interests of the two Nations; Aud to prevent, by this previous Concert, any Difference which might arise, in the Course of the Treaty, between the Queen and the States, they were further directed toadjuft, in Confidence, with him, such a Plan for the General Peace, as it might be proper finally to inlist upon: And, in this Cafe, her Ma-jeliy would have been ready, jointly with the States, to have broke the Conferences, if these Terms had not been granted without Exception, and without Delay: But such was the publick Misfortune at that time, that this Minister was only impowered to hear, and not to speak; and could not take upon him so much as to conclude, or even sign fub f a new offensive and

defensive Alliance betwixt the Queen and the States; which, in those Circurastances of Affairs, hejudged, and Iter Majesty’s Servants concurred with him, to be extremely necessary.

But the Conferences which were held with Monsieur Buys here, by the Accounts which came from abroad, and by the Representations which some of the Allies made, about the same time, to her Majesty, it appeared undeniably evident, not only that the War was become on the present Foot, absolutely impracticable; but also, that no Alteration could be attempted, either in the Method of carrying it on, or in the views towards which it was directed, without dissolving at once the Confederacy: And that the Dispute was, in fact, not whether a Peace, by which Spain, and the Indies would be left to Philip, should be made, but who Iliould have the making of it.

The real annual Expence of this Kingdom amounting to more than Seven millions; whereas it is certain, that we were not in a Condition effectually to raise near Six Millions, in the Course of a Year: From whence it follows, that, if this Proportion had been continued, about Nine Millions had been the true Charge of a Second Year, and about Eleven Millions that of a Third.

This was the State of oar Affairs, whilst the House of Austria contributed nothing but One Regiment to the War of Spain, little to that of Italy, had but few Forces, and those entirely unactive, on the Rhine; and sent none into the Netherlands, except such as those harafi'ed Provinces were obliged to maintain, and were thereby rendered unable to furnish Troops, or make the necessary Provisions for the Operations of the Arm}'; both which they might otherwise have done, and both which they did, in an eminent Degree, whilti they were under the Government of the present King of Spain.

The States General bore a cor.tiderable Burthen: But as they had from the Year 1708 sent no Supplies of any Kind, either to Portugal, or to; and had drawn themselves ahnoft entirely out of the Spanish War; as they furnished in no Proportion their Quota lor the Sea Service; as they had reduced their joint Contributions with the Queen, in all Payments, to One-third of the Whole; and as they were very backward in answering even this Share of Expence; so the Load of Great Britain came, upon their Account, as well as upon the Emperor’s, to be vastly increased: As to the rest of the Allies, all the Troops which they furnished were maintained by the Queen, and the States, except Voi. 17.

a few, and those almost wholly employed in covering peace with their own Fortifications. Allies and

In this Situation of Affairs her Majesty declared to an,i the Imperialists, and to the Dutch, That if they would 5pa'n‘ not allow France to have given sufficient Grounds for opening the Conferences; if they were desirous to carry on the War, and determined to accept of no Terms of Peace inferior to those which had been formerly demanded, and refused: Ihe was, on her Part, ready to concur with them: But that, in Justice to herself, and to them. Hie thought herself bound to let them know, that file could no longer bear so disproportionable a Burthen; that it was evident, that the common Effort must be still greater than it was, or that there would remain no Prospect of arriving at the Ends which they proposed; and that for these Reasons, it would be incumbent upon them, if the War continued, to increase their Expences, whilst the Queen reduced hers.

The Ministers of the States General were very candid and opeu upon this Head: Monsieur Buys asserted.

That his Mailers had done their utmost already, and could be obliged to do no more; and many of the others had, on several Occasions, declared their Country unable to support the Charge they were at another Summer;

And the Pensionary himself, in a Deputation of the States appointed to attend the Earl of Strafford in her 1711, declared, that it was impossible to think of continuing the War another Year: that, what from the Emperor, and what from the Princes of the North, we should be in the utmost Danger, Iliould we attempt to do it; and finally, that they were Traitors to their Country who were against the Peace.

Many Instances might be produced to {hew, that there was, at least, as little Reason to expect from the House of Austria, as from the States General, a greater Effort than they had hitherto made: The Peace of Hungary was concluded about the Mouth of May 1711; and that constant Excuse which the Ministers of Vienna used to make, for all their Deficiencies, did, by Consequence, no longer subsist: Yet her Majesty found it impossible, at the latter End of that Year, to obtain a Reinforcement of no more than 8,000 Men from thence; although her Minister was impowered to have offered £.40,000 for the March of them; and, although the present King of Sicily, then Duke of Savoy, undertook, if he might be assured of this Reinforcement any time before the Close of the Campaign, to establish his Winter-quarters on that Side of France; which would have been in that Point of time, the more decisive; because a Project was then formed, and would have been executed, could the States have been in time induced to have taken even less than their own Share upon them (her Majesty supplying their Deficiency, as well as her own Proportion), to have kept a great Body of Horse, all the Winter, on the Frontiers of the Low Countries, by which means Picardy, and the Isle of France, would have been ravaged; no Magazines could have been erected; and the French must have gone, in the Spring, a great Way back into their Country to assemble their Army.

The Imperial Ministers confessed very freely, that their Master expected the Queen Iliould furnish all the Money, and that the utmost lie could do was to fend Troops at her Expence; in the same Breath avowing the Emperor’s Intention to break the Negotiation of Peace, and to continue the War till Spain was conquered; the entire Monarchy whereof he expected: But if there had remained any Doubt of the little Assistance which was to be hoped for from the House of Austria, who arrived at fuel) great Acquisilions, this Matter would have been put ent irely oil! of Dispute by the Pcopofals which Prinee Eugene himself made, in Holland first, and afterwards to the Queen.

These Proposals, it must be thought, were carried at lead as high as his Imperial Majesty judged himself able to make good; fmee it is notorious, that he would have stuck at nothing which might have broke the Measures of Peace, and have encouraged the Resolution of pro-

From what has been said it is manifest, that the Method in which the War was proposed to be carried on could no longer be supported; and that there was not any Glimpse of Hope left, that the Allies could be brought to make any considerable Augmentation of Force: To have prosecuted the War, therefore, in this manner, mud have been the Ruin of Britain: To have infilled on an Impossibility, as a Condition without which the Queen would not proceed, mult have disunited the Alliance, and suspended the Operations of the Armies in all Parts: In both these Cafes, the Consequences are too evident to be enlarged on.

In the Beginning of the Year 1711, died the late ."Emperor Joseph; and the Eyes, not only of the Princes of the Empire, but of all the Confederates, and of her Majesty in the first place, were immediately fixed 011 his Brother: This Event occasioned a great Alteration in the Councils of Europe, and gave a new Turn to the Sentiments of many Princes.

There was reason to believe, that the Ministers of Vienna themselves began to cool in the Project of recovering Spain and the Indies.

They seemed to intend nothing more than to get the present Emperor into G, and to secure the Possession of Italy to themselves; and the former, as well as the late, Instances they had made, for attempting the Reduction of Sicily, though at the Expence of diverting Part of that Force which was applied to the War of Spain, pointed the same Way.

In Holland, a Partition of the Monarchy

seemed almost the general Scheme; and the conduct of that Republick, as well as the Confection of its Ministers, shewed, that the Project of driving Philip out of Spain, was looked on thereto, to be a pure Chimera.

Soon after the death of the Emperor , her Majesty had been acquainted, that some of the Princes of the Empire thought it a Point which deserved themost . serious Reflection, whether they should suffer the Imperial and Spanish Crowns to he united on the same Head;

and whether it might not be proper, in the Capitulation of the Empire, to infill on the Separating of them: Other Members of the grand Alliance, and those the only Two with whom her Majesty had entered into any formal Engagement for recovering the entire Spanish Monarchy, represented, upon the fameOccasion, against placing this Crown on the Emperor’s Head: It was urged, by one of the most considerable Princes in the Alliance, that the Principle upon which he engaged into the War was now altered; and that, instead of fighting to procure the Spanish Monarchy to the House of tria, his filtered, and even his Safety, required, that he should tight to prevent it.

The same therefore Hood thus: The present Emperor, even after his Brother’s Death, and his own Election, would content himself with nothing less than the whole Spanish Monarchy; and iniifted that the War should be prosecuted in this View: Of the other Allies, some looked on this Project as chimerical, others as dangerous: Prom whence it follows, that to keep the grand Alliance united in this Principle was impracticable; and it must be allowed, that, to alter this Principle, to have changed so many Treaties, to have reconciled so many different Interests, and to have formed a System entirely new in the midst of the War, was an Experiment too hazardous to be attempted.

Io this Situatiou of Affairs no Time was to be loft: The Queen knew very well, that Attempts to of«n a Treaty with France, separately from her, were made

by those who clamoured the loudest against her Mea-fpres: And the present Emperor had thought fit, on board one of her Majesty’s Ships, and by her own Mi-nifter to fend her a Message of the same Nature: She therefore infilled with the Imperial ills, and with the Dutch, that Hie would beat some certainty; and that they should comply with her in the Measures either of War, or of Peace.

How the War became impracticable, has already appeared: What Objections there were to the carrying on a Treaty of Peace, come next to be related.

The principal, and indeed the only avowed, Dispute between her Majesty and the States, at this time, concerned the Method of carrying a Negotiation forward: The States pretended, that a fair Opportunity would be given the Mmillers of France to divide the Confederates, if they were fullered to meet together in a general Congress, before the essential Articles of Peace were settled by specifick Preliminaries: The Use which had been made of this Method, on a former Occasion, to evade the concluding of any Peace; when, according to the Confession of the Dutch Ministers themselves, the Differences on which the Allies and France broke off did not deserve the Life of a single SoLier; gave no great Encouragement to pursue the same again: Besides which, as the Queen would uot take upon her to settle the Interests of others; so neither would lhe suffer others to determine those of her own Kingdoms: And if all the Confederates were to assemble, in order to adjust a Preliminary Treaty, the Objection made by the States returned upon them.

In December 1711 the States concurred with her Majesty in fixing the Place of the Treaty, appointing the Day on which the Congress should open, inviting the Allies to fend their Ministers thither, and giving the necessary Passports to the Plenipoteutiar'ej of And, if nothing had happened to revive the Spirit of those who were bent against the Peace, it is highly probable, by the little time which it cod to conclude most of the Treaties after the Conferences, that had been interrupted, were resumed at and the

Allies proceeded in earned to negotiate, that the Treaties of all the Confederates with France might have been finiftied before the Season of opening the Campaign in 1712: But before Motifieur Buys returned into Holland, or the Conferences could begin, the Efforts were renewed with the greatest Vigour to break off the Negotiation: The Cry against a Peace, by which Spain, and the Indies, should be left to any Branch of the House of Bourbon, liecame louder than ever; and, letters and Memorials were not only delivered, hut printed; and Appeal made against her Majesty’s Proceedings to all Europe, and even to her own Subjects.

On these Encouragements, the good Dispositions towards Peace received a Check; and some of those who had owned themselves against the Prosecution of the War, to recover the whole Spanish Monarchy to the House of Austria, joined now, under this very Pretence

to break the Measures of Peace: The Treatment which her Majesty met with at this time will appear in the cleared Light from this Circumstance: The Miiiifter of the States General proposed to her Majesty’s Servants, that, considering the Difficulties the Queen lay under; how impossible it was to recover by War, or by Treaty, the Spanish Monarchy from King Philip-, and how im-possible lie hkewile apprehended it to be, in the present Circunistances of Affairs, for her Majesty to carry any Negotiation on, by which this Monarchy should he left to Philip; he was ready to extricate her Majesty from this Dilemma, and to fereen her Ministers . in carrying on the Work which they had begun, in the Name of his Masters to present a Memorial, by which the Point of obtuitiing Spain, and the Indies (h add be given up, provided he might be assured, that the Dutch should have an equal Share with her Majesty’s Subjefcls in the AJJiento, which Contract he sup-poled it was stipulated should be made with Great Britain.

From the Causes, and by the Steps, which have been here mentioned, was the Disunion among the Allies arrived to the high'eft Pitch at the Opening of the Conferences in the Month of January 1714; when the ftrifleft Union amongst them was more than ever necessary, and when the whole Fruit of those Successes wherewith God had blessed their Cause, in the Course of the War, depended on it; They sent their several Plenipotentiaries to Utrecht; but it was very apparent, that most of them acted on that Maxim which one of them professed; that giving into the Measures of Peace was the surest way to continue the War: They flattered themselves, that the Imperial Ministers, in Conjunction with those of Britain, had, Two Years before, baffled the Designs of Holland to make Peace; and that it would be at lead as easy for the Ministers of the Emperor, in Conjunction with those of the States General, to render fruitless, at this time, all her Majesty’s Endeavours to the same End: After this, it will not appear surprising, if the utmost Dexterity was exerted to delay the entering on Business at UtreAil, and to Wait for the Event of the Campaign.

On the 29th January 1744-. the First general Conference was held between the Ministers of the Allies and those of France; and by the Beginning of April a Dispute was set on Foot concerning the Method of proceeding; which made all Treaty impracticable; and which was kept up till a Quarrel happening between one of the Plenipotentiaries of France,*n& One of those of the Suites, a new Obstruction was created, to take place, and answer the Ends of the First.

The French had made their Overtures in Writing, the Allies had likewise given in their Demands in Writing: A nd the Question arose. Whether the French were obi iged to give a speciGc Answer in Writing; or whether they should now proceed in the Negotiation, fcy debating with the several Allies, agreeably to the Method used in funner Congresscs.

By the Minutes of the Protocol, to which the French Ministers appealed, it appeared that they were under no such Obligation: But, between the ad April and the 5th, Count Zinzendorf had been at the where the

Resolution was taken to carry things to Extremity; that is, not to treat with the Ministers of the most Christian King, unless they gave an Answer in Writing: And Orders were accordingly sent by the States to their Plenipotentiaries: Tile Design Was laid, upon this, to have broke off all further Treaty; but this Deflgn was difap-poiuted by the Declaration which the French Ministers made on the 6th: That their Instructions allowed them to go no further than they had offered; but that they would write to the King their Master, to know his Pleasure: After which, during Three Months Time, there was not so much as any Step made on the Part of the Allies for an Answer from the French; though, at the same time, the Imperialists were pulhing to get the Congress broke, or, at least, her Majesty’s Ministers excluded.

In August the Second Obstruction took place; and that, trifling as the Occasion of it may seem, was so managed, that till the 30th N. S. 1744* the

Difficulty could not be overcome.

Ten Months having been loft at Utrecht, and the Success of the Campaign not having answered the Deflgn of those who projected the breaking off the Treaty by the Operations of the Army, the Ministers of the Allies made no further Difficulty to proceed in the very Method which her Majesty’s Plenipotentiaries had from the first advised: This Metlrod succeeded so well, that, in Two Months after the Negotiation was resumed, all the Par-tiesin the War made their Peace with France, except the Emperor, and the Empire; and the Ministers of these Powers had likewise broughttheir Disputes to so narrow aCompals, that, on the 15th May 1713, the only Difference between them was concerning the Marquisate of Burgaio, eftiinatedat the yearly Value of about 12,000 Crowns.

In this State of Things, Monsieur Kirchner, the last of thelmperial Ministers who continued at , left

Vol. 17.

57*

that Place; and the Emperor’s Resolution was declared of supporting that War, Angle, which, assisted by the Queen and the States, he had not been able to carry on with any tolerable Vigour.

It was from this time easy to foresee, that the Emperor intended to treat no more at; and that a separate

Negotiation between the Courts of Vienna and France, whenever it should happen, would not prove very advantageous to the Emperor, or. favourable to the Protestant Interest in Germany; of which her Majesty had taken early, and as Ihe hoped, effectual Care, by obliging France toconsent, that all things concerning the State of Religion in the Empire should be settled comformably to the Tenor of the Treaties of iVeJlphalia, in such manner, as to make it plainly appear, that the most Christian King neither would make, nor-would have made, any Alteration in the said Treaties: Thus Oneof the contracting Parties had already, in effect, yielded to the Abolition of that Clause in the 4th Article of the Treaty of Byfwick, so fatal to the Protestant Religion: And, if his Imperial Majesty had concluded his Treaty at Utrecht, it is hardly to be believed, that in the Midll of so many Allies, whose Blood had been Ihed, and whose Treasure had "been exhausterl, in his Cause, he would have refused to their Intercession, what France had complied with on the Angle Infiances of the Queen.

It has been already observed, that if the Allies, when the Congress at Utrecht was opened in the Beginning of the Year, had, in good earnest, gone about the several Treaties, the Peace might, in all Probability, have been made before the Armies could have taken the Field: It may be necessary here to observe the State of Affairs at a'nother Period of Time; and another Opportunity loft of treating with the greatest Advantage on our Side and with the greatest Probability of Succels.

On the 6th of June 1712 her Majesty communicated to both Housesof Parliament upon what Terms ageneral Peace might be made: Those who were against any Treaty, and who entertained Hopes, that the Sense of the Nation would not go along with her Majesty; and that Obstructions would arise, even in Britain, to the Couclufion of the Peace; might havefeen how vain those Expectations were, by the Returns which the Two Houses made to this Instance of her Majesty’s Conde-feension; by the Adurances they gave of their Confidence in her, and of their entire Relianceon her Wisdom to finifti this great and good Work; and by their humble Delire.that Ihe would please to proceed in the present Negotiations for obtaining a speedy Peace: Those who pretended only lo be against the Method of treating, and who were lond ofspecifick Preliminaries, had now the very thing which they desired; his most Christian Majesty having declared himself explicitly, and particularly, on the most important Points that were to be settled in the Treaties of Peace: The Queen was, even at that time, not under the least Obligation, but at full Liberty, to have proceeded in the Negotiation, or to have broke it off, according as the French had behaved themselves; but France was under the strongest Obligations to her Majesty, and, by her Majesty’s means, to the Allies; the Coiiceffious then made on the Part of France, were made without any Concession whatever on the Part of the Confederates.

If therefore they could, even then have been prevailed upon to unite with the Queen, and with one another, during a short Cessation of Arms, the general Peace might have been secured; or, if that had failed, we should have got, by the Cessation, into our Hands, a Place of greater Importance than we could have expected by the most successful Campaign to conquer: But, instead of applying themselves to improve this happy Conjuncture, the Ministers who met to treat of Peace seemed attentive only to what passed in the Field; and Utrecht seemed the Scene of no oilier Business than unnecessary Disputes concerning the Forms of proceeding, and Negotiations to accommodate Differences which the Quarrels of Servants had begun.

From this State of the several Treaties between her Majesty, her Allies, and France and Spain $ and by this Account of the general Negotiations of Peace; the Reasonableness of all the Steps her Majesty has taken, and those Designs which have been pursued, at first, to wrest the Negotiation out of her Hands, and, since, to unravel all that had been done, and to throw us into Confusion, will sufficiently appear.

Extract of a Letter to the Commissioners of the Cnf-toms, from Mr. Edward Hill, Collector of the Customs in the Upper District of James River, in Virginia’, dated 15th October 1713.

I beg Leave to inform your Honours, That, of latfe, the Out-ports, and North Britain, nay, London itself, has given Directions to their Agents and Factors Wife purchasing Tobacco, to receive none other than TraSfi, discoloured, and unmerchantable; such as, before they encouraged it, was flung away, and never packt: We could not but wonder such Tobaccoes should answer any Profit, when we found, that the belt We sent brought us oftentimes in Debt.

’Tis now no longer a Mystery; and we are informed, That such discoloured Tobacco, when it comes for England, or North Britain, is all allowed for Damage, and so no Custom paid; in which, the Ships beitfg their own, they find their Account.

The Council of Virginia having in their Memorial to the Lords for Trade and Plantations mentioned this Evil in particular, I presume that will be Inducement sufficient for your Honours to believe the Fact; else would have been very easy to have produced particular Instances.

I only have just mentioned this Evil, that your Honours may be apprised of it.

Ex. Cha. Cdrkejfe, Secretary.

That, by ancient Laws, Aliens and Strangers are liable to pay Customs for all Merchandizes imported into this Realm; and, for securing thereof, several Laws was made against Englishmens colouring Aliens Goods, and entering them in their Names, to obviate which, every Person, on4his Admission to Freedom, takes an Oath against the Doing thereof; That several Foreigners, not being under an Oath, as Freemen are, have, on purpose to defraud her Majesty, and this City of those Customs, and still do enter Aliens Goods in their Names, to the great Decay ofsaid Customs, and Revenues of this City: And praying, That, for the future, all Merchants, and others, passing inwards, may be obliged to take an Oath, That the said Merchandizes do not belong to any Alien; and, upon Refusal, to be deemed Aliens Goods.

Upon the Petitions of John Burgh and Henry Watkins Esquires, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Paul Methuen, and the honourable Wm. Eger/on, Esquires, to serve for the Borough of Brack ley, in the County of Northampton,
