That the Petitioners Counsel infilled, That the Right of Election for this Borough is in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses.

That the Sitting Members Counsel infified, That the Right of Election, is in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, resident within the Borough.

That it appeared, by the Journal of the House of Commons, in January 1710, That, in the then controverted Election for this Borough, the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Mayer, Aldermen, and Burgefifes; the whole Number of which are Thirty-three. That the Petitioners Counsel called,

William Blunt: W ho said, He has known the Borough Seven Years; and takes the Right of Election to be in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses: That Robert Wilkins junior, who has been removed to London a considerable time, voted in the lad Election before this, for Mr. Eger/on, and was not objected to; and he has always voted in the Corporation Courts: And that Edward Butler has claimed to vote; but the Lord Bridgewater’s Steward would not allow it, because he lived out of Town:

Being cross-examined, the Witness said, has

a House in the Borough of; but had not any

Sen nuts there: That he pays the Queen’sTaxes for it; and his Landlord pays to Church and Poor: That he comes to all the Courts: That Butler lives in the Town) but they never admit him to vote among them.

That the Sitting Members Counsel called,

Mr. Francis Neale: Who said, He has been Steward of the Borough above Twenty Years: That the Right of Elect:on is in those Capital Burgesses only, who are 16

brilis. 1714.

resident within the Town and Borough: If they have a Being the re, they have a Right to vote: When a Capital Burgess removes, and lives out of the Town, his Place is void, ip/o fa£io; and they choose another in his stead: Some, upon coming again, have been reelected; but they are not in without a Re-election:

That William Philips and Matthew Harding, who were Burgesses, and had removed out of the Borough, were, upon their Return, re-eleCled: Phillips his Election is mentioned in the Minutes of 94; and Harding's in the Roll of 97: It appears, by those Minutes and Rolls,

That this has been the Practice there for above 20 Years last pall: And the Witness said. There are no Rolls before the Year 95 in being:

That Butler never was Burgess in the Witness’s time:

That, after 12 Years Absence, he applied to the Witness to be re-eleCled; and in 1708 was named by the Mayor; but George Bull, who was named by the Witness, was chosen:

That Wilkins always attended the Courts, and voted ’ in all Elections; had a good Estate in the Borough j and paid Scotland Lot there.

Simon Butcher, aged 63, said, He has belonged to the Courts 40 Years: That the Custom is, when a Burgess removes, his Place is void, and they choose another; but, if he leaves Part of his Family there, he has a Right to vote: If he removes his Family, and returns, he has no Right, without being elected again; of which he mentioned the Inllances of Philips and Harding, produced by Mr. Neale; And said, That Wilkins attended all the Courts; and all along, during his Absence, paid Scotland Lot.

Geo. Loveday, called, said, He collected the Church-rates for Mr. Wilkins' House: That the Tenant told him, He paid them for his Landlord: And that Wilkins, and not the Tenant, is in the Levy.

And that the Committee came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Brackley, in the County of Northampton, is in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the said Borough, residing in the said Borough.

That the Petitioners Counsel offered to disqualify the aforesaid Three Voters for the Sitting Member, viz. John Hawes, John Reaper, and John Maxwell; by calling Witnesses to prove their Confessions, That they had not taken the Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper within One Year next before their Elections into Office, as is required by the Corporation Act; these Persons being elected, One in 1710, and the other Two in 1711, to be Three of the 33 Burgesses, who have the Government of this Corporation;

But the Sitting Members Counsel alleging, these Voters are Churchmen; That they had no Notice of this Objection; and were surprised in it;

That the Committee did not think fit admit the Petitioners to produce the Evidence they offered to this Point.

Then the Petitioners Counsel called,

John Welchman: Who produced a Certificate from the Churchwardens, and Overseers of the Poor of the Parish of Tingwick; in the County of Bucks, dated 7th

April 1701, owning Henry Whitmell to be an Inhabitant there j and that he will be received as such whenever he, or any of his Family, become chargeable to the Parish he lives in at Brackley:

And said, That Whitmell, at the time of his Election to be a Burgess, rented only a House of 50 a Year at Brackley: That he lives there; is a Burgess; is reckoned One of the Corporation; and rents about £.5 per Annum in another Parish.

James Slit said, That at the time of this Election;

Edward Butler lived at Tingxvick, in Bucks: That he long since went from the Borough, and lived iu and his Place was filled up; and that, after his Return, he lived several Years in the Town, and never pretended any Right to be a Burgess; and, a Year ago, Weljk-man owned to the Witness, That Butler, had no Right; but said, He would keep him for a Handle.

Robert Hilton, called, said. That Butler has not voted for a Member of Parliament these Twenty Years: That Five Years ago he desired, and actually flood, to be re-elected a Burgess; and asked the Witness’s Voteforhim:

That they have several times elected Burgesses upon the same Day they elect Members of Parliament: Their Usage is, first to fill up the Corporation, and then proceed to the Election to Parliament.

Mr,. Neale said, When he came first to the Borough, it was declared to be the Custom to fill up any Vacancies in the Corporation upon the same Day they elect to Parliament:

There were Two controverted Elections in King William's Reign; and then all the old Members declared, and unanimously agreed, this was the Custom immemorial: Upon both those Occasions it was put in Practice; and such Elections, in 1702, are entered upon the Roll, to prevent the like Disputes for the future.

William Thonger laid, That he voted for the Sitting Members; but that Mr. Bush, Mr. Collis, and Mr.

Walton, who made Interest for the Petitioners, asked his Vote for them; and told him. He now might raise his Family; they had done the Business; and, if they could get his Vote, they should carry. the Election:

They bid him take 100 or 200 Guineas, or write down what he would have, and he should have it; and swore.

They had Money enough in Town, and would not lose the Election for want of it.

Robert Hilton said, That, being in Brackley Street, a Fellow of Magdalen College asked him to go with hitn to drink a Glass of Wine; He went; was made drunk, and carried away, he cannot tell whither; was kept without seeing any Light, till the Election was over, and was then attended home with Four Horses; but knows not where he was, nor any of the Company, except Mr. Jackson, Bishop Crew's Gardener: That he would have voted for the Sitting Members, had he been at the Election.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions;

Mr. Chetwynd, reported from the Committee appointed to inquire into the Management and Application of all Sums of Money, which have been collected for repairing any particular Highways, by virtue of any Act, of Parliament passed frnce her Majesty’s Accession to the Crown, That they bad received a Complaint of the ill Repair of the Roads between Stratford, in the County of Northampton, and Dunchurch, in the County ’of Warwick, which were to be_ repaired by the Act,

made in the 9th and 10th Years of her Majesty’s Reign, for repairing the said Highways; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report, and Resolutions, in at the Clerk's Table: Where they were read; and are as follow; viz.

That, upon Complaint to the Committee of the ill Repair of the Roads between Old Stratford, in the County of Northampton, and Dunchurch, in the County of Warwick, they proceeded to the Examination of the

Incomes of the Toll from the Turnpike erected in Wol-scotl-lane, in the County of Warwick, by virtue of an Act of Parliament, made in the Ninth and Tenth Years of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for repairing the Highways from Old Stratford, in the County of Northampton, to Dunchurch, in the County of Warwick; and find, That there hath been expended on that Part of the said Road lying in Warwickshire, near as much Money as hath been collected and bor-. rowed upon the Toll aforesaid; and that the Reason why it is no better repaired, proceeds from the very great Distance, and extraordinary Charge of CarHage, of Materials proper to amend the fame; as also, from the Turnpike not raising so much Money as it might dor had the Commissioners a Power to erect one in a convenient Part of the Road between Dunchurch and Coventry, that Passengers might not avoid it as they now do, by travelling a By-way.

Upon which the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Toll continuing to be collefcted, and the Roads between Old Stratford and Dunchurch being no better repaired, is a great Grievance to all People travelling that Road.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Sums of Money, borrowed and collected by virtue of the said Act, as far as relates to the Warwkkfiire Part of the Road, have been duly applied towards the Repair thereof, according to the Directions of the said Act, as appeared by the particular Accounts laid before the Committee.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Commissioners of Warwickshire may have Power to erect another Turnpike on the Road between Coventry and Dunchurch, to hinder Passengers from evading, as they now do, by travelling a By-way, the Vo j..-17.

Mr. Conyers, according to Order, reported from the Ways Committee of the whole House, who were to consider of and Way* and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, the Resolution they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Table: Where it was read: and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That.it is the Opinion of this Committee,

ThatTwo Shillings in the Pound, and no more, be raised, in the Year 1714, upon all Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments, Pensions, Offices, and personal Estates, in that Part of Great Britain called England, Wales, and the Town of Berwick upon Tweed; and that a proportionable Cess, according to the 9th Article of the Treaty for the Union, be laid upon that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

The said Resolution being read a Second lime.

Refolded, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That Two Shillings in the Pound, and no more, be raised in the Year 1714, upon all Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments, Pensions, Offi-' ces, and personal Estates, in that Part of Great Britain called England, Wales, and the Town of Berwick upon Tweed; and that a proportionable Cess, according to *' the gth Article of the Treaty for the Union, be laid upon that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolution: And that Mr. Conyert, Mr. Attorney General, Mr. Solicitor General, and Mr. Lowndes, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Ordered, That the Knights of Shires, and other Members of the House, do prepare Lifts, fairly written, of Commissioners Names for executing the said Act, for> the respective Counties, Cities, and Places, for which] there have been used to be particular Commissioners.

The House, according to Order, took into Considera- Addrefle* on tion the Message from the Lords on Saturday last; Conclufien of which was as followeth; viz. . the Peace.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, in Parliament aftemfiled, beg Leave to express the just Sense which we have of your Majesty’s Goodnels to your People, in delivering them by a safe, honourable, and advantageous, Peace with France and Spain, from the heavy Burthen of a consuming Land War, unequally carried on, and become, at lull, impracticable: And we do most earnestly entreat your Majesty, That you will be pleased with the same Steadiness, notwithstanding all the Obstructions which have been, or may be, thrown in your Way, to pursue such Measures as you shall judge necessary for completing the Settlement of Europe, on the Principles laid down by your Majesty in your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

Refolded, That the Blank in the Address be filled up with the Words " and Commons."

Refolded, That the House doth agree with the Lords in the said Address to be presented to her Majesty.

Ordered, That Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer do carry the Address to the Lords, and acquaint them.

That this House hath filled up the Blank, and agreed with their Lordships in the said Address to be presented

to her Majesty. .

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Sir Gilbert Dolben, according to Order, reported from st. Alban’* the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, Eletfion. as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of St. Albans, in the County of Hertford, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report and Resolutions, in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read; and are as follow;

Upon the Petition of John Gape Esquire complaining of an undue Election and Return of Hale Esquire to serve for the Borough of Saint Albans, in the County of Hertford:

That the Petitioner’s Counsel alleged this Borough to be a Borough by Prescription, confirmed by several Charters; and that the Right of Election is in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Freemen, and such Hou (holders only as pay Scotland Lot.

That the Sitting Member’s Counsel alleged, That honorary Freemen have no Right to vote.

That, to prove the Right of Election to be as the Petitioner’s Counsel alleged, they produced the Charter of nMay7° Ed. the VI. which incorporates the Mayor,

and 10 Aldermen; and gives Power to them, or the major Part of them, to elect Burgesses, habit antibus burgi:And,

The Resolution of the House of Commons of iotli March 1700, That the Right of Election for this Borough is in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Freemen, and such Housholders only as pay Scotland Lot:

And the Petitioner's Counsel called,

Wm.Maston Who said, He has known the honorary Freemen vote for 68 Years without Objection; he was Mayor in 1705, and then they voted on both Sides without Exception; and, since that time, they have been always admitted.

Wm. Hunt said, That for 32 Years he has known the honorary Freemen vote without Exception:

That the Right of Election is in the Freemen at large; and the being honorary Freemen, or not re-~* fident, is no Disqualilication:

That,

.13 Ann. 27* Aprilis.

597

That in all Elc&ions since 1705 the honorary Freemen have voted on all Sides, without Exception:

That Freemen ought not to be made without the Mayor, and a Majority of the Aldermen present; but several have been made by a Minority, and not objected to in the Town; but that some, made free in Mr. Sea-brook's Mayoralty, were set alideby the Court of Queen’s Bench, as illegally made, because only Two Aldermen were present.

Francis Halford said. He has known the Borough rear 40 Years: That the Right of Election is in the Freemen in general; and that since 1705 the Freemen at large have been polled on both Sides, and were so polled in the lait Election; and he never knew any honorary Freemen refused.

That the Sitting Member’s Counsel alleged, That before the Year 1700 honorary Freemen were admitted sparingly; but that in September 1705 Mr. Stone, the then Mayor, called Two Courts, and admitted 50 Freemen; which being complained of in the next Parliament, the House of Commons set aside the honorary Freemen. They called,

Edmund Ay heard-, who has been 20 Years Town-clerk, and has known the Corporation above 30 Years; He produced the Town-book; by which it appears, that upon 5th September 1705, 45 Freemen were admitted; but it is not distinguished, nor could he say, how many of them were honorary Freemen; but he said several of them had a Right:

That the Sitting Member did object against honorary Freemen at this Election; but that ever since the Witness has known the Corporation they have polled on all Sides, and were never disputed till 1705.

T/10. Down said. That he supposed all those who were admitted the 5th of September 1705, except One or Two, were honorary Freemen; because the Question was put, whether honorary Freemen should be made.

That the Petitioners Counsel argued. That these Actions against the Men of this Town; and this Release being to them, and their Successors; and their Disclaimer being for them, and Successors; were an Evidence of their being a Community, and a Corporation: and that thereby, and by the other Records produced, it appeared they were an ancient Community; had an ancient Guild, and a prescriptive Right to fend Members to Parliament; and that such Community and Privileges were suppressed by this Agreement, and the Power of the Abbot; so that the Corporation durll not afterwards claim a Right to fend Members to Parliament:

That they farther argued, as an Evidence of such Prescription, That the head of this Town is styled Alderman; and that every Town in England whoseHead or chief Officer is so styled, was founded in the time of the Saxons.

That they produced the Journal of the 3d, and of the 14th, of May 1660: whereby it appeared. AP ETITIO N of the Fishmongers of the City of Fish caught London was presented to the House, and read; set- b> ^reign-ting forth, That the Fishermen of Dover, Folkjione, and ers-Hyth, have each petitioned for Leave to bring in a Bill to prevent the Importation into England, Wales, or Berwick upon Tweed, in any Ship or Vessel, any fresh Fish caught by Foreigners; and should the same affect Stock-fiffi, live Eels, and Lobsters, it will be of ill Consequence, great Quantities of Stockfish being used in victualing Merchant Ships to the East Indies; besides which, the Eels and Lobsters imported are larger and better than those caught about England: And praying, Provision may be made, in the said Bill, for the Importation of Stockfish, live Eels, and Lobsters, in English Property, into the Port of London, though caught by Foreigners.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for the effectual preventing the Importation into England, Wales, and Town of Berwick, any fresh Fish caught by Foreigners, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Wardens and Fellows of New College, in Oxon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have an Estate in the Levels of Havering and Dagenham, in Essex, which was drowned by a Breach in the Walls of Dagenham Six Years ago; and on Monday the 15th of February there happened a violent Storm, which occasioned new Breaches; inso much that the-Tenants are wearied with making any Attempts to flop the fame; and the said Level will be loft: That the Petitioners said Estate is a considerable Branch of the Revenue of this College; and the Petitioners are likely to receive great Damage, if not speedily prevented: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Common-council, of the City of London, is referred.

A Petition of the several Land-owners of the Levels of Eastbury, Ripple, and Wejin the County of

E/fex, on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners Lands, being 1,500 Acres, are now underWater, occasioned by a Breach at Dagnam: That the Petitioners have been at great Charge, ever since the Breach which happened Six Years ago, in preferring the said Levels; by which vastExpence the Land-owners have been at, they are unable to attempt any more the Recovery of the said Levels; which if not speedily prevented, the Water will reach the Town of Barkin, lying about Three Miles distant: And praying to be relieved in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Common-council, of the City of London, is referred.

A Petition of the Dean and Canons of the King’s free Chapel of St. George, within the Castle of Wind for, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners have an Estate in the Levels of Dagenham, in Essex, which, Six Yearsfince, was overflowed by a Breach in the River Walls: That the Petitioners, and Tenants, paid above the Value of their Lands, and happily succeeded in the Stopping thereof; but, in February last, received very great Damage by a violent Storm, inso much that the Land-owners will not be able to attempt the Recovery; which will be a great Loss to the Petitioners, and Successors: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Common-council, of the City of London, is referred.

A Petition of several Owners of Land in the Levels of Havering and Dagnam, in the County of Essex, now under Water, on behalf of themselves and others, was. presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners, ever since the Breach Six Years ago, which happened in the Walls of the said. Levels, have been attempting to recover the fame: and completed the fame, at the Expence of at least 30 Years Value of the said Lands: That, in February last, by a great Storm, all the Walls adjoining were overflowed, and carried away great Part of the new Work; by which several Families have been ruined; and, others thinking the Attempts hazardous, the Land must be loft, and the Navigation interrupted: That the Petitioners have been charged with a Land Tax, though the Lands produced nothing but Expence for Six Years: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Common-council, of the City of London, is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Capital Burgesses, as also several of the Inhabitants, Merchants, and Traders, of the ancient Borough and Town of Bridgwater, in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That Minehead is an ancient and commodious Port, and 'a great Security for harbouring and discharging all Ships failing on the Se-verne, coming and going from all Parts, to the Town of Bridgwater, and City of Br: That the Lnttrell's Family have expended great Sums in making the said Port safe: That the Port of Watchet is incommodious to be made a staple Port; first, by the Danger of the Rocks; next, the Shallowness of the Water, that none but small Vessels can come in, unless on high Spring-tides, and then subject to Wind and Weather; and another Reason, the Town of Taunton has been at great Expences to make the River navigable, from Bridgwater to 'aunton, by an Act by the Petitioners lately obtained; and those trading in Wool there, and importing it at Bridgwater, have it carried to Taunton in Barges, and from t lienee to all adjacent Places, much to the Ease and Advantage of the Inhabitants of Somerset, and other Parts: That

the Petitioners can’t perceive any Benefit will accrue, by making Watchet a liaple Port; but a great Prejudice to the Owners of Ships, and their Trade, who belong to Bridgwater Port, Bristol, and other Ports up the Severne: And praying the Bill may not pal’s, in Prejudice to the ancient Port of Minehead-, and that Watchet may dill continue a Creek to Minehead.

' The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for encouraging the Tobacco-trade;

A Petition of the Merchants, and Traders to Virginia and Maryland, in the City of Bristol, was presented to

the House, and read; setting forth. That the Tobacco brought to this Port is in lieu of the Manufactures sent from hence, but designed by the Planters for; so

our Factors abroad are often imposed on, and fend home Vol. 17.

Tobacco of mean Quality, the felling Planters falsely packing the Hogsheads; by which means the Duty paid is sometimes more than the real Value; and, at this time, the presentCrop of Tobacco expected from Virginia is spoiled by the Hurricane there, in August last, damnifying it to an uncommon Degree: And praying the Allowance of Damage may not be prohibited; but a reasonableTime allowed for Importation of Tobacco this Year expected.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

That they like wife produced the following Entries in the Town-book; viz.

23d Mar. 1696. The Order of Common-council for admitting several Persons to Freedom, upon Payment of such Fines as this House shall think reasonable; provided the free Burgesses fhalhconsent thereunto:

27th April 1697. An Order of Common-council against Foreigners felting up their Trade before they have agreed with the Mayor and Aldermen, or the major Part of them, for Freedom:

6 July 1697. An Order of Common-council, That, from henceforth, no Person, being a Foreigner, and not having a Right to Freedom, shall be admitted a free Burgess, without the Consent of the free Burgesses assembled in the Common-hull, or tire major Part of them. And,

That the Petitioners Counsel called,

Henry Lamb, Miles Bull, and Robert:

"Whose Evidence was. That they have known 20, 30, and 40 Years: And that the Usage of making Foreigners free Burgesses is by calling a Common-floor, which conlilts of near 1,000 free Burgesses; who are summoned by Proclamation, made by the Serjeant, in the several Wards, by Order of the Mayor:

That this Usage was infringed in 1705, when Mr. Rain ham was Mayor: Some few Instances were before that time, of Admitfions by the Mayor alone; others by the Mayor and Common-council: Since that time there have been many such; but they look upon all such Admaliens to be illegal, for want of free Bur--gefl’es being present:

That if the free Burgesses giveConlent, in a Common-floor, to the admitting any particular Freemen, they may be admitted by the Mayor; and are good Freemen.

That it appeared by the Town-book, that 125 were admitted to Freedom by Mr. Rainham in his Mayoralty in 1705, without the Town-clerk; 80 of which the Sitting Members Counsel admitted were Foreigners.

That it appeared by the Journal, that, in the last controverted Election for this Borough, the Question was, "Whether the Mayor, of his own Authority, without Consent of the Common-council, could make Foreigners free: And, upon

27 January 1710, The House resolved. That the

Mayor could not make Foreigners free, without Consent of the Majority of the Aldermen and Common-council.

After which Determination by the House, there is an Order in the Town-book, made by the Common-council, upon the 17th Day of July 1711; whereby the Order of Common-council, of 6 July 1697, against admitting Foreigners, without Consent of the Mayor, Aldermen, Assistants, Common-counoil, and free Burgesses, or the major Part of them, is repealed: And divers Foreigners having of late Years been admitted; some for Money paid; and others for Honour and Services to the Corporation; for Peace and Tranquillity of the Town, all Persons who have been sworn free Burgesses before any Mayor, upon taking the Oath again before the Mayor, are, by the said Order, declared to be duly admitted, and sworn free Burgesses: And, for the future, the Admission and Swearing of any Person a free Burgess, having uo antecedent Right by Birth, or actual Service of Seven Years Apprenticeship, is declared to be void;

and no free Burgess to be hereafter admitted and sworn in any other Place than the Common-hall.

That the Petitioners Counsel argued, That this, and the precedent Orders of the Common-council, are declaratory of a prescriptive Right in the free Burgesses to be present at the Autniiiion of Foreigners.

That the Sitting Members Counsel infilled, That the Mayorand Common-council do all corporate Acts; and have the Right of admitting Foreigners to Freedom: That there is no Instance to the contrary, in any of the Town-books; and that it does not appear in any of those Books, that free Burgesses were ever present at any Admission of Foreigners: They denied >C was necessary to have such Burgesses present at such Adaiiflions:

And they called,

Mr. Nathaniel Laurence: Who fairl, Me was Mayor Colcheftrr in 1711: That the Order of 1 7th Juhj in that Year was Flection, made by the Common-council, in pursuance of the last Refutation of tin; House of Commons; which Resolution they then took into Consideration: And they also considered the Conditions of a great many Persons who had paid for Freedom; which Sums the Town was not in a Condition to repay; therefore they made that Order:

And he said, they had, at that time, an Account of those who had l>een sworn by the several Mayors:

And said farther. That the Common-council confills of 1.2 Aldermen, 18 Assistants, and 1$ Burgesses of the Common-council: That the free Burgesses are not of the Common-council: That he has known the Borough 30 Years; and never knew an Instance of free Burgesses being present, or summoned to be present, at any Ad-million of Freemen.

Mr. Conyers reported front the Committee, to whom _ the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, of the City of London j and also of several Merchants, Owners and Mailers of Ships, on behalf of themselves, and others; and also several other Petitions, relating to a Breach in the Banks of the River of Thames, within the Leyels of Havering and Dagenham, were referred: That they had considered the Matter thereof; and had directed him to report the same to the House, and the Resolutions the Committee had come to thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Report, and Resolutions, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read > and are as follow; viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, That the Lord Mayor of i.owd<3n, as Conservator of the River of upon Information given him of aBreach, which happened in February last, in the Walls of the Levels of Havering and 'Dagenham, in the County of Essex, adjoining to the said River, whereby a great Part of the said Levels was overflowed, appointed a Survey of the said River lobe taken by his Water Bailiff; by whose Report it doth appear, that the Navigation of the said River is already very much prejudiced, by the said Breach, of Four Miles above, and Two Miles below, the fame; as by the said Report, as also by a Report from the Mailer, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Trinity-House of Deptford Strand, thereunto annexed, will more fully appear:

Which Reports were likewise confirmed by the Testi-ir.ony, of the said Mailer, and several of the Brethren, of the Trinity House, the Commissioners of Sewers for the said Levels, and Mr. Butler, the Water Bailiff of the City of London, then attending this Committee.

That it appeared, upon the Examination of several of the Commissioners of Sewers, who attended the said Committee, and of the Clerk of Sewers, and the respective Expenditors for the Levels, That the Taxes charged . upon the Land-owners, from 1707,

to the 19th of December 1713, upon the Level of Havering, amounted to £.13,723 and upon the Level

of Dagnam, to£. 14,364, which Sum amounts to £.28,08 7 95. c d.besides several Debts, amounting to about£. 2,000 contracted by the Land-owners, and not yet provided for by any Rate charged upon the said Levels.

That it farther appeared to the Committee, upon examining the said Matter and Brethren of Trinity House, as to their Opinion what the Charge of repairing the said Breach will amount to, they declared themselves not competent Judges thereof; but believed, that it may coll as much, or more, to repair the said Breach, as has already been expended towards the Recovery thereof by the Land-owners, which appeared to the Committee to be upwards of .30,000.

And, upon Examination of Thomas Hall,a Carpenter, '

who was employed several Years in the said Work till the said Breach was flopped, he, by an Estimate hereunto annexed, made it appear to the Committee, That the said Breach will cost, flopping, and making good the Walls ruined by the said Breach, £36,000.

And it further appeared, upon Examination of the Commissioners of Sewers of the aforesaid Levels, That the several Sums of Money before mentioned to have been raised upon the said Levels were justly and truly applied towards recovering the said Breach; and that the several Accounts thereof, together with the Vouchers for the fame, were always ftrt&ly examined by Four of the said Commissioners, who, for several Years past, met once a Month, for taking care to forward the said Work, and to afft fs Taxes, and make Decrees for Sale of Lands, in Default of Payment of Taxes for defraying the Charges of the said Work.

any Neglect, to be applied towards the erecting, or maintaining, such Bridges:

Bristol Poor- A Petition of the principal Freeholders, Merchants, Citizens, and Inhabitants, of the City of who

pay towards the Maintenance of the Poor, on behalf of them selves, and many other Freeholders, Merchants, and Inhabitants, there, who liken ife pay towards the Maintenance of the same Poor, was prefen ted to the House, and read; setting forth. That, by an Act in 1696, the Corporation had Power to take upon them the Maintenance of the whole Poor within the said City, and to raise a yearly Sum, not exceeding the greatest Sum for that Use raised in any of the Three Years pall, which they endeavoured to do; but met with great Opposition from the Churchwardens and Overseers of the several Parishes, and others; which hindered their Discovery; but, by the Rates which were collected from the Inhabitants of the said City, and upon Perusal thereof, the greatest Sum raised thereby was £.2,376. i6r. sd. which the Corporation, not being then able to make any further Discovery, did accept of, for Maintenance of the whole Poor; in hopes that, by employing the Poor that were able to work, it might have been sufficient; and, proceeding thereon, did effectually complete the same for several Years: That there was concealed from the said Corporation above f. 500 per Annum, charitable Gifts; which was yearly employed towards maintaining the Poor, called casual Poor, and not brought into the said Rates: That the whole Charge of the casual Poor have fallen upon the said Corporation: for which they have had no Allowance: That several Sums, given by Benefactors, did amount to £.4,360 15 s. for carrying on the fame; the Interest only to be applied for the Maintenance of the said Poor, although not so expressed; but the Poor increasing, and for want of the said £. 500 per Annum, the Corporation have- been forced toexpend the said Sum of £. 4,360 15 s. and likewise. to eontraft several great Debts, for carrying on the said charitable Work; which Debts remain on them; and thereby are unable to maintain the said Poor, unless farther supplied, for the Reasons following: First, For want of the said £.500 per Annum, from the Year 1696 to 1713, which amounts to £.8,500 Principal: 2dly, Since the passing the Act in 1696, the Buildings in the said City ate increased, which greatly increased the Charge of the Poor: 3dly, That, by the late War, many Fathers of Families have been loft: 4thly, And, since the said Act, there hath been great Scarcity of Provisions in many Years: 5thly, There hath been a great Decay in the Woollen and other Manufactures, which hath greatly increased the Poor: That the Inhabitants are not raised above 6d. in the Pound; whereas the neighbouring Parishes of this City, who, at the passing the said Act, did not raile above 12 d.in the Pound, are now forced to raise above qs. 6 d.for Maintenance of the Poor: That the said

ir Corporation, till of late, not only maintained their aged

Poor, without Begging; but took care of the Young, by educating them, and placing them out Apprentices: VoL. 17.

That the Petitioners are satisfied, that the said Corporation have duly applied all the Money tljat came to their Hands, in Maintenance of their Poor, their Accounts being ready to be produced; which if not otherwise supplied, it will breed Confusion and Disorder in the said City: And praying a further Supply maybe granted to the said Corporation for the Maintenance of the Poor.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for racking more effectual an Act, passed in the 7th and 8th Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King IVm.III. intituled, An Act for erecting Hospitals and Work-houses within the City of Bristol, for the better employing and maintaining the Poor thereof) be read a Second time.

Alienr A Petition of several Merchants, as well Freemen of Good*. London, and Denizens, as other naturalized Foreigners, in behalf of themselves. and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, by the Bill for the better preventing the Covering Aliens Goods imported into this Kingdom, every Merchant shall be obliged to subscribe One of his Bills of every Entry of Goods; and shall likewise, by himself. Agent or Servant, make Oath, That the Goods therein mentioned do truly belong to, or are imported on Account of, some of her Majesty’s Subjects; and that the fame, nor any Part thereof, doth not belong to, or are imported on account of, any Alien, to his or their Knowledge; and, in case of Refusal, the Goods shall be deemed Aliens Goods, and pay accordingly: And, should the said Bill pass, it would obstruct the general Trade of this Realm; as well Natives, as Foreigners, would lie under Incapacities of trading, either in Ships or Cargoes, one with another: What is more grievous, the British Merchant being obliged to trade with none unknown to him, or to lie under the fatal Ne-celfity of being perjured, in case he takes the intended Oath; or his Correspondent, whether Alien, or Native, shall be liable to have his Goods deemed Aliens Goods without regard, inCafethe Persons so entering the Goods shall have Conscience to fear an Oath: That the Laws hath already provided against the real Mischiefs, set forth in the Bill, to the Forfeiture of the Goods on the Breakers thereof: And praying the said Bill may not pass; and to be heard, by Counsel, against the fame.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the better preventing the Covering of Aliens Goods imported, is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard by their Counsel, before the Committee thereupon, if they think fit.

in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Petitioner, in order to make good the Allegations of his Petition, called, as Witnesses.

Mr. Ralph Mitchell: Who said, He was sent, some Years past, by Order of the Trinity-house, to view the Edifion, and had other Instructions to make a View of Whitfand Bay, and the Place proposed by the Petitioner for a Light-house; and has twice re-fnrveyed the fame; and fays. That the Foundation of the Light-house will be at least 80 Fathom above High-water-mark, and may be seen at least Seven Leagues at Sea, even off St. Ives in the North, and the Lizzard in the South; and will be of great Use for directing Sailors to distinguish the North and South Chanels, and to prevent Ships being cast away on those Coasts:

That the Rock Cowloe is 15 Acres, at least; and the Harbour, when made, 33 Acres, or more; the Depth at Low-water Four Fathom, and at High Seven: And that it washisOpinion the said Places are capableof making the most convenient Harbour and Light-house in Great Britain, being at the Lands End, the In and Outlet of the Nation, and opposite to Brejl: That there hath been, and still continues to be, more LolTes at and nigh that Place, tlran in all the Coasts of Great Britain besides.

Mr. William Clapp said, He had been upon Coioloe Rock, and had viewed the Place proposed for the Harbour in Whitfand Bay j and, according to his Judgment, he believes the making a Light-house and Harbour there very practicable, there being vast Quantities of large loose Moor-stones, fit for flopping up the said Gap; and that the Gap intended to be stopped was on Spring-tides dry, that People walked over to Cowloe Rock; and, for want of such an Harbour and Light-house, there have been considerable Losses by Wrrecks and Privateers, and may be more in time of War.

Mr. Chrifopher Davis said, He had been upon the said Cowloe Rock, and also measured the Depth of the Water, which he found to be more than Four Fathom at Low-water in the proposed Harbour; and thereby confirms Mr. Ralph Mitchell's Evidence.

And further, the Petitioner produced the Hands of the eminent Merchants and Commanders of Ships of London, Exon, Topham, DLooe,

Foy, Penzance, Gentlemen living nigh the Land’s End,

St. Ives, Barnfable, BiddifoBridgwater,

Trinity-house of Hull, and Ports adjacent, to prove it was their Opinions, That an Harbour in Whitfand Bay would be of Advantage to Great Britain, and greatly encourage Trade and Navigation.

That it appearing to this Committee, That the said Whitfand Bay, for want of a Harbour there, was fer-viceable to our Enemies during the late War;

And also that a great many Ships of this Kingdom, loft and taken by the Enemy during the late War, would have been sheltered and protected in Whitfand Bay, had there been an Harbour there;

And that the making such Harbour, and the erecting such Light-house, will be undertaken for «£. 30,000.

And that the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Harbour to be made in Whitfand Bay, near the Lands End, in Cornwall, will be of great Benefit for the Preservation of Shipping, and a publick Advantage to this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Two Lights at PordeNack Point, near the Land's

End, will be of great Use to direct Sailors to distinguish the North and South Chanels, and to prevent Ships being cast away upon those Coasts.

A Petition of several Planters of the Sugar Colonies, Afr.fu now residing in Great Britain, was presented to the Tr.dc. House, and read; letting forth, That the Importing Negroes into the Sugar Plantations by th Company, who imported great Numbers annually, and fold them at moderate Prices, and gave the Planters great Credit, until the said Company was paid out of the Negroes Labour: That, on the opening the Trade to Africa, what from the separate Traders not 'oeinglkilled in a right Management of trafficking with the Natives, and from the different Smugglings and Over-reachings amongst themselves, as well as the Contentions as have arisen between them and the Company’s Agents on the Coalt, hath not only advanced the Price of Negroes from 50 s.to near £.20 per Head, but hath so retarded the Voyages, that greatMortalities have happened onShipboard; by which the Planters were obliged to greater Prices for those brought them, to the great Decrease in the Produce of our Sugars, and the Consumption of British ]

Manufactures, and in the Revenue; as well as the Dif-couragement to Navigation: That the Traders, finding the Planters could not afford such Prices for Negroes as answered the great Rates they gave for them on the Coast, conveyed them to the Sugar Settlements of other Nations; by which those Nations have much increased in the making Sugar; which they, from the Fertility of their Lands, can do much easier than we; and so supply the foreign Markets cheaper than we can; which, if not prevented, will be the utter Ruin and Loss of the British Plantations, amounting to £.2,000,000 annually to this Kingdom; there being no other Way to prevent it, but by recovering and securing the Trade to Africa, by establishing a Company, with a considerable Stock, exclusive, with all doe Encouragement from the Government: And praying the Trade to Africa may be established as aforesaid; and that such Company may be obliged to take Subscriptions for raising a sufficient Stock, or Fund; and be obliged to export annually so much Goods and Mer- y

chand ize, as will purchase a convenient Number of Slaves

for the Plantations; and that they transport them thither, and fell them at reasonable Rates; and, if the said Company shall fail to furnish the Plantations with Negroes aforesaid, that they may be made liable to such Inquiries and Penalties as this House shall inflict.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, that this House will, upon Tuesday Sevennight, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Trade to Africa;

And the same was read; and is as follows;

Copy of the Instrufition given to the Earl of Strafford, with relation to the Declaration made by him, on the Part of her Majesty, to the Generals of the several Allies who had any Troops in her Majesty s Pay before the Cessation of Arms; given at Kensington, the 21st Day of June 1712.

YOU will declare to the Generals and Commanders in Chief of the foreign Troops in our Pay, and in the joint Pay of us and the States General, with how much Surprize we heard, That there was the least Doubt of their obeying such Orders as they should receive from the Duke of Ormond, Captain General and Commander in Chief of our Forces.

You will declare to them in our Name, That, if this same should happen, we shall esteem it not only as an Indignity and Affront offered to us, but as a Declara-, tion against us; and that from that Moment they mull look on themselves as no further entitled either to future-Pay, or to Arrears of Pay, or Subsidies.

0rrfera/, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, an Act for regulating, improving, and encouraging, the Woollen Manufacture of Mixed or Medley Broad-cloths; and for the better Payment of the Poor employed therein; is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard before the said Committee thereupon, by their Counsel, if they think fit,

A Petition and Representation of the Mixture or Medley Broad-clothiers in and about in the County of Gloucester, whose Names are subscribed, on

behalf of themselves, and the rest of their Fraternity, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Merchants, and Dealers in Mixed or Medley Broad-cloths, have obtained Leave to bring in a Bill to explain and amend an Act, of the 10th of Queen , for regulating, improving, and encouraging, the Woollen Manufacture of Mixed or Medley Broad-cloths; and for the better Payment of the Poor employed therein: That the Intention of the said Act was to settle the Measure of every Cloth between Buyer and Seller, and to prevent Frauds, by straining of Mixed Cloths; and it was enacted, That every Owner or Occupier of Mills thouid measure every Mixed Cloth upon a Table of Four Yards, allowing One Inch to each Yard; and, as soon as milled and scoured, the Millman to fix on a Seal with the Length and Breadth of each Cloth, and to take an Oath first. to qualify him; and the Merchant, Draper, and Clothier, to be liable to a Penal* Vol. 17.

9 Matu 39

ty of 20s. for each Cloth hot conformable to the Act .* That the Petitioners have printed their Reasons, in order to obtain the said explanatory Act; And the First Objection is, touching the Country Millmens Qualification for (tamping the Measures of these Cloths; and that they Cannot be indifferent or impartial Judges in this Affair, though sworn, by reason their Dependence is on their Master, and they dare not refuse stamping much longer Measure than is just; where to the Petitioners answer, and appeal, Whether a Countryman may not be as honed, and capable of measuring Cloth, as a Citizen ? The 2d Objection is, That the Penalty of 20 is too little; and, if too little for thcClothier, it is too little for the Draper, or Buyer; it extending to both, and therefore equal; The Third Objection is, The Manner of recovering the said Penalty is defective: to which the Petitioners would willingly join with them in procuring any better Method: But all their Grievances and Designs are comprised in the Conclusion of their Reasons; which are. They hope, that the Length and Breadth of all mixed Cloths shall not be ascertained at the Place of Making, but at the Place of Sale; which the Petitioners submit to this House; and should the Petitioners be forced to go or fend xoo Miles before they know what to enter in their Books, which will be the same of the Petitioners, and the rest of the Clothiers, if these Clothsare to be ascertained and (tampt in London \ and will occasion the utterRuin of many diligent, honed, and laborious, Men, and their Families: And praying the said Act may be continued, and preserved entire, without any Explanations, Alterations, or Additions, or such only as may equally extend to her Majesty’s Subjects in general.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for explaining and amending an Act passed in the Tenth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for regulating, improving, and encouraging, the Woollen Manufacture of Mixed or Medley Broad-cloths; and for the better Payment of the Poor employed therein; is committed: And that the Petitioners be heard before the said Committee thereupon, by their Counsel, if they think fit.

X. D. Some of the Out-port Books for the Year 1688 not being now to be found, the Amount of the Aliens Duty at such Ports cannot be known, which if it could, it would increase the Total of the said Year.

One reason why the Aliens Duty on Wines is so much greater in 1713 than in 1683 is, that in 1688 there was only One Subsidy on Wines; whereas, in 1713, there is Old Subsidy, New Subsidy, -f and 4-ds Subsidies; all which have Aliens Duty in them. R. Paul.

A Petition of the Merchants, and other Traders in the Woollen Manufactures, in the Town of was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, since the Opening the Trade to Africa in 1698, greater Quantities of the said Manufactures have been vended, than in the time of the African Company’s having the foie Trade in a Joint Stock, but now lies under great Discouragements, by the Endeavours of the African Company to exclude all others from the said Trade; which, if obtained, will ruin the said Manufacture, and be very grievous to the Petitioners, and others concerned therein: And praying the Trade to Africa may be preserved free and open to all her Majesty’s Subjects.

A Petition of the Proprietors of certain Lands and Lands taken , Tenements at Portsmouth, Chatham, and Harwich, was

presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That F0rtific»-by an Act 8° Anna, the Petitioners Lands and Tene- tions. ments are veiled in Trustees, for the Use of her Majesty, for the better fortifying Portsmouth, Chatham, and Harwich, on certain Contracts between her Majesty’s Commissioners and the Trullees, for the Purchase thereof, which Contracts were made, pursuant to an Inquisition taken, on Oath, before the salt! Commissioners, by Juries appointed to inspect the Value of each Proprietor’s Estate; That, by Report of a Committee of last Parliament, it appeared, that a sufficient Sum was paid into the Treasury of the Ordnance, to pay off the Petitioners respective Purchase-money: That the Petitioners have had several expensive Journies to London, in hopes of receiving the fame: That several of the Proprietors Tenants, upon passing the said Act, have left their Houses; and the Petitioners, being divelled of their Power to make Leases, or assurance to Tenants for Continuance, could neither keep their old, nor get new, Tenants; yet are forced to pay Taxes for those empty Houses; and several of the Petitioners Houses, being built on short Leases, will revert to the Lessors, for want of renewing their said Leases, to the Ruin of some of the Petitioners; and some of the Proprietors depending on the said Act, have suffered great Loss of Trade, and lie under great Distresses: and that the Damages reported by the Commissioners, at the Tower of London, are not proportioned to the real Damages fuilained by the Proprietors: And praying the Corn-million, granted by her Majesty in 1711, may be execute.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table

until the said Report be taken into Consideration: And that the said Petitioners be then heard at the Bar of the House, thereupon, by their Counsel, if they think fit.

" And whereas several Bonds, pursuant to several " Acts of Parliament in that behalf, have been entered into by Merchants, or others, for the additional Duty, " New Subsidy, One-third Subsidy, and Impost-duties, " upon Tobacco imported into this Kingdom; upon " which Bonds, the whole Monies, or Part of the Monies, " specified in the Conditions of the same respectively, " have, according to such Conditions, incurred, or become payable, at several Days, or Times of Payment, " before the Fifteenth Day of June One thousand Seven " hundred and Fourteen; and do remain unsatisfied; or usuch Bonds are not delivered up; Be it Enacted, by the " Authority aforesaid, That in all and every Case and " Cases, where, the Obligors in such Bonds being Principals or Sureties, their Heirs, Executors, or Administrators, or any of them, shall have, before the First Day " of September One thousand Seven hundred and Fourteen, paid to the proper Officer or Officers the principal Monies so incurred, or grown due, before the " said Fifteenth Day of June One thousand Seven hun-" dred and Fourteen, such Payment shall be of the same " Force and Effect as if the same had been made at, or " before, the respective Day or Days in such Condition " or Conditions mentioned for Payment thereof:

" And be it further Enacted, by the Authority aforesaid, That in all Cases where the whole principal " Monies due, or to be due, by the Conditions of such Bonds as are before-mentioned, are, or shall be, paid " by the said First Day of September One thousand Seven hundred and Fourteen, such Bond and Bonds " respectively shall, upon Demand, be delivered up to " the Party or Parties who hath, or shall have, so paid the " same, his, her, or their. Heirs, Executors, or Administrators, without any further or other Demand whatsoever: Nevertheless, it is hereby Declared, That in case " any of the Bonds before-mentioned shall not be satisfied within the time by this Act limited, as aforesaid;

The said Report is as follows; viz.

To the most honqurableRo&er/Earl of Or/brd and Earl Mortimer, p>rd High Treasurer of Great Britain. May it please your Lordship,

JN Obedience to your Lordship’s Order of Reference, dated the 25th Instant, and signified to me by Mr. Lowndes, on the Memorial of John Hallungius Esquire, Minister of his Highness the D. of Saxe Gotha; wherein hesets jbrth, That, being sent by his said Highness to adjust and solicit the Payment of the Arrears due to his Troops, lately employed in her Majesty’g Service m Italy, upon examining the Votes of Parliament, of the 3d of June last, in jvhich the Sum only o(£. 9,300. i2r. 6d. is voted foV the Ordinary pay of the said Troops, from the 2 ad December, preceding, to the time of their Dismission; including One Month’s pay for their Return; he finds that, in that Computation, no Consideration is had of what is stipulated by the 10th Article of the Treaty, for the Two Months Advertisement to be given them, before their March; his said Highness being reciprocally pbliged, by the 16 Article of the said Treaty, to give the like Notice of Two Months, before hecould take the said Troopsqut ofher Majesty’s Service; therefore humbly hopes Payment may be ordered of the said Twq Months ordinary Pay, pursuant to the Treaty, amounting to the Sum of Fifty-six thousand One hundred Eighty-five Guilders, according to the Establishment; and that such proper Method maybe takeu, as tjiqt this Sun?, together with the Extraordinaries, may provided for this present Session of Parliament.

' I do humbly report to your Lordship, That I find, as is represented in the said Memorial, the Sum of Nine Thousand Three hundred Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence was voted, the last Year, by Parliament, for har Majesty’s Share; being a Moiety of the Pay of 2,600 Men, of the Troops of his Highness the D. of Saxe Gotha, ffom the 22d of Deceviber 1712, to the 3d of April foil, inch when they were dismissed her Majesty’s Service; and for One Month’s Pay more to be allowed the.no on their Dismission, according to the Treaty; which Demand appears to have been founded on a Declaration made by her Majesty’s Plenipotentiaries at IItvecht, dated the 14th of April 1713, N. S.; That his Said Highness the Duke of Saxe Gotha, was then at Liberty to cause his said Troops to march out of Italy, and to dispose of them as he pleased, they being no longer engaged in her Majesty’s Service:

But Mr. Hallungiusalleges. That, in that Computation, no Consideration is had of what is stipulated by the Treaty for the Two Months Advertisement to be given them before their March.

I have perused the said Treaty; and do find, in the . 1 oth A rticle thereof, it is expressed. That upon the Con-

elusion of the Peacc, his highness shall have Two Months Notice given, before his Troops put themselves on their March for their Return home; and shall be paid all their , Arrears before their Dismission: And in the t ithArticle , it isstipulated, That, upon sending back the said Troops,

they shall be paid One Month’s Pay for their March home: As also, in the 16 Article of the said Treaty, his Highness is reciprocally obliged to give the like Notice of Two Months, before he could take his Troops out ofher Majesty’s Service, as is alleged in the Memorial: But it-does not appear; That any Notice was given

them, according to the 1 oth Article aforesaid, by which they ought to have had Two Months, other than the Declaration of her Majesty ^Plenipotentiaries of thet4th of April 1713, N. S.: So that, in the Estimate given in to Parliament last Year, the Account of their Pay was determined on the Day of the Date of the said Declaration, with One Month’s Allowance more for their March-money, according to the Tenor of the nth A:* ticle of the said Treaty, without any Regard to the said Two Months Notice; and a Certificate is now produced to me, from the Bishop of London, testifying. That the Declaration afore-mentioned, made by his Lordship, and the Earl of Strafford, concerning the Two Regiments of the Duke of Saxe Gotha, paid by her Majesty, importing, That the Service of the said Two Regiments was no longer needed, was not intended to determine any other Point or Article in the Treaty, by which the said Troops were taken into the Service: And as these Troops were actually in Italy, at the time the said Declaration was made at Utrecht;

I humbly submit it to your Lordship, whether, considering the Distance of time before they could receive Notice of that Declaration, and the length of their March afterwards to his Highness’s Dominions, they ought not to be allowed the said Two Months, pursuant to the Treaty; their Pay for which Time amounting, according to the Establishment, to 56,185 Guilders; and, at 10 Guil, 10 St. to the Pound Sterling, to Five thousand One hundred Seven Pounds Fifteen Shillings;

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordship,

28th May 1714.

the Petitioners Counsel alleged, the Right of Election is in the Mayor, Aldemten, Bailiffs, Capital Burgesses, and Freeholders, having a Freehold in the Corporation: The Sitting Members Counsel alleged it to be in the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, Bailiffs, Capital Burgesses, Town-clerk, and Freeholders, having a Freehold in the Corporation: ‘

The Committee found themselves discharged, by Order of the House, from proceeding upon so much of the said Petition as relates to Mr. Ward.

' The Petitioners Counsel admitted Mr. Littleton was duly chosen:

'1 hey complained of Partiality in the Mayor against the Petitioners; and alleged, They should add 59 to their Poll, and take off 165 from the Sitting Members Poll: And called,

Mr. Thomas Cowperjunior: Who said, He took the Poll for the Mayor: That the Mayor rejected above 100 Voters for the Petitioners, and admitted a great many of the same Date for the Sitting Members:

That many Voters for the Petitioners came from distant Places, with Conveyances just wrote; of which they would give no Account; nor whether they were in Possession; nor whether the Grantors had a Freehold: Several for the Petitioners were split Votes, and from Grantors who had only Leaseholds:

That the first splitting of Votes for this Borough, which began to be any-way notorious, was in October 1710: In 1711 they went farther; and, in this last Election, they went as far as, he thinks, they could go, on all Sides: That he believes the new Votes on all Sides are of the same Nature: There are upon the Poll 58 new Votes for the Petitioners, and 186 for the Sitting Members: He could not tell how many of the Petitioners Voters are bad; but said, Those made in 1710 are of the same Nature with those made since.

Then Negative Questions were moved; and, being insisted upon, wereput, and passed in the Negative: Which, if thereby made affirmative Resolutions, are thus;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That those Persons who had no Right of voting in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Weymouth and in the County of

Dorset, at Lady-day 1710; and not claiming by Purchase for a valuable Consideration, or by Will, or Descent, since that Time; had a Right to vote in the last Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough.

Resolved, That, it appearing to this Committee, That divers scandalous and illegal Practices have been lately carried on, in the Borough of Weymouth and Melcomb Regis, in the County of Dorset, to multiply Votes, in order to the last Election of Members to serve in Parliament; it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all such Persons, whose Votes were not admitted at the Determination of the last contested Election in Parliament for the said Borough, and who have not acquired a Right by Descent or Devise since that time, had a Right of voting in the last Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough.

Mr. Speaker reported. Mr. Wykes reported from the Committee to whom it Leather was referred -to consider of the State of the Leather Manufeftw^. Manufactures in this Kingdom; and what further Encouragement may be proper to be given to the same;

That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Clerk’s Table: Where they were read j and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That considerable Quantities of tanned Leather, made into Boots, Shoes, and other Wares, are, in the Currying and Making, cut off, wasted, and rendered of no Use and yet the Makers, or Exporters, on Exportation of the said made Wares, being allowed to draw back no more than Two-thicds of the Duty charged on the said tanned Leather, according to the Weight of the said made Wares, without any Allowance for such Waste; the same is a great Discouragement to the Leather-mapufacture in this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That if a Drawback of the whole Duty of One Peny Halfpeny per Pound Weight be allowed on all tanned Leather which shall bemauufactured, and actually made into Wares or Goods, and exported out of Great Britain, to be ascertained according to the Weight of fuel) Good# or Wares respectively, the same will be a reasonable

Encouragement

feriftol

Poor,

Army Debts.

d. 1714.

Encouragement to the Leather Manufacture of this

j Kingdom;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That great Quantities of raw Hides from Ireland were heretofore imported into, and tanned in, this Kingdom; but, by the Exportation of Bark to , great Num-

bers of Hides are tanned there, and pay no Duty; and foreign Parts being supplied from thence not only with Leather, but with Shoes, Boots, and other Wares, made of Leather, which, before the Exportation of Bark to Ireland, were supplied with Leather, and with Shoes, Boots, and other Wares made of Leather, from Great Britain; is not only a Loss to her Majesty’s Revenue but a great Prejudice to the Manufactures of Leather of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That for preventing Deficiencies in Duties arising from tanned Leather, and for encouraging the Manufactures of tanned Leather, the Exportation of all Bark useful for the Tanning of Leather be discouraged for the future.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the making of Shoes and Slippers of Canvas, or Ticking, is a great Discouragement to the Leather Manufacture of this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to her Majesty.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the D-Report from the Committee, who were to consider of the^Longw5 what Encouragement was fit to be given to such as tude. should find out the longitude at Sea:

And the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon: Which Report, and Resolutions, are as follow; viz.

That it appeared to the said Committee as followeth; viz.

Mr. Ditton and Mr. Wiston, being examined, did inform the Committee, That they had made a Discovery of the Longitude; and were very certain, that the same was true in the Theory; and did not doubt but that, upon due Trial made, it would prove certain and practicable at Sea:

That they had communicated the whole History of their Proceedings towards the said Discovery to Sir Isaac Newton, Dr. Clark, Mr. Haley, and Mr. Cotes; who all seemed to allow of the T ruth of the Proposition, as to the Theory: but doubted of several Difficulties that would arise in the Practice.

Sir Isaac Newton, attending the Committee, said.

That, for determining the Longitude at Sea, there have been several Projects, true in the Theory, but difficult to execute:

One is, by a Watch to keep Time exactly: But, by reason of the Motion of a Ship, the Variation of Heat and Cold, Wet and Dry, and the Difference of Gravity in different Latitudes, such a Watch hath not yet been made:

Another is, by the Eclipses of But, by reason of the Length of Telescopes requisite to observe them, and the Motion of a Ship at Sea, those Eclipses cannot yet be there observed:

A Third is, by the Place of the Moon: But her Theory is not yet exact enough for this Purpose: It is exact enough to determine her Longitude within Two or Three Degrees, but not within a Degree:

8 K A Fourth

678 11° Junii. 1714.

Discovering A Fourth is, Mr. Dills Project: And this is rather for keeping an Account ofthcLongitude at Sea, than for finding; it, if at any time it should be lost, as it may easily be in cloudy Weather: How far this is practicable, and with what Charge, they that are skilled in Sea-affairs are . best able to judge: In sailing by this Method, whenevet they are to pass over very deep Seas, they must sail due East, or West, without varying their Latitude; and if their Way over such a Sea doth not lie due East, or West, they must first sail into the Latitude of the next Place to which they are going beyond it; and then keep due East, or West, till they come at that Place:

In the Three first Ways there must be a Watch regulated by a Spring, and rectified every visible Sun-rise and Sunset, to tell the Hour of the Day, or Night: In the Fourth Way, such a Watch is not necessary: In the First Way, there must be Two Watches; this, and the other mentioned above:

In any of the Three first Ways, it may be of some Service to find the Longitude within a Degree; and of much more Service to find it w ithin Forty Minutes, or Half a Degree, if it may be; and the Success may deserve Rewards accordingly:

In the Fourth Way, it is easier to enable Seamen to know their Distance, and Bearing from the Shore, 40, 60, or 80, Miles off, than to cross the Seas; and some Part of the Reward may be given when the First is performed on the Coast of Great Britain, for the Safety of Ships coming Home; and the rest, when Seamen shall be enabled to sail to an assigned remote Harbour without losing their Longitude, if it may be.

Dr. Clarke said, That there could no Discredit arise to

the Government, inpromisinga Reward in general, without respect to any particular Project, to such Person or Persons who should discover the Longitude at Sea.

Mr. Haley said. That Mr. Method for find-

ing the Longitude did seem to him to consist of many Particulars, which first ought to be experimented, before he could give his Opinion; and that it would cost a considerable Sum to make the Experiments; but what the Expence would amount to, he could not tell.

Mr. Whislonaffirmed, That the undoubted Benefit which would arise on the Land, and near the Shore, would vastly surmount the Charges of Experiments.

Mr. Cotes said, That the Project was right in the Theory near the Shore; and the practical Part ought to be experimented.

And, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions; viz.

JResolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Reward be settled by Parliament upon such Person or Persons as shall discover a more certain and practicable Method of ascertaining the Longitude, than any yet in Practice; and the said Reward be proportioned to the Degree of Exactness to which the said Method shall reach.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved. That Leave be given for a Bill to be brought in accordingly.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That a Reward be settled by Parliament upon such Person or Persons as shall discover a more certain and practicable Method of ascertaining the Longitude, than any yet in Practice; and the said Reward be proportioned to the Degree of Exactness to which the said Method shall reachl

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, upon the said Resolution: And that Mr. Clayton, Mr. Aislaby, Sir George Beaumont, Sir Wm. Mr.

Boscaiven, Sir Thomas Hardy, Mr. Addison, General Stanhope, and Sir John Leake, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Derby, and Stafford, navigable, was committed:

And the Amendments, made by the Committee, to the Bill, were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question put thereupon, with Amendments to some of them, agreed unto by the House. '

A Clause wras offered, to be added to the Bill, That, for effectually making the River navigable from Gainsborough to Burton, the Assignee or Occupier of the Locks upon the River, and his Servants and Agents, shall, when there shall be Occasion, open the Gates of the Locks, and allow Flashes of Water, upon Request, sufficient to enable Vessels to pass up and down the said Locks; and, in case of Refusal, shall forfeit the Sum of And, for want of Distress, the Offender

shall be committed to the House of Correction for

there to be kept to hard Labour; but nothing in the Act contained, shall be construed to extend to damage the Mills, upon the River, called King's , or prevent their Grinding or Working:

And the same was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up:

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill,

That no Person should wilfully or maliciously turn the Water out of the navigable Channel or Passage thereof, so as to give any Obstruction to the Navigation.: all Persons offending should forfeit within

Months, to be recovered in any of her Majesty’s Courts of Record, or before Justices of Assize, or Justices of the Peace, in their General Quarter Sessions for the County where such Offence or Offences should be committed; but, if the Plaintiff or Prosecutor should be nonsuited, then he, she, or the}"-, should pay unto the Defendant, his, her, or their. Costs:

And the same was twice read, with Blanks; which were filled up:

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

And other Amendments were made by the House to the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

A Petition of Edward Warnford Esquire was pre- Cricklade sen ted to the House, and read; setting forth, That at Election, the Election for Cricklade, in Wilts, in the room of Wm. Gore Esquire; the Petitioner, and Sam. Robinson Esquire, stood Candidates: That the said Robinson, by Bribes, tec. has procured himself to be returned; in Wrong of the Petitioner: That Joint Lane Bailiff, polled several who had no Right, for Mr. Robinson-, and refused others who had a Right, for the Petitioner; and denied to return the Petitioner, although he had a legal Majority of 63; and declared, before the Election,

That if Mr. Robinson had but Five Votes, he would return him: And praying to be relieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to ihe Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections:

And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

An ingrossed Bill for the more effectual preventing, and punishing, the Stealing, and unlawful Killing, of Cattle, was read the Third time.

The Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 1. L. To leave out " and for Discovery " thereof:"

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, aDuty belaidupon all Soap made mGreat Britain, or imported into the same, over and above allDuties chargeable thereupon by any Act or Acts of Parliament nowin Force.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said further Duty upon foreign Soap imported be after the Rate of One Peny per Pound Weight Avoirdupois.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said further Duty upon all Soap made in Great Britain be after the Kate of One Halfpeny per Pound W eight Avoirdupois.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Stocks of Soap in the Hands of any Persons trading or dealing the rein, for the Sale, be chargeable with the like further or additional Duties.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the whole additional Duties aforesaid upon such Soap as shall be exported be drawn back.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all the said additional Duties for such Soap as shall be used in the Woollen Manufacture, or in Goods mixed with Wool, whereof the greatest Part of the Value shall he Wool, shall be drawn back.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, certain Duties be laid upon all Paper, Pasteboards, Mil-boards, and Scaleboards, imported into Great Britain, Books and Prints excepted; and upon all Paper, Paste-

boards, Milboards, and Scaleboards, made in Great Britain; and upon all Paper painted, printed, or stained, for Hangings, within the same; over and above the present Duties on the said Commodities respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee; That such new and additional Duties on the said Paper, Pasteboard, Milboards, and Scaleboards; and on printed, painted, and stained, Paper; be One Moiety of the Rates or Duties chargeable on them respectively by One Act made in the Tenth Year of her Majesty’* Reign, in that behalf.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Stock of such Paper and Boards, as aforesaid, in the Hands of Dealers therein, for Sale, be charged with the like new or additional Duties.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to her Majesty, certain Duties be laid upon such imported Linens, excepting La w'ns, Canvas, Barras, and Silesia Neckcloths; and upon such Silks, Callicoes, Linens, and Stuffs, to be printed, painted, stained, or dyed, in Great;

as are chargeable with Duties by the Act made in the Tenth Year of her Majesty’s Reign, in that behalf; over and above the present Duties on those Commodities respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such new or additional Duties on the Commodities last mentioned, except as aforesaid, be the like Rates or Duties as are chargeable on the same Commodities respectively by the said Act made in the Tenth Year of his Majesty’s Reign.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Stocks of such Linens, Silks, Callicoes, and Stuffs, as aforesaid, in the Hands of Dealers therein, for Sale, be charged with One Moiety of such new additional Duties to be laid thereupon respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said further Duty upon Starch made in Great Britain be after the Rate of 1 d. per Pound Weight.
